One of the most important concepts in non-Hermitian system is the exceptional point [194], a branch point singularity in the complex eigenvalue plane [195, 196, 197, 198]. At the exceptional point, two or more eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors coalesce, and the norm of the eigenvectors becomes zero. The avoided crossing in non-Hermitian systems occurs in the vicinity of an exceptional point [199, 200]. It is advantageous to study the avoided crossing of BH QNMs in the context of non-Hermitian physics. However, as we will see in Section 2.5, the standard inner product used for bound states in quantum mechanics does not extend to QNMs or, more broadly, to open systems.

In nuclear physics, a wave function for resonances, analogous to the QNM wave function, is known as the Gamow-Siegert state [188, 187]. An appropriate finite norm is realized by the so-called Zel’dovich regularization [201] (see also earlier work [202]), where the norm is defined by introducing a regularization factor which decays faster than the wave function itself, maintaining the divergent contribution from the boundary. This formulation allows one to develop a Rayleigh-Schrödinger-like perturbation theory for resonance states [201, 203] (see [189, 190] for more developments in quantum resonances and non-Hermitian physics).

For BH QNMs, a finite scalar product obtained by subtracting the divergent boundary term was introduced in [204, 205, 206]. Several other definitions of the scalar product for QNMs of BHs have been considered, as discussed in Section 2.5 below. By means of such scalar products, avoided crossings and resonances in the QNM spectrum of BHs can be understood as a universal phenomenon occurring near exceptional points [154]. Generalizing the scalar product of [204, 205, 206] for Schwarzschild BHs, and employing an analogy with the scalar product used in quantum resonances [189, 190], a scalar product (or more precisely a “biorthogonal” product) can be introduced for the Weyl scalars of Kerr BHs [154]. Using this biorthogonal product, one can develop a Rayleigh-Schrödinger-like perturbation theory and predict small changes δ​ω\delta\omega of the QNM frequencies induced by small changes of the BH parameters. Similar results have also been obtained for other products [205, 207, 77, 208, 102, 209, 210].

Consider two overtone QNM frequencies, ωn1\omega_{n_{1}} and ωn2\omega_{n_{2}}, that are isolated from other QNMs, and approach closely each other in the complex frequency plane when the BH parameters are varied (here, the subscripts ℓ,m\ell,m are suppressed for simplicity). An argument analogous to the quantum two-level system can be applied to predict how two QNM frequencies will behave under a small change of the BH parameters. In quantum two-level system, the energy eigenvalues such that the Hamiltonian matrix is diagonal are obtained by solving the eigenvalue equation. Similarly, solving the eigenvalue equation, the resulting QNM frequencies are given by [104, 154]

ω±2=ℰc±ℰd2+Δ2,\displaystyle\omega^{2}_{\pm}=\mathcal{E}_{c}\pm\sqrt{\mathcal{E}_{d}^{2}+\Delta^{2}}, (2.33)

where ℰc,d≔(ℰn1±ℰn2)/2\mathcal{E}_{c,d}\coloneqq(\mathcal{E}_{n_{1}}\pm\mathcal{E}_{n_{2}})/2, ℰnj≔ωnj2+δ​ωnj2\mathcal{E}_{n_{j}}\coloneqq\omega_{n_{j}}^{2}+\delta\omega_{n_{j}}^{2} with j=1,2j=1,2, and Δ\Delta captures a small change in the BH parameters. The present derivation of Eq. (2.33) follows [154]. An analogous formula can be found in Eq. (4.6) of [104]. However, in [104], the squared frequencies ω2\omega^{2}’s in (2.33) are replaced with linear terms in ω\omega, predicting different values in general.

From Eq. (2.33), we see that the frequencies ω±\omega_{\pm} are degenerate if ℰd2+Δ2=0\mathcal{E}_{d}^{2}+\Delta^{2}=0. Solutions to this equation correspond to exceptional points. Since this condition involves complex variables, in general it cannot be satisfied by tuning a single real parameter. This corresponds to the crossing between two QNM frequencies [108, 104, 133, 154]. On the other hand, if one can tune two independent parameters, it is possible to satisfy the condition and reach the exceptional point. The hysteresis-like effects in the QNM spectrum [167, 166] can also be understood as geometric phases associated with an exceptional point [211, 212, 213, 214].

The anomalous enhancement of the excitation factors at the avoided crossing can be understood as follows. The excitation factor BnB_{n} for the QNM frequency ωn\omega_{n}, defined in Eq. (2.32), can be rewritten by using the norm squared An2A_{n}^{2} defined by the biorthogonal product as [154]

Bn=i​𝒜out22​ωn​An2,\displaystyle B_{n}=\frac{i\mathcal{A}_{\rm out}^{2}}{2\omega_{n}A_{n}^{2}}, (2.34)

where 𝒜out\mathcal{A}_{\rm out} is the asymptotic amplitude for the outgoing wave at infinity in Eq. (2.30). In general, the norm vanishes at an exceptional point, and hence An2A_{n}^{2} becomes small at the avoided crossing near the exceptional point. From Eq. (2.34), this leads to the enhancement of the excitation factor observed above. Further, arguments based on Eqs. (2.33) and (2.34) can be used to derive analytically some peculiar features of the phenomenon we reviewed in this section, namely, the hyperbolic avoidance curve in the complex frequency plane and the lemniscate-shaped resonance in the excitation factor plane, characterized by a quarter-power Lorentzian peak (see [154] for more details). Note that different features can appear in resonances of QNMs in coupled systems [215]. Additional insights regarding the structure of QNMs near exceptional points and avoided crossings, along with observational implications for time domain (TD) waveforms, are provided in Refs. [216, 217, 218].

In summary: numerical and analytical calculations in Ref. [154] have firmly established that the resonant excitation of QNMs at the avoided crossings is a universal phenomenon in BH QNM spectra. In analogy with other areas of physics [196, 197, 148, 149, 150], the recently discovered exceptional points, avoided crossings and resonances in BH spectra can be expected to lead to further theoretical developments and possibly to new observational discoveries, especially in view of upcoming accurate GW observations of ringdown waves over a wide range of spin parameters (see Section 7.2).

2.4 Light-ring physics

Initial contributors: Fransen

The event horizon is the defining feature of a BH. Yet BHs are also the only known bodies (with the possible exception of exotic ultracompact objects [8]) supporting a “light-ring,” i.e., bound orbits of null geodesics [219]. The importance of these geodesics for the ringdown rests on two observations. First, congruences of null geodesics provide the leading order geometrical optics approximation to the linearized wave equation. Second, congruences which come neither from the BH nor from asymptotic infinity in the past must instead asymptote to bound null geodesics. The light-ring thus provides the boundary conditions to start approximating QNMs in the high-frequency limit. As a result, essential features of these QNMs are fixed by spacetime properties around the light-ring, and the ringdown carries the imprint of light-ring physics.

2.4.1 Geometrical optics

The geometrical optics approximation constructs solutions for (say) trace-reversed gravitational perturbations of the following form [220, 221, 222, 223, 224]

h¯μ​ν​(x)=ϵμ​ν​(x,λ̄)​ei​S​(x)/λ̄,ϵμ​ν​(x,λ̄)=∑i=0∞ϵμ​ν(i)​(x)​λ̄i.\bar{h}_{\mu\nu}(x)=\epsilon_{\mu\nu}(x;\lambdabar)e^{iS(x)/\lambdabar}\,,\quad\epsilon_{\mu\nu}(x;\lambdabar)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\epsilon^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}(x)\lambdabar^{i}\,. (2.35)

More properly, one should take the real part of Eq. (2.35). Here λ̄\lambdabar is a small parameter, while ϵμ​ν​(x,λ̄)\epsilon_{\mu\nu}(x;\lambdabar) and S⁡(x)S(x) are to be determined. To leading order in λ̄\lambdabar, the wave equation reduces to the “eikonal” equation [225]. For both electromagnetic and gravitational perturbations in the Lorenz gauge, the eikonal equation and its first subleading correction are fixed by the d’Alembertian. Explicitly, in our gravitational example [226, 224]:

gμ​ν​(∇μS)​(∇νS)=0,((∇μS)​∇μ+12​(∇μ∇μ​S))​ϵα​β(0)=0,(∇μS)​ϵμ​ν(0)​(x)=0.g^{\mu\nu}(\nabla_{\mu}S)(\nabla_{\nu}S)=0\,,\quad\left((\nabla^{\mu}S)\nabla_{\mu}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\nabla^{\mu}\nabla_{\mu}S\right)\right)\epsilon^{(0)}_{\alpha\beta}=0\,,\quad(\nabla^{\mu}S)\epsilon^{(0)}_{\mu\nu}(x)=0\,. (2.36)

The geodesic equation follows from the first equation in (2.36) by taking a covariant derivative and using [∇μ,∇ν]​S=0[\nabla_{\mu},\nabla_{\nu}]S=0. Higher order ϵα​β(i)\epsilon^{(i)}_{\alpha\beta} will satisfy the second equation in (2.36), but with source terms constructed from lower-order quantities ϵα​β(k<i)\epsilon^{(k<i)}_{\alpha\beta}. Often, it is useful to write ϵμ​ν(0)=𝒜(0)​ϵ^μ​ν(0)\epsilon^{(0)}_{\mu\nu}=\mathcal{A}^{(0)}\hat{\epsilon}^{(0)}_{\mu\nu} in terms of an amplitude and a normalized, parallel transported polarization tensor [220, 222, 224].

As an example, the null geodesic congruence with critical impact parameter bc=L/E=3​3​Mb_{c}=L/E=3\sqrt{3}M and L=LϕL=L_{\phi} around the equatorial bound null geodesic, which we shall denote γ\gamma, at rc=3​Mr_{c}=3M of a Schwarzschild BH is described to first subleading order by [227]

S⁡(x)=E⁡(−t+ϕΩorb+32​M​δ​r2+i​3​3​M​δ​θ2+O⁡(δ​r3,δ​θ3)),δ​r=r−rc,δ​θ=θ−π2,S(x)=E\left(-t+\frac{\phi}{\Omega_{\rm orb}}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2M}\delta r^{2}+i3\sqrt{3}M\delta\theta^{2}+O(\delta r^{3},\delta\theta^{3})\right)\,,\;\delta r=r-r_{c}\,,\;\delta\theta=\theta-\frac{\pi}{2}\,, (2.37)

where it follows from (2.36) that Ωorb=(∇tS/∇ϕS)|γ=1/3​3​M\Omega_{\rm orb}=(\nabla_{t}S/\nabla_{\phi}S)|_{\gamma}=1/3\sqrt{3}M and

((∇μS)​∇μ+1+i2​3​EM)​𝒜(0)​(t,ϕ)=0,𝒜(0)​(t,ϕ)=F⁡(Ωorb​t−ϕ)​e−12​(1+i)​(Ωorb​t+ϕ).\left((\nabla^{\mu}S)\nabla_{\mu}+\frac{1+i}{2\sqrt{3}}\frac{E}{M}\right)\mathcal{A}^{(0)}(t,\phi)=0\,,\quad\mathcal{A}^{(0)}(t,\phi)=F(\Omega_{\rm orb}t-\phi)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(1+i\right)\left(\Omega_{\rm orb}t+\phi\right)}\,. (2.38)

Here, F⁡(x)F(x) is an arbitrary function, and 𝒜(0)\mathcal{A}^{(0)} is evaluated at r=rcr=r_{c} and θ=π2\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}. Demanding that the full azimuthal mode number is unchanged fixes F⁡(x)F(x) up to a constant and allows us to determine, by comparison with ∼e−i​ω​t+i​ℓ​ϕ\sim e^{-i\omega t+i\ell\phi}, the “eikonal” ωℓ​0\omega_{\ell 0} mode. Instead, a slightly more general congruence around the bound null geodesic leads to the benchmark relation between QNMs and “light-ring” physics [228, 67, 229, 68]

ωℓ​n=Ωorb​(ℓ+12)−i​ΛL​(n+12)+O⁡(ℓ−1),ΛL=13​3​M.\omega_{\ell n}=\Omega_{\rm orb}\left(\ell+\frac{1}{2}\right)-i\Lambda_{L}\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)+O(\ell^{-1})\,,\quad\Lambda_{L}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}M}\,. (2.39)

Here, ΛL\Lambda_{L} highlights the relation to the instability timescale of the reference bound null geodesic, as could be deduced from (2.37) by considering (d​S)μ(dS)^{\mu} at linear order in δ​r\delta r [68].

Similar eikonal QNM frequencies have been derived in higher-dimensional [230, 231], Reissner-Nordström [232, 233, 234], Kerr [69, 70], Myers-Perry [68], Kerr-Newman [234, 128], and various other BHs [235, 236]. Typically, an expansion similar to (2.35) is applied only after a symmetry reduction. When the reduction results in an ODE, Eq. (2.35) essentially becomes the WKB method, which has been extensively applied to study BH perturbations [237, 238, 232, 239, 240, 231, 241, 242]. Rather than reviewing these well-known methods, we highlight a more recent variation of the geometrical approach which, instead of approximately solving the wave equation, directly approximates the spacetime around the light ring, and is therefore well-suited to studying the interplay between QNMs and light-ring physics [243, 244].

2.4.2 Near-ring spacetime

As a starting point, observe that the eikonal equations (2.36) can be simplified by going to adapted coordinates (see e.g. [245] for a construction of adapted coordinates for Kerr BHs)

d​s2=2​d​U​d​S+D⁡(xμ)​d​S2+Bi​(xμ)​d​S​d​Xi+Ci​j​(xμ)​d​Xi​d​Xj,ds^{2}=2dUdS+D(x^{\mu})dS^{2}+B_{i}(x^{\mu})dSdX^{i}+C_{ij}(x^{\mu})dX^{i}dX^{j}\,, (2.40)

with D⁡(xμ)D(x^{\mu}), Bi​(xμ)B_{i}(x^{\mu}), and Ci​j​(xμ)C_{ij}(x^{\mu}) functions of the coordinates xμ={U,S,Xi}x^{\mu}=\left\{U,S,X^{i}\right\} and the indices ii, jj running over the d−2d-2 “transverse” directions (i,j,…∈{1,…,d−2}i,j,\ldots\in\left\{1,\ldots,d-2\right\}). Specifically, S⁡(x)S(x) itself has been made into a coordinate, and the null congruence is generated by the coordinate vector field ∂U\partial_{U}. Therefore, Eq. (2.36) is automatically satisfied, and the geometrical optics solution (2.35) to first subleading order can be written explicitly as

h¯μ​ν​(x)=(𝒜0(0)​(Xi,S)​ϵ^μ​ν(0)​(xμ)(det​(Ci​j​(xμ)))1/4+O⁡(λ̄))​ei​S/λ̄.\bar{h}_{\mu\nu}(x)=\left(\frac{\mathcal{A}^{(0)}_{0}(X^{i},S)\hat{\epsilon}^{(0)}_{\mu\nu}(x^{\mu})}{\left(\text{det}\left(C_{ij}(x^{\mu})\right)\right)^{1/4}}+O(\lambdabar)\right)e^{iS/\lambdabar}\,. (2.41)

To obtain a high-frequency approximation to QNMs it is appropriate (as illustrated by the example (2.37)) to simultaneously expand around a reference bound null geodesic, say γ\gamma, with conserved charges appropriate to the QNM of interest. The adapted coordinate system (2.40) can be chosen such that γ\gamma is located at S=Xi=0S=X^{i}=0. Now, an expansion around S=Xi=0S=X^{i}=0 which keeps U∼λ̄0U\sim\lambdabar^{0} but lets S∼λ̄S\sim\lambdabar and Xi∼λ̄X^{i}\sim\sqrt{\lambdabar} corresponds, to leading order, to a spacetime limit proposed by Penrose [246]. In this Penrose limit, the metric (2.40) reduces to a plane wave spacetime in Rosen coordinates [247]:

d​sγ2=2​d​U​d​S+Ci​j​(U)​d​Xi​d​Xj,Ci​j​(U)=Ci​j​(xμ)|S=Xi=0.ds^{2}_{\gamma}=2dUdS+C_{ij}(U)dX^{i}dX^{j}\,,\quad C_{ij}(U)=C_{ij}(x^{\mu})|_{S=X^{i}=0}\,. (2.42)

The approximate solution (2.41), with 𝒜0(0)\mathcal{A}^{(0)}_{0} reduced to a constant by the limit, satisfies the wave equation on the Penrose limit spacetime exactly. In this sense, the Penrose limit acts on the spacetime analogously to a truncation after the first subleading order in the geometrical optics approximation, at least when simultaneously expanded close to a reference null geodesic as in (2.37).

Neither the adapted coordinates (2.40) nor the Rosen coordinates (2.42) are globally well-defined. They (roughly speaking) break down at caustics of the congruence ∂U\partial_{U}. The related breakdown of the geometrical optics approximation, in the local form (2.35), is a starting point for more sophisticated global mathematical treatments [225]. However, for the plane wave (2.42) it is well-known [248, 246] that the coordinate singularities of the Rosen coordinates can be removed by going to Brinkmann coordinates {u,v,xa}\left\{u,v,x^{a}\right\} with a,b,…∈{1,…,d−2}a,b,\ldots\in\left\{1,\ldots,d-2\right\}, in which the metric takes the form [249]

d​sγ2=2​d​u​d​v−Ha​b​(u)​xa​xb​d​u2+δa​b​d​xa​d​xb.ds_{\gamma}^{2}=2dudv-H_{ab}(u)x^{a}x^{b}du^{2}+\delta_{ab}dx^{a}dx^{b}\,. (2.43)

The Penrose limit of an arbitrary null geodesic can be found in [250], or more implicitly in [251, 252]. Closely related geodesic deviation equations for Kerr are also discussed in [253]. In terms of the original spacetime, the “wave-profile” Ha​b​(u)H_{ab}(u) is exactly related to the geodesic deviation along the reference null geodesic [254]

Ha​b​(u)=(Rμ​ν​α​β​Eaμ​uν​Ebα​uβ)|γ,H_{ab}(u)=\left(R_{\mu\nu\alpha\beta}E^{\mu}_{a}u^{\nu}E^{\alpha}_{b}u^{\beta}\right)|_{\gamma}\,, (2.44)

where EaμE^{\mu}_{a} is a transverse frame, parallel propagated along γ\gamma, while uμu^{\mu} is its tangent; locally, uμ=(d​S)μ|γu^{\mu}=(dS)^{\mu}|_{\gamma}. The Penrose limit (2.43) can be viewed as the leading order of a Fermi null coordinate expansion, closely related to keeping higher orders in adapted coordinates (2.40) beyond the Rosen coordinate plane wave (2.42) [254].

2.4.3 Eikonal spectrum

Plane wave metrics of the form (2.43) are particularly simple. They generally act precisely as a harmonic oscillator with square frequency matrix Ha​bH_{ab}. Explicitly, for a massless free scalar Ψ⁡(x)=ei​v​pv​ψ​(u,x1,x2)\Psi(x)=e^{ivp_{v}}\psi(u,x_{1},x_{2}) we have

ipv∂uψ=(−12​pv2δa​b∂a∂b+12Ha​b(u)xaxb)ψ.\frac{i}{p_{v}}\partial_{u}\psi=\left(-\frac{1}{2p_{v}^{2}}\delta^{ab}\partial_{a}\partial_{b}+\frac{1}{2}H_{ab}(u)x^{a}x^{b}\right)\psi\,. (2.45)

Electromagnetic and gravitational perturbations can be constructed from massless free scalar solution to (2.45) by a spin-raising operator [255, 256]. This is the origin of the spin-independence of the eikonal QNMs at the order (2.39) from the Penrose limit point of view. Note also that v|xa=0=Sv|_{x^{a}=0}=S and pv∼1/λ̄p_{v}\sim 1/\lambdabar acts as the inverse Planck constant in (2.45). Its value is fixed by the choice of γ\gamma and a single-valuedness condition, just like EE was fixed in (2.37) at δ​r=δ​θ=0\delta r=\delta\theta=0. Instead, the λ̄0\lambdabar^{0} pieces in eikonal QNMs directly correspond to the eigenstates of (2.45) under the affine time evolution uu, with two important subtleties. First, Ha​b​(u)H_{ab}(u) is explicitly time-dependent in important cases of interest, such as nonequatorial orbits of a Kerr BH. On the other hand, in that case, it is periodic, so there is a well-defined notion of Floquet states [257]. Second, there is an unstable direction in the oscillator (2.45), which is of course expected as the modes are quasinormal [67, 258].

For a Schwarzschild BH, Ha​bH_{ab} is diagonal, and using the same implicit affine parameter as in (2.37) one finds −H11=H22=3​Lc2​M/rc5=E2/9​M2-H_{11}=H_{22}=3L_{c}^{2}M/r_{c}^{5}=E^{2}/9M^{2}. Taking into account the transformation from the affine parameter uu to the Schwarzschild time tt, Eq. (2.45) represents a stable harmonic oscillator with frequency Ωprec=1/3​3​M\Omega_{\rm prec}=1/3\sqrt{3}M and an unstable one with Lyapunov exponent ΛL=1/3​3​M\Lambda_{L}=1/3\sqrt{3}M, consistent with Eq. (2.39). From the perspective of the plane wave (2.43), −H11=H22-H_{11}=H_{22} follows directly from the Einstein equations. In combination with spherical symmetry, this fixes (2.45) entirely up to Ωorb\Omega_{\rm orb}. The eikonal QNMs of a dd-dimensional (vacuum) spherically symmetric BH follow from the same logic, with d−3d-3 stable oscillators and an unstable one [230, 231]. While more complicated for less symmetric cases, it is still striking how directly the Einstein equations are reflected in the O⁡(λ̄0)O(\lambdabar^{0}) eikonal QNM frequencies.

The gravitational wave functions near the light ring can be constructed by solving Eq. (2.45) and using a spin raising operator [255, 256]. Alternatively, (mode) raising and lowering operators can be constructed from the isometry algebra of (2.43), which in that example includes ∂u\partial_{u} in addition to the algebra of Killing vectors {Q(a),P(a),Z}\left\{Q^{(a)},P^{(a)},Z\right\}

[Q(a),P(b)]=δa​b​Z,[Q(a),Q(b)]=[P(a),P(b)]=[Z,P(b)]=[Z,P(b)]=0,\left[Q_{(a)},P_{(b)}\right]=\delta_{ab}Z\,,\quad\left[Q_{(a)},Q_{(b)}\right]=\left[P_{(a)},P_{(b)}\right]=\left[Z,P_{(b)}\right]=\left[Z,P_{(b)}\right]=0\,, (2.46)

present in any plane wave spacetime. In Eq. (2.46), the central element Z=∂vZ=\partial_{v} while {Q(a),P(a)}\left\{Q^{(a)},P^{(a)}\right\} are more complicated (see e.g. [259, 260]), but note that d−2d-2 of these are manifest as coordinate vector fields in Rosen coordinates (2.42). After constructing raising and lowering operators using the additional symmetry X=∂uX=\partial_{u} from

[X,Q(a)]=Q(a),[X,P(a)]=−Ha​b​Q(b),\left[X,Q_{(a)}\right]=Q_{(a)}\,,\quad\left[X,P_{(a)}\right]=-H_{ab}Q_{(b)}\,, (2.47)

one can act on the Gaussian solutions to (2.45), associated to (2.37) with resulting QNM frequency ωℓ​0\omega_{\ell 0}, to obtain the overtone wavefunctions corresponding to ωℓ​n\omega_{\ell n}. For an alternative approach to this “emergent” symmetry structure in eikonal QNMs see [227]. The nature of the simplifications involved perhaps necessitates that some effective emergent symmetry governs the eikonal QNM spectrum. It is less obvious that this symmetry should be realized in terms of local spacetime isometries, which reflects that, while QNMs are ordinarily sensitive to the global spacetime structure, eikonal QNMs become localized at the light-ring.

Another instance where a subset of QNMs organizes according to a “spacetime-limit” isometry are the ZDMs of near-extremal rotating BHs (see also Section (2.1.5)). These QNMs take the form [12, 44, 46, 81]

ωℓ​m​n≈m​ΩH−i⁡(n+hℓ​m)​2​π​TH,\omega_{\ell mn}\approx m\Omega_{\rm H}-i(n+h_{\ell m})2\pi T_{\rm H}\,, (2.48)

where TH→0T_{\rm H}\to 0 is the BH temperature, ΩH→1/2​M\Omega_{H}\to 1/2M is the horizon angular velocity, and Re​(hℓ​m)=1/2\text{Re}(h_{\ell m})=1/2 for modes with m∼ℓm\sim\ell [47]. The modes (2.48) are closely related to interesting phenomenology near-extremal rotating BHs, such as a “polynomial ringdown” phase [47, 77, 78, 261, 262]. They organize themselves (approximately) into representations of the SL​(2,ℝ)×U​(1)\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})\times U(1) isometry of the near-horizon, near-extremal limit metric [263, 264], a warped version of the limiting AdS2×S2\text{AdS}_{2}\times\text{S}^{2} (AdSp+2×Sd−p−2\text{AdS}_{p+2}\times\text{S}^{d-p-2}) near-horizon of extremal charged BHs (p-branes) [265].

The Penrose limit can capture the eikonal limit of Eq. (2.48) as (near-equatorial) corotating bound null geodesics go into the near-horizon region [266]: see [267, 243] for the interplay between the near-horizon and the Penrose limit descriptions. Notably, the isometries of a spacetime are a “hereditary property”; any limit spacetime will have at least as much isometries as its parent [268, 259, 269]. Nevertheless, the nature of the isometries changes through a group contraction [270], which is clearly illustrated in the interplay between the near-horizon and Penrose limits [271]. For the interpretation of the near-horizon Penrose limit within the context of the AdS/CFT conjecture, see [272, 273].

As discussed in detail in Section 2.6, even “small” changes can drastically alter the QNM spectrum. The connection between the light ring and the eikonal QNMs can similarly be broken. For instance, if an effective cavity forms – either because of exotic physics at the horizon or because the BH is immersed in some environment – waves can go back and forth between the light ring and the other features involved, such as AdS asymptotics or the surface of an exotic compact star (see also Section 3.3). The argument that null congruences around the light ring are the only ones consistent with the QNM boundary conditions no longer holds, and the direct relation of the light ring with the eikonal QNMs is broken. Alternatively, the leading eikonal equation can be modified such that null geodesic congruences no longer provide the relevant geometrical optics limit. Given that the eikonal equation is determined by the “principal symbol” of a PDE, the terms with the maximal number of differential operators, this routinely happens in higher-derivative theories [274].

The remainder of the review indicates that observational opportunities are pushing for an understanding of the ringdown in more quantitative detail. This comes with computational challenges and results that are not always easy to interpret. The eikonal limit can provide helpful clarifications. However, to do so, it too must be developed further. The Penrose limit perspective has natural (Penrose-Güven limit) extensions to include additional fields [275] which would for instance be applicable to the Kerr-Newman case (see Section 2.2). The limiting plane waves are almost universal solutions to higher-derivative gravity theories in which they are naturally incorporated [276]: see Section 3.1 for potential applications. The Penrose limit also may also lead to a better understanding of qualitative aspects of nonlinearities (see Sections 4.3 and 4.4 and Refs. [277, 278, 279, 280] for preliminary work in this direction). Higher-order Fermi null coordinate expansions could help relate higher-order eikonal results directly to curvature properties around the light-ring [254]. Finally, it is precisely the nearly bound null geodesics that are responsible for a distinctive “photon ring” in BH images [281, 282]. Current Event Horizon Telescope images are not yet able to resolve the universal, accretion-independent features of this photon ring, but future observations have the potential to do so [283, 284]. For this reason, the eikonal limit of QNMs is a direct link between GW and very-long-baseline interferometry observations of BHs.

2.5 Mode scalar products: completeness, orthogonality, and other properties

Initial contributors: Green, London, Panosso Macedo, Sberna

2.5.1 Introduction

Perturbed BHs are inherently nonconservative systems, as they generally emit gravitational radiation that can escape to infinity or fall into the BH horizon. This means that to understand the properties of their QNM spectrum – in mathematical terms, of QNMs as a kind of vector space – we cannot rely on the familiar theory of conservative systems. In conservative systems (e.g., a particle in a box in quantum mechanics), the equations of motion are Hermitian, their spectrum consists of real eigenvalues, and the related eigenfunctions are referred to as normal modes [285, 286, 287]. Normal modes are orthogonal with respect to an inner product and constitute a complete set. These properties can be exploited to build general solutions, to compute mode excitation coefficients, and to build perturbative solutions to more complex problems. They also ensure the stability of the spectrum [194].

Nonconservative (or non-Hermitian) problems are not unique to gravity, but rather they are ubiquitous in physics, from electromagnetism to nuclear physics, in either classical or quantum systems [193]. It is therefore not surprising that the first scalar product for BH QNMs, appearing as far back as 1993, was inspired by QNMs in optical cavities [204, 288] (see also [289, 290] for reviews). The scalar product introduced there was a bilinear form for Schwarzschild QNMs. Here, a distinction needs to be made between inner products (commonly used in conservative systems) and bilinear forms. An inner product is a map from a vector space to a field that is (i) conjugate-symmetric, i.e., linear in one argument and conjugate linear in the other; and (ii) positive definite. An example of an inner product in quantum mechanics is the integral ⟨f,g⟩=∫abf⁡(x)¯​g​(x)​𝑑x\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{a}^{b}\overline{f(x)}g(x)\mathrm{d}x between two continuous, complex-valued functions on the interval [a,b][a,\,b]. A bilinear form is also a map from a vector space to a field, but one that is linear in both arguments and is not guaranteed to be positive definite. Such a Schwarzschild QNM bilinear form was connected to the QNM excitation coefficients [204], and it was used to compute frequency shifts due to a perturbation in the potential of the mode equation [205, 207]. This approach was later extended to Kerr, and applied to compute perturbative corrections to the Kerr frequencies [77, 208, 102, 209]. Later, motivated by the practicalities of GW signal modeling, situations in which the Kerr QNM spheroidal harmonics are complete have been pointed out [40], and this motivates special functions which enable QNM orthogonality over the solid angle [291, 292, 293, 294]. More recently, a product under which the Kerr QNMs display full spatial orthogonality was presented [295].

A notable technical complication in the definition of Kerr QNM products arises from the asymptotic behavior of QNMs at the bifurcation surface and spatial infinity, located at r=r+r=r_{+} and r→∞r\to\infty, respectively, in the Boyer-Lindquist coordinates. The QNM radial eigenfunctions diverge exponentially in these two limits, so inner products must be modified to give finite results (this same issue is encountered in other physical systems with QNMs, such as resonators in electromagnetism [296]). The simplest resolution is to compute the inner product by deforming the radial integration into regions of the complex plane where modes decay exponentially [155, 295, 297, 298]. An example of such a contour in the Boyer-Lindquist radial coordinate, for modes with Re⁡(ω1+ω2)>0{\rm Re}(\omega_{1}+\omega_{2})>0, is given in Fig. 11. In certain cases, convergence may be accomplished also by subtracting appropriate boundary terms: see e.g. [204, 288, 299, 210, 154]. Alternatively, it has long been suggested [300, 301] that selecting suitable hypersurfaces, correctly foliating both the BH horizon and future null infinity, should yield QNM regular functions asymptotically. The hyperboloidal framework in BH perturbation theory, discussed in Section 2.5.4 below, exploits this geometrical strategy. By constructing time-translation invariant hyperboloidal coordinates in BH spacetimes [302] and identifying their relation to regularization schemes in the FD [303, 66], the framework has become a widespread approach in BH perturbation theory over the past decades (see [304, 305] for recent reviews). Besides addressing the asymptotic divergence of QNMs, the hyperboloidal framework offers a powerful approach to go beyond the linear regime and to properly resolve late-time tails (see Sections 4.4, 4.5, and 5.3).

This body of work, reviewed in more detail in the following subsections, demonstrated that some properties of conservative systems can be recovered – at least to some extent, and at the cost of additional mathematical complexity. There is indeed a sense in which Kerr QNMs are vectors within a topological space and orthogonal. Simple extensions of time-independent perturbation theory can be used to compute QNM frequency shifts. We will review a number of these product spaces for QNMs, as summarized in Table 3. Scalar products of QNMs have been used in several applications, including the calculation of perturbative frequency shifts [102, 306, 210], the study of avoided crossings and resonances in Kerr QNMs (see Section 2.3.3), and the modeling of GWs from BBHs [294, 307]. Other properties of conservative systems, such as spectral stability (see Section 2.6) and completeness (discussed briefly here and in Section 4.1), are unfortunately lost for Kerr QNM spectra. For this reason we will also review some recent developments in the field achieved by importing tools from the theory of non-normal operators [308, 309] to gravity via the hyperboloidal framework, including the notion of pseudospectrum [308, 310, 311] and the so-called Keldysh projection scheme [312].

In the subsections that follow we will pay considerable attention to the spatial properties of Kerr QNMs, in particular their spatial orthogonality [40, 295, 313], as well as ongoing efforts to understand whether QNMs may be spatially complete [40, 42, 43].

Primer: QNMs as a vector space in the azimuthal variable ϕ\phi. We will begin by considering the azimuthal dependence ei​m​ϕe^{im\phi} in Eq. (2.3). This provides an unambiguous yet restrictive avenue to better understand QNM orthogonality and completeness. It is also a reference relative to which some nontrivial aspects of QNM vector spaces may be framed.

The requirement that QNM eigenfunctions be continuous and smooth as one rotates around the BH spin direction (i.e., along ϕ\phi) means that mm may only take on integer values. Therefore, for fixed ss, ℓ\ell and nn, the QNMs constitute a countably infinite set whose natural label or order is m∈ℤm\in\mathbb{Z}. The related complex exponential functions, ei​m​ϕe^{im\phi}, are known to be orthogonal and complete:

⟨ψm∗|ψm′⟩ϕ\displaystyle{\langle{\psi^{*}_{m}}\,|\,{\psi_{m^{\prime}}}\rangle}_{\phi} =∫02​πe−i​m​ϕ​ei​m′​ϕ​𝑑ϕ=2​π​δm′​m,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\,e^{-im\phi}\,e^{im^{\prime}\phi}\,d\phi={2\pi}\,\delta_{m^{\prime}m}\;, (2.49a)
𝕀ϕ\displaystyle\mathbb{I}_{\phi}\; =∑m=−∞∞|ψm⟩​⟨ψm∗|ϕ.\displaystyle=\;\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\,\ket{\psi_{m}}\bra{\psi^{*}_{m}}_{\phi}\;. (2.49b)

In Eq. (2.49a), we define ψm=ei​m​ϕ\psi_{m}=e^{im\phi}, and ψm∗\psi^{*}_{m} is the complex conjugate of ψm\psi_{m}. In Eq. (2.49b), |ψm⟩​⟨ψm∗|ϕ\ket{\psi_{m}}\bra{\psi^{*}_{m}}_{\phi} signals that all products must be performed according to ⟨⋅|⋅⟩ϕ{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{\cdot}\rangle}_{\phi}, as is done in the right-hand side of Eq. (2.49a). Note that the scalar product in Eq. (2.49a) differs from an inner product in that complex conjugation is not treated as an inherent property of the bra-ket operation ⟨⋅|⋅⟩ϕ{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{\cdot}\rangle}_{\phi}; rather, we treat ψm∗\psi^{*}_{m} and ψm\psi_{m} as members of different sets. This is characteristic of the scalar products encountered throughout this section, and reflects the complex nature of the QNM frequencies. In Eq. (2.49b), 𝕀ϕ\mathbb{I}_{\phi} is simply the identity operator, meaning that if Ψ⁡(ϕ)\Psi(\phi) is an arbitrary function of ϕ\phi with domain [0,2​π][0,2\pi], then

𝕀ϕ​|Ψ⟩=∑m=−∞∞|ψm⟩​⟨ψm∗|Ψ⟩ϕ.\displaystyle\mathbb{I}_{\phi}\ket{\Psi}=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\,\ket{\psi_{m}}{\langle{\psi^{*}_{m}}\,|\,{\Psi}\rangle}_{\phi}\;. (2.50)

Together, Eqs. (2.49) and (2.50) define a topological vector space, specifically: a set of vectors, ψm\psi_{m}, and a way to compute distances between them with ⟨⋅|⋅⟩ϕ{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{\cdot}\rangle}_{\phi}. We will refer to this as the ϕ\phi scalar product space, or 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi}, where

𝒬ϕ\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} ={⟨⋅|⋅⟩ϕ,𝒰ϕ}\displaystyle=\{{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{\cdot}\rangle}_{\phi},\mathcal{U}_{\phi}\} (2.51)

In Eq. (2.51), we have defined 𝒰ϕ={ei​m​ϕ|m∈ℤ}\mathcal{U}_{\phi}=\{e^{im\phi}\,|\,m\in\mathbb{Z}\}. Since 𝒰ϕ\mathcal{U}_{\phi} is complete, and norms may be defined via ⟨⋅|⋅⟩ϕ{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{\cdot}\rangle}_{\phi}, 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi} is a Hilbert space.

In summary, the azimuthal functions used in QNM solutions are orthogonal and complete, and can thereby serve as a basis for general decomposition. Indeed, these functions are widely used throughout GW theory (see e.g. [314, 315]). Note that, since Eqs. (2.49) and (2.50) are independent of the QNM frequency, they apply to all QNM eigenfunctions equally. In the following, we will discuss how QNMs may share these properties, either as full spatial functions, or in single spatial dimensions. Historically, these possibilities have been most commonly studied using Sturm-Liouville theory.

2.5.2 Sturm-Liouville theory in the Teukolsky formalism

Given Teukolsky’s master equation, one can apply ideas from Sturm-Liouville theory to construct scalar-product spaces for the QNMs. These spaces provide a foundation for understanding whether it is possible to use the QNMs for projection and decomposition, much as is done with special functions in electromagnetism and quantum mechanics. Key to this program is the intersection between Sturm-Liouville theory and complex operator theory [42, 316, 317].

According to Sturm-Liouville theory, a multi- or uni-variate ordinary differential operator may be used to (i) construct a scalar product under which the operator is self-adjoint, (ii) combine the operator’s eigenfunctions with the scalar product to define a vector space, and (iii) study the properties of that scalar product space in the context of physical applications. These applications include (but are not limited to) the estimation of separation constants, the approximation of QNM angular and radial functions, and potential “spectral decomposition” with QNMs, for which it is required that the QNMs be spatially complete in some way. The points above apply to the full spatial dependence of the QNMs, as well as to their angular and radial functions, Sℓs​(θ,ω~ℓ​m​n){{}_{s}S_{\ell}(\theta;\tilde{\omega}_{\ell mn})} and Rℓs​(θ,ω~ℓ​m​n){{}_{s}R_{\ell}(\theta;\tilde{\omega}_{\ell mn})}, respectively. Therefore, it is possible to construct a scalar product space over (r,θ,ϕ)(r,\theta,\phi), as well as spaces over rr, θ\theta and ϕ\phi separately. We have already encountered the scalar product space in ϕ\phi, 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi}. Like 𝒬ϕ\mathcal{Q}_{\phi}, the remaining spaces are defined by a scalar product, as well as a set of functions (abstract vectors) which span the space.

In this subsection, we will briefly review the construction and properties of select Sturm-Liouville scalar product spaces, namely 𝒬θ\mathcal{Q}_{\theta} and 𝒬r​θ\mathcal{Q}_{r\theta} [208, 40, 295]. The reader should note that, since Teukolsky’s master equation is an operator with complex coefficients, it is possible to have degenerate eigenvalues, as well as related Jordan chains [318, 319]. As it has been observed that this is not the case for Schwarzschild BHs and for Kerr BHs below the extremal limit, we will henceforth focus only on cases in which Teukolsky’s radial and angular problems have unique eigenvalues [40, 42, 43]. Lastly, in what follows we will include within Sturm-Liouville theory two types of situations: one in which we consider a single QNM frequency (“single-frequency” case), and another in which we consider two QNM frequencies concurrently (“two-frequency” case). These two cases are built upon slightly different versions of Sturm-Liouville arguments [285, 286].

Sturm-Liouville theory and indefinite scalar products. Let 𝒯t​r​θ​ϕ\mathcal{T}_{tr\theta\phi} be the linear differential operator corresponding to Teukolsky’s equation in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates, as shown in Eq. (2.2). With a QNM frequency ω\omega in mind, we wish to consider the action of 𝒯t​r​θ​ϕ\mathcal{T}_{tr\theta\phi} on functions whose tt and ϕ\phi dependence is defined by an overall proportionality to e−i⁡(ω​t−m​ϕ)e^{-i(\omega t-m\phi)}, as in Eq. (2.3). Since the result will still be proportional to e−i⁡(ω​t−m​ϕ)e^{-i(\omega t-m\phi)}, it is useful to consider a new operator, 𝒯r​θ\mathcal{T}_{r\theta},

𝒯r​θ\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{r\theta}\; =ei⁡(ω​t−m​ϕ)​𝒯t​r​θ​ϕ​e−i⁡(ω​t−m​ϕ)​𝕀.\displaystyle=\;e^{i(\omega t-m\phi)}\;\mathcal{T}_{tr\theta\phi}\;e^{-i(\omega t-m\phi)}\,\mathbb{I}\;. (2.52)

On the right-hand side of Eq. (2.52), 𝒯t​r​θ​ϕ\mathcal{T}_{tr\theta\phi} acts on the quantity (e−i⁡(ω​t−m​ϕ)​𝕀)(e^{-i(\omega t-m\phi)}\;\mathbb{I}), where 𝕀\mathbb{I} (the identity operator) stands in for an arbitrary function of rr and θ\theta. Sturm-Liouville theory provides a simple framework for the construction of scalar products. Since 𝒯r​θ\mathcal{T}_{r\theta} involves derivatives scaled by complex-valued functions, related scalar products will typically be nonpositive definite or, equivalently, indefinite [320, 321].

The key idea is that one may attempt to define a weight function, W\mathrm{W}, such that W​𝒯r​θ\mathrm{W}\mathcal{T}_{r\theta} is formally self-adjoint:

⟨f|W​𝒯r​θ​g⟩=⟨W​𝒯r​θ​f|g⟩,\displaystyle{\langle{f}\,|\,{\mathrm{W}\mathcal{T}_{r\theta}\,g}\rangle}={\langle{\mathrm{W}\mathcal{T}_{r\theta}\,f}\,|\,{g}\rangle}\,, (2.53)

where ⟨⋅|⋅⟩{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{\cdot}\rangle} refers to an integral over a domain volume. Note that formally self-adjoint operators may not satisfy Sturm-Liouville boundary conditions [286]. Any second order linear operator may be formatted by coordinate and/or similarity transformation to be formally self-adjoint; however, the required transformations may involve impractical or nonalgebraic functions [286, 287]. One then redefines the scalar product to implicitly include the weight function, making the operator self-adjoint with respect to the newly defined product [286]. As demonstrated in many texts [322, 286, 287, 285, 139, 323, 324], the property of self-adjointness imposes constraints on an operator’s form, and has the simplifying benefit of requiring that an operator’s matrix elements are symmetric in a suitably chosen vector space. All linear differential operators may be reformatted (via coordinate transformation and/or appropriate scaling of a weight function) such they are formally self-adjoint.

Single-frequency Sturm-Liouville weights. For example, let us consider the polar space, 𝒬θ\mathcal{Q}_{\theta}. Using Sturm-Liouville theory, we will construct a polar scalar product, ⟨⋅|⋅⟩θ{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{\cdot}\rangle}_{\theta}, and then briefly discuss the radial scalar product. According to Sturm-Liouville theory, ⟨⋅|⋅⟩θ{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{\cdot}\rangle}_{\theta} is defined such that 𝒯r​θ\mathcal{T}_{r\theta} is self-adjoint by first rewriting it as

𝒯r​θ=p0(r,θ,∂r)+p1(θ)∂∂θ+p2(θ)∂2∂θ2.\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{r\theta}=p_{0}(r,\theta,\partial_{r})+p_{1}(\theta)\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}+p_{2}(\theta)\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta^{2}}\;. (2.54)

In Eq. (2.54), the functions p0p_{0}, p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} are simply the coefficients of derivatives with respect to θ\theta. Their explicit form may be determined by inspection. Since there are no cross-derivatives between rr and θ\theta, we have grouped derivatives in rr (i.e., ∂r\partial_{r}) into p0p_{0}. Following standard Sturm-Liouville arguments [286, 287], a weight Wθ\mathrm{W}_{\theta} for which Wθ​𝒯r​θ\mathrm{W}_{\theta}\mathcal{T}_{r\theta} is self-adjoint is

Wθ\displaystyle\mathrm{W}_{\theta} =1p2​(θ)​∫θp1​(θ′)p2​(θ′)​d​θ′\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{2}(\theta)}\,\int^{\theta}\frac{p_{1}(\theta^{\prime})}{p_{2}(\theta^{\prime})}\,d\theta^{\prime}\; (2.55a)
=sin⁡θ.\displaystyle=\sin\theta\,. (2.55b)

The resulting Sturm-Liouville scalar product is ⟨f|g⟩θ=∫0πf​g​Wθ​𝑑θ{\langle{f}\,|\,{g}\rangle}_{\theta}=\int_{0}^{\pi}fg\mathrm{W}_{\theta}d\theta. Unlike tt and ϕ\phi, rr and θ\theta appear explicitly in 𝒯t​r​θ​ϕ\mathcal{T}_{tr\theta\phi}, making it possible to derive single variable weights from Eq. (2.54). Applying the algorithm encapsulated by Eqs. (2.54) and (2.55a) to rr yields

Wr\displaystyle\mathrm{W}_{r} =Δ​(r)s=(r−r+)s​(r−r−)s.\displaystyle=\Delta(r)^{s}=(r-r_{+})^{s}\,(r-r_{-})^{s}\,. (2.56)

Recall that r+r_{+} and r−r_{-} are defined below Eq. (2.1). Equations (2.55) and (2.56) may also be derived by considering Teukolsky’s radial and angular equations separately.

Sturm-Liouville weights depend strongly on coordinate and scaling choices. Coordinate choices affect the weight function via the chain rule applied to the scalar product’s integrand [42]. Choices about spacetime-slicing affect the spatial asymptotic behavior of the QNMs, and are therefore interchangeable with different similarity transformations, akin to Eq. (2.52) [325, 42, 35]. These similarity transformations are sometimes referred to as scaling or “s-homotopic” transformations [42, 41, 326]. In the context of Frobenius-series solutions to the QNM problem, these transformations correspond to solutions with different spatial asymptotic behaviors [42, 43, 327].

The spatial behavior of QNM solutions is constrained by their phase velocity near the BH horizon and spatial infinity [15]. Therefore, while one may consider arbitrary similarity transformations on the QNM problem, the underlying physics is only consistent with transformations that preserve the QNM ingoing-outgoing boundary conditions [42, 15, 52, 48].

For example, Wr\mathrm{W}_{r} has been used in the context of operator perturbation theory for QNMs [208, 297]; however, as it fails to incorporate the QNM asymptotic boundary conditions, this weight is not the most appropriate for studying the potential spatial completeness of QNMs [42, 43]. Upon imposing the QNM boundary conditions [42], Wr\mathrm{W}_{r} transforms into a complex valued Pollaczek-Jacobi weight [328, 329],

Wξ=ξB0​(1−ξ)B1​eB21−ξ\displaystyle{\mathrm{W}}_{\xi}=\xi^{\mathrm{B}_{0}}\,(1-\xi)^{\mathrm{B}_{1}}\,e^{\frac{\mathrm{B}_{2}}{1-\xi}} (2.57)

where ξ=(r−r+)/(r−r−)\xi=(r-r_{+})/(r-r_{-}), and B0\mathrm{B}_{0} through B2\mathrm{B}_{2} are defined in terms of aa, ss, MM and ω\omega [42]. Polynomials derived from Wξ{\mathrm{W}}_{\xi} enable one to express Teukolsky’s radial operator for QNMs as a symmetric tridiagonal matrix, and Eq. (2.5) as a simple matrix eigenvalue problem [43]. These observations point to intersections between QNMs, matrix representations of Sturm-Liouville operators, and the study of orthogonal polynomial systems [330, 40, 42, 43, 331, 316]. In the case of the spheroidal harmonics for QNMs, these intersections are one avenue through which QNM spatial completeness may be studied [40, 294].

The Sturm-Liouville weights defined in Eqs. (2.55) and (2.56) have a few important properties that are relevant to their potential use in defining a unique projection operator, similar to 𝕀ϕ\mathbb{I}_{\phi} in Eq. (2.50). Both Wr{\mathrm{W}}_{r} and Wθ{\mathrm{W}}_{\theta} are independent of the QNM frequency; as a result, the related scalar products could be applied equally to different QNMs that make up GW signals. Concurrently, Wr{\mathrm{W}}_{r} and Wθ{\mathrm{W}}_{\theta} were derived using 𝒯r​θ\mathcal{T}_{r\theta} which is, by construction, frequency-dependent [42]: see Eq. (2.2). This is illustrated by the fact that Wr{\mathrm{W}}_{r} can be similarity-transformed into the explicitly frequency-dependent weight Wξ{\mathrm{W}}_{\xi}, without affecting the underlying physics. Thus, similarity transformations enable the conversion of frequency-agnostic Sturm-Liouville weights into single-frequency weights, and vice-versa.

Two-frequency weights, and the 22D space 𝒬r​θ\mathcal{Q}_{r\theta}. Using a variant of the Sturm-Liouville construction [285], two-frequency weights may be constructed from the action of the (r,θ)(r,\theta) part of Teukolsky’s operator on two different QNM solutions [154, 297, 295]. The (r,θ)(r,\theta) part of Teukolsky’s operator, 𝒯r​θ\mathcal{T}_{r\theta}, was shown in Eq. (2.52). Here, it is useful to refer to this operator as 𝒯r​θ​(w)\mathcal{T}_{r\theta}(w), to explicitly indicate its dependence on a single QNM frequency. Following the logic of Eq. (2.55a), 𝒯r​θ​(ω)\mathcal{T}_{r\theta}(\omega) is self-adjoint with respect to the 22D product whose weight is Wr​Wθ{\mathrm{W}}_{r}\,{\mathrm{W}}_{\theta}, and whose domain of integration is the BH exterior. For two arbitrary functions, f⁡(r,θ)f(r,\theta) and g⁡(r,θ)g(r,\theta), this product is

⟨f|g⟩r​θ=∫r+∞∫0πf⁡(r,θ)​g​(r,θ)​WθSL​WrSL​𝑑θ​𝑑r.\displaystyle{\langle{f}\,|\,{g}\rangle}_{r\theta}=\int_{r_{+}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\pi}\;f(r,\theta)\,g(r,\theta)\;{\mathrm{W}}^{\mathrm{SL}}_{\theta}\,{\mathrm{W}}^{\mathrm{SL}}_{r}\,d\theta\,dr\;. (2.58)

We now consider two different QNM frequencies, ωj\omega_{j} and ωk\omega_{k}. For compactness, let 𝒯k=𝒯r​θ​(ωk)\mathcal{T}_{k}=\mathcal{T}_{r\theta}(\omega_{k}), and let ψk\psi_{k} be the (r,θ)(r,\theta) dependence of a single QNM. Thus, for QNMs, 𝒯k​ψk=0\mathcal{T}_{k}\,\psi_{k}=0. Using this fact, and the properties of ⟨⋅|⋅⟩{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{\cdot}\rangle}, it can be shown that [297]

⟨ψj|𝒯j​ψk⟩r​θ−⟨ψj|𝒯k​ψk⟩r​θ=⟨ψj|(𝒯j−𝒯k)|ψk⟩r​θ=0,\displaystyle{\langle{\psi_{j}}\,|\,{\mathcal{T}_{j}\,\psi_{k}}\rangle}_{r\theta}-{\langle{\psi_{j}}\,|\,{\mathcal{T}_{k}\,\psi_{k}}\rangle}_{r\theta}={\langle{\psi_{j}}\,|\,{(\mathcal{T}_{j}-\mathcal{T}_{k})\,|\psi_{k}}\rangle}_{r\theta}=0\;, (2.59)

where 𝒯j−𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{j}-\mathcal{T}_{k} can be written as

(𝒯j−𝒯k)=(ωj−ωk)​Wr​θ,\displaystyle(\mathcal{T}_{j}-\mathcal{T}_{k})=\left(\omega_{j}-\omega_{k}\right){\mathrm{W}}_{r\theta}\,, (2.60)

and where Wr​θ{\mathrm{W}}_{r\theta} is

Wr​θ=−(ωj+ωk)\displaystyle{\mathrm{W}}_{r\theta}=-\left(\omega_{j}+\omega_{k}\right) ((a2+r2)2Δ⁡(r)−a2​sin2⁡(θ))\displaystyle\left(\frac{\left(a^{2}+r^{2}\right)^{2}}{\Delta(r)}-a^{2}\sin^{2}(\theta)\right)
+2​i​s​(M⁡(r2−a2)Δ⁡(r)−i​a​cos⁡(θ)−r)+4​M​a​m​rΔ⁡(r).\displaystyle+2is\left(\frac{M(r^{2}-a^{2})}{\Delta(r)}-ia\cos(\theta)-r\right)+\frac{4Mamr}{\Delta(r)}. (2.61)

In effect, Eq. (2.59) implies that Wr​θ{\mathrm{W}}_{r\theta} is a frequency-dependent weight function such that two QNM functions of rr and θ\theta are orthogonal,

⟨ψj|Wr​θ|ψk⟩r​θ∝δj​k.\displaystyle{\langle{\psi_{j}}\,|\,{{\mathrm{W}}_{r\theta}\,|\psi_{k}}\rangle}_{r\theta}\propto\delta_{jk}\;. (2.62)

Equations (2.59)–(2.62) echo standard arguments for the orthogonality of linearly independent eigenfunctions of a self-adjoint operator [287, 40, 286], but differ in that one focuses on the operator’s null space. With Eq. (2.62), we may define the rr-θ\theta scalar product space as

𝒬r​θ\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{r\theta} ={⟨⋅|Wr​θ|⋅⟩ϕ,𝒰r​θ},\displaystyle=\{{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{{\mathrm{W}}_{r\theta}|\cdot}\rangle}_{\phi},\mathcal{U}_{r\theta}\}\,, (2.63)

where 𝒰r​θ={Sℓs​(θ,a​ωℓ​m​n)​Rns​(r,ωℓ​m​n)|ℓ≥max⁡(|s|,|m|)​, ​n≥0}\mathcal{U}_{r\theta}=\{{{}_{s}S_{\ell}(\theta;a{\omega}_{\ell mn})}\,{{}_{s}R_{n}(r;{\omega}_{\ell mn})}\;|\;\ell\geq\max(|s|,|m|)\text{, }n\geq 0\}. It is presently unknown whether this space is complete. It may be over-complete [48, 65, 42, 43], which would mean that an identity operator constructed from 𝒬r​θ\mathcal{Q}_{r\theta} would not be unique.

Like Wθ{\mathrm{W}}_{\theta} and Wr{\mathrm{W}}_{r}, the weight Wr​θ{\mathrm{W}}_{r\theta} is strongly coordinate-dependent. Although Wr​θ{\mathrm{W}}_{r\theta} depends on two QNM frequencies, the sum of QNM frequencies in Eq. (2.61) may be replaced with time derivatives, resulting in a weighting operator that is frequency-independent [295, 297]. The product (2.62) is equivalent to the result of [295], discussed in the next subsection (see [297]).

Lastly, the algorithm encapsulated in Eqs. (2.59)–(2.62) also applies to Teukolsky’s radial and angular equations. For example, the resulting angular weight is

Wθ(2)=1+a​cos⁡(θ)​ωj−ωkA⁡(ωj)−A⁡(ωk)​[−2​s+a​cos⁡(θ)​(ωj+ωk)].\displaystyle{\mathrm{W}}_{\theta}^{(2)}=1+a\cos(\theta)\,\frac{\omega_{j}-\omega_{k}}{A(\omega_{j})-A(\omega_{k})}\,\left[\;-2s+a\cos(\theta)\,\left(\omega_{j}+\omega_{k}\right)\;\right]\,. (2.64)

Since the separation constants, A⁡(ω)A(\omega), are generally nonlinear functions of ω\omega (see e.g. [332, 330, 333]), it is unlikely that Wθ(2){\mathrm{W}}_{\theta}^{(2)} can be rewritten in a frequency-independent manner. Consequently, it is unlikely that Wθ(2){\mathrm{W}}_{\theta}^{(2)} can be used to construct a frequency-agnostic projection operator. Equivalently, it is unclear whether Wθ(2){\mathrm{W}}_{\theta}^{(2)} is compatible with numerical decomposition.

The polar space, 𝒬θ\mathcal{Q}_{\theta}. An alternative perspective [40, 294] concludes that decomposition is possible with the QNM spheroidal harmonics, but that it requires a generalization of orthogonality called biorthogonality (i.e., orthogonality between members of two different sets), as well as the use of special functions called adjoint-spheroidal harmonics. The resulting decomposition can be applied, for example, to extreme and comparable mass-ratio BBHs [294]. Below, we briefly review the treatment of the QNM spheroidal harmonics as a Hilbert space. In what follows, we will drop the labels of ss, mm and nn, as they will all be considered fixed, and we will refer only to the θ\theta-dependence of the spherical and spheroidal harmonics; e.g., Sℓ=Sℓs​(θ,a​ωℓ​m​n)S_{\ell}={{}_{s}}S_{\ell}(\theta;a\omega_{\ell mn}).

For fixed values of ss, mm and nn, the following properties hold [40]: (i) the QNM angular separation constants are unique, even for very large values of ℓ\ell, and (ii) there is a close relationship between the spherical and spheroidal harmonics, meaning that there exists a one-to-one mapping between them. The related spherical-spheroidal mixing coefficients may be used to construct an invertible operator, 𝕋\mathbb{T}, that converts spin-weighted spherical harmonics into the QNM spheroidal harmonics,

𝕋=∑ℓ,ℓ′|Yℓ′⟩​⟨Sℓ′|Yℓ⟩θ​⟨Yℓ|.\displaystyle\mathbb{T}=\sum_{\ell,\ell^{\prime}}\,\ket{Y_{\ell^{\prime}}}{\langle{S_{\ell^{\prime}}}\,|\,{Y_{\ell}}\rangle}_{\theta}\bra{Y_{\ell}}\;. (2.65)

In Eq. (2.65), all scalar products are defined using the Sturm-Liouville weight, Wθ=sin⁡(θ){\mathrm{W}}_{\theta}=\sin(\theta), with θ∈[0,2​π]\theta\in[0,2\pi]. Note that we have represented 𝕋\mathbb{T} in the basis of spherical harmonics, where it is a matrix with elements ⟨Sℓ′|Yℓ⟩θ{\langle{S_{\ell^{\prime}}}\,|\,{Y_{\ell}}\rangle}_{\theta}. Using the orthogonality and completeness of the spherical harmonics, it is easy to show that 𝕋​Yℓ=Sℓ\mathbb{T}\,Y_{\ell}=S_{\ell}. The invertibility of 𝕋\mathbb{T} is underpinned by the bounded inverse theorem [40]. Given 𝕋−1\mathbb{T}^{-1}, it follows that Yℓ=𝕋−1​SℓY_{\ell}=\mathbb{T}^{-1}\,S_{\ell}. One can then recast the orthogonality relationship for the spherical harmonics in terms of the QNM spheroidal harmonics,

⟨Yℓ|Yℓ′⟩θ=⟨Yℓ|𝕋−1​𝕋​Yℓ′⟩θ=⟨𝕋−⁣†​Yℓ|𝕋​Yℓ′⟩θ=⟨S~ℓ|Sℓ′⟩θ=δℓ′​ℓ.\displaystyle{\langle{Y_{\ell}}\,|\,{Y_{\ell^{\prime}}}\rangle}_{\theta}={\langle{Y_{\ell}}\,|\,{\mathbb{T}^{-1}\mathbb{T}Y_{\ell^{\prime}}}\rangle}_{\theta}={\langle{\mathbb{T}^{-\dagger}Y_{\ell}}\,|\,{\mathbb{T}Y_{\ell^{\prime}}}\rangle}_{\theta}={\langle{\tilde{S}_{\ell}}\,|\,{S_{\ell^{\prime}}}\rangle}_{\theta}=\delta_{\ell^{\prime}\ell}\;. (2.66)

𝕋−⁣†​Yℓ\mathbb{T}^{-\dagger}Y_{\ell} can be identified [40] as an “adjoint-spheroidal” harmonic

S~ℓ=𝕋−⁣†​Yℓ.\displaystyle\tilde{S}_{\ell}=\mathbb{T}^{-\dagger}\,Y_{\ell}\;. (2.67)

In Eq. (2.67), one should read that S~ℓ\tilde{S}_{\ell} is represented in the basis of spherical harmonics, where the expansion coefficients are the matrix elements of 𝕋\mathbb{T} inverted and conjugate-transposed [40]. Using similar arguments, the QNM spheroidal harmonics may be shown to be complete,

𝕀θ=∑ℓ|Sℓ⟩​⟨S~ℓ|θ.\displaystyle\mathbb{I}_{\theta}=\sum_{\ell}\,\ket{S_{\ell}}\bra{\tilde{S}_{\ell}}_{\theta}\;. (2.68)

With the weight WθW_{\theta}, we may define the scalar product space in θ\theta as

𝒬θ={⟨⋅|⋅⟩θ,𝒰θ},\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\theta}=\{{\langle{\cdot}\,|\,{\cdot}\rangle}_{\theta},\mathcal{U}_{\theta}\}\;, (2.69)

where 𝒰θ={Sℓs​(θ,a​ωℓ​m​n)|ℓ≥max⁡(|m|,|s|)}\mathcal{U}_{\theta}=\{\,{{}_{s}}S_{\ell}(\theta;a\omega_{\ell mn})\,|\,\ell\geq\max(|m|,|s|)\,\} [40, 42]. Te small spin expansion of S~ℓ\tilde{S}_{\ell} was computed and 𝒬θ\mathcal{Q}_{\theta} was used to estimate ringdown amplitudes by projection for extreme mass-ratio, comparable mass-ratio, and precessing BBH simulations in [294]. An approximation of 𝒬θ\mathcal{Q}_{\theta} is used in PhenomXHM [307] and related GW signal models [291, 292, 293].

We have the freedom to define the norm of the spheroidal harmonics based on the scalar product [40]. This, along with completeness of the spheroidal harmonics [319, 40], means that 𝒬θ\mathcal{Q}_{\theta} is a Hilbert space.

2.5.3 QNM orthogonality product.

A bilinear form with respect to which the time-translation operator is symmetric can be constructed to show that QNMs of the spin-ss Teukolsky equation are orthogonal [295]. This construction, inspired by the physics of leaky optical cavities [334] and other open systems, and already applied to scalar waves in Schwarzschild [204, 288, 205, 207], provides a more general derivation of the orthogonality of QNMs.

The starting point is a conserved current defined by the Teukolsky operator. Here the Teukolsky operator acting on spin-ss solutions Ψ\Psi [the left-hand side of Eq. (2.3)] is denoted by 𝒪\mathcal{O}. The current also involves the spacetime adjoint of the Teukolsky equation, denoted by 𝒪†\mathcal{O}^{\dagger} and acting on spin −s-s solutions Ψ~\tilde{\Psi} (we denote this “spacetime adjoint” to stress the fact, often left implicit in the literature, that the product defining the adjoint is the spacetime integral). The current πa\pi^{a} is a functional of a spin ss and a spin −s-s solution, and is implicitly defined by

(𝒪†​ψ~)​ψ−ψ~​(𝒪​ψ)=∇aπa​[ψ~,ψ].(\mathcal{O}^{\dagger}\tilde{\psi})\psi-\tilde{\psi}(\mathcal{O}\psi)=\nabla_{a}\pi^{a}[\tilde{\psi},\psi]. (2.70)

The current is evidently conserved on solutions, i.e., ∇aπa​[ψ~,ψ]=0\nabla_{a}\pi^{a}[\tilde{\psi},\psi]=0 for ψ∈ker⁡𝒪,ψ~∈ker⁡𝒪†\psi\in\ker\mathcal{O},\tilde{\psi}\in\ker\mathcal{O}^{\dagger}. A “base product” can then be built as the associated conserved quantity on any spacelike hypersurface,

Π⁡[ψ~,ψ]=∫d​Σa​πa​[ψ~,ψ].\Pi[\tilde{\psi},\psi]=\int{\rm d}\Sigma_{a}\pi^{a}[\tilde{\psi},\psi]. (2.71)

To build a product on two modes of the same spin ss, one can map a mode of spin ss into a mode of spin −s-s using the operator 𝒥\mathcal{J} associated to the discrete t−ϕt-\phi reflection symmetry of Kerr [295]. The resulting product is

⟨⟨ψ1,ψ2⟩⟩=∫d​Σa​πa​[Ψ22​s/3​𝒥​ψ1,ψ2],\langle\langle\psi_{1},\psi_{2}\rangle\rangle=\int{\rm d}\Sigma_{a}\pi^{a}[\Psi_{2}^{2s/3}\mathcal{J}\psi_{1},\psi_{2}], (2.72)

where Ψ2\Psi_{2} is the only nonzero Weyl scalar of the Kerr metric. The product possesses the following key properties [295]: (i) it does not rely on the spatial separability of the Teukolsky equation; (ii) it is bilinear (a bilinear form); (iii) it is symmetric, ⟨⟨ψ1,ψ2⟩⟩=⟨⟨ψ2,ψ1⟩⟩\langle\langle\psi_{1},\psi_{2}\rangle\rangle=\langle\langle\psi_{2},\psi_{1}\rangle\rangle. Moreover, the time-translation symmetry operator LtL_{t} of Kerr is symmetric with respect to the product, ⟨⟨ψ1,Lt​ψ2⟩⟩=⟨⟨Lt​ψ1,ψ2⟩⟩\langle\langle\psi_{1},L_{t}\psi_{2}\rangle\rangle=\langle\langle L_{t}\psi_{1},\psi_{2}\rangle\rangle. Consequently, for two QNMs, (ω1−ω2)​⟨⟨ψ1,ψ2⟩⟩=0(\omega_{1}-\omega_{2})\langle\langle\psi_{1},\psi_{2}\rangle\rangle=0, implying that modes with different frequencies are orthogonal. Equivalently, {ψn}\{\psi_{n}\} and {ψ~n≡Ψ22​s/3𝒥ψn}\{\tilde{\psi}_{n}\equiv\Psi_{2}^{2s/3}\mathcal{J}\psi_{n}\} form biorthogonal sets under the product Π\Pi. In other words, QNM orthogonality arises from the orthogonality between QNMs and “anti-QNMs” [298]. Thanks to this understanding, this construction has been extended to scalar fields on black holes in AdS, exploiting the CPT operator to map the two families of QNM solutions [298].

In Boyer-Lindquist coordinates, the product takes the form

⟨⟨ψ1,ψ2⟩⟩\displaystyle\langle\langle\psi_{1},\psi_{2}\rangle\rangle
=4M4/3∫ΣdrdθdϕsinθΔs[ψ1|t→−tϕ→−ϕ(ΛΔ∂t+2​M​r​aΔ∂ϕ−2s[−r−iacosθ+MΔ(r2−a2)])ψ2\displaystyle={}4M^{4/3}\int_{\Sigma}\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta\mathrm{d}\phi\,\sin\theta\Delta^{s}\Bigg[\psi_{1}\Big|_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\to-t\\ \phi\to-\phi\end{subarray}}\left(\frac{\Lambda}{\Delta}\partial_{t}+\frac{2Mra}{\Delta}\partial_{\phi}-2s\left[-r-ia\cos\theta+\frac{M}{\Delta}(r^{2}-a^{2})\right]\right)\psi_{2}
+ψ2(ΛΔ∂t+2​M​r​aΔ∂ϕ−2s[−r−iacosθ+MΔ(r2−a2)])ψ1|t→−tϕ→−ϕ]\displaystyle\quad+\psi_{2}\left(\frac{\Lambda}{\Delta}\partial_{t}+\frac{2Mra}{\Delta}\partial_{\phi}-2s\left[-r-ia\cos\theta+\frac{M}{\Delta}(r^{2}-a^{2})\right]\right)\psi_{1}\Big|_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\to-t\\ \phi\to-\phi\end{subarray}}\Bigg] (2.73a)
=8πM4/3δm1​m2e−i⁡(ω2−ω1)​t∫𝒞dr∫0πdθ{sinθΔsS1(θ)S2(θ)R1(r)R2(r)\displaystyle={}8\pi M^{4/3}\delta_{m_{1}m_{2}}e^{-i(\omega_{2}-\omega_{1})t}\int_{\mathcal{C}}{\rm d}r\int_{0}^{\pi}{\rm d}\theta\,\bigg\{\sin\theta\Delta^{s}S_{1}(\theta)S_{2}(\theta)R_{1}(r)R_{2}(r)
(−i​ΛΔ(ω1+ω2)+2​i​M​r​aΔ(m1+m2)−2s[−r−iacosθ+MΔ(r2−a2)])},\displaystyle\quad\left(-\frac{i\Lambda}{\Delta}(\omega_{1}+\omega_{2})+\frac{2iMra}{\Delta}(m_{1}+m_{2})-2s\left[-r-ia\cos\theta+\frac{M}{\Delta}(r^{2}-a^{2})\right]\right)\bigg\}, (2.73b)

where Λ≡(r2+a2)2−Δ​a2​sin2⁡θ\Lambda\equiv(r^{2}+a^{2})^{2}-\Delta a^{2}\sin^{2}\theta, and in the second line we have explicitly applied it to QNMs. An example of the regularization contour, 𝒞\mathcal{C}, is shown in Fig. 11.

The bilinear form defined in Eq. (2.73a) can be used, for example, to compute the excitation coefficients of QNMs given data ψ\psi on a space-like hypersurface [295],

Cn​ℓ​m=⟨⟨ψn​ℓ​m,ψ⟩⟩⟨⟨ψn​ℓ​m,ψn​ℓ​m⟩⟩,C_{n\ell m}=\frac{\langle\langle\psi_{n\ell m},\psi\rangle\rangle}{\langle\langle\psi_{n\ell m},\psi_{n\ell m}\rangle\rangle}\,, (2.74)

providing an alternative to the Green’s function formalism described in Sections 4.1 and 4.2 below. It also provides an alternative to the Sturm-Liouville product Eq. (2.58) to compute perturbative frequency shifts [210]. Finally, it enables to calculate corrections to linear ringdown predictions [299, 335, 336].

2.5.4 The hyperboloidal framework, the energy product, and the pseudospectrum

The study of scalar products was initially motivated by attempts to understand the completeness properties of the QNM eigenfunctions [337, 338]. As previously mentioned, however, the radial integration used in all of the products introduced so far requires a regularization of the QNM eigenfunctions via a deformation of the relevant integration contour in the complex rr plane, as in Fig. 11. Over the past decades, the so-called hyperboloidal framework [302, 303, 66, 304, 305] has become a widespread geometrical approach in BH perturbation theory to avoid the divergence of QNMs on spacelike hypersurfaces near the bifurcation sphere and spatial infinity.

In Riemannian geometry, spherical coordinates (or their spheroidal deformations) play a crucial role to capture symmetries of the manifold or to simplify the equations. Hyperboloids play a similar role in Lorentzian geometries [339], as they capture key features of the spacetime’s casual structure. In the particular case of BH spacetimes, the level sets of constant hyperboloidal time coordinate are regular spacelike hypersurfaces, extending smoothly from the BH event horizon to future null infinity. Most importantly, they reveal that QNM eigenfunctions are regular in the BH exterior [340, 341, 342, 343, 66, 344, 345, 346].

In essence, a hyperboloidal foliation x¯μ=(τ,σ,θ,φ)\bar{x}^{\mu}=(\tau,\sigma,\theta,\varphi) follows from the usual Boyer-Lindquist coordinates xμ=(t,r,θ,ϕ)x^{\mu}=(t,r,\theta,\phi) via

t=r+​(τ−H⁡(σ)),r=r0+r+−r0σ,ϕ=φ−ϕ∗​(r).t=r_{+}\bigg(\tau-H(\sigma)\bigg),\quad r=r_{0}+\dfrac{r_{+}-r_{0}}{\sigma},\quad\phi=\varphi-\phi_{*}(r). (2.75)

Each element in Eq. (2.75) contributes to the regularity of the QNM eigenfunctions at the BH horizon and at future null infinity in different ways. For instance, the azimuthal angle transformation defined by the relation d​ϕ∗/d​r=a/Δd\phi_{*}/dr=a/\Delta is well-known for the ingoing Kerr coordinates, and it ensures the regularity of observables across the BH horizon.

To properly obtain a hyperboloidal surface, the height function H⁡(σ)H(\sigma) in Eq. (2.75) must satisfy specific asymptotic conditions [302, 303, 304]. The so-called minimal gauge retains just these minimal conditions when constructing a hyperboloidal foliation, and H⁡(σ)H(\sigma) reads [347, 304]

H⁡(σ)=−1−r0/r+σ+2​Mr+​ln⁡σ+12​r+​κ+​ln⁡(1−σ)+12​r+​κ−​ln⁡(1−σσ−),H(\sigma)=-\dfrac{1-r_{0}/r_{+}}{\sigma}+\dfrac{2M}{r_{+}}\ln\sigma+\dfrac{1}{2r_{+}\kappa_{+}}\ln(1-\sigma)+\dfrac{1}{2r_{+}\kappa_{-}}\ln\left(1-\dfrac{\sigma}{\sigma_{-}}\right), (2.76)

with κ±=(4​M)−1​(1−a2/r±2)\kappa_{\pm}=(4M)^{-1}\left(1-a^{2}/r_{\pm}^{2}\right) denoting the surface gravity of the horizons.

The radial compactification in Eq. (2.75) includes only the minimal structure necessary to bring the infinitely far wave zone into a finite range of coordinate values. Indeed, σ=0\sigma=0 represents future null infinity, whereas the choice in Eq. (2.75) conveniently fixes the BH horizon r=r+r=r_{+} to σ+=1\sigma_{+}=1. This minimal compactification is not unique, as it allows for an arbitrary initial offset r0r_{0} in the radial coordinate. In terms of this parameter, the Cauchy horizon at r=r−r=r_{-} is mapped into σ−=(r+−r0)/(r−−r0)\sigma_{-}=(r_{+}-r_{0})/(r_{-}-r_{0}).

This arbitrary constant offers some freedom to understand and explore the Kerr spacetime extremal limit from this geometrical perspective [347]. A straightforward option is to choose r0=0r_{0}=0, which implies σ−=r+/r−\sigma_{-}=r_{+}/r_{-}, i.e., the coordinate value of the Cauchy horizon depends on the BH rotation parameter aa. As a consequence, the hyperboloidal hypersurfaces τ=\tau= constant foliate the Cauchy horizon smoothly, and the extremal Kerr limit is directly achieved when |a|→M|a|\rightarrow M and r−→r+r_{-}\rightarrow r_{+} [347, 325]. This option is equivalent to the hyperboloidal implementation used in [348].

A second option is to fix the Cauchy horizon at a coordinate value independent of the BH rotation parameter. The choice r0=r−r_{0}=r_{-}, for instance, is such that σ−→∞\sigma_{-}\rightarrow\infty for all values of aa. In this way, the hypersurfaces τ=\tau= constant do not cross the Cauchy horizon [325], and the extremal limit provides a discontinuous transition into the Kerr near-horizon geometry [347]. This option is the spacetime counterpart of Leaver’s strategy [326, 349, 66, 350, 347].

The construction of Eqs. (2.75),(2.76) automatically yields a configuration where outgoing boundary conditions at both the BH horizon and the wave zone are satisfied. The physically relevant scenario is described by the regular solution to the resulting hyperboloidal wave equation [303, 304, 305], ∂τu→=L^​u→\partial_{\tau}\vec{u}={\hat{L}}\vec{u}. The operator L^{\hat{L}}, acting only on the spatial dimensions, is schematically represented as

L^=(01𝑳1𝑳2).\quad{\hat{L}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\ {\boldsymbol{L}}_{1}&{\boldsymbol{L}}_{2}\end{array}\right). (2.77)

The second-order differential operator 𝑳1{\boldsymbol{L}}_{1} assumes a singular Sturm–Liouville form, and the first-order differential operator 𝑳2{\boldsymbol{L}}_{2} incorporates the energy flow into the BH and towards ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+} [310, 351].

An early objective of this approach was to utilize the fact that QNMs defined on hyperboloidal surfaces “are represented by proper eigenvalues and eigenfunctions” [301]. A FD transformation u→∼e𝔰​τ​u→\vec{u}\sim e^{\mathfrak{s}\tau}\vec{u} leads to the eigenvalue problem L^​u→=𝔰​u→\hat{L}\vec{u}=\mathfrak{s}\vec{u}, with the dimensionless parameter 𝔰=−i​r+​ω\mathfrak{s}=-ir_{+}\omega. Consequently, the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of L^{\hat{L}} correspond directly to the QNM eigenfrequencies and eigenfunctions [310]. Advances in this framework for spherically symmetric spacetimes have been significant [310, 304], with successful applications to the Kerr spacetime [347, 348].

The regularity of the QNM eigenfunctions allows one to revisit the completeness properties of the QNM eigenfunctions [337, 338] via the representation of solutions as a complete spectral decomposition in terms of a superposition of a discrete spectrum (the QNMs) and of a continuous spectrum from the branch cut contribution [66, 350]:

ϕ¯ℓ​m​(τ,σ)=∑n=0∞ηn​ℓ​m​ϕ¯n​ℓ​m​(σ)​e𝔰n​ℓ​m​τ+∫Re⁡(𝔰)≤0​ηℓ​m​(ω)​e𝔰​τ​ϕ¯n​ℓ​m​(𝔰,σ)​d​ω.\bar{\phi}_{\ell m}(\tau,\sigma)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\eta_{n\ell m}\bar{\phi}_{n\ell m}(\sigma)e^{\mathfrak{s}_{n\ell m}\tau}+\underset{{\rm Re}(\mathfrak{s})\leq 0}{\int}\eta_{\ell m}(\omega)e^{\mathfrak{s}\tau}\bar{\phi}_{n\ell m}(\mathfrak{s};\sigma)d\omega. (2.78)

The notation ϕ¯\bar{\phi} emphasizes that these fields are defined in terms of the hyperboloidal coordinate system, with ϕ¯n​ℓ​m​(σ)\bar{\phi}_{n\ell m}(\sigma) the regular QNM eigenfunctions. An extension of Leaver’s algorithm [66, 350] allows one to define QNMs as the poles of a discrete Green’s function (see e.g. Eq. (73) in [66]) and to compute the QNM and branch cut amplitudes, ηn\eta_{n} and η⁡(𝔰)\eta(\mathfrak{s}), from a given set of initial data via a discrete projection operator (see e.g. Eqs. (106) and (109) in [66]). The orthogonality of QNMs is verified in terms of these discrete projection operators. The spectral decomposition of Eq. (2.78) has been recently revisited in terms of the so-called Keldysh scheme [351, 290, 312], that extends the analysis in [66] beyond one-dimensional problems. This scheme relies on defining the QNM projection solely in terms of quantities in the dual vector space [312], in particular not requiring a scalar product. Proof-of-principle studies indicate that the transpose operator LtL^{t} provides the elements to express Eq. (2.78) with QNM/tail amplitudes fixed by projections of the initial data into the dual vector space [312].

The early studies on the completeness properties of the QNM eigenfunctions [337, 338] also noticed a peculiar feature: the QNM spectrum changed drastically when considering a discrete approximation to the Regge-Wheeler potential. In particular, the (continuum representation) QNMs were not recovered, even in the limit where the discrete representation was pushed closer to the continuous counterpart. Since this FD instability did not seem to directly affect the TD signal at moderately early times, the issue was regarded as a mostly technical curiosity. However, spectral instability is now understood to be a broad property of BH spectra which occurs quite generically in the presence of environmental perturbations (see [352, 353] for early work, and Section 2.6 for a more extensive discussion). The issue of spectral instabilities – possibly introduced by dilute astrophysical environments or even corrections to Einstein’s theory – is of paramount importance. We discuss it more thoroughly below in Section 2.6, but note that detection strategies and systematic effects, discussed in Section 6.1.7, are directly impacted by such possible instabilities.

The development of a hyperboloidal framework was a crucial tool in our understanding of these instabilities as it also enabled the application of non-self-adjoint operator theory [308, 309] to gravitational studies [310]. In particular, the notion of pseudospectrum [308] provides a formal explanation for QNM spectral instability, and it facilitates a nonmodal analysis [311]. The ϵ\epsilon-pseudospectrum ςϵ​(ω)\varsigma_{\epsilon}(\omega) is defined as the set of points in the complex frequency plane such that

ςϵ​(𝔰)≡||(L^−𝔰)−1||E>1/ϵ.\varsigma_{\epsilon}(\mathfrak{s})\equiv\left|\left|\left(\hat{L}-\mathfrak{s}\right)^{-1}\right|\right|_{\rm E}>1/\epsilon. (2.79)

The limit ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 recovers the spectrum of the operator L^\hat{L}. For ϵ≳0\epsilon\gtrsim 0, the pseudospectrum reveals the spectral properties of the operator as a topographic map on the complex plane, with peaks located at the complex eigenvalues. Unlike the spectrum, the computation of the pseudospectrum requires a well-defined notion of norm to distinguish “large” from “small” ϵ\epsilon values. A norm reflecting the field’s energy on a constant-time hypersurface, based on the scalar product of the field and its derivatives, is given schematically by [310, 351]

⟨ϕ¯|ψ¯⟩E∝∫τ=const.(q1μ​ν(x¯)ϕ¯,x¯μ∗ψ¯,x¯ν+q0(x¯)ϕ¯∗ψ¯)dΣτ.\braket{\bar{\phi}|\bar{\psi}}_{\rm E}\propto\underset{\tau={\rm const.}}{\int}(q_{1}^{\mu\nu}(\bar{x})\bar{\phi}^{\ast}_{,\bar{x}^{\mu}}\bar{\psi}_{,\bar{x}^{\nu}}+q_{0}(\bar{x})\bar{\phi}^{\ast}\bar{\psi})\,d\Sigma_{\tau}. (2.80)

The functions qiμ​ν​(x¯)q_{i}^{\mu\nu}(\bar{x}) (i=0,1i=0,1) are directly related to the spacetime metric and to the structure of the wave equation. A common example of such an energy norm is derived from the energy-momentum tensor of a scalar field, where the integrand components reflect the field’s kinetic and potential energy contributions. The product (2.80) is positive-definite and makes the non-self-adjoint character of the operator L^\hat{L} evident [310, 351]. Indeed, calculating the formal adjoint with respect to the energy norm ⟨ϕ¯|L^​ψ¯⟩E=⟨L^†​ϕ¯|ψ¯⟩E\braket{\bar{\phi}|\hat{L}\bar{\psi}}_{\rm E}=\braket{\hat{L}^{\dagger}\bar{\phi}|\bar{\psi}}_{\rm E} yields L^†=L^+L^2∂\hat{L}^{\dagger}=\hat{L}+\hat{L}_{2}^{\partial}, with L2∂L_{2}^{\partial} a boundary term resulting from 𝑳2\boldsymbol{L}_{2} that carries information about the energy loss at the horizon and at future null infinity.

As an example, Fig. 12 shows the pseudospectra for the Schwarzschild spacetime (Regge-Wheeler operator) constructed under the energy norm (2.80). Open contour lines in the complex plane indicate spectral instability: small perturbations of the potential completely destabilize the QNMs overtones. The astrophysical implications of this phenomenon are discussed in Section 2.6 below.

Despite the solid mathematical foundation of this program, there are some technical open issues. The numerical calculation of the pseudospectrum with the energy norm does not always converge to a fixed, nonvanishing value with increasing numerical resolution [354, 355, 356, 357, 358]. In such cases, the continuum limit indicates that the pseudospectrum goes to zero in the entire complex half-plane Re⁡(ω)<0{\rm Re}(\omega)<0. This result would imply that any point ω\omega in this half-plane is an eigenvalue of the operator, and not only the discrete values corresponding to the well-known QNMs. Thus, the numerical calculation of pseudospectral contour lines under the energy norm offers a correct qualitative understanding and interpretation of the underlying structure of the operator, but quantitative assessments must be performed carefully [354, 355, 356, 357, 358].

The origin of this feature is not directly related to the particular numerical scheme used in the calculation, but it is rooted in the definition of QNMs. The intuitive notion that QNMs are mode solutions to Eq. (2.4) that “forbid waves to travel in from infinity or out of the event horizon of the BH” (see Section 2.1) is a necessary, but not sufficient condition [3, 359, 360]. In other words, outgoing boundary conditions at the horizon and at infinity are not the only defining structure of QNMs, as there exist further unphysical solutions satisfying such boundary conditions [3, 343, 66, 344, 345, 305, 346] precisely in the entire complex half-plane Re⁡(ω)<0{\rm Re}(\omega)<0. The numerical nonconvergence of the pseudospectrum in the energy norm captures this subtlety.

The traditional definition of QNMs as poles of the Green’s function [3, 359, 360] removes the ambiguities from the intuitive approach based on the boundary conditions. By exploiting the hyperboloidal framework, an alternative definition for QNMs arises as isolated eigenvalues of the infinitesimal generator of time translations acting on an appropriately defined Hilbert space [361, 342, 343, 66, 344, 345, 346].

This definition relies on an inner product controlling higher derivatives of the functions belonging to the functional space. Such product generalizes the energy norm, and it is often known in the mathematical literature as the HpH^{\rm p} Sobolev norm

⟨ϕ¯|ψ¯⟩Hp∝∑k=0p∫τ=const.​qkμ​ν​(x¯)​∂μ¯kϕ¯∗​∂ν¯kψ¯​d​Στ.\braket{\bar{\phi}|\bar{\psi}}_{H^{\rm p}}\propto\sum_{k=0}^{\rm p}\underset{\tau={\rm const.}}{\int}q_{k}^{\mu\nu}(\bar{x})\partial^{k}_{\bar{\mu}}\bar{\phi}^{\ast}\partial^{k}_{\bar{\nu}}\bar{\psi}\,d\Sigma_{\tau}. (2.81)

Then, QNM eigenfunctions belong to the so-called Gevrey-2 class: roughly speaking, they are more regular than a smooth function, but less than an analytic function [361, 342, 343, 344, 345, 346]. In this context, recent investigations show that the higher-order derivatives in the HpH^{\rm p} scalar product permit to address certain technical issues in the calculation of the pseudospectrum, providing a better mathematical control of the convergence of the pseudospectrum and offering additional insight into the stability properties of the overtones [312, 362].

All in all, the discussion in this section summarizes the ongoing effort to tackle open mathematical questions underlying the theory of BH QNMs. By revisiting seminal works from the nineties [337, 338] with novel approaches and strategies, the scalar products listed here have found application in the study of many physical problems, such as mode avoidance (Section 2.3), environmental perturbations (Section 2.6), nonlinearities (Sections 4.4 and 4.5) and tails (Section 5.3). There is an ongoing effort to explore and synthesize these different strategies to establish a unified understanding of QNM theory that reconciles their orthogonality properties, (in)completeness, non-self-adjointness, and the geometric insights offered by the various methods.

2.6 Spectral instabilities and environmental effects

Initial contributors: Cardoso, Destounis, Duque, Panosso Macedo

So far, we have reviewed the structure of the QNM spectrum for electrovacuum spacetimes. This assumption is justified for BHs in isolation, but the Universe is filled with various forms of matter, including interstellar clouds, gas, plasma and dust in galaxies, dark matter, populations of compact objects, and cosmic radiation. There are hints that some of the GW events already observed by ground-based detectors may originate in gas-rich environments, ranging from somewhat controversial claims of electromagnetic counterparts to BBH mergers [363] to statistical hints that at least a fraction of the observed BBH population may have originated in Active Galactic Nuclei [364]. In fact, there is an ongoing effort to place direct bounds on the density of the medium surrounding these BBH merger events [365]. The effect of environments is definitely a concern for space-based instruments like LISA that will target the merger of supermassive BH binaries in galactic centers, where the two BHs are brought to coalesce by dynamical friction and migration driven either by gas or stars [366, 367]. It is therefore important to ask how astrophysical environments will affect the BH spectroscopy program [368, 369]. This is the topic of this section.

One would expect that the BH response should be only slightly perturbed in the presence of external matter with sufficiently small density, localized away from the BH light ring. However, numerical investigations revealed the surprising fact that even small perturbations of the BH potential, due to e.g. astrophysical environments, can lead to considerable changes in the BH vibrational spectra, potentially orders of magnitude away from the QNM frequencies computed in vacuum [337, 338, 352, 353, 368, 310, 370, 371, 354, 372, 373, 374, 375]. This phenomenon is known as spectral instability.

The BH spectroscopy program is based on perturbative calculations of the vacuum BH spectrum in GR [376, 377, 378] and it implicitly assumes a reasonable physical robustness against “small” changes in the system. Thus, understanding spectral instabilities is of paramount importance for the interpretation of GW data.

2.6.1 Spectral instabilities

There are two major classes of spectral instabilities: fundamental mode and high overtone instabilities. A simple toy model illustrating fundamental mode instabilities in the context of massless perturbations of nonspinning BHs (see Section 2.1) is helpful to better understand the issue. To mimic possible environments, let us assume the master equation to be of the form of Eq. (2.7), but with a perturbed potential VϵV_{\epsilon} [368, 372]:

d2​Ψ2−d​r∗2+[ω2−Vϵ]​Ψ2−=0,\dfrac{d^{2}\Psi_{2}^{-}}{dr_{*}^{2}}+\left[\omega^{2}-V_{\epsilon}\right]\Psi_{2}^{-}=0\,, (2.82)

where the tortoise coordinate is defined as d​r/d​r∗=1−2​M/rdr/dr_{*}=1-2M/r, and a small, localized “bump” is added to the effective potential V2−V_{2}^{-} in vacuum (see Fig. 13), i.e.,

Vϵ≡V2−+ϵ​Vbump.V_{\epsilon}\equiv V_{2}^{-}+\epsilon\,V_{\rm bump}\,. (2.83)

Note that when ϵ=0\epsilon=0, Eq. (2.82) is equivalent to the RWZ equation (2.7), i.e., it governs gravitational perturbations around nonrotating BHs in GR. The functional form of the unperturbed potential is not crucial for the discussion, and for simplicity we will consider the Regge-Wheeler potential V2−V_{2}^{-} defined in Eq. (2.8).

In this ad hoc modification, external environments conspire to produce the “bump” located at r∗=Lr_{*}=L, such that VbumpV_{\rm bump} goes to zero as r∗→±∞r_{*}\to\pm\infty. In Fig. 13 we consider two possible choices for VbumpV_{\rm bump}, i.e., a Pöschl-Teller [379] potential and a Gaussian:

Vbump=sech2​(r∗−L),Vbump=exp⁡(−(r∗−L)22​σ).V_{\rm bump}={\rm sech}^{2}\left(r_{*}-L\right),\qquad V_{\rm bump}=\exp\left(-\frac{(r_{*}-L)^{2}}{2\sigma}\right)\,. (2.84)
