The QNM spectra of the perturbed potentials are shown in Fig. 14 (top left panel) for ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6}. Here, ω(ϵ)\omega^{(\epsilon)} denotes the fundamental mode resulting from the original potential under a perturbation of order ϵ\epsilon, while ϖ\varpi is the actual perturbed dominant/fundamental mode – i.e., the mode with the smallest (in absolute value) imaginary part, which does not necessarily coincide with ω(ϵ)\omega^{(\epsilon)}. For small LL, ϖ\varpi is initially quasi-stable and it coincides with the perturbed fundamental mode of the original potential, ω(ϵ)\omega^{(\epsilon)}, which spirals outward from its unperturbed Schwarzschild value (thick gray line). Notice how the fundamental mode can change by a factor of two or more even for such a small value of the perturbation amplitude ϵ\epsilon, indicating spectral instability.

As LL increases, something even more dramatic happens: the trapped modes localized between the two potential barriers migrate downwards and to the left in the complex plane. Eventually (at L≃34L\simeq 34) one of these modes overtakes ω(ϵ)\omega^{(\epsilon)}. This causes the first of several discontinuous jumps in ϖ\varpi (shown with dotted lines, and highlighted in the bottom-right panel). Figure 14 illustrates that, quite independently of the functional form of VbumpV_{\rm bump}, the fundamental mode ϖ\varpi is unstable in large regions of the relevant phase space ([L,ϵ][L,\epsilon] for the Pöschl-Teller bump, and [L,σ][L,\sigma] for the Gaussian bump). The nature of this FD instability, its relation with TD waveforms, and the location of the edges between the various regions were clarified analytically in various works [380, 381].

The crucial observation is that “two bump” systems have distinct scales. When the characteristic distance LL between the bump and the peak of the unperturbed BH potential (located near the light ring) is much larger than the other scale in the problem (i.e., the BH mass), a cavity is formed by the two potential peaks. This cavity supports “trapped modes” of frequency ∼1/L\sim 1/L which are trapped as long as 1/L2≪ϵ​Vbump1/L^{2}\ll\epsilon V_{\rm bump}. In these conditions, the fundamental BH QNM is destabilized [368, 372, 382, 374]: for any arbitrarily small ϵ​Vbump\epsilon V_{\rm bump} there is a scale LL where an extremely low-frequency mode appears ends up dominating over the fundamental BH QNM associated with the light ring [383, 8, 382], and this low-frequency mode is never “close” to the original fundamental mode (“close” meaning that the mode perturbation is at most of order ϵ\epsilon [382]). Similar phenomenology occurs if new scales are present close to the horizon, under the form of matter or new boundary conditions [383, 8]; see e.g. [154, 381, 380, 384, 357] for more detailed analyses of the spectra of double-peak potentials and of the consequent spectral instabilities, and [357] for a discussion of the high energetic content of the apparent “small” bump. The mode avoidance and resonance phenomena discussed in Section 2.3 occur quite generally in double-peak potentials [154].

The above discussion shows that the fundamental mode is generally unstable when a second (large) length scale is present in the problem. What about the overtones?

In an attempt to capture possible ultraviolet quantum effects and to identify spectral instabilities under small-scale changes to the effective potential, one can use the notion of the ϵ\epsilon-pseudospectrum defined in Section 2.5.4 to predict the occurrence of spectral instabilities without the need of introducing ad hoc perturbations of order 𝒪⁡(ϵ)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon) of the BH potential [310]. The pseudospectrum is very useful to understand the phenomenon of QNM spectral instability in perturbation theory beyond the usual modal analysis [310, 311]. Mathematical tools from the theory of non-normal operators [308, 309] were successfully adapted to gravitational physics through a careful treatment of the QNM boundary conditions, in which a geometrical strategy was used to adapt the time coordinates to the asymptotic spacetime structure around the BH horizon and in the wave zone, i.e., at future null infinity [303, 310] (see Section 2.5.4). An appropriate norm is necessary to measure the “strength” or “smallness” of the perturbation: see the discussion around Eq. (2.80). The energy norm is well-defined under certain conditions [310, 351, 374, 357], and it is a useful discriminator to understand why the spectrum is destabilized under apparent “small” perturbations of the potential [357]. By plotting pseudospectral contour lines, that identify the maximal migration of perturbed QNMs in the complex plane under a perturbation of order |ϵ|≪1\left|\epsilon\right|\ll 1, one finds that asymptotically flat [310, 385, 311, 386], de Sitter [387, 388, 389], and anti-de Sitter [390, 356, 355, 391] BHs all exhibit spectral instabilities. See discussion in Section 2.5.4 and fig. 12.

An example of spectral instability in the high-overtone regime concerns charged BHs [392, 393, 394, 5, 395, 374, 370, 371]. The asymptotic structure of the spectrum for any massless field perturbation of nonspinning, neutral BHs is

Mω∼log⁡3−i⁡(2​n+1)​π8​π+𝒪(n−1/2),Q=0,M\omega\sim\frac{\log 3-i(2n+1)\pi}{8\pi}+{\cal O}(n^{-1/2})\,,\quad Q=0\,, (2.85)

in the large-nn limit [5]. On the other hand, the asymptotic spectrum of slightly charged BHs is found to be

Mω∼log⁡5−i⁡(2​n+1)​π8​π+𝒪(n−1/2),Q→0,M\omega\sim\frac{\log 5-i(2n+1)\pi}{8\pi}+{\cal O}(n^{-1/2})\,,\quad Q\to 0\,, (2.86)

As a consequence, for any arbitrarily small charge QQ the BH spectrum differs by 𝒪⁡(Q0){\cal O}(Q^{0}) from the spectrum of a Schwarzschild BH. This is a clear example of spectral instability in the large-nn regime [374].

To conclude, a few important remarks are in order concerning the spectral instability of both the fundamental mode and overtones. Despite the large shift to the spectrum found above, in all realistic cases studied in the literature the corresponding early-time signal in the TD is smooth and receives only small corrections (as quantified e.g. by the unfaithfulness, see Section 2.6.2). In other words, the initial prompt response in the TD is very close to the vacuum BH signal, while the destabilized modes dominate only at late times. The information of the dominant ringdown at early time signals is imprinted in the phase shift defined analogously to quantum scattering [396], which is only perturbatively modified even with the spectral instability. This fact can also be easily captured by causality argument for signals propagating in a cavity [368, 382]: at late times, the double-bump-cavity filters the high-frequency content of the outgoing GW, and all that remains is the new low-frequency fundamental mode, which is approached via a sequence of “echoes” [383, 8, 397, 398, 399, 400] (see Section 3.3 below). The second observation concerns the existence of actual physical systems that produce “double-bump” potentials as solutions to the Einstein field equations. There are no known viable astrophysical setups whose perturbations to the gravitational field are described by a single decoupled master equation as in Eq. (2.82). Indeed, there are indications that spacetimes described by a double-peak effective potential have at least two light rings, and are therefore not a small perturbation of a vacuum BH spacetime [374].

Spectral instability has nevertheless been observed and studied in a consistent description of BH environments [401, 402, 403], which requires coupling matter to gravitational perturbations. No matter how small the strength of the coupling, the gravitational sector will always be “contaminated” (or destabilized) by the mode content in the matter sector. However, there is now widespread consensus [368, 382, 396, 374] that the prompt ringdown is only perturbatively affected, as discussed in detail in Section 2.6.2 below.

2.6.2 Environmental effects

The analysis outlined above leads to the intriguing conclusion that astrophysical environments can, in principle, produce considerable changes in BH QNM spectra. What is left to understand is how the perturbed QNMs appear in the TD ringdown signal, as computed from self-consistent solutions of the Einstein field equations. This question is of paramount importance because large deviations from the vacuum predictions, if they occur in nature, may either hamper our ability to infer the properties of BHs or (if properly understood) carry important information on BH environments.

There are several physical mechanisms that can affect the BH spectroscopy program in astrophysical environments (see [368] for a thorough list and simple order-of-magnitude estimates). Here we will focus on the effect of galaxies, dark matter halos, and dark matter spikes. To understand why environmental corrections could be relevant in this context, recall for example that the BH at the center of the Milky Way, with a mass M∼4×106​M⊙M\sim 4\times 10^{6}M_{\odot}, is surrounded by stars and dark matter of total mass MH∼5×1011​M⊙M_{\rm H}\sim 5\times 10^{11}M_{\odot} within a radius of aH∼20​kpca_{\text{H}}\sim 20\,\text{kpc} (corresponding to aH∼104​MHa_{\text{H}}\sim 10^{4}\,M_{H} in geometrical units) [404, 405].

In the simple case of spherical symmetry, a fully relativistic solution can be found in closed form [401]. Other matter distributions are, of course, possible, but the qualitative conclusions discussed below are expected to hold also in other cases [406].

The qualitative setup is shown in Fig. 15. A BH of mass MM is surrounded by a halo of matter (stars, dark matter, etc.) of mass MHM_{\rm H} with characteristic length scale aH\text{a}_{\text{H}}. The environment’s compactness 𝒞\mathcal{C} and typical density ρ\rho are given by

𝒞=MHaH,ρ∼MHaH3.\mathcal{C}=\frac{M_{\text{H}}}{\text{a}_{\text{H}}},\qquad\rho\sim\frac{M_{\text{H}}}{\text{a}_{\text{H}}^{3}}\,. (2.87)

For the Milky Way, an order of magnitude estimate yields 𝒞∼10−6\mathcal{C}\sim 10^{-6} [405]. In general, the halo size and mass are orders of magnitude larger than the BH’s.

Stationary and spherically symmetric solutions to the Einstein equations for an anisotropic fluid surrounding a BH are known in closed form for specific density profiles [401], but similar procedures can be used to model generic astrophysical environments around BHs either analytically or numerically [407, 408, 409, 410, 411, 412, 413, 406, 414, 415, 416]. Given these fully relativistic background spacetimes, computing geodesic motion and perturbations is a relatively simple matter [401, 402, 417, 410, 406, 415].

The scales in the problem can be sufficiently distinct to make the computation of QNMs in the general case challenging. However the axial sector of gravitational perturbations does not couple to matter (under mild assumptions, such as being nondissipative [335, 418]), and it is easier to handle [401, 419]. An accurate calculation of the corresponding QNMs relies on casting the wave equation in terms of an eigenvalue problem of a (non-self-adjoint) operator, achieved by means of the hyperboloidal approach described in Section 2.5.4 [66, 304, 305].

The resulting (nonvacuum) axial QNM frequencies are shown in Fig. 16, and they clearly depend on the properties of the BH environment. As the compactness 𝒞\mathcal{C} of the halo increases from 10−610^{-6} to 10−110^{-1}, the QNM frequencies ω20​n\omega_{20n} are redshifted towards smaller values with respect to the vacuum frequencies ω20​nvacuum\omega^{\textrm{vacuum}}_{20n}. For ℓ=2\ell=2, a fit gives

δn≡ω20​n−ω20​nvacuumω20​nvacuum≈−𝒞+0.17​𝒞2.\delta_{n}\equiv\frac{\omega_{20n}-\omega_{20n}^{\rm vacuum}}{\omega_{20n}^{\rm vacuum}}\approx-{\cal C}+0.17{\cal C}^{2}\,. (2.88)

This behavior, which is common to other multipoles and applies over a large range of halo masses, is in essence a redshift of axial waves as they cross the galactic gravitational potential, after being generated close to the light ring. A calculation in the geometric optics approximation predicts δn=−𝒞+𝒞2/6\delta_{n}=-{\cal C}+{\cal C}^{2}/6 in the small compactness limit, in very good agreement with the numerical results. Indeed, it can be shown that any sufficiently dilute environment produces, to leading order, a redshift 1+U1+U of the axial frequencies and damping times, where U∼−𝒞U\sim-{\cal C} is the Newtonian potential of the environment [419].

The polar sector of GWs couples to matter and triggers richer phenomenology [402, 403]. A QNM analysis in the FD is still lacking, but this case can be studied through TD evolutions. The TD signal for a BH excited by a particle plunging radially, computed in a fully relativistic setting, is shown in Fig. 17 [402, 403]. The plunge excites a prompt ringdown signal (highlighted in the inset) corresponding to direct excitation of the light ring QNMs. As in the axial sector, these ringdown waves cross the gravitational potential and are redshift to lower frequencies as a consequence of the additional gravitational pull exerted by the halo mass. However, the signal structure is substantially different from vacuum after this prompt ringdown. The intermediate-time strain in vacuum is dominated by a “tail,” i.e., a superposition of a large number of power laws [420] due to waves backscattering off the nonzero curvature of the background [421, 155, 422]. These terms slowly decay, leaving place to a single power law h+∼t−ph_{+}\sim t^{-p} (with p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}), as discussed in Section 5.3 below. In the presence of a halo of matter, one observes instead a slowly decaying fluid mode with characteristic period T∼aH/cs,rT\sim a_{\text{H}}/c_{s,r}, where cs,rc_{s,r} is the speed of sound in the radial direction, and with amplitude determined mostly by the halo’s compactness. The excitation of this fluid mode is an interesting example of how spectral instabilities can arise quite generically via mode coupling [374]. In conclusion, astrophysical environments can significantly alter the QNM spectrum of a BH, but these modifications in the spectrum do not necessarily imply that the signal will drastically change at early times, when it has the highest amplitude.

A measure of the contribution of environmental effects in the ringdown signal is the so-called “faithfulness” between the numerical signal generated in the nonvacuum case and the numerical vacuum waveform [403]. In real observations the BH mass is a priori unknown, so the faithfulness must be maximized over a “stretching” of the time component which is different at each spacetime location, to model redshift as the wave propagates. The result of this calculation is shown in Fig. 18. For example, for a halo configuration with MH=MM_{\textrm{H}}=M and aH=58​Ma_{\text{H}}=58M, the faithfulness is maximized for a redshift factor 0.9870.987, whereas 1−MH/aH=0.9821-M_{\text{H}}/a_{\text{H}}=0.982. For smaller values of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the mismatch follows a power-law decay. This allows extrapolation to even smaller values of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, for which numerical calculations are computationally prohibitive.

Are differences between the ringdown template and the real signal measurable at very large signal-to-noise ratios? Current observations from the motion of the S2 star in our own Galactic center limit the additional mass enclosed within its orbit to be ≲103​M⊙\lesssim 10^{3}\,M_{\odot} [423], but distributed over a semi-major axis aS2∼2×104​MSgr A*a_{\text{S2}}\sim 2\times 10^{4}M_{\text{Sgr\penalty\ A*}} (in units of Sgr A* mass). Figure 18 suggests that for a typical galactic halo compactness 𝒞≲10−4{\cal C}\lesssim 10^{-4} the SNR must to be larger than several thousands to detect any environmental effects other than the gravitational redshift. Therefore BH spectroscopy is not expected to be able to probe astrophysical environments, even in the optimistic case of a signal from a plunge of a 40​M⊙40\,M_{\odot} compact object into Sgr A* (unless the plunge happens to occur in some exotic, highly compact environment).

Recent work explored NR simulations of collapsing and merging neutron stars leading to BH formation, and used them to perform BH spectroscopy by extracting QNMs as a function of the starting time [424]. The resulting ringdown signals can be classified into “clean”, “modified”, and “distorted” cases, depending on the amount of matter present in the system. Even in the presence of matter, possible deviations of the QNM frequencies from the expected Kerr values seem to be dominated by ringdown modeling systematics. Incorporating multiple QNMs drastically reduces mismatches and errors in estimating the final BH mass at early times. If not treated carefully, deviations in the fundamental QNM might artificially be overestimated and falsely attributed to the presence of matter or violations of GR.

In summary, the last decade has seen substantial progress in our understanding of how astrophysical environments affect BH spectroscopy. The emerging consensus is that environments have a small impact, but further research is necessary to confirm this finding. First of all, the conclusions summarized above are mostly based on the assumption of a time-independent, nonrotating backgrounds. As discussed in Section 4.5.3 below, mass accretion can change the QNM spectrum [299, 335, 425, 426, 427], but in most situations of astrophysical interest the resulting modifications are expected to be negligibly small [368, 428]. The ringdown radiation produced by spinning BHs within astrophysical environments is poorly understood. Tidal modifications to the spectrum of Schwarzschild and Kerr BHs also deserve further scrutiny [429]. Even if environmental modifications to the vacuum QNM spectrum turn out to be large, it may be possible to test the BH nature of the underlying spacetime in other ways (e.g. through perturbative quantities that may be observable and have been found to be largely unaffected by instabilities in the spectrum, such as the greybody factors [396, 430, 431]).

3 Ringdown beyond general relativity and the Standard Model

Ci sono soltanto due possibili conclusioni: se il risultato conferma l’ipotesi, allora hai appena fatto una misura; se il risultato è contrario all’ipotesi, allora hai fatto una scoperta. (There are only two possible conclusions: if the result confirms the hypothesis, then you have just made a measurement; if the result disproves the hypothesis, then you have made a discovery.)

Enrico Fermi

Part of the current experimental interest in BH spectroscopy comes from the possibility of finding experimental smoking guns of new physics or modifications of GR in the large and growing catalog of GW events. This possibility has motivated an intense effort, reviewed in this chapter, to (i) compute QNM spectra in specific classes of modified theories (Section 3.1); (ii) develop theory-agnostic ringdown parameterizations, similar in spirit to the parameterized post-Newtonian formalism [432] (Section 3.2); and (iii) investigate the effects of physics beyond the Standard Model that could produce characteristic signatures – e.g., “echoes” – in the ringdown waveform (Section 3.3).

3.1 Theory-specific spectra

Initial contributors: Blázquez-Salcedo, Cano, Chung, Khoo, Yunes

In recent years, there has been substantial progress in understanding the QNM spectrum of rotating BHs in theories beyond GR and the Standard Model of particle physics. Most of the work concerns higher-derivative theories that modify the Einstein equations in a continuous way in terms of free parameters (coupling constants). The regime where these couplings are small and the new theory is close to GR is currently the best understood scenario, but there are also results that apply to large couplings.

The space of possible theories is too large to enumerate [433, 434]. The theories we will discuss here can be split into two main classes.

The first class assumes a pure metric theory, for which a general effective field theory (EFT) extension of GR [435, 436], up to eight derivatives, reads

SEFT=116​π​G∫\displaystyle S_{\rm EFT}=\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int d4​x​|g|​[R+L4​(λev​ℛ3+λodd​ℛ~3)+L6​(λ1​𝒞2+λ2​𝒞~2+λ3​𝒞​𝒞~)],\displaystyle d^{4}x\sqrt{|g|}\bigg[R+L^{4}\left(\lambda_{\rm ev}\mathcal{R}^{3}+\lambda_{\rm odd}\tilde{\mathcal{R}}^{3}\right)+L^{6}\left(\lambda_{1}\mathcal{C}^{2}+\lambda_{2}\tilde{\mathcal{C}}^{2}+\lambda_{3}\mathcal{C}\tilde{\mathcal{C}}\right)\bigg]\,, (3.1)

with

ℛ3=Rμ​νρ​σ​Rρ​σδ​γ​Rδ​γμ​ν,ℛ~3=Rμ​νρ​σ​Rρ​σδ​γ​R~δ​γμ​ν,𝒞=Rμ​ν​ρ​σ​Rμ​ν​ρ​σ,𝒞~=Rμ​ν​ρ​σ​R~μ​ν​ρ​σ.\mathcal{R}^{3}=R_{\mu\nu}^{\,\,\,\,\,\,\rho\sigma}R_{\rho\sigma}^{\,\,\,\,\,\,\delta\gamma}R_{\delta\gamma}^{\,\,\,\,\,\,\mu\nu}\,,\quad\tilde{\mathcal{R}}^{3}=R_{\mu\nu}^{\,\,\,\,\,\,\rho\sigma}R_{\rho\sigma}^{\,\,\,\,\,\,\delta\gamma}\tilde{R}_{\delta\gamma}^{\,\,\,\,\,\,\mu\nu}\,,\quad\mathcal{C}=R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\,,\quad\tilde{\mathcal{C}}=R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\tilde{R}^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\,. (3.2)

Here R~μ​ν​ρ​σ=12​ϵμ​ν​α​β​Rρ​σα​β\tilde{R}_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_{\mu\nu\alpha\beta}R^{\alpha\beta}_{\,\,\,\,\,\,\rho\sigma} is the dual Riemann tensor, ϵμ​ν​α​β\epsilon_{\mu\nu\alpha\beta} is the Levi-Civita tensor density, defined such that ϵ0123=+|g|\epsilon_{0123}=+\sqrt{|g|}, λq\lambda_{\rm q} (with q=ev,odd,1,2,3\rm q=ev,odd,1,2,3) are free dimensionless coupling constants, and LL is the characteristic length scale of new physics. The EFT is applicable for BHs larger than LL, i.e. r+≫Lr_{+}\gg L, and it describes the most general diffeomorphism-invariant metric modification of GR. For a BH of mass MM, it is useful to introduce the dimensionless coupling constants

ζq=λq​(LM)n,\zeta_{\rm q}=\lambda_{\rm q}\left(\frac{L}{M}\right)^{n}\,, (3.3)

where n=4n=4 for q=ev,odd{\rm q=ev,odd} and n=6n=6 for q=1,2,3{\rm q=1,2,3}. These control the relative deviations with respect to GR and are assumed to satisfy |ζq|≪1|\zeta_{q}|\ll 1. We will work at first order in these couplings.

The second class of theories that we will consider involves additional fields (typically chosen to be scalar fields, for simplicity) coupled to curvature invariants. Including up to quadratic curvature invariants, these scalar-tensor theories are described by the action

SST=116​π​G​∫d4​x​|g|​[R−12​∇μΦ​∇μΦ−V⁡(Φ)+α​f​(Φ)​𝒬],S_{\rm ST}=\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int d^{4}x\sqrt{|g|}\left[R-\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{\mu}\Phi\nabla^{\mu}\Phi-V(\Phi)+\alpha f(\Phi)\mathcal{Q}\right]\,, (3.4)

where Φ\Phi is a scalar field that couples to the spacetime metric, V⁡(Φ)V(\Phi) is a potential governing the self-interactions of the scalar field, α\alpha is a dimensionful coupling constant that measures the strength of modifications to GR, f⁡(Φ)f(\Phi) is a coupling function, and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is a scalar constructed from the curvature tensor. The quantities V⁡(Φ)V(\Phi), 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and f⁡(Φ)f(\Phi) determine the nature of the gravity theory. For example, for the class of Einstein-scalar-Gauss-Bonnet (EsGB) theories [437, 438], 𝒬=𝒢≡R2−4​Rα​β​Rα​β+Rα​β​γ​δ​Rα​β​γ​δ\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{G}\equiv R^{2}-4R_{\alpha\beta}R^{\alpha\beta}+R_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}R^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}, where 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the Gauss-Bonnet invariant, while different choices of f⁡(Φ)f(\Phi) define different members in the class. For dynamical Chern-Simons (dCS) gravity, 𝒬=𝒞~=Rν​μ​ρ​σ​R~μ​ν​ρ​σ\mathcal{Q}=\tilde{\mathcal{C}}=R_{\nu\mu\rho\sigma}\tilde{R}^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}, where 𝒞~\tilde{\mathcal{C}} is the parity-odd Pontryagin invariant, while f⁡(Φ)=Φf(\Phi)=\Phi and V⁡(Φ)=0V(\Phi)=0, so that the theory is shift-symmetric [439, 440]. In both of these cases, 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is built from quadratic curvature invariants, so α\alpha has units of length squared. Analogously to (3.3), we introduce

ζEsGB/dCS=αM2,\zeta_{\text{EsGB/dCS}}=\frac{\alpha}{M^{2}}\,, (3.5)

as the dimensionless coupling that determines the order of magnitude of the deviations with respect to GR.

A theory with two scalars that couple simultaneously to the Gauss-Bonnet and Pontryagin invariants can also be considered [441]. Such a theory is a natural prediction of string theory [442], where one of the scalars is the dilaton and the second one is an axion dual to the Kalb-Ramond two-form. However, QNM calculations in this theory are in their infancy, hence it will not be discussed below.

For other classes of theories beyond the higher-derivative corrections discussed above, the study of QNMs is less complete. One such example concern so-called DHOST theories, for which it is not possible (in general) to write down the linearized perturbations in a compact Schrödinger-like form [443, 444, 445]. Moreover, the presence of additional terms and couplings may change the implementation of the boundary conditions [446]. A possible way out for studying perturbations of BHs in alternative theories of gravity is to use full-fledged TD numerical relativity (NR) evolutions. Although the required numerical resolution to extract QNMs is not always met, a few preliminary results in this direction have been achieved [447, 448, 449]. One of the biggest challenges in studying linear perturbations and computing QNMs in Lorentz-violating theories of gravity is that BH solutions in these theories possess multiple horizons, and there is ongoing research on how to impose boundary conditions [450]. There are exceptional cases (such as a subclass of the so-called Hořava gravity theories [451]) in which all of the additional degrees of freedom have the same propagation speed as the gravitational ones, but the QNM spectrum in these cases is indistinguishable from GR.

The remainder of this section is structured as follows. We first review rotating BH solutions in the theories defined by the actions (3.1), (3.4), which are no longer given by the Kerr metric. Then we discuss several methods to analyze perturbations and QNMs in these (and more general) theories. Finally, we summarize current state-of-the-art calculations of QNM frequencies in specific cases.

3.1.1 Modified Kerr black holes

The calculation of the modified Kerr metric describing rotating BHs in the theories under consideration is not a completely solved problem: there are no exact analytic solutions for BHs with arbitrary rotation and coupling. Most current efforts focus either on analytical approximations valid for small couplings or slow-rotation, or on numerical solutions.

Small-spin and small-coupling expansion A common strategy to obtain corrections to the Kerr metric is to find approximate analytical solution through a double series expansion in small angular momentum and small coupling [452, 453, 454, 455, 456, 457, 458]. While the small coupling approximation can be justified from the perspective of EFTs and current tests of GR [432, 459, 434, 460, 461], restricting to small spin is not sufficient to describe the BH remnants resulting from binary mergers, which typically have dimensionless spin χ≃0.7\chi\simeq 0.7. This problem can be addressed by extending the spin expansion to very high orders [436].

The corrected Kerr metric is typically written in Boyer-Lindquist like coordinates (t,r,x,ϕ)(t,r,x,\phi), where x=cos⁡θx=\cos{\theta}, as

d​s2=\displaystyle ds^{2}= −(1−2​M​rΣ−H1)​d​t2−(1+H2)​4​a​M​r​(1−x2)Σ​d​t​d​ϕ\displaystyle-\left(1-\frac{2Mr}{\Sigma}-H_{1}\right)dt^{2}-(1+H_{2})\frac{4aMr(1-x^{2})}{\Sigma}dtd\phi (3.6)
+\displaystyle+ (1+H3)​Σ​(d​r2Δ+d​x21−x2)+(1+H4)​(r2+a2+2​a2​M​r​(1−x2)Σ)​(1−x2)​d​ϕ2,\displaystyle\left(1+H_{3}\right)\Sigma\left(\frac{dr^{2}}{\Delta}+\frac{dx^{2}}{1-x^{2}}\right)+(1+H_{4})\left(r^{2}+a^{2}+\frac{2a^{2}Mr(1-x^{2})}{\Sigma}\right)(1-x^{2})d\phi^{2}\,,

where (Σ,Δ)(\Sigma,\Delta) are the known functions of rr and θ\theta that define the Kerr metric, while the four functions Hi​(r,x)H_{i}(r,x) admit the expansion

Hi=∑n=0∞χn​∑p=0n∑k=0kmax​(n)Hi(n,p,k)​(Mr)k​xp.H_{i}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\chi^{n}\sum_{p=0}^{n}\sum_{k=0}^{k_{\text{max}}(n)}H_{i}^{(n,p,k)}\left(\frac{M}{r}\right)^{k}x^{p}\,. (3.7)

Here χ=a/M\chi=a/M is the dimensionless spin parameter for a BH with mass MM and angular momentum M​aMa. The coefficients Hi(n,p,k)H_{i}^{(n,p,k)} are functions of the various coupling constants that can be determined by solving the modified field equations. We will consider only the solution to linear order in the ζ\zeta couplings (3.3), (3.5), but expressions of the form (3.7) in principle also work at higher order in the small coupling expansion. For theories defined by the action (3.4) with V⁡(Φ)=0V(\Phi)=0, the scalar field can also be written as

Φ=∑n=0∞χn​∑p=0n∑k=0kmax​(n)ϑ(n,p,k)​(Mr)k​xp,\Phi=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\chi^{n}\sum_{p=0}^{n}\sum_{k=0}^{k_{\text{max}}(n)}\vartheta^{(n,p,k)}\left(\frac{M}{r}\right)^{k}x^{p}\,, (3.8)

where the coefficients ϑ(n,p,k)\vartheta^{(n,p,k)} are functions of the coupling constants that can similarly be determined by solving the modified field equations. The spin expansion is convergent, and 10–20 terms are usually enough to accurately describe typical post-merger BHs with χ∈[0.5,0.9]\chi\in[0.5,0.9] [462]. The functions HiH_{i} and Φ\Phi have been derived to the 1414-th order in χ\chi in [436], but these calculations can in principle be extended to arbitrary orders. A Mathematica notebook allowing to construct such extensions is publicly available [436, 463] (see Appendix A). The small-spin expansion, however, becomes inefficient when approaching extremality (see e.g. [464] for a discussion in dCS gravity).

Numerical solutions Full numerical approaches are typically required to search for solutions with arbitrary rotation and coupling constants, or solutions with nontrivial coupling functions f⁡(Φ)f(\Phi). For example, in Einstein-dilaton-Gauss-Bonnet (EdGB) gravity (a member of the EsGB class 𝒬=𝒢\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{G} with V⁡(Φ)=0V(\Phi)=0 and f⁡(Φ)=e−γ​Φf(\Phi)=e^{-\gamma\Phi}, where γ\gamma is the dilaton coupling constant), both static spherically symmetric [438, 465] and rotating configuration [466, 467, 468, 469] have been obtained. Static spherically symmetric [470, 465] and rotating BH solutions [469, 471] are also known in linear EsGB gravity (another member of the massless EsGB class, but with coupling function f⁡(Φ)=Φf(\Phi)=\Phi). Interestingly, when the coupling function satisfies certain conditions (examples of which include f⁡(Φ)∝Φ2f(\Phi)\propto\Phi^{2} [472, 473, 474, 475] and f⁡(Φ)∝exp⁡(−Φ2)f(\Phi)\propto\exp(-\Phi^{2}) [476]), BHs can become “spontaneously scalarized,” with a stable branch of modified BH solutions arising nonperturbatively for large enough curvature: see [477] for a recent review. In dCS gravity, static and spherically-symmetric BH solutions are described by the Schwarzschild metric just as in GR, while rotating configurations were studied in [478, 479, 480, 469, 481].

To obtain stationary and axially symmetric BHs one typically uses “quasi-isotropic” spherical coordinates, with the generic metric ansatz

d​s2=−f​d​t2+bf​(d​r2+r2​d​θ2)+lf​r2​sin2⁡θ​(d​ϕ−wr​d​t)2,\displaystyle ds^{2}=-fdt^{2}+\frac{b}{f}\left(dr^{2}+r^{2}d\theta^{2}\right)+\frac{l}{f}r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta(d\phi-\frac{w}{r}dt)^{2}, (3.9)

where f,b,l,wf,\,b,\,l,\,w are functions of rr and θ\theta. With this ansatz for the metric, together with the background field Φ\Phi (also a function of rr and θ\theta), the field equations are reduced to a system of elliptic, PDEs that are solved numerically. The metric and scalar field functions satisfy a number of boundary conditions that are derived from requiring the standard conditions for astrophysical BHs: regularity of the solution on the rotation axis, asymptotic flatness of the metric at spatial infinity, and regularity of the Killing horizon.

The domain of existence of the resulting solutions in some modified theories can sometimes have interesting properties, as shown e.g. in Fig. 5 of [468] for EdGB gravity. For instance, in EdGB gravity with γ=1\gamma=1 and fixed α\alpha, the scalar charge of the solution grows as the mass of the static BH decreases, and eventually a critical solution with a minimum mass is reached [438, 437, 482]. At this point, the BH mass increases again along a small unstable branch of solutions before a singular solution is reached. For an analysis of this branch structure with other values of γ\gamma, see [483]. The situation is similar when introducing angular momentum [466, 467, 468]: for fixed values of coupling constant α\alpha and χ\chi, there is a BH solution with minimum mass. For large enough angular momentum there is no second branch, and the singular solutions also possess a minimum mass. For even larger values of the angular momentum, it is possible to reach a set of extremal BHs in EdGB gravity. Hence, the boundary of the domain of BH existence is given by the set of static EdGB BHs, the set of critical solutions, the set of extremal BHs, and the set of Kerr BHs.

3.1.2 Black hole perturbations in modified gravity: methods

Besides the lack of analytical BH solutions in modified gravity, other challenges plague the analysis of perturbations in these theories. First of all, these solutions are not of Petrov type D [484], and the Teukolsky equation is not valid. Separability is also generically lost, even in the case of the wave operator for a scalar field. In addition, the equations of motion for these theories are extremely intricate, containing higher-order derivatives and/or extra degrees of freedom. For these reasons, up until recently, QNM frequencies were known only for static and slowly rotating BHs [485, 486, 458, 487, 488, 489, 440, 490, 491, 492, 493, 494], since these can be computed by conventional methods using metric perturbations. These results are useful to learn about some generic features of beyond-GR effects, like the breaking of isospectrality (we will say more about this below), but they are not applicable to the typical angular momenta of post-merger BHs. Two different classes of methods, reviewed below, have been devised to overcome these challenges and compute QNMs in the case of large rotation.

Modified Teukolsky equation The first approach aims at extending the Teukolsky equation [15] to encompass theories of gravity that permit algebraically general BH spacetimes. It was first constructed within the Newman-Penrose formalism [495, 306], and reformulated using the Geroch-Held-Penrose formalism [496]. Practical implementations of this “modified Teukolsky formalism” have been developed for higher-derivative gravity [496, 497, 498] and dCS gravity [499, 500]. The main idea behind these approaches is to find an equation, valid for arbitrary theories, that reduces to the usual Teukolsky equation when the theory reduces to GR and the background is of Petrov type D. Any equation with such properties is enough to perform perturbation theory in a regime close to GR.

The key is the introduction of a two-parameter expansion scheme, which helps circumvent certain algebraic constraints due to the possible non-Petrov-type-D nature of the background BH spacetime. Using ζ\zeta (denoting one of the dimensionless couplings defined in (3.3), (3.5) above) to characterize the deviation from GR and ϵ\epsilon to characterize the strength of gravitational perturbations, one can expand all geometrical quantities in a bivariate series. For example, the Weyl scalars Ψn\Psi_{n} with n∈(0,4)n\in(0,4) can be expanded as

Ψn=Ψn(0,0)+ζ​Ψn(1,0)+ϵ​Ψn(0,1)+ζ​ϵ​Ψn(1,1)+⋯.\Psi_{n}=\Psi_{n}^{(0,0)}+\zeta\Psi_{n}^{(1,0)}+\epsilon\Psi_{n}^{(0,1)}+\zeta\epsilon\Psi_{n}^{(1,1)}+\cdots\,. (3.10)

The quantities Ψn(0,0)\Psi_{n}^{(0,0)} and Ψn(1,0)\Psi_{n}^{(1,0)} are Weyl scalars evaluated on the BH background and expanded to zeroth- and first-order in ζ\zeta, respectively. Similarly, Ψn(0,1)\Psi_{n}^{(0,1)} and Ψn(1,1)\Psi_{n}^{(1,1)} represent the Weyl scalars induced by GWs in GR and their leading-order, beyond-GR corrections, respectively.

To generalize the Teukolsky equation one can consider the same combination of Bianchi identities of the Riemann tensor that lead to the usual Teukolsky equation, but without making any assumptions on the form of the curvature tensor, the equations of motion, or the Petrov type of the background spacetime. Using these combinations and the two-parameter expansion, the perturbed Newman-Penrose equations can be decoupled to obtain the modified Teukolsky equation at first order in (ζ,ϵ)(\zeta,\epsilon)

𝒪0(0,0)​Ψ0(1,1)=𝒮0(1,0)​[Ψn(0,1),ea⁡(0,1),γa​b​c(0,1)]+𝒯0(0,0)​[ϕs(1,1)],\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{0}^{(0,0)}\Psi_{0}^{(1,1)}=\mathcal{S}_{0}^{(1,0)}[\Psi_{n}^{(0,1)},e^{a(0,1)},\gamma_{abc}^{(0,1)}]+\mathcal{T}_{0}^{(0,0)}[\phi_{s}^{(1,1)}]\,, (3.11)
𝒪4(0,0)​Ψ4(1,1)=𝒮4(1,0)​[Ψn(0,1),ea⁡(0,1),γa​b​c(0,1)]+𝒯4(0,0)​[ϕs(1,1)],\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{4}^{(0,0)}\Psi_{4}^{(1,1)}=\mathcal{S}_{4}^{(1,0)}[\Psi_{n}^{(0,1)},e^{a(0,1)},\gamma_{abc}^{(0,1)}]+\mathcal{T}_{4}^{(0,0)}[\phi_{s}^{(1,1)}]\,, (3.12)

where 𝒪0,4\mathcal{O}_{0,4} are the original Teukolsky operators as defined in Eq. (2.2), acting on a spin 2 or spin −2-2 scalar, respectively, while 𝒮0(1,0)\mathcal{S}_{0}^{(1,0)}, 𝒮4(1,0)\mathcal{S}_{4}^{(1,0)}, 𝒯0(0,0)\mathcal{T}_{0}^{(0,0)}, and 𝒯4(0,0)\mathcal{T}_{4}^{(0,0)} are source operators. The latter depend on background Newman-Penrose quantities and act on the perturbed Weyl scalars Ψn(0,1)\Psi_{n}^{(0,1)}, the perturbed tetrad ea⁡(0,1)e^{a(0,1)}, and the perturbed spin coefficients γa​b​c(0,1)\gamma_{abc}^{(0,1)}. Similarly, the extra field ϕs\phi_{s} satisfies

𝒪s(0,0)​ϕs(1,1)=𝒮ϕ(1,0)​[Ψn(0,1),ea⁡(0,1),γa​b​c(0,1)],\mathcal{O}_{s}^{(0,0)}\phi_{s}^{(1,1)}=\mathcal{S}_{\phi}^{(1,0)}[\Psi_{n}^{(0,1)},e^{a(0,1)},\gamma_{abc}^{(0,1)}]\,, (3.13)

where 𝒪s(0,0)\mathcal{O}_{s}^{(0,0)} is the original Teukolsky operator acting on the perturbed spin-weight-s field ϕs(1,1)\phi_{s}^{(1,1)}, while 𝒮ϕ(1,0)\mathcal{S}_{\phi}^{(1,0)} is another source operator. These equations are still coupled PDEs, complicating the analysis.

To proceed, one needs to compute the solution to the Teukolsky equation in GR for a Kerr background, and reconstruct the metric perturbation in vacuum hμ​ν(0,1)h_{\mu\nu}^{(0,1)} using standard methods [501, 502, 503, 504, 505, 506]. In turn, from this metric perturbation one can calculate the perturbed Weyl scalars, tetrad and spin coefficients, obtaining explicit expressions for the right-hand sides of Eqs. (3.11)-(3.13). At this point, the shift in the QNM frequencies is obtained by applying eigenvalue perturbation theory [306]. The first-order in ζ\zeta correction to the frequency can then be found as an integral of 𝒮0,4,ϕ(1,0)​[δ​Ψn,δ​ea⁡(0,1),δ​γa​b​c(0,1)]\mathcal{S}^{(1,0)}_{0,4,\phi}[\delta\Psi_{n},\delta e^{a(0,1)},\delta\gamma_{abc}^{(0,1)}] and 𝒯0,4(0,0)​[ϕs(1,1)]\mathcal{T}^{(0,0)}_{0,4}[\phi_{s}^{(1,1)}] over the angular coordinates and over a complex contour for the radial coordinate. Alternatively, Eqs. (3.11)-(3.13) can be reduced to a more manageable system of radial equations by assuming a decomposition of the Teukolsky variables as

Ψ0(1,1)=e−i​ω​t+i​m​ϕ​∑ℓR0ℓ​m​(r)​S0ℓ​m​(x,a​ω),\displaystyle\Psi_{0}^{(1,1)}=e^{-i\omega t+im\phi}\sum_{\ell}R^{\ell m}_{0}(r)S^{\ell m}_{0}(x;a\omega)\,, (3.14)
ρ−4​Ψ4(1,1)=e−i​ω​t+i​m​ϕ​∑ℓR4ℓ​m​(r)​S4ℓ​m​(x,a​ω),\displaystyle\rho^{-4}\Psi_{4}^{(1,1)}=e^{-i\omega t+im\phi}\sum_{\ell}R^{\ell m}_{4}(r)S^{\ell m}_{4}(x;a\omega)\,, (3.15)
ϕs(1,1)=e−i​ω​t+i​m​ϕ​∑ℓRsℓ​m​(r)​Ssℓ​m​(x,a​ω),\displaystyle\phi_{s}^{(1,1)}=e^{-i\omega t+im\phi}\sum_{\ell}{R}^{\ell m}_{s}(r)S^{\ell m}_{s}(x;a\omega)\,, (3.16)

where mm is the magnetic mode number, ω\omega is the complex frequency of the QNM, Ssℓ​m​(x,a​ω)S^{\ell m}_{s}(x;a\omega) are spin-weighted spheroidal harmonics, ρ=(r−i​a​x)−1\rho=(r-iax)^{-1}, and [R0ℓ​m​(r),R4ℓ​m​(r),Rsℓ​m​(r)][{R}^{\ell m}_{0}(r),{R}^{\ell m}_{4}(r),{R}^{\ell m}_{s}(r)] are unknown radial functions. One can then project Eqs. (3.11)-(3.13) onto the spheroidal harmonics in order to get decoupled equations for the radial variables [496, 499] (see also [507, 508]).

For the EFT of GR (3.1), containing no extra fields ϕs\phi_{s}, this procedure yields a modified Teukolsky radial equation which, after redefinitions of the radial variable, can be written as [497, 498]

Δ−s​dd​r​[Δs+1​d​Rsd​r]+(Vs+ζq​δ​Vs(q))​Rs=0,\Delta^{-s}\frac{d}{dr}\left[\Delta^{s+1}\frac{dR_{s}}{dr}\right]+\left(V_{s}+\zeta_{\rm q}\delta V^{(\rm q)}_{s}\right)R_{s}=0\,, (3.17)

for the total Teukolsky variable Ψ0,4(0,1)+ζq​Ψ0,4(1,1)\Psi_{0,4}^{(0,1)}+\zeta_{\rm q}\Psi_{0,4}^{(1,1)}, where s=±2s=\pm 2. For nonextremal BHs, the correction to the potential can always be put in the form

δ​V−2(q)=1Δ​[A−2(q)r2+A0(q)+A1(q)​r+A2(q)​r2].\delta V^{(\rm q)}_{-2}=\frac{1}{\Delta}\left[\frac{A^{\rm(q)}_{-2}}{r^{2}}+A^{\rm(q)}_{0}+A^{\rm(q)}_{1}r+A^{\rm(q)}_{2}r^{2}\right]\,. (3.18)

The coefficients Ak(q)A^{(\rm q)}_{k} can be found analytically as a power series in the angular momentum. They depend on the polarization of the perturbation, hence leading to a breaking of isospectrality. For EsGB and dCS gravity, a similar process can be implemented by decomposing the scalar fields in spheroidal harmonics. In this case, one expects that scalar and gravitational modes of different ℓ\ell will be coupled, leading to a set of coupled radial PDEs that need to be solved numerically. In the case of dCS gravity, these coupled Teukolsky radial equations have been analyzed at first order in the angular momentum expansion [499], and the corresponding QNM frequencies have been computed [500].

Further insights can be gained by employing the parity operator [509]. This operator enables separation of the modified Teukolsky equation into two distinct components: an odd-parity equation coupled to the scalar field perturbations and an even-parity equation that remains entirely decoupled, thereby exhibiting isospectrality breaking in dCS gravity. Similarly, in EsGB gravity, one obtains an even-parity equation coupled to the scalar field perturbations and an odd-parity equation that remains entirely decoupled, again exhibiting isospectrality breaking.

All these findings are consistent with those obtained through the metric perturbation framework discussed below, reinforcing the validity of both approaches [440, 490, 510, 489, 493, 486, 483, 511, 512, 513, 514, 515].

The METRICS approach A different approach, known as Metric pErTuRbations wIth speCtral methodS (METRICS) [516, 517], models both gravitational and scalar perturbations by expressing them in a product decomposition (by peeling off a certain asymptotic factor) and then applying a spectral expansion in Legendre polynomials of (cosine of) the polar angle and Chebyshev polynomials of a (compactified) radial variable [516, 517]. The linearized field equations then become a linear algebra problem for the spectral coefficients and the QNMs frequencies.

The METRICS approach is as follows. First, small perturbations of both the background metric (gμ​ν(0))(g_{\mu\nu}^{(0)}) and scalar field background (Φ(0))(\Phi^{(0)}) in Boyer-Lindquist-like coordinates are written as

gμ​ν=gμ​ν(0)+ϵ​ei​m​ϕ−i​ω​t​h^μ​ν,Φ=Φ(0)+ϵ​ei​m​ϕ−i​ω​t​h^ϑ,\begin{split}g_{\mu\nu}&=g^{\rm(0)}_{\mu\nu}+\epsilon\;e^{im\phi-i\omega t}\hat{h}_{\mu\nu},\\ \Phi&=\Phi^{\rm(0)}+\epsilon\;e^{im\phi-i\omega t}\hat{h}_{\vartheta}\,,\end{split} (3.19)

where h^μ​ν\hat{h}_{\mu\nu} and h^ϑ\hat{h}_{\vartheta} are functions of rr and χ\chi only, and the quantity ϵ≪1\epsilon\ll 1 is a perturbative bookkeeping parameter. Enforcing the Regge-Wheeler gauge, the metric perturbation is completely specified by 6 unknown metric variable hj=1,…,6h_{j=1,...,6} [13], plus h^ϑ\hat{h}_{\vartheta}. The linearized field equations governing hj=1,…,7h_{j=1,...,7} read

∑β=γ=0∑j=17𝒞k,β,γ,j​(r,cos⁡θ)​∂rβ∂cos⁡θγhj=0,\sum_{\beta=\gamma=0}\sum_{j=1}^{7}\mathscr{C}_{k,\beta,\gamma,j}(r,\cos\theta)\partial^{\beta}_{r}\partial^{\gamma}_{\cos\theta}h_{j}=0\,, (3.20)

where β\beta and γ\gamma are nonnegative integers, 𝒞k,β,γ,j\mathscr{C}_{k,\beta,\gamma,j} are complex functions of (r,cos⁡θ)(r,\cos\theta) that also depend on (M,a,m,ω,ζ)(M,a,m,\omega,\zeta), and k∈[1,11]k\in[1,11] labels the equations (10 metric field and 1 scalar field equation). Instead, the upper limit of β\beta and γ\gamma depends on the theory. For example, in GR and EsGB gravity, the summation ranges from β=γ=0\beta=\gamma=0 to β+γ=2\beta+\gamma=2; in dCS gravity, 0≤β+γ≤30\leq\beta+\gamma\leq 3. Assuming the expansion of Eq. (3.7), 𝒞k,β,γ,j\mathscr{C}_{k,\beta,\gamma,j} are rational functions. Upon appropriate factorization and manipulation, 𝒞k,β,γ,j\mathscr{C}_{k,\beta,\gamma,j} can be converted into polynomials [517, 516].

The divergent behavior of hjh_{j} at the event horizon and spatial infinity due to coordinate singularities, governed by the linearized field equations, is accounted for by factorizing or “peeling off” an asymptotic factor Aj​(r)A_{j}(r), which in GR reads

Aj​(r)=ei​ω​r​r2​i​M​ω+ρ∞(j)​(r−r+r)−i​M​ω−m​ΩH2​κ+−ρH(j),A_{j}(r)=e^{i\omega r}r^{2iM\omega+\rho_{\infty}^{(j)}}\left(\frac{r-r_{+}}{r}\right)^{-iM\frac{\omega-m\Omega_{H}}{2\kappa_{+}}-\rho_{H}^{(j)}}, (3.21)

where ρ∞(j)\rho_{\infty}^{(j)} and ρH(j)\rho_{H}^{(j)} are positive integers that depend on jj, and κ+=M2−a2/(2​M​r+)\kappa_{+}=\sqrt{M^{2}-a^{2}}/(2Mr_{+}) is the surface gravity of the outer horizon. For general, axially symmetric BHs whose event horizon is a Killing horizon, Aj​(r)A_{j}(r) can be derived by imposing ingoing and outgoing wave boundary conditions at the event horizon and at spatial infinity, while using the beyond-GR ΩH\Omega_{H} and κ+\kappa_{+} expressions for the modified Killing horizon [512]. In terms of Aj​(r)A_{j}(r), one can express hjh_{j} as

hj=Aj​(r)​∑p=1Nr∑l=1Nlvj,p,l​φp,l​(r,cos⁡θ).h_{j}=A_{j}(r)\sum_{p=1}^{N_{r}}\sum_{l=1}^{N_{l}}v_{j,p,l}\penalty\ \varphi_{p,l}(r,\cos\theta)\,. (3.22)

Here φp,l​(r,cos⁡θ)\varphi_{p,l}(r,\cos\theta) encodes all of the radial and polar angle dependence, which in the METRICS approach is represented through a spectral expansion. That is, φp,l​(r,cos⁡θ)\varphi_{p,l}(r,\cos\theta) is modeled through a complete and orthogonal spectral basis of rr and cos⁡θ\cos\theta (typically, Legendre polynomials in cos⁡θ\cos\theta and Chebyshev polynomials in a compactified radial coordinate [512]); NrN_{r} and NlN_{l} are the spectral order of the spectral projection along the radial and angular coordinates; finally, pp and ll label the degree of the spectral basis, with vj,p,lv_{j,p,l} constants. The approach has been validated in GR, showcasing its high accuracy, with relative fractional errors smaller than 10−510^{-5} for all dimensionless spins below up to 0.95.

For EsGB and dCS gravity, this method simultaneously solves all 11 partial differential equations for the 7 unknowns by transforming Eq. (3.22) into a generalized eigenvalue problem. The solution has been found using the Newton-Raphson algorithm and the generalized Moore-Penrose inverse [512].

Generalized spectral method (collocation) An alternative approach is the generalized spectral collocation method [513]. The method can be used for a range of theories (e.g., linear EsGB gravity), but for concreteness is exemplified below for EdGB gravity. Under linear perturbations of the metric tensor and dilaton fields, Eq. (3.19), the equations take the form

𝒢μ​ν\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\mu\nu} =\displaystyle= 𝒢μ​ν(b​g)+ϵ​δ​𝒢μ​ν​(r,θ)​ei⁡(m​ϕ−ω​t)=0,\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\mu\nu}^{(bg)}+\epsilon\,\delta\mathcal{G}_{\mu\nu}(r,\theta)e^{i(m\phi-\omega t)}=0\,, (3.23)
𝒮\displaystyle\mathcal{S} =\displaystyle= 𝒮(b​g)+ϵ​δ​𝒮​(r,θ)​ei⁡(m​ϕ−ω​t)=0.\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{(bg)}+\epsilon\,\delta\mathcal{S}(r,\theta)e^{i(m\phi-\omega t)}=0\,. (3.24)

where the subscript “(b​g)(bg)” denotes background quantities (see [513] for the full expressions). The background can be generic and numerical if desired. The perturbations are also generic and do not require special coordinates, leading to results valid beyond the small-coupling and small-spin approximations. Rotating background solutions satisfy 𝒢μ​ν(b​g)=0\mathcal{G}_{\mu\nu}^{(bg)}=0 and 𝒮(b​g)=0\mathcal{S}^{(bg)}=0, leaving a system of coupled PDEs in rr and θ\theta for the perturbation functions, δ​𝒢μ​ν=0\delta\mathcal{G}_{\mu\nu}=0 and δ​𝒮=0\delta\mathcal{S}=0. Imposing standard QNM boundary conditions and regularity on the rotation axis yields a set of constraints through a perturbative analysis of the asymptotic behavior at asymptotic infinity and near the horizon [513].

The perturbations are then expanded using Chebyshev polynomials and Legendre functions, employing a compactified radial coordinate z=(r−r+)/(r+1)z=(r-r_{+})/(r+1) and x=cos⁡(θ)x=\cos(\theta). After the Chebyshev and Legendre expansions of the perturbation functions, the partial differential system can be expressed as a quadratic eigenvalue problem

(ℳ0+ℳ1​ω+ℳ2​ω2)​C→=0,\left(\mathcal{M}_{0}+\mathcal{M}_{1}\omega+\mathcal{M}_{2}\omega^{2}\right)\vec{C}=0\,, (3.25)

with square matrices ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0}, ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2} that depend on the background solution.

At variance with the METRICS approach, the quadratic eigenvalue is obtained directly, without factorization and simplification of the perturbed field equations, on a discretized grid of Nx×NyN_{x}\times N_{y} points (typically of order 20 in both directions). The unknown expansion coefficients that lie in the vector C→\vec{C} can be accurately determined. One can then find accurate numerical solutions [513] for the eigenvalue ω\omega, for example through Maple and MATLAB with Multiprecision Computing Toolbox Advanpix [518]. The method has been validated in the GR rotating case, confirming its high accuracy: at least 10−610^{-6} accuracy up to about 80%80\% of the maximum angular momentum [519]. Besides the modified gravity results covered below, this method was also applied to study the QNMs of rapidly rotating wormholes [520].

3.1.3 Black hole perturbations in modified gravity: results

We now summarize the state of the art of QNM frequency calculations that applied the methods described above to a variety of theories.

EFT extensions of GR In these theories, defined by the action (3.1), the modified Teukolsky equation allows one to obtain the modifications to the Kerr QNM frequencies to linear order in the coupling constants ζq\zeta_{\rm q}:

ωℓ​m​n±=ωℓ​m​nKerr+ζqM​δ​ωℓ​m​n±(q)​(χ)+𝒪⁡(ζq2).\omega_{\ell mn\pm}=\omega^{\rm Kerr}_{\ell mn}+\frac{\zeta_{\rm q}}{M}\delta\omega_{\ell mn\pm}^{({\rm q})}(\chi)+\mathcal{O}\left(\zeta_{\rm q}^{2}\right)\,. (3.26)

Here ±\pm denotes the mode polarization, and we have introduced the factor of 1/M1/M so that the target of the computations, δ​ωℓ​m​n±(q)​(χ)\delta\omega_{\ell mn\pm}^{({\rm q})}(\chi), is dimensionless.

The frequency shifts can be found by solving Eq. (3.17) through, e.g., a generalized continued fraction method through a higher-step recursive relation [521] or eigenvalue perturbation techniques [208, 306]. The frequency shifts can also be obtained by mapping Eq. (3.17) to the parameterized formalism reviewed in Section 3.2.3 below. Achieving a reliable result for large angular momentum requires computing Eq. (3.17) at very high order in the spin expansion, which is computationally challenging.

Shifts δ​ωℓ​m​n±(q)​(χ)\delta\omega_{\ell mn\pm}^{({\rm q})}(\chi) for all the EFT theories, for the modes ℓ=2,3,4\ell=2,3,4, m∈[−ℓ,ℓ]m\in[-\ell,\ell], n=0,1,2n=0,1,2 and up to angular momentum χ∼0.7−0.9\chi\sim 0.7-0.9 were computed up to expansion order χ18\chi^{18} [498]. In Fig. 19 we show the (ℓ,m,n)=(2,m,0),(2,m,1)(\ell,m,n)=(2,m,0),(2,m,1) modes in the even-parity cubic theory case. The results agree with previous computations for static and slowly rotating BHs obtained via modified RWZ equations [458, 487, 492] and are publicly available [522] (see Appendix A).

One of the most generic beyond-GR effects is the breaking of isospectrality, so that even and odd modes receive different corrections [523, 524]. This works differently for parity-preserving and parity-breaking theories. In the former case, δ​ω+\delta\omega_{+} and δ​ω−\delta\omega_{-} are unrelated to each other, while in the latter δ​ω+=−δ​ω−\delta\omega_{+}=-\delta\omega_{-}. Interestingly, combining parity-preserving corrections (with shifts δ​ωpres±\delta\omega_{\rm pres\pm}) and parity-breaking ones (with shifts δ​ω±=±δ​ωbreak\delta\omega_{\pm}=\pm\delta\omega_{\rm break}) the total shift is not just the sum of each of them. Instead, the following combination rule holds [524, 492, 497]

δ​ωtot±=12​(δ​ωpres++δ​ωpres−)±14​(δ​ωpres+−δ​ωpres−)2+δ​ωbreak2.\delta\omega_{\rm tot\pm}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\delta\omega_{\rm pres+}+\delta\omega_{\rm pres-}\right)\pm\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}\left(\delta\omega_{\rm pres+}-\delta\omega_{\rm pres-}\right)^{2}+\delta\omega_{\rm break}^{2}}\,. (3.27)

This relationship arises from the coupling between perturbations of different parity. While all of the analyzed higher-derivative theories break isospectrality, it has been recently observed that the special quartic theory 𝒞2+𝒞~2\mathcal{C}^{2}+\tilde{\mathcal{C}}^{2} preserves isospectrality in the eikonal limit [274]. In this theory, isospectrality is still broken for low-ℓ\ell modes, but the difference between even and odd modes is small. Additional results for other theories and more modes are available online [522] (see Appendix A).

These results have recently been applied to test EFT corrections against real ringdown data from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) observations in [525], finding a bound on the scale of new physics ℓ≲35\ell\lesssim 35 km. Future ground-based detectors will substantially improve these bounds, as discussed in Section 7.2.2 below.

dCS gravity In this theory, the QNM frequencies are also obtained as a linear expansion in the coupling, similar to Eq. (3.26). Results are known for the static and spherically symmetric (Schwarzschild) background [485, 510, 526, 524], and for rotating (non-Kerr) BHs at linear order in the small-spin expansion [440, 490, 499] and for χ\chi up to ∼0.75\sim 0.75 using METRICS [527]. All of these studies relied on a metric perturbation approach, except for [499], which employed the modified Teukolsky approach, expanded to linear order in the spin.

All the existing calculations show that, in dCS gravity, the axial frequency is shifted more significantly than the polar frequency, due to the stronger coupling of the perturbations of the pseudoscalar to axial metric perturbations. In particular, when the background has zero spin (a=0a=0), the perturbations of the pseudoscalar field completely decouple from the polar metric perturbations. Fig. 20 shows the lead-order QNM-frequency shift in ζ\zeta (i.e. δ​ω\delta\omega defined by Eq. (3.26)) of the axial metric perturbations for the ℓ​m​n=220,330\ell mn=220,330 and 320 modes of a rotating BH background with 0≤χ≤0.7530\leq\chi\leq 0.753. Observe that δ​ω\delta\omega of the polar perturbations to nonrotating BHs is zero for all modes, because the polar metric perturbations are decoupled from the dCS terms when χ=0\chi=0. Analytical fitting expressions of the QNM-frequency shift obtained by METRICS that are valid for χ\chi up to 0.750.75 are available in [527], and obtained by a separate analytical calculation valid up to linear order in the spin are also available [490].

Linear EsGB gravity Initial results for this theory were obtained using either numerical solutions or analytic (slow-rotation) approximations for the background metric and scalar field [486, 483, 489, 493, 528]. The extension to rapidly rotating BH backgrounds, with a≲0.85​Ma\lesssim 0.85M, and small coupling were instead computed using the METRICS approach [511, 512]. Results are shown in Fig. 21 for n​ℓ​m=022n\ell m=022, both axial and polar perturbations, and an illustrative value of the coupling ζEsGB=0.1\zeta_{\text{EsGB}}=0.1, where we recall that ζEsGB\zeta_{\text{EsGB}} is defined in (3.5). The figures confirms the breaking of isospectrality, as in the case of cubic EFTs and dCS gravity. Fitting formulas and calculations for other modes are also available [512].

For small spin, the numerical results are consistent with second-order in spin perturbative predictions [486, 483, 489, 493], confirming that polar frequency corrections are shifted by a larger extent compared to axial ones. The relative fractional uncertainty of the real (imaginary) frequency varies between [10−8,10−2][10^{-8},10^{-2}] ([10−6,10−1][10^{-6},10^{-1}]), depending on the spin [511]. This level of accuracy is good enough to analyze individual ringdown GW signals observed by the LVK ground-based detectors in the third observing run [529, 460]. The polar frequencies were used to construct an effective one body (EOB) waveform model [530] employed to search for modified gravity signatures in GW data (see Section 6.3.2).

A calculation of the QNM frequencies in linear EsGB gravity that is fully nonperturbative in the coupling can be found in [514].

EdGB gravity In Fig. 22 we show fully nonperturbative results for the QNM frequencies of EdGB BHs for a dilaton coupling with γ=1\gamma=1 as a function of coupling constant ζEdGB\zeta_{\text{EdGB}} for two representative values of the spin. The frequencies of the longest-lived modes with ℓ=2,3\ell=2,3 and m=2m=2 were computed using the spectral collocation method described above [513], and the vertical lines mark the critical values of ζEdGB\zeta_{\text{EdGB}} beyond which no regular BHs exist in EdGB theory for the given dimensionless spin χ=J/M2\chi=J/M^{2}.

As we see in Figure 22, the isospectrality of the Kerr axial-led and polar-led modes is broken in EdGB gravity. This happens already in the static case [486, 483], becoming more prominent as the coupling strength and BH spin increase, approaching the boundary of the domain of existence of BH solutions. The figure also shows the scalar-led modes of the dilaton field, smoothly connecting with the modes of a minimally coupled scalar field on the Kerr background as the coupling strength is decreased. The lowest value of the frequency M​ωRM\omega_{R} always corresponds to the ℓ=2\ell=2 metric modes. Typically, polar modes have smaller values of M​ωRM\omega_{R}, but the difference with respect to the axial modes is always small.

Another interesting property of the spectrum is the switch of mode dominance as the critical coupling strength is approached, and the scalar charge of the solutions increases. While for Kerr the gravity-led modes are always longer lived than the scalar-led modes, here, depending on the angular momentum and coupling strength, it is possible to find solutions for which (vice versa) the scalar-led modes are longer lived than the gravity-led modes. This dominance switch is displayed in Fig. 22 for χ=0.4\chi=0.4 and ℓ=2\ell=2, stressing the importance of scalar-led modes when modeling the ringdown phase in EdGB theory.

These general results also reproduce with excellent accuracy the static limit [486, 483] obtained with a different shooting method, and the analytical predictions in the slow-rotation approximation [489, 493]. The computed QNMs satisfy all the PDEs and boundary conditions of the perturbations with an accuracy of at least 10−410^{-4}. More details can be found in [513] as well as [515], where the modes with a negative real part are also computed. Like the positive-frequency modes, the modes with negative frequency have damping times that depend strongly on the angular momentum and on the coupling constant, and they present dominance switch between gravity-led and scalar-led modes in some cases.

Future directions

Despite the remarkable progress summarized above, several outstanding problems remain in order to complete our understanding of the linear ringdown in theories beyond GR. An important open question is the case of very highly rotating BHs, χ≳0.95\chi\gtrsim 0.95. None of the methods reviewed above has achieved reliable results in this regime yet, as this is technically challenging and may require alternative approaches [531] (see also Section 2.1.5). The computation of overtones has also been quite limited so far. In addition, some of the results we have discussed only consider corrections to the QNMs perturbative in the coupling. For the purpose of testing these theories, it is important to have reliable predictions for the QNM frequencies for arbitrary values of the coupling constants. Beyond the QNM frequencies, one should also analyze the effect of beyond-GR physics on the QNM amplitudes [494] and, more broadly, on the TD signal. In a context where extensions of GR are treated as EFTs, it is important to have reliable predictions for the QNMs for arbitrary values of the coupling constants or an estimate of the regime validity of QNM calculations. This validity regime may depend on the harmonic or overtone number [532, 494, 498].

Addressing these issues is important in order to perform accurate ringdown-based tests of theories beyond GR with next-generation (XG) GW observatories (see Section 7).

3.2 Theory-agnostic parameterization

Initial contributors: Franchini, Kimura, Völkel

Rather than computing QNM frequencies on a theory-by-theory basis, an alternative approach is to develop a theory-agnostic, parametric framework to compute QNMs when the underlying theory of gravity or the corresponding BH solutions are unknown. This approach is strongly motivated by the large amount of modified theories of gravity or new physics scenarios that could induce deviations from the Kerr spectrum in the data. Note however that the terminology “theory-agnostic” can be somewhat misleading, as specific theoretical constraints are often imposed, either implicitly or explicitly. For example, if we start from the ansatz that modifications to the QNM spectrum can be described by modifications of the perturbation potentials in GR we must necessarily assume separability, which selects only certain classes of beyond-GR theories (see e.g. [533]). Similarly, the eikonal limit (see Section 2.4), may not hold in some theories; approaches using parameterized BH metrics requires a choice of test fields (e.g., the Klein-Gordon equation in a background spacetime); and so on.

Any parameterization must resolve a tension between generality and simplicity. The parameterization should be general enough to encompass the largest possible amount of new physics, yet limit the number of free parameters so that they will not be degenerate or unconstrained, thus making measurements uninformative. If the aim is to understand fundamental properties of QNMs beyond GR without focusing on a given theory, one must assume some general structure for the equations of motion or even for the action of the theory, either starting from first principles or using known cases as a guide. Finally, assuming a metric theory, one might be interested in linking the modifications to the QNM spectrum (as induced, e.g., by environmental effects) to modifications in the underlying spacetime metric.

Despite these limitations, theory-agnostic approaches allow us to study a rich phenomenology capturing several classes of modifications, and they provide a valuable, interpretable observational framework to search for new physics. In this chapter we review the most commonly used parameterized models. We first introduce the simplest parameterization of possible deviations from the gravitational QNM spectrum in Section 3.2.1, then we discuss the “parameterized spectroscopy” (or ParSpec) framework in Section 3.2.2, and finally we discuss parameterizations of the perturbation potentials in Section 3.2.3. In Section 3.2.4 we describe approaches based on parameterized BH metrics and ideas based on the eikonal limit (see Section 2.4). Finally, in Section 3.2.5 we discuss parameterizations at the level of the action and the so-called “EFT of QNMs.”

3.2.1 Agnostic QNM deviations

Quite generally, if there are any deviations from vacuum GR, the gravitational QNMs can be parameterized in the form

fℓ​m​n\displaystyle f_{\ell{m}n} =fℓ​m​nKerr​(1+δ​fℓ​m​n),\displaystyle=f_{\ell{m}n}^{\mathrm{Kerr}}\,(1+\delta f_{\ell{m}n})\,, (3.28)
τℓ​m​n\displaystyle\tau_{\ell{m}n} =τℓ​m​nKerr​(1+δ​τℓ​m​n),\displaystyle=\tau_{\ell{m}n}^{\mathrm{Kerr}}\,(1+\delta\tau_{\ell{m}n})\,, (3.29)

where here ff refers to the real component of the complex QNM frequency ω\omega, and τ\tau to the inverse of its imaginary component. This parameterization has been proposed and used extensively in GW data analysis for tests of GR and searches of new physics [534, 535, 536, 529, 460] (see also Section 6 below). The parameterization is extremely flexible and general, as it can accommodate any shift to a given QNM with respect to the Kerr spectrum. Its main limitation is that Eq. (3.28) does not take into account new modes that are not given by continuous deformations of the Kerr gravitational spectrum which may appear in the signal (see [537, 538]). In general, additional modes and polarizations will appear in the spectrum whenever a specific modified theory of gravity involves additional degrees of freedom (such as dynamical scalar, vector or tensor fields). While the parameterization will not capture the power contained in such new modes, any additional degrees of freedom should only contain a small fraction of the signal power if the modified theory is close enough to GR. In this sense, the deviation parameters are still expected to capture the main modifications to the GR signal. Any deviation from the Kerr spectrum would flag the detection of an anomalous feature, that can later be followed up with informed searches including additional modes.

From the data analysis point of view, the main disadvantage of this parameterized model is that it requires two new degrees of freedom for each mode (ℓ,m,n)(\ell,m,n) to describe potential deviations from the GR spectrum. For this reason the parameterization can be very inefficient when the number of observed modes increases, resulting in uninformative measurements (see Section 6). A second important limitation is that the parameterization is “too general,” in the sense that it does not fold in the dependence of the frequencies and of their modifications on the BH parameters (mass and spin). This makes it impossible to exploit the properties of the underlying source population: individual sources with different masses and spins are better at probing different modifications from GR, and by combining multiple sources it should be possible to obtain better bounds on any specific modification. More fundamentally, if a deviation is detected, one would like a physical understanding of its origin – something which is not provided by Eq. (3.28).

In conclusion, the parameterization of Eq. (3.28) is useful for null tests, but it cannot be used to extract the underlying physics without further assumptions. Due to the generality of the parameterization, it is also very difficult to give a physical interpretation of nonzero deviation parameters in multi-modal scenarios if the underlying GR signal model is incomplete. This can happen when the number of detectable modes is unknown (and especially for overtones), even in idealized situations [378, 539, 540, 541].

In the following we will show how including more assumptions based on the underlying physics affects QNM parameterizations.

3.2.2 The ParSpec framework

A simple and reasonable ansatz is to assume the deviations from GR to be small, i.e.,

δ​fℓ​m​n≪1,δ​τℓ​m​n≪1.\delta f_{\ell{m}n}\ll 1\,,\qquad\delta\tau_{\ell{m}n}\ll 1\,. (3.30)

This ansatz is based on the reasoning that even if modifications of GR are present in nature, the stringent experimental bounds imposed by existing tests of GR [432, 434, 542, 543, 544, 545, 546, 529, 460, 461] imply that the modifications must be hidden in the noise, and the relative size of any frequency modifications to the Kerr spectrum can be expected to be much smaller than unity. From a theoretical perspective, this assumption fits well with an EFT description of gravity, where GR is the low-energy limit of some as yet unknown theory (see Section 3.1 for theory-specific examples).

A phenomenological model for “universal” modifications of spinning BH spectra that incorporate the key features of the remnant mass and spin dependence was proposed in [547]. In this parameterized spectroscopy, or “ParSpec” model, the modifications are written in the form of parameterized ringdown spin expansion coefficients as follows:

fℓ​m​n\displaystyle f_{\ell mn} =1M​∑k=0Kχk​fℓ​m​n(k)​(1+γ​δ​fℓ​m​n(k)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{k=0}^{K}\,\chi^{k}\,f_{\ell mn}^{(k)}\left(1+\gamma\,\delta f_{\ell mn}^{(k)}\right)\,, (3.31)
τℓ​m​n\displaystyle\tau_{\ell mn} =M​∑k=0Kχk​τℓ​m​n(k)​(1+γ​δ​τℓ​m​n(k)),\displaystyle=M\sum_{k=0}^{K}\,\chi^{k}\,\tau_{\ell mn}^{(k)}\left(1+\gamma\,\delta\tau_{\ell mn}^{(k)}\right)\,, (3.32)

where fℓ​m​n(k)f^{(k)}_{\ell mn} and τℓ​m​n(k)\tau^{(k)}_{\ell mn} come from a Taylor expansion of the GR values around χ=0\chi=0, γ\gamma is a theory-dependent and (possibly) source-dependent parameter, and δ​fℓ​m​n(k)\delta f^{(k)}_{\ell mn} and δ​τℓ​m​n(k)\delta\tau^{(k)}_{\ell mn} are the source-independent beyond-GR deviations expanded around χ=0\chi=0.

Depending on the underlying theory of modified gravity, we can consider three different cases:

(i) Scale-free corrections If the corrections to GR are given by a single dimensionless coupling α\alpha, we can set γ=α\gamma=\alpha and reabsorb it within δ​fℓ​m​n(k)\delta f^{(k)}_{\ell mn} and δ​τℓ​m​n(k)\delta\tau^{(k)}_{\ell mn}. This case includes certain scalar-tensor and Lorentz-violating theories, such as Einstein-Aether and Hořava gravity (to leading order) [548].

(ii) Single dimensionful coupling The corrections to GR are given by a dimensionful coupling α\alpha with dimensions [α]=M^p[\alpha]=\hat{M}^{p}, with pp a (usually positive) integer, and M^\hat{M} the typical length scale of the problem. We can set γ=α/Msp=α​(1+z)p/Mp\gamma=\alpha/M_{\mathrm{s}}^{p}=\alpha(1+z)^{p}/M^{p}, where MsM_{\mathrm{s}} is the BH mass in the source frame and zz is the source redshift. For example, for p=4p=4 this captures the scaling of the curvature-dependent modifications in EsGB and dCS gravity, and for p=6p=6 it captures the scaling of some of the EFTs discussed in Section 3.1.

(iii) Individual charges BHs in the modified theory possess what is sometimes called “primary hair,” i.e., a new charge QQ that is completely independent on the BH mass and spin, with dimensions [Q]=M^p[Q]=\hat{M}^{p}. The simplest examples are Kerr-Newman BHs (see [549] for a review of “hairy” BH solutions). In this case, we can set γ=Q/Msp\gamma=Q/M_{\mathrm{s}}^{p}.

This parameterization was used to derive constraints from current observational data in the case of scale-free and dimensionful couplings [550], in the case of individual charges with p=2p=2 (i.e., Kerr-Newman BHs) [551, 552], and in some specific theories of gravity with selected values of pp [553]. Projected bounds with XG detectors were computed in [554] (see Sections 6.3 and 7.2 for an extensive discussion).

3.2.3 Parameterized QNM framework

This section deals with the parameterized QNM framework, which is one step closer to the theory-specific case. Instead of assuming a mass and spin dependence in the parameterization of the QNM spectrum, in this framework one assumes a parameterization of the effective potentials. In this way we can make direct contact with the numerous specific models in which the perturbation equations can be cast in the form of a modified RWZ equation (in the nonrotating case) or of a modified Teukolsky equation (in the rotating case). The power of the method is that one can compute the QNM spectrum in all of these beyond-GR theories in one sweep without assuming any specific theory. The main (important) assumption is that, in the perturbative spirit discussed above, the modifications of the RWZ or Teukolsky potentials must be small, in a sense that can be made precise. We will first focus on the nonrotating case for simplicity, and then generalize the treatment to rotating BHs.

The parameterized QNM framework was first introduced to compute linear QNM corrections due to small modifications of single-field (scalar, gravitational axial, gravitational polar) perturbation equations of the Schwarzschild BH [523]. Then it was extended to include quadratic corrections, systems with multiple coupled fields [524], QNM overtones [555, 532] and the TD evolution of initial data [556].

In the nonrotating or slowly rotating case, let us assume that single or multi-field perturbations 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi} are well approximated by the wave equation

f​dd​r​(f​d​𝚽d​r)+[ω2−f​𝐕]​𝚽=0,f\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r}\left(f\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{\Phi}}{\mathrm{d}r}\right)+\left[\omega^{2}-f\mathbf{V}\right]\mathbf{\Phi}=0\,, (3.33)

where f=1−r+/rf=1-r_{+}/r, r+=2​Mr_{+}=2M, and the effective potential is

Vi​j\displaystyle V_{ij} =Vi​jGR+δ​Vi​j,\displaystyle=V^{\mathrm{GR}}_{ij}+\delta V_{ij}, (3.34)
δ​Vi​j\displaystyle\delta V_{ij} =1r+2​∑k=0∞αi​j(k)​(r+r)k.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{r_{+}^{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha^{(k)}_{ij}\left(\frac{r_{+}}{r}\right)^{k}\,. (3.35)

Here the diagonal elements of the matrix Vi​jGRV^{\mathrm{GR}}_{ij} stand for the scalar (s=0s=0) potential, the gravitational axial (Regge-Wheeler) potential, or the polar gravitational (Zerilli) potential. This way of writing the unperturbed wave equations differs slightly from standard conventions in the literature due to the extra factor of ff. Many models are included in this parameterized potential [458, 523, 524, 557, 555, 558, 559, 487, 560, 561, 532], which allows for the inclusion of coupling functions between multiple fields through the off-diagonal matrix elements.

The QNM frequencies ω\omega (where we omit the ℓ,m,n\ell,\,m,\,n indices for simplicity) can be expanded in powers of the small modifications αi​j(k)\alpha^{(k)}_{ij}, and the resulting corrections up to quadratic order can be written as

ω≈ω0+αi​j(k)​d(k)i​j+αi​j(k)​α​d(k)i​jp​q′(s)​d(s)p​q+12​αi​j(k)​αp​q(s)​e(k​s)i​j​p​q,\omega\approx\omega^{0}+\alpha^{(k)}_{ij}d_{(k)}^{ij}+\alpha_{ij}^{(k)}\alpha{}_{pq}^{\prime(s)}d^{ij}_{(k)}d^{pq}_{(s)}+\frac{1}{2}\alpha^{(k)}_{ij}\alpha^{(s)}_{pq}e^{ijpq}_{(ks)}\,, (3.36)

where ω0\omega^{0} is the unperturbed QNM. In Eq. (3.36), αi​j(k)\alpha_{ij}^{(k)} and its derivative with respect to ω\omega, denoted by a prime, are evaluated at ω0\omega^{0}. Note that the coefficients d(k)i​jd_{(k)}^{ij} and e(k​s)i​j​p​qe^{ijpq}_{(ks)} do not depend on αi​j(k)\alpha^{(k)}_{ij}, and thus only need to be computed once. Numerical data for the coefficients are publicly available in [89, 91, 90, 532] (see Appendix A).

It was shown that the number of deviation parameters can be conveniently reduced by suitable field redefinitions, thus limiting the total number of free parameters to just a few low-order coefficients [562, 563]. This makes the computation of QNM corrections extremely fast and stable, which is particularly interesting for data analysis applications or theoretical explorations of the parameter space [558]. The parameterized QNM framework was applied to describe deviations at the level of the background metric [564] and to reconstruct modifications of the potential in the case where a deviation is detected [555].

In the large-kk limit, the amplitude of the coefficients d(k)i​jd_{(k)}^{ij} in the decoupled case is proportional to k−1−2​r+​ωI0k^{-1-2r_{+}\omega_{I}^{0}}, where ωI0\omega_{I}^{0} is the imaginary part of the unperturbed QNM [523, 532]. Since −r+​ωI0-r_{+}\omega_{I}^{0} is large and positive for higher overtones, k−1−2​r+​ωI0k^{-1-2r_{+}\omega_{I}^{0}} also becomes large as kk increases. This implies that the deviation from the GR spectra in the large-kk limit is particularly significant for higher overtones. Since large-kk modifications of the effective potential are largest close to the horizon, at r∗≃−r+​ln⁡(k/e)r_{*}\simeq-r_{+}\ln(k/e), this is yet another illustration of the spectral QNM instability discussed in Section 2.6: overtones are easily destabilized by near-horizon modifications of the effective potential [565, 532].

The parameterized QNM framework has been extended to encompass modifications of the Teukolsky equation, which describes curvature perturbations of the Kerr BH [521]. There are several nontrivial differences with the nonrotating case, which are only briefly summarized below. First, as in GR, the angular separation constant becomes ω\omega-dependent. The linear QNM shifts and separation constants are given by

ωn​ℓ​m\displaystyle\omega_{n\ell m} ≃ωn​ℓ​m0+∑kdω,n​ℓ​m(k)​α(k),\displaystyle\simeq\omega_{n\ell m}^{0}+\sum_{k}d_{\omega,n\ell m}^{(k)}\alpha^{(k)}\,, (3.37)
Bℓ​m​(a​ω)\displaystyle B_{\ell m}(a\omega) ≃Bℓ​m0​(a​ω)+∑kdB,ℓ​m(k)​α(k),\displaystyle\simeq B_{\ell m}^{0}(a\omega)+\sum_{k}d_{B,\ell m}^{(k)}\alpha^{(k)}\,, (3.38)

where the α(k)\alpha^{(k)} describe deviations from the generalized Teukolsky equation. In Fig. 23 we plot the thresholds at which the linear QNM shifts differ by more than 1%1\,\% from fully nonlinear results for different α(k)\alpha^{(k)}’s, focusing on the fundamental mode. The regime in which the beyond-Teukolsky framework is valid clearly shrinks as the BH spin increases, underlining the limitations of the nonrotating parameterized QNM framework to model the typical BBH ringdown signals observed in GWs (which have OPENχ≃0.7)\chi\simeq 0.7). The beyond-Teukolsky framework has been applied to specific higher-derivative gravity theories in [498].

The coefficients of the parameterized QNM framework beyond Schwarzschild/Kerr can be found in a public github repository [566], presented in [521] (see Appendix A).

3.2.4 Parameterized black hole metrics with test fields and the eikonal approximation

In the following, we discuss two closely related approaches for exploring QNMs beyond GR. We start by studying test fields on a parameterized BH background, and then we outline how the eikonal limit can be used in this context.

While the parameterized QNM framework from Section 3.2.3 connects QNM deviations with modifications of the effective potential, it cannot directly be used to infer the background metric unless the equations of motions beyond GR are being provided (e.g., in a theory-specific application). However, deviations from the GR QNMs in terms of the background spacetime deviations can be studied under certain assumptions – for instance considering test-field perturbations (as discussed below), or assuming the validity of the eikonal limit (discussed in Section 2.4). Since perturbations of test fields, e.g. the massless Klein-Gordon equation on the background spacetime, share qualitatively similar properties with gravitational perturbations in GR, one might still identify certain smoking gun features of new physics. A comprehensive overview of the literature on parameterized BH metrics is beyond the scope of this review [567, 568, 569, 570, 571, 572, 573, 574]; here we discuss QNM studies based on some of the most commonly used parameterizations.

The simplest cases are those where the background metric is static and spherically symmetric. Here, the master equation for a massless scalar field is simply given by

d2​Φd​r∗2+[ω2−V0​(r)]​Φ=0,\displaystyle\frac{\text{d}^{2}\Phi}{\text{d}r_{*}^{2}}+\left[\omega^{2}-V_{0}(r)\right]\Phi=0\,, (3.39)

where

V0​(r)=−gt​t​(r)​[ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)r2+12​r​gt​t​(r)​dd​r​gt​t​(r)gr​r​(r)]\displaystyle V_{0}(r)=-g_{tt}(r)\left[\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^{2}}+\frac{1}{2rg_{tt}(r)}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}\frac{g_{tt}(r)}{g_{rr}(r)}\right] (3.40)

and d​r=−gr​r(r)/gt​t(r)​d​r∗\text{d}r=\sqrt{-g_{rr}(r)/g_{tt}(r)}\text{d}r_{*}.
