Scalar [570, 575] and axial gravitational perturbations (assuming the GR background equations) [576, 374, 375] have been studied for some of these parameterizations. It is also possible to construct scalar-tensor theories of gravity such that these static, spherically symmetric parameterized metrics can be “reverse engineered” to be exact solutions of the theory, so that one can consistently compute the QNMs in the full theory [577]. The QNM overtones are very sensitive to the properties of the parameterized metrics close to the horizon [565].

The problem becomes significantly more complicated for rotating BHs because even test fields do not, in general, yield separable perturbation equations. Some progress is possible for special classes of axisymmetric BHs for which separability holds [578]. In particular, scalar QNMs of rotating spacetimes that describe deviations from Kerr BHs through a single parameter have been analyzed using Leaver’s method [579]. There has also been some progress on computing the QNMs of nonseparable scalar perturbations in non-Kerr backgrounds, with analytical or numerical tools [507, 508, 580].

Next we outline how the eikonal approximation, reviewed in Section 2.4, has been used in the present context. The key aspect of the “eikonal limit” (the limit of large angular numbers ℓ\ell) is that the QNMs of perturbations induced by test fields can be directly related to properties of the unstable photon orbit at the light ring. This connection implies that, in GR, the QNM frequencies can be expressed solely in terms of the properties of the background metric. This is a very convenient simplification that opens a variety of theory-agnostic tests based on beyond-Kerr spacetimes.

The correspondence was first established by connecting the QNM frequency to the peak of the effective potential and to circular photon orbits [228, 581]. It has then been shown that the orbital period Ω\Omega and Lyapunov exponent λ\lambda can be used to approximate both the real and imaginary part of the fundamental QNM [582, 67, 234, 68]. This is also in agreement with a WKB analysis [237, 68], yielding

ω=Ω​ℓ−i⁡(n+12)​|λ|.\displaystyle\omega=\Omega\ell-\mathrm{i}\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)|\lambda|\,. (3.41)

Further GR-related studies can be found in [68, 69, 70, 46, 47, 583].

In a series of works [68, 584, 236, 585, 586, 491], the eikonal limit was also studied in theories beyond GR. In a theory-agnostic approach, one could attempt to use the eikonal limit in modified theories of gravity in order to compute QNMs from the modified background metric, provided there are no additional fields that lead to coupled perturbation equations [584]. However, the correspondence does not always hold [587, 588], in particular when considering theories with additional scalar or vector field that lead to coupled perturbation equations. Moreover, a practical limitation of the method is that small-ℓ\ell multipoles are dominant in GW data, whereas the eikonal approximation (while still accurate at the percent level even for ℓ=2\ell=2) is more accurate for large ℓ\ell. Despite complications due to its low accuracy for the dominant quadrupolar mode ℓ=2\ell=2, the eikonal approximation has been applied to obtain bounds for different types of modifications to the Kerr spacetime using both current (observational) and future (simulated) GW data [589, 590, 591, 592].

3.2.5 Effective field theory of QNMs

Yet another possibility for parameterizing the QNMs of a gravity theory is to do so directly at the level of the action. In the Schwarzschild case this can be done by listing all the possible covariant terms at first order in perturbations, including possible contributions from scalar and vector fields [445], following a covariant version of the formalism developed for cosmological perturbations in [593, 594]. A more general result is the EFT of QNMs of any spherically symmetric metric plus a scalar field coupled to gravity [595]. By assuming a spin-2, unitary, Lorentz invariant theory of gravity coupled to a spin-0 field, perturbations of a generic nonrotating background metric of the form

d​s2=−a​(r)2​d​t2+d​r2b​(r)2+c​(r)2​(d​θ2+sin2⁡θ​d​ϕ2)\mathrm{d}s^{2}=-a(r)^{2}\mathrm{d}t^{2}+\frac{\mathrm{d}r^{2}}{b(r)^{2}}+c(r)^{2}\left(\mathrm{d}\theta^{2}+\sin^{2}\!\theta\,\mathrm{d}\phi^{2}\right) (3.42)

can be studied for a generic background scalar field Φ⁡(r)\Phi(r). By choosing the unitary gauge, the scalar field perturbations can be set to vanish (i.e., δ​Φ=0\delta\Phi=0), and the most general action for linear perturbations at leading order in derivative terms for both axial and polar perturbations reads [595]

S\displaystyle S =∫d4​x​−g​[R−Λ⁡(r)−f⁡(r)​gr​r+M2​(r)​(δ​gr​r)2].\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}^{4}x\sqrt{-g}\left[R-\Lambda(r)-f(r)g^{rr}+M_{2}(r)\left(\delta g^{rr}\right)^{2}\right]\,. (3.43)

The only free functions of this action are Λ⁡(r)\Lambda(r), f⁡(r)f(r) and M2​(r)M_{2}(r). However, a condition from the constraint equation can be imposed to relate Λ⁡(r)\Lambda(r) and f⁡(r)f(r) with the background metric. These two functions are the only ones responsible for the perturbations in the odd sector, meaning that the modified Regge-Wheeler equation only depends on the background metric, and it reads

d2​Ψd​r∗2+[ω2+a2​b2​(c′′c−2​c′2c2+a′​c′a​c+b′​c′b​c−ℓ2+ℓ−2b2​c2)]​Ψ=0,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}\Psi}{\mathrm{d}r_{*}^{2}}+\left[\omega^{2}+a^{2}b^{2}\left(\frac{c^{\prime\prime}}{c}-2\frac{c^{\prime 2}}{c^{2}}+\frac{a^{\prime}c^{\prime}}{ac}+\frac{b^{\prime}c^{\prime}}{bc}-\frac{\ell^{2}+\ell-2}{b^{2}c^{2}}\right)\right]\Psi=0\,, (3.44)

where the tortoise coordinate is d​r∗=d​r/a​b\mathrm{d}r_{*}=\mathrm{d}r/ab. The equation for polar perturbations is more involved [595]. This calculation was also extended to the slowly rotating case [596]. These EFTs of QNMs have been constructed for the case of a scalar field coupled to gravity, but one could in principle follow the same strategy to add relevant operators for other cases, including different couplings. At present, the EFT of QNMs for the fully rotating case is still lacking.

3.3 New physics at the horizon

Initial contributors: Afshordi, Maggio, Pani

3.3.1 Motivation

Einstein’s theory of GR is in agreement with all of our experimental evidence for BHs so far, but it leaves unsolved some of the deepest theoretical puzzles unveiled by these mysterious objects. In particular, the semi-classical picture of Hawking’s BH evaporation is incompatible with quantum unitarity, the microstates underlying the enormous BH entropy are unknown, and the singularities hidden by the BH horizon signal a breakdown of classical physics inside BHs. These far-reaching problems are dramatic manifestations of the incompleteness of our fundamental laws of nature.

Motivated by Penrose’s weak cosmic censorship conjecture [597], the incompleteness of GR has traditionally been overlooked in observations of astrophysical BHs, as it was assumed to manifest only near singularities, safely concealed behind event horizons. However, a drastic violation of the classical causal structure of event horizons, beyond small corrections [598, 599], appears necessary to evaporate away BH information. In particular, the so-called “firewall paradox” [600] has been invoked to suggest that it is impossible to reconcile the three (apparently modest) assumptions of locality, causality, and unitarity outside regular event horizons if the entropy SBHS_{\rm BH} of an evaporating BH follows its horizon area AH=4​π​(r+2+a2)A_{\rm H}=4\pi(r_{+}^{2}+a^{2}). The relation between the two, according to Bekenstein and Hawking, reads:

SBH=AH4​G​ℏ.S_{\rm BH}=\frac{A_{\rm H}}{4G\hbar}\,. (3.45)

While the paradox only manifests itself about halfway through the BH evaporation (after the so-called Page time tPage∼G2​M3/ℏt_{\rm Page}\sim G^{2}M^{3}/\hbar), it has been argued [600] that due to the fast scrambling of quantum states within BHs [601], a significant quantum modification of the classical horizon, or “firewall,” would happen much earlier, i.e., within a “scrambling time”:

tscr≃ℏ2​π​kB​TH​ln⁡SBH=κ+−1​ln⁡(AH4​ℏ​G)∼G​M​ln⁡(G​M2ℏ)≪tPage,t_{\rm scr}\simeq\frac{\hbar}{2\pi k_{B}T_{\rm H}}\ln S_{\rm BH}=\kappa_{+}^{-1}\ln\left(A_{\rm H}\over 4\hbar G\right)\sim GM\ln\left(GM^{2}\over\hbar\right)\ll t_{\rm Page}, (3.46)

where TH=2​(r+−M)/AHT_{\rm H}=2(r_{+}-M)/A_{\rm H} is the horizon (or Hawking) temperature, and κ+\kappa_{+} is the surface gravity of the event horizon. This coincides with the time scale to reflect a signal off a mirror, within a Planck proper distance from the BH horizon [602].

An alternative derivation comes from studying a BH in equilibrium with a thermal bath of radiation at the Hawking temperature. Due to the blueshift effect near the BH horizon, the total entropy of the radiation bath (even within a finite box) is infinite. However, if we consider the microstates of radiation near the horizon as contributing to the BH entropy, then we would require Srad<SBHS_{\rm rad}<S_{\rm BH}, which suggests that the free radiation needs to be cut off by a “firewall” near the horizon. The inequality Srad<SBHS_{\rm rad}<S_{\rm BH} provides an upper limit on the time for null signals to be reflected off the firewall, which coincides with the scrambling time in Eq. (3.46) [603]. If the bath temperature deviates from the Hawking temperature, then the dynamical backreaction of the quantum vacuum stress on the geometry would truncate the classical spacetime even farther out, resulting in shorter time scales, as small as half of Eq. (3.46) [604].

The executive summary of the state of affairs is that the assertion of a Bekenstein-Hawking area law for thermodynamic entropy (3.45) suggests significant deviations from classical GR dynamics near BH event horizons (e.g., [598, 605]). This challenges the classical BH paradigm, and thus cosmic censorship, which posits that the fate of the gravitational collapse of sufficiently massive and compact stars is a classical BH, surrounded by regular event horizons. Therefore, horizonless compact objects can emerge due to quantum modifications at the horizon scale (e.g., gravastars [606] and wormholes [607, 608, 609]) or due to a modified theory of gravity describing the interior of compact objects (e.g., fuzzballs [610, 611, 612, 613] and nonlocal stars [614, 615]).

3.3.2 General signatures of horizon-scale structures

If the remnant of a compact binary coalescence is a horizonless compact object, the QNM spectrum is predicted to deviate from the BH one [383, 397], also showing a breaking of isospectrality between axial and polar modes [399, 616, 617, 618]. When the horizonless remnant is ultracompact (i.e., featuring a photon sphere [8]), a characteristic cavity in the effective potential of the perturbation exists between the light ring and the object. In the TD, the prompt ringdown signal would be nearly indistinguishable from the signal from a BH, since it is excited at the light ring. After a travel time in the cavity of the effective potential, an additional signal could be emitted in the form of GW echoes [383, 397, 619]. Therefore, GW echoes in the postmerger phase of a compact binary coalescence are possible smoking guns for the formation of a horizonless ultracompact object [2, 620, 621, 397] (see also [622, 623, 624, 625]). Assuming that these horizonless compact objects are stabilized outside a proper Planck length of the would-be classical horizon results in echo time delays that precisely match the quantum scrambling time τecho=tscr\tau_{\rm echo}=t_{\rm scr} of Eq. (3.46) in generic circumstances [626].

Since their conception, GW echoes have been studied in a variety of contexts, including near-horizon quantum structures [383, 397, 627], ultracompact stars [628, 621, 629, 630, 631], BHs in modified theories of gravity in which the graviton reflects effectively on a hard wall [632, 633], or any other scenarios producing a BH effective potential with multiple peaks. Echoes have also been studied in the fuzzball scenario. The cavity reflections of low-energy scalars can be expressed as a sum over the number of bounces at the throat of these geometries [634, 635]. More recently, GW echoes have been studied for specific BH (or fuzzball) microstates in string theory [636, 637, 638].

The cavity picture of GW echoes we have presented so far is semi-classical, and limited to linearized perturbations. Therefore, it is fair to ask whether such a naive description would survive a fully quantum and/or nonlinear treatment, a point that we shall come back to later in this subsection. However, it is interesting to note that a fully quantum language for the very same dynamics was already proposed by Bekenstein back in 1972 [639], in terms of quantized BH horizon area. Roughly speaking, the QNMs of the cavity (significantly different and much more long-lived than those of a GR BH) have frequencies ωn≃2​π​n​τecho−1\omega_{n}\simeq 2\pi n\tau^{-1}_{\rm echo} + const., where nn is an integer. If we conceive the ringdown of a horizonless compact object as the spontaneous emission of gravitons, the gravitons appear to be emitted at discrete energy quanta of Δ​E=2​π​ℏ​τecho−1\Delta E=2\pi\hbar\tau^{-1}_{\rm echo}. Using the first law of BH thermodynamics, κ+​Δ​AH/(8​π)=Δ​E\kappa_{+}\Delta A_{\rm H}/(8\pi)=\Delta E (and ignoring the BH spin for now), the BH area/entropy can only vary by a discrete amount:

Δ​AH=16​π2​ℏ​Gκ+​τecho.\Delta A_{\rm H}=\frac{16\pi^{2}\hbar G}{\kappa_{+}\tau_{\rm echo}}. (3.47)

This suggests that the discretization of the horizon area proposed by Bekenstein [639] is directly related to the presence of echoes in the semi-classical cavity description [640]. This connection was also extended to spinning BHs [641], where the picture is more complex [642]. The connection was initially proposed to apply to the prompt ringdown QNM emission [643], but this would require a more drastic departure from current understanding [644].

A similar quantum description of the emission mechanism for GW echoes can be provided. Considering Hawking radiation as quantum spontaneous emission of gravitons in vacuum, incident GWs onto a quantum BH should lead to quantum stimulated emission [645], amplifying the amplitude of Hawking radiation. This stimulation is caused by the classical infalling GWs during ringdown, which in turn can lead to the emergence of GW echoes [646, 627].

Given the uncertainty on the nature of quantum physics that replaces the classical description of event horizons, it is reasonable to seek a model-agnostic EFT approach allowing for generic deviations, as a systematic expansion [647]. An ambiguity in this approach is to decide on the correct small parameter (e.g., distance, frequency, energy, curvature, or something else) that controls the expansion. For example, strictly local EFT approaches to modifications of GR (e.g., [458, 648]) are unlikely to accommodate the nonlocal or highly unusual physics necessary to replace horizons by ultracompact objects, or to address the BH information paradox.

3.3.3 QNM spectrum beyond Kerr

If the remnant is not compact enough to feature a photon sphere, cavity effects are absent, and so are echoes in the post-merger phase. Nevertheless, the ringdown would still show deviations from the ordinary BH QNMs, different QNM excitation [649], or excitation of new nongravitational modes [537] (e.g. extra fluid modes in objects containing matter [544, 650], or scalar excitations in boson star models [651, 652, 653, 654]). These deviations are mostly degenerate with those predicted by beyond-GR theories (see Sections 3.1 and 3.2). They may also resemble the post-merger phenomenology of neutron star remnants, featuring long-lived modes, fluid-mode excitations, and in general being qualitatively different from the ordinary BH ringdown. The QNMs of exotic compact objects have been computed for boson stars [655, 656], gravastars [657, 658, 659], BH microstates within the fuzzball paradigm [636, 637, 660, 638], and generic compact objects described within the membrane paradigm [399, 618].

3.3.4 Echo morphology

For a classical BH, the ringdown phase can be understood as the spacetime’s response to perturbations occurring near the photon sphere [661]. Part of the signal produced near the light ring propagates outward, reaching distant observers, while the remainder travels inward towards the horizon, without influencing the observables at large distances. This occurs because classical BHs are by definition perfect absorbers, with their horizon serving as a one-way, null hypersurface.

However, this property relies on the existence of a classical horizon and is dramatically different for horizonless ultracompact objects or in any model predicting new physics at the horizon scale (see [8] for a detailed overview). In this case, perturbations can probe the inner boundary of compact objects (such as the regular core of an ultracompact object, or a modified horizon) and reach an observer at large distance, carrying crucial information about putative effects occurring at the horizon scale.

Simply by causality, the effects of the horizon-scale structure cannot show up in the signal before a time of the order of the (round-trip) light crossing time from the photon ring to the boundary. Assuming that the background spacetime is sufficiently close to the Kerr metric, this time scale is no shorter than [383, 397, 662]

τecho∼2M[1+(1−χ2)−1/2]|lnϵ|,\tau_{\rm echo}\sim 2M\left[1+(1-\chi^{2})^{-1/2}\right]|\ln\epsilon|\,, (3.48)

where ϵ∼d2/M2≪1\epsilon\sim d^{2}/M^{2}\ll 1, and dd is the proper distance between the would-be horizon and any putative effective surface. If such distance is Planckian, d∼ℏ1/2≈10−35​md\sim\hbar^{1/2}\approx 10^{-35}{\rm m}, then ϵ∼SBH−1\epsilon\sim S^{-1}_{\rm BH}, and this time scale is comparable to the scrambling time (3.46). Depending on the model, the radiation can take significant time to probe the object’s interior, in which case the time scale above should be augmented by the corresponding time delay. Therefore, if the spacetime geometry is similar to Kerr, the prompt ringdown is essentially indistinguishable from that of an ordinary BH for times shorter than τecho\tau_{\rm echo}.

On longer time scales, the reflected pulse is semi-trapped between the object and the light ring. With each interaction at the light ring, a portion escapes to distant observers, producing a series of echoes with progressively diminishing amplitudes. These reflections occur at intervals defined by a characteristic echo delay time, which is no shorter than τecho\tau_{\rm echo}. Remarkably, owing to the logarithmic dependence of Eq. (3.48), even if the proper distance of the effective surface is Planckian, the delay time is only a factor |ln⁡ϵ|=|ln⁡(ℏ/M2)||\ln\epsilon|=|\ln(\hbar/M^{2})| (≈175\approx 175 for a solar-mass object) longer than the BH light crossing time 4​M4M, and therefore potentially observable in the post-merger phase following the prompt ringdown.

Consideration of possible exotic classical interiors for some ultracompact horizonless objects have led to proposals for much longer (geometric) echo time delays [663, 664, 665]. However, as noted above, the quantum vacuum backreaction [604] appears to truncate these geometries, and/or their entropy is likely to significantly exceed the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy (3.45) [603]. This suggests that, even if such long echo time delays with τecho≳tscr\tau_{\rm echo}\gtrsim t_{\rm scr} exist, they cannot be understood within a semi-classical geometric description.

The photon sphere barrier acts as a frequency dependent high-pass filter. The characteristic frequencies governing the prompt ringdown are very similar to the BH QNM frequencies, being essentially governed by the excitation of the photon sphere [383]. The frequencies governing each subsequent GW echo become progressively smaller and, at very late times, the GW signal is dominated by low-frequency QNMs associated with the partially reflecting boundary conditions at the inner boundary [666, 667, 398].

Echoes appear in the transient regime following the universal prompt ringdown, and developing while the remnant reaches stationarity on long time scales. While such echoes are generic smoking guns of nonconventional horizon-scale physics, their actual detectability crucially depends on the object’s effective reflectivity, ℛ{\cal R}, since the amplitude of each subsequent echo is suppressed by a factor of ℛ{\cal R} relative to the previous one (see Fig. 24 for an illustration). The reflectivity is a model-dependent, complex function of the frequency which can be conveniently defined from the asymptotic behavior of the perturbations near the effective surface [399]

Ψ∼e−i​ω​(x−x0)+ℛ⁡(ω)​ei​ω​(x−x0),\Psi\sim e^{-i\omega(x-x_{0})}+{\cal R}(\omega)e^{i\omega(x-x_{0})}\,, (3.49)

where Ψ\Psi is a suitably-defined wave function describing the radial component of the perturbation [669, 670], and x0x_{0} is the location of the effective surface in the tortoise coordinate. The ordinary boundary condition for a classical BH is ℛ=0{\cal R}=0 for any frequency (perfect absorption). On the contrary, an object whose interaction with GWs is negligible would have |ℛ|2=1|{\cal R}|^{2}=1 (perfect “reflection,” which can actually correspond to radiation crossing the object without being absorbed). Overall, the frequency-dependent phase factor in ℛ{\cal R} accounts for any time delay within the object. As discussed in the next section, the effective reflectivity modulates the signal and governs the amplitude of subsequent echoes, which depends also on the initial conditions for the perturbation [671, 672, 673, 674, 675]. A list of models for which the reflectivity has been explicitly computed is given in Table 4. Recently, the effective reflectivity has been linked to the shear and bulk viscosity parameters within the membrane paradigm [676].

Finally, using WKB theory, the effective perturbation potential of certain types of exotic compact objects can be reconstructed from a knowledge of their QNM spectrum [677, 678], which is imprinted in the ringdown at very late times.

3.3.5 Echo templates

Several phenomenological templates for GW echoes have been developed based on standard GR ringdown templates, augmented with additional parameters representing the echoes emission [8].

A first proposal is a TD template based on a GR inspiral-merger-ringdown (IMR) template ℳ⁡(t)\mathcal{M}(t) with five additional parameters [662],

h⁡(t)=A​∑n=0∞(−1)n+1​γn​ℳ​(t+tmerger−techo−n​Δ​techo,t0),h(t)=A\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}\gamma^{n}\mathcal{M}(t+t_{\rm{merger}}-t_{\rm{echo}}-n\Delta t_{\rm{echo}},t_{0})\,, (3.50)

where AA is the overall amplitude of the echo template, γ\gamma is the damping factor of successive echoes, techot_{\rm echo} is the time of arrival of the first echo, τecho\tau_{\rm echo} is the time-interval in between successive echoes, (−1)n+1(-1)^{n+1} is the term due to the phase inversion in each reflection, ℳ⁡(t,t0)=Θ⁡(t,t0)​ℳ​(t)\mathcal{M}(t,t_{0})=\Theta(t,t_{0})\mathcal{M}(t), and t0t_{0} quantifies which part of the GR merger template is truncated to produce the subsequent echoes. The smooth cut-off function is defined as

Θ⁡(t,t0)=12​{1+tanh⁡[12​ω​(t)​(t−tmerger−t0)]},\Theta(t,t_{0})=\frac{1}{2}\left\{1+\tanh\left[\frac{1}{2}\omega(t)\left(t-t_{\rm merger}-t_{0}\right)\right]\right\}\,, (3.51)

where ω⁡(t)\omega(t) is the frequency of the model as a function of time, and tmergert_{\rm merger} is the time at which the GR template peaks. This template (publicly available at [681]; see also Appendix A), was used to search for GW echoes using Bayesian model selection [682], and to analyze the events in the second Gravitational Wave Transient Catalog (GWTC) of the LVK Collaboration [529]. Phenomenological TD templates for the echoes in terms of superposition of individual modes were also studied [683], together with their detectability via a Fisher-information matrix approach.

A different FD template is based on a standard GR ringdown signal with two additional parameters, related to the object’s compactness and reflectivity [398]. At infinity, the perturbation is a purely outgoing wave

Ψ∼Z~HCO∞​(ω)​ei​ω​r∗,r∗→∞,\Psi\sim\tilde{Z}_{\rm{HCO}}^{\infty}(\omega)\ e^{i\omega r_{*}}\,,\qquad r_{*}\to\infty\,, (3.52)

(3.53)

The BH response at infinity for the fundamental ℓ=m=2\ell=m=2 QNM is the Fourier transform of

A FD template with three search parameters was also proposed [686] (publicly available at [681]; see also Appendix A):

h~​(ω)=1−ℛBH2​(ω)​h~0​(ω)​∑n=1NechoℛBH​(ω)n−1​e−i⁡(ω​τecho+ϕ)​(n−1),\tilde{h}(\omega)=\sqrt{1-\mathcal{R}_{\rm{BH}}^{2}(\omega)}\ \tilde{h}_{0}(\omega)\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\rm echo}}\mathcal{R}_{\rm{BH}}(\omega)^{n-1}e^{-i(\omega\tau_{\rm echo}+\phi)(n-1)}\,, (3.57)

where h~0​(ω)\tilde{h}_{0}(\omega) is obtained by cutting off the inspiral part of the best fit IMR waveform with a smooth function as in Eq. (3.51) with t0=−0.1​τechot_{0}=-0.1\tau_{\rm echo}, and ϕ\phi is a phase shift due to reflections between the surface and the potential barrier. The search parameters of the template are therefore (M,χ,ϕ)(M,\chi,\phi), where τecho\tau_{\rm echo} is determined by (M,χ)(M,\chi). This template was used to search for GW echoes from BBH events in the third observing run of the LVK Collaboration [687]. For additional details on the data analysis methodology and results, see Section 6.4.

3.3.6 Nonlinear effects and echoes in numerical relativity

In closing, let us address the question of whether our understanding of GW echoes (or any signature of new horizon physics) may survive beyond linear perturbation theory. Energy loss due to emitted echoes inevitably changes the background spacetime at third order in perturbation theory, decreasing τecho\tau_{\rm echo} for subsequent echoes [688, 689]. More drastically, one may imagine that the expansion of an apparent horizon due to the backreaction of an infalling wave packet may trap it before any potential reflection is possible [690] (but see [689] for a counterpoint).

Arguably, the holy grail for modeling any nonlinear novel horizon physics in the ringdown phase is its implementation into NR codes, which currently provide state-of-the-art full gravitational waveforms from compact binary mergers. This is a hard problem, especially given the uncertain nature of the quantum gravity physics under consideration. Studies of the post-merger signal from coalescing boson stars in the large mass-ratio regime [654] showcase the subsequent emission of bursts at high frequencies, sourced by perturbations of the remnant’s internal degrees of freedom. However, in this case the maximum compactness is far from the values discussed above, which makes a systematic separation of ringdown and echoes impossible. Another approach [675] stitches a numerical GR simulated volume into an outer region that obeys linearized perturbations, with a dissipative dispersion relation that models Boltzmann echoes [646, 627]. Recently, a numerical implementation of novel near-horizon physics has been carried out in the form of a numerical solver for the GR initial-boundary value problem [689, 691]. While these studies have provided examples of fully nonlinear evolution of GR within an effective numerical “membrane paradigm,” the correct scheme to evolve this membrane depends on the new physics responsible for its formation and thus remains a challenging open problem, both theoretically and numerically.

3.3.7 Other proposals for new physics at the horizon scale

In addition to predicting deviations in the standard BH QNMs, new modes in the ringdown, or echoes in the post-merger phase, specific models can introduce other subtle effects.

For example, while models of horizonless ultracompact objects are expected to have the same ringdown phenomenology at least qualitatively, peculiar effects departing from this picture might arise. The ringdown of BH microstates emerging in the fuzzball scenario is much richer and more complex than in other models due to the absence of spatial isometries [636]. This introduces mode mixing and effectively quenches the echoes, even in the absence of effective absorption.

In the frozen-star model [692, 693], the pressure is maximally negative in the radial direction and vanishes in the tangential directions. The interior is not described by a classical geometry but, at the microscopic level, is described by a fluid of highly excited, interacting, closed, fundamental strings. Due to the peculiar equation of state, perturbations in the interior vanish identically at the classical level, but display low-frequency, long-lived modes whose lifetime depends on the string length, which is parametrically longer than the Planck length [694].

Finally, if massless modes propagate at different speeds (as predicted, for instance, in Lorentz-violating theories), each would possess its own distinct horizon. One mode could potentially probe the interior of the other’s horizon, leading to energy extraction from the BH and a distinctive late-time relaxation behavior [450].

Compact objects with an ergoregion but without a horizon might be affected by an ergoregion instability when spinning sufficiently fast [597, 186]. The instability time scale is much longer than the decay time of the BH ringdown and the GW echo delay time [669]. The ergoregion instability was studied in uniform-density stars [695], gravastars [696], and boson stars [697]. The only way to prevent the instability is by absorbing the negative-energy states in the ergoregion with dissipation mechanisms [669].

4 Quasinormal mode amplitudes

One thought spectra are marvelous, but it is not possible to make progress there. Just as if you have the wings of a butterfly, then certainly it is very regular with the colors and so on, but nobody thought one could get the basis of biology from the coloring of the wing of a butterfly. So that was the way to look at it.

Niels Bohr, Interview by T.S. Kuhn, L. Rosenfeld, E. Rudinger, and A. Petersen,

October 31, 1962, AHQP.

After decades of work, we now have a deep understanding of the ornate structure of BH QNM spectra in GR and beyond GR. However, to make progress in the experimental implementation of BH spectroscopy we need a similar understanding of QNM excitation; more specifically, we must be able to predict the amplitudes of the dominant modes resulting from a binary merger, and their dynamical excitation in the full nonlinear theory. The mode amplitudes are usually computed by solving the radial perturbation equation using Green’s functions techniques (Section 4.1), and then computing the so-called “excitation factors” and “excitation coefficients” (Section 4.2). These basic techniques have recently been extended to compute the QNM amplitudes at quadratic order, both in Schwarzschild (Section 4.3) and in Kerr (Section 4.4). The analytical results obtained in this way are complementary to more empirical approaches, where the amplitudes of linear and nonlinear QNMs are extracted by direct fits of TD evolutions of the perturbation equations for single perturbed BHs, or from NR simulations of BBH mergers. These efforts are reviewed in Section 4.5.

4.1 Green’s functions

Initial contributor: Lagos

Standard spectroscopic tests of gravity are concerned with testing the exponential temporal evolution of the signal by measuring the QNM frequencies of different angular harmonics. However, the complete ringdown solution is characterized by additional nontrivial temporal dependence, as well as a spatial evolution. Both of these bring information about the causal structure of the signal, when QNMs are expected to dominate the emission, and the process setting the initial conditions of ringdown relaxation (e.g., the merger of a BBH system).

At linear order in perturbation theory, the ringdown signal satisfies the RWZ equations (2.7) for Schwarzschild BHs and the Teukolsky equation (2.5) for Kerr BHs. These are linear differential equations that can be formally solved with the Green’s function approach.

The properties of the Green’s function of ringdown signals have been thoroughly analyzed [155, 359, 165, 338, 698, 241, 699, 700, 701, 702, 703]. Since the equations of interest have a separable angular dependence in the FD, let us consider the following representative Schrödinger-like 1D equation in space:

[∂r∗2+ω2−V2(ω,r∗)]Ψ2(ω,r∗)=0,\left[\partial_{r_{*}}^{2}+\omega^{2}-V_{2}(\omega,r_{*})\right]\Psi_{2}(\omega,r_{*})=0\,, (4.1)

where r∗r_{*} is the tortoise coordinate, defined by d​r∗/d​r=(r2+a2)/Δdr_{*}/dr=(r^{2}+a^{2})/\Delta with Δ\Delta given in Eq. (2.1c), and ranging from r∗→−∞r_{*}\rightarrow-\infty towards the horizon (r→r+r\rightarrow r_{+}) and r∗→+∞r_{*}\rightarrow+\infty towards spatial infinity (r→+∞r\rightarrow+\infty). Here, contrary to the ansatz made in Eq. (2.3), a Fourier transform of the solution has been performed

Ψ⁡(r∗,t,θ,ω)=∑ℓ,m∫−∞+∞d​ω2​π​e−i​ω​t​Ψ2​(ω,r∗)​Sℓ​ms​(θ,ϕ,a​ω).\Psi(r_{*},t,\theta,\omega)=\sum_{\ell,m}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}{d\omega\over 2\pi}e^{-i\omega t}\Psi_{2}(\omega,r_{*}){}_{s}S_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi;a\omega). (4.2)

Avoiding the exact ansatz in Eq. (2.3) is important for the solution to include not only QNM contributions, but to allow for additional time dependence.

The exact form of the effective potential V2​(ω,r∗)V_{2}(\omega,r_{*}) depends on the type of BH and perturbation variable. For Schwarzschild BHs, V2​(ω,r∗)V_{2}(\omega,r_{*}) matches the effective potentials V2±V_{2}^{\pm} defined in Eqs. (2.8)-(2.9), which are purely real, and do not depend on mm nor ω\omega. For Kerr BHs, the original radial Teukolsky equation (2.5) in terms of the Boyer-Lindquist coordinates does not take the form of Eq. (4.1). Nonetheless, a change of variables for the field will bring Eq. (2.5) into the form of Eq. (4.1) for the tortoise coordinate [704, 705, 706]. In this case, the potential V2​(ω,r∗)V_{2}(\omega,r_{*}) of Kerr will generally depend on mm and ω\omega, and it can be made real when ω\omega is real [704, 706]. For both types of BHs, Schwarzschild and Kerr, the effective potentials are short range. Specifically, the Kerr potential decays to zero towards spatial infinity, and to V2→ω2−(ω−a​m/(2​M​r+))2V_{2}\rightarrow\omega^{2}-(\omega-am/(2Mr_{+}))^{2} towards the horizon r+r_{+} [706]. For Schwarzschild, both potentials decay to zero in both limits.

A different radial field redefinition transforms the radial Teukolsky equation into the Sasaki-Nakamura equation [18], which has the form of Eq. (4.1) with an additional first-order derivative on the left-hand side, and a short-ranged potential that reduces to the Regge-Wheeler potential when a=0a=0. The Green’s function for Kerr can also be studied in the Sasaki-Nakamura formalism, but here our starting point will be that fields are chosen such that no first derivatives are present, and hence Eq. (4.1) holds.

The radial Green’s function, Gω​ℓ​mG_{\omega\ell m}, satisfies

[∂r∗2+ω2−V2(ω,r∗)]Gω​ℓ​m(r∗|r¯∗)=δ(r∗−r¯∗),\left[\partial_{r_{*}}^{2}+\omega^{2}-V_{2}(\omega,r_{*})\right]G_{\omega\ell m}(r_{*}|\bar{r}_{*})=\delta(r_{*}-\bar{r}_{*})\,, (4.3)

and it is related to the Green’s function in the TD by a Laplace transform:

G(t,r∗,θ,ϕ|t¯,r¯∗,θ¯,ϕ¯)=∑ℓ​m∫−∞+i​ϵ+∞+i​ϵd​ω2​πe−i​ω​(t−t¯)Gω​ℓ​m(r∗|r¯∗)Sℓ​ms(θ,ϕ;aω)Sℓ​m∗s(θ¯,ϕ¯;aω).G(t,r_{*},\theta,\phi|\bar{t},\bar{r}_{*},\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi})=\sum_{\ell m}\int_{-\infty+i\epsilon}^{+\infty+i\epsilon}{d\omega\over 2\pi}e^{-i\omega(t-\bar{t})}G_{\omega\ell m}(r_{*}|\bar{r}_{*}){}_{s}S_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi;a\omega){}_{s}S_{\ell m}^{*}(\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi};a\omega). (4.4)

The integral is performed slightly above the real axis, such that G=0G=0 if t−t¯<0t-\bar{t}<0 – i.e., this is a retarded Green’s function.

Once the Green’s function is known, one can use it to evolve any initial conditions on the perturbation field Ψ\Psi and obtain its general solution. Consider the initial conditions

ψ0​(r∗,θ,ϕ)≡Ψ⁡(t=0),ψ˙0​(r∗,θ,ϕ)≡∂tΨ⁡(t)|t=0,\displaystyle\psi_{0}(r_{*},\theta,\phi)\equiv\Psi(t=0)\,,\quad\dot{\psi}_{0}(r_{*},\theta,\phi)\equiv\partial_{t}\Psi(t)|_{t=0}\,, (4.5)

where we set t=0t=0 as the initial time. The Green’s function can be used to evolve the initial linear perturbation forward in time as follows:

Ψ⁡(t,r∗,θ,ϕ)=∫d​ω2​π​d​r¯∗​𝑑Ω¯​e−i​ω​t​Gω​ℓ​m​(r∗|r¯∗)​ℐ0​(r¯∗,θ¯,ϕ¯)​Sℓ​ms​(θ,ϕ,a​ω)​S∗ℓ​ms​(θ¯,ϕ¯,a​ω),\displaystyle\Psi(t,r_{*},\theta,\phi)=\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}d\bar{r}_{*}d\bar{\Omega}e^{-i\omega t}G_{\omega\ell m}(r_{*}|\bar{r}_{*})\mathcal{I}_{0}(\bar{r}_{*},\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi}){}_{s}S_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi;a\omega){}_{s}S_{\ell m}^{*}(\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi};a\omega), (4.6)
ℐ0​(r¯∗,θ¯,ϕ¯)≡i​ω​ψ0​(r¯∗,θ¯,ϕ¯)−ψ˙0​(r¯∗,θ¯,ϕ¯).\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{0}(\bar{r}_{*},\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi})\equiv i\omega\psi_{0}(\bar{r}_{*},\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi})-\dot{\psi}_{0}(\bar{r}_{*},\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi}).

Therefore, the Green’s function allows us to understand the time evolution and causality properties of ringdown signals. The Green’s function solution can be constructed from two homogeneous solutions gout​(r∗)g_{\rm out}(r_{*}) and gin​(r∗)g_{\rm in}(r_{*}) satisfying Eq. (4.1) with the appropriate asymptotic boundary conditions:

gin→e−i​kH​r∗forr∗→−∞,\displaystyle g_{\rm in}\rightarrow e^{-ik_{H}r_{*}}\,\,\,\,\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad{\rm for}\quad r_{*}\rightarrow-\infty,
gin→𝒜in​e−i​ω​r∗+ℬin​ei​ω​r∗forr∗→+∞,\displaystyle g_{\rm in}\rightarrow{\cal A}_{\rm in}e^{-i\omega r_{*}}+{\cal B}_{\rm in}e^{i\omega r_{*}}\,\,\quad\quad\quad{\rm for}\quad r_{*}\rightarrow+\infty, (4.7)
gout→𝒜out​ei​kH​r∗+ℬout​e−i​kH​r∗forr∗→−∞,\displaystyle g_{\rm out}\rightarrow{\cal A}_{\rm out}e^{ik_{H}r_{*}}+{\cal B}_{\rm out}e^{-ik_{H}r_{*}}\quad{\rm for}\quad r_{*}\rightarrow-\infty,
gout→ei​ω​r∗forr∗→+∞,\displaystyle g_{\rm out}\rightarrow e^{i\omega r_{*}}\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\,\,\quad{\rm for}\quad r_{*}\rightarrow+\infty\,, (4.8)

where kH=ω−m​a/(2​M​r+)k_{H}=\omega-ma/(2Mr_{+}), we have used the fact that the potential VV vanishes towards spatial infinity and asymptotes a constant towards the horizon (which vanishes when a=0a=0), and we have suppressed the dependence of the coefficients 𝒜in,ℬin,𝒜out,ℬout{\cal A}_{\rm in},{\cal B}_{\rm in},{\cal A}_{\rm out},{\cal B}_{\rm out} on (ω,m,ℓ)(\omega,m,\ell) to avoid clutter. Combining this asymptotic radial dependence with the decomposition in Eq. (4.2), gout​(r∗)g_{\rm out}(r_{*}) describes outgoing plane waves toward spatial infinity, while gin​(r∗)g_{\rm in}(r_{*}) describes ingoing plane waves toward the horizon.

The radial Green’s function Gω​ℓ​mG_{\omega\ell m} can then be constructed as:

Gω​ℓ​m​(r∗|r¯∗)=1W​gout​(r∗⁣>)​gin​(r∗⁣<),\displaystyle G_{\omega\ell m}(r_{*}|\bar{r}_{*})={1\over W}g_{\rm out}(r_{*>})g_{\rm in}(r_{*<}), (4.9)

where r∗⁣>=max⁡(r∗,r¯∗)r_{*>}=\max(r_{*},\bar{r}_{*}), r∗⁣<=min⁡(r∗,r¯∗)r_{*<}=\min(r_{*},\bar{r}_{*}), and WW is the Wronskian:

W⁡(ω)≡gin​(r∗)​∂r∗gout​(r∗)−gout​(r∗)​∂r∗gin​(r∗).\displaystyle W(\omega)\equiv g_{\rm in}(r_{*})\partial_{r_{*}}g_{\rm out}(r_{*})-g_{\rm out}(r_{*})\partial_{r_{*}}g_{\rm in}(r_{*})\,. (4.10)

Note that the Wronskian depends on ω\omega, but it is independent of r∗r_{*}, since both gout​(r∗)g_{\rm out}(r_{*}) and gin​(r∗)g_{\rm in}(r_{*}) satisfy Eq. (4.1). In particular, one obtains:

W=2​i​ω​𝒜in=2​i​ω​𝒜out.W=2i\omega{\cal A}_{\rm in}=2i\omega{\cal A}_{\rm out}. (4.11)

Replacing into Eq. (4.6), the general ringdown solution is

Ψ⁡(r∗,t,θ,ω)=\displaystyle\Psi(r_{*},t,\theta,\omega)= ∫d​ω2​π​𝑑Ω¯​e−i​ω​t​Sℓ​ms​(θ,ϕ,a​ω)​S∗ℓ​ms​(θ¯,ϕ¯,a​ω)\displaystyle\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}d\bar{\Omega}e^{-i\omega t}{}_{s}S_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi;a\omega){}_{s}S_{\ell m}^{*}(\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi};a\omega)
×[gout​(r∗)W​∫−∞r∗d​r¯∗​gin​(r¯∗)​ℐ0​(r¯∗,θ¯,ϕ¯)+gin​(r∗)W​∫r∗+∞d​r¯∗​gout​(r¯∗)​ℐ0​(r¯∗,θ¯,ϕ¯)].\displaystyle\times\left[\frac{g_{\rm out}(r_{*})}{W}\int_{-\infty}^{r_{*}}d\bar{r}_{*}g_{\rm in}(\bar{r}_{*})\mathcal{I}_{0}(\bar{r}_{*},\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi})+\frac{g_{\rm in}(r_{*})}{W}\int^{+\infty}_{r_{*}}d\bar{r}_{*}g_{\rm out}(\bar{r}_{*})\mathcal{I}_{0}(\bar{r}_{*},\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi})\right]. (4.12)

Hence, the overall radial evolution of ringdown signals is fully determined by gout​(r∗)g_{\rm out}(r_{*}) and gin​(r∗)g_{\rm in}(r_{*}), whereas the temporal evolution is fully determined by the ω\omega dependence of the Green’s function Gω​ℓ​mG_{\omega\ell m} and the spheroidal harmonics. The initial conditions determine the value of the constant factors in the ringdown signal.

The exact form of Gω​ℓ​mG_{\omega\ell m} depends on the potential V2V_{2}, and to date an analytical closed-form expression for Gω​ℓ​mG_{\omega\ell m} in the full parameter space (ω,r∗)(\omega,r_{*}) is not known, although expressions as infinite expansion series [241, 707, 708], qualitative, and asymptotic features are well known, at least for Schwarzschild BHs [155, 165, 698]. As discussed below, approximate expansions have also been calculated for Kerr BHs, and they have analogous features. Since the derivations for Kerr are more complicated, from now on we will focus on Schwarzschild BHs and discuss general features of the Green’s function.

In particular, the functions ging_{\rm in} and goutg_{\rm out} for Schwarzschild BHs can be expressed as infinite series [155]

gin​(r)\displaystyle g_{\rm in}(r) =r2​i​ω​(r−1)−i​ω​ei​ω​(r−2)​∑n=0∞an​(1−1/r)n,\displaystyle=r^{2i\omega}(r-1)^{-i\omega}e^{i\omega(r-2)}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}(1-1/r)^{n}, (4.13)
gout​(r)\displaystyle g_{\rm out}(r) =(2​ω)−i​ω​ei​ϕ+​(1−1/r)−i​ω​∑ℓ=−∞∞bℓ​[Gℓ​(η,ρ)+i​Fℓ​(η,ρ)],\displaystyle=(2\omega)^{-i\omega}e^{i\phi_{+}}(1-1/r)^{-i\omega}\sum_{\ell=-\infty}^{\infty}b_{\ell}\left[G_{\ell}(\eta,\rho)+iF_{\ell}(\eta,\rho)\right], (4.14)

in terms of the Schwarzschild radial coordinate rr, instead of the tortoise coordinate r∗r_{*}. Here, ana_{n} and bℓb_{\ell} are coefficients satisfying specific recurrence relations, the functions Gℓ​(η,ρ)G_{\ell}(\eta,\rho) and Fℓ​(η,ρ)F_{\ell}(\eta,\rho) are the Coulomb wave functions with η=−ω\eta=-\omega and ρ=ω​r\rho=\omega r, and ϕ+\phi_{+} is a normalization phase. Using Eq. (4.9), these expressions for ging_{\rm in} and goutg_{\rm out} can be used to obtain an expansion series for the Green’s function.

Since GW signals are observed as time series, the temporal/frequency dependence of the Green’s function deserves particular attention. For Schwarzschild BHs, the spheroidal harmonics do not depend on ω\omega, and thus only the ω\omega dependence of Gω​ℓ​mG_{\omega\ell m} in Eq. (4.9) determines the TD Green’s function:

G(t,r∗,θ,ϕ|t¯,r¯∗,θ¯,ϕ¯)=∑ℓ​mGℓ​m(t,r∗|t¯,r¯∗)Yℓ​ms(θ,ϕ)Yℓ​m∗s(θ¯,ϕ¯),\displaystyle G(t,r_{*},\theta,\phi|\bar{t},\bar{r}_{*},\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi})=\sum_{\ell m}G_{\ell m}(t,r_{*}|\bar{t},\bar{r}_{*}){}_{s}Y_{\ell m}(\theta,\phi){}_{s}Y_{\ell m}^{*}(\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi}),
Gℓ​m(t,r∗|t¯,r¯∗)=∫−∞+i​ϵ+∞+i​ϵd​ω2​πe−i​ω​(t−t¯)Gω​ℓ​m(r∗|r¯∗).\displaystyle G_{\ell m}(t,r_{*}|\bar{t},\bar{r}_{*})=\int_{-\infty+i\epsilon}^{+\infty+i\epsilon}{d\omega\over 2\pi}e^{-i\omega(t-\bar{t})}G_{\omega\ell m}(r_{*}|\bar{r}_{*}). (4.15)

For a general value of ω\omega, the boundary conditions for goutg_{\rm out} and ging_{\rm in} cannot be satisfied at the same time; therefore these are two independent solutions of the homogeneous equation, and W≠0W\not=0. However, for ω\omega values that coincide with the linear QNM spectrum, goutg_{\rm out} and ging_{\rm in} are given by the same single solution. In that case, 𝒜in=𝒜out=0{\cal A}_{\rm in}={\cal A}_{\rm out}=0 and thus W=0W=0: see Eq. (4.11). As a consequence of the fact that G∝1/WG\propto 1/W, Gω​ℓ​mG_{\omega\ell m} has poles at the (linear) QNM frequencies ω=ωℓ​m​n\omega=\omega_{\ell mn}.

The integral on the displaced real axis involved in the computation of the TD Green’s function Gℓ​mG_{\ell m}, Eq. (4.1), is obtained by deforming the integration contour in the complex-frequency plane according to the features of Gω​ℓ​mG_{\omega\ell m} [155]. The main features are: (i) it contains first-order poles at the linear QNM frequencies ω=ωℓ​m​n\omega=\omega_{\ell mn} [706]; (ii) it contains a pole at ω=0\omega=0, due not to the Wronskian alone, but its combination with goutg_{\rm out} and ging_{\rm in}; (iii) it contains a branch cut running along the negative imaginary ω\omega values, connected to the pole at ω=0\omega=0. According to these features, the Green’s function in the TD may be obtained using the residue theorem, following a closed contour integral as shown in Fig. 25.

As a result of the frequency integration, the TD Green’s function can be expressed in terms of three contributions:

Gℓ​m(t,r∗|t¯,r¯∗)=GQ+GF+GB,G_{\ell m}(t,r_{*}|\bar{t},\bar{r}_{*})=G_{Q}+G_{F}+G_{B}, (4.16)

with GQG_{Q}, GFG_{F} and GBG_{B} known as the QNM, flat, and branch cut contributions, respectively.

  • (1)

    GQG_{Q} comes from a sum over the residues at the linear QNM frequency poles (black dots in Fig. 25), and leads to exponentials with frequencies ω=ωℓ​m​n\omega=\omega_{\ell mn}, thus producing the usual QNM solutions. This implies that the linear QNM frequencies will be contained in the ringdown signal, unless the initial conditions are fine-tuned [709].

  • (2)

    GFG_{F} comes from the arcs of the semi-infinite circle of the integration contour (green long-dashed lines in Fig. 25), and its contribution includes information about high-magnitude frequency contributions and asymptotically far signals, that propagate effectively in free space since they are insensitive to the potential. For this reason, GFG_{F} is expected to be responsible for the prompt response in ringdown solutions, which will mostly depend on the details of the initial conditions.

  • (3)

    GBG_{B} comes from the branch cut contribution (red dotted line in Fig. 25) and is interpreted to arise from the long-range decay of the potential, corresponding to low-frequencies. It generally leads to polynomial tails in ringdown solutions, which can dominate the late-time signal, and are understood as the result of waves back-scattering off the potential [710] (see Section 5.3).

While their complete expressions are not known, details on different asymptotic limits for GQG_{Q} and GBG_{B} can be found in [155]. An intuition on their effect can be gained by looking at the limit of large |r∗||r_{*}| and |r¯∗||\bar{r}_{*}|, using the asymptotic forms of ging_{\rm in} and goutg_{\rm out} in Eqs. (4.7)-(4.8), leading to

GF∼−12​[Θ⁡(t−t¯−|r∗−r¯∗|)−Θ⁡(t−t¯−|r∗|−|r¯∗|)],\displaystyle G_{F}\sim-{1\over 2}\left[\Theta(t-\bar{t}-|r_{*}-\bar{r}_{*}|)-\Theta(t-\bar{t}-|r_{*}|-|\bar{r}_{*}|)\right]\,, (4.17)
GQ∼∑n−i​fℓ​m​nWℓ​m​n′​e−i​ωℓ​m​n(1)​(t−t¯−|r∗|−|r¯∗|)​Θ​(t−t¯−|r∗|−|r¯∗|),\displaystyle G_{Q}\sim\sum_{n}{-if_{\ell mn}\over W^{\prime}_{\ell mn}}e^{-i\omega_{\ell mn}^{(1)}(t-\bar{t}-|r_{*}|-|\bar{r}_{*}|)}\Theta(t-\bar{t}-|r_{*}|-|\bar{r}_{*}|), (4.18)

where Θ⁡(x)\Theta(x) is the step function (unity if x>0x>0, zero otherwise), and Wℓ​m​n′W^{\prime}_{\ell mn} is the derivative of the Wronskian with respect to the frequency, evaluated at the QNM frequencies ωℓ​m​n\omega_{\ell mn}. The term fℓ​m​nf_{\ell mn} is a constant factor depending on the QNM frequencies ωℓ​m​n\omega_{\ell mn}, with fℓ​m​n=1f_{\ell mn}=1 when r∗r_{*} and r¯∗\bar{r}_{*} have opposite signs, fℓ​m​n=ℬin​(ωℓ​m​n)f_{\ell mn}=\mathcal{B}_{\rm in}(\omega_{\ell mn}) when r∗,r¯∗>0r_{*},{\bar{r}}_{*}>0, and fℓ​m​n=ℬout​(ωℓ​m​n)f_{\ell mn}=\mathcal{B}_{\rm out}(\omega_{\ell mn}) when r∗,r¯∗<0r_{*},{\bar{r}}_{*}<0. The step functions in the above expressions represent nontrivial causality constraints coming from how the contour in the ω\omega integral is closed.

The causality constraints that ringdown solutions have to satisfy in the asymptotic limit considered here are shown in Fig. 26. In this figure (t¯,r¯∗)(\bar{t},\bar{r}_{*}) is interpreted as an event with a nonzero initial condition, and (t,r∗)(t,r_{*}) corresponds to the observer. In particular, the step function for GQG_{Q} implies that the QNM piece of the Green’s function does not vanish only if the point (t¯,r¯∗)(\bar{t},\bar{r}_{*}) is causally connected to (t,r∗)(t,r_{*}) via the potential (approximated to be at r∗=0r_{*}=0 in these asymptotic expressions). This means that QNM solutions will build in time, as a given initial condition gets causally connected to the potential and then has enough time to travel towards the observer. For initial conditions with compact support, the QNM solutions will eventually reach a stationary regime, when the entire initial condition has been connected to the potential and the observer, and the solution will be well approximated by a superposition of QNM frequencies with constant amplitudes. This causality constraint will thus lead to a time variation of the linear QNM amplitudes beyond the complex exponential dependence in the initial ringdown regime (e.g., near the merger of two BHs) [165, 702, 378]. The time taken to stabilize will depend on the initial condition, as exemplified by calculations with toy models [709]. Since these results were obtained in the asymptotic limit of the Green’s function, the actual causality conditions at smaller radii are expected to be analogous but with fuzzier boundaries.

In addition, the causality constraints from GFG_{F} imply that part of the initial conditions will travel directly towards the observer. Compared to GQG_{Q}, a signal produced by GFG_{F} is thus expected to arrive earlier than those produced by GQG_{Q}. For this reason, GFG_{F} is said to generate a “prompt response.” The effect of GQG_{Q} and GFG_{F} has been studied with toy model initial conditions [155, 165]. An example is given in Fig. 27.

The GBG_{B} component does not appear in the asymptotic study of the Green’s function, since the potential vanishes in that limit. However, a number of studies of its polynomial form have been performed in other limits [711, 155, 710, 712, 713, 714, 700]. For instance, at late times such that r∗,r¯∗≪(t−t¯)r_{*},{\bar{r}_{*}}\ll(t-{\bar{t}}) and for static initial conditions one finds

GB∼(r∗​r¯∗)ℓ+1​(t−t¯)−2​ℓ−3,G_{B}\sim(r_{*}\bar{r}_{*})^{\ell+1}(t-\bar{t})^{-2\ell-3}\,, (4.19)

which describes the propagation of low-frequency waves. From this expression, the dominant multipole will have ℓ=2\ell=2, with higher multipoles decaying faster. This Green’s function component also leads to polynomial tails in ringdown solutions. Since QNM solutions decay exponentially fast, polynomial tails dominate ringdown signals at late times. For a detailed discussion of their physical interpretation and impact on signal modeling, see Section 5.3.

Analogous features for the Green’s function are expected for Kerr BHs. In particular, as previously mentioned, the Schwarzschild and Kerr cases can both be cast in the form of Eq. (4.1), with the same asymptotic behavior towards the horizon and infinity. The main difference between the two cases lies in the fact that the angular separation in Kerr uses spheroidal harmonics, which depend on ω\omega and may thus introduce additional nontrivial time dependence on the TD Green’s function. As discussed in [700], which analyzes the Kerr Green’s function to obtain late-time tail solutions, the ω\omega dependence of the spheroidal harmonics leads to apparent branch points that are not present for Schwarzschild BHs, yet such angular branch cuts are spurious artifacts of the spheroidal decomposition, which will vanish when performing the infinite sum over ℓ\ell to obtain the full Green’s function. Analytical series approximations of the Kerr Green’s function have been obtained in [715, 716, 157, 156] (see also the review [158]). The Green’s function for a scalar field around a Kerr BH has also been studied in [699]. As opposed to the Teukolsky formalism discussed here, a different approach to the Kerr Green’s function useful for reconstructing the full metric perturbation hμ​νh_{\mu\nu} can be found in [703].

An important observation is that the Green’s function approach can also be used to analyze the behavior of higher-order BH perturbations, iteratively. In fact, at any perturbative order, perturbations will satisfy the same linear differential equation, with the only difference being the presence of an additional source term fixed by lower order perturbations. For example, second-order ringdown solutions Ψ2(2)\Psi^{(2)}_{2} satisfy the equation

[∂r∗2+ω2−V2(ω,r∗)]Ψ2(2)(ω,r∗)=S(2)[Ψ2],\left[\partial_{r_{*}}^{2}+\omega^{2}-V_{2}(\omega,r_{*})\right]\Psi^{(2)}_{2}(\omega,r_{*})=S^{(2)}[\Psi_{2}], (4.20)

where S(2)S^{(2)} is a second-order source, a function of quadratic terms in the linear perturbation Ψ2\Psi_{2} and its derivatives. While a homogeneous solution to this equation will simply renormalize the linear solution, its particular solution can be obtained with the Green’s function in a way analogous to Eq. (4.6):

Ψ2(2)(t,r∗,θ,ϕ)=∫dr¯∗dt¯dΩ¯G(t,r∗,θ,ϕ|t¯,r¯∗,θ¯,ϕ¯)S(2)(t¯,r¯∗,θ¯,ϕ¯).\Psi^{(2)}_{2}(t,r_{*},\theta,\phi)=\int d\bar{r}_{*}d\bar{t}d\bar{\Omega}\;G(t,r_{*},\theta,\phi|\bar{t},\bar{r}_{*},\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi})S^{(2)}(\bar{t},\bar{r}_{*},\bar{\theta},\bar{\phi}). (4.21)

Applications of the Green’s function approach to second-order ringdown perturbations for Schwarzschild BHs predict the presence of nonlinear polynomial tails in toy models [717] and shed light on the causal formation and evolution of nonlinearities [702]. Analogous results are expected for Kerr BHs.

4.2 Kerr amplitudes in the time domain and excitation factors

Initial contributors: Oshita

4.2.1 Kerr perturbations

Gravitational waveforms in the Kerr background can be computed by solving the Teukolsky equation (see Section 2.1). A useful feature of the Teukolsky equation is that it can be separated into two ODEs for the angular and radial part of the perturbations, Eqs. (2.4) and (2.5). The full waveform can be obtained by solving the Teukolsky equation using the Green’s function approach, possibly including a matter source term. In this “Teukolsky formalism,” an apparent obstacle is that the required integrals can be divergent. An appropriate regularization, equivalent to introducing a Green’s function that is well-behaved at infinity, can resolve this issue [718]. Alternatively, the effective potential in the wave equation can be made short-range by transforming the Teukolsky equation using the “generalized Darboux” or “Chandrasekhar” transformation [705, 719, 706, 720], which reads

Xℓ​m​ω≡α⁡(r)​Rℓ​m​ω+β⁡(r)Δ​d​Rℓ​m​ωd​r,X_{\ell m\omega}\equiv\alpha(r)R_{\ell m\omega}+\frac{\beta(r)}{\Delta}\frac{dR_{\ell m\omega}}{dr}\,, (4.22)

in terms of certain functions α⁡(r)\alpha(r) and β⁡(r)\beta(r). By properly choosing the functions α\alpha and β\beta in (4.22), the radial Teukolsky equation is transformed into another ODE for Xℓ​m​ωX_{\ell m\omega} with a short-range potential (see e.g. [721] for a detailed review of the generalized Darboux transformation). With a specific choice of α⁡(r)\alpha(r) and β⁡(r)\beta(r), the radial perturbation equation has a short-range real potential, and it is known as the Chandrasekhar-Detweiler equation [705]. This equation features a potential with four distinct branches. For certain combinations of the Kerr parameter and of the mode frequency, one of the potential branches may become singular, necessitating a switch between branches. A different choice of α⁡(r)\alpha(r) and β⁡(r)\beta(r) leads to a second radial perturbation equation with a short-range complex potential, known as the Sasaki-Nakamura equation [18], which (for perturbations with s=−2s=-2) has the form

[d2d​r∗2−ℱ⁡(r)​dd​r∗−𝒰⁡(r)]​Xℓ​m​ω​(r)=Iℓ​m​ω​(r).\left[\frac{d^{2}}{dr_{*}^{2}}-{\cal F}(r)\frac{d}{dr_{*}}-{\cal U}(r)\right]X_{\ell m\omega}(r)=I_{\ell m\omega}(r). (4.23)

The explicit expressions of ℱ⁡(r){\cal F}(r), 𝒰⁡(r){\cal U}(r) and Iℓ​m​ω​(r)I_{\ell m\omega}(r) are given in [18]. The Sasaki-Nakamura equation is convenient for numerical work due to its short-range complex potential, and it has also been extended to other values of the spin weight [722]. The equation reduces to the Regge-Wheeler equation in the limit a→0a\to 0. In the Sasaki-Nakamura formalism, the source term Iℓ​m​ωI_{\ell m\omega} is also short-range, hence the full waveform can be obtained by performing a convergent integral. The calculation of the source term requires a double integral of the Teukolsky source term, with two corresponding integration constants determined so that the inhomogeneous solution of the Teukolsky equation is purely outgoing at infinity [18, 16]. The source term of the Sasaki-Nakamura equation for a point particle in geodesic motion on the Kerr background was computed in [18, 723, 724]. An important property of the source term is that it redshifts to zero as the particle approaches the Kerr event horizon. Since solutions of the source-free Teukolsky equation are QNMs, this ensures that the waveform for a plunging particle terminates in QNMs which are phase-coherent with the inspiral preceding the plunge.

Another possibility to study the excitation of Kerr amplitudes is to directly solve the Teukolsky equation (2.2) with a point-particle source, without switching to an equation which uses a short-range potential [725, 726]. Key to this method is that the source is approximated as a variant of an impulse response function which preserves integral identities of the Dirac delta function and its derivatives. By combining adiabatic backreaction data (see e.g. [727] for an overview) with a prescription to describe how the adiabatic evolution ends as the particle begins plunging into the Kerr BH, one can construct a worldline describing a small body’s inspiral and plunge for a wide range of initial conditions. This method, initially developed in [728], was extended to a larger class of inspirals and improved in [729]. Given the worldline, the Teukolsky equation source term (e.g. [341, 730]) and the gravitational waveforms can be computed by numerically solving the evolution equation. The final cycles of these waveforms consist of QNMs, so these time evolutions can be used to numerically study the relative excitation of the modes as a function of the geometry of the point-particle orbit.

4.2.2 Kerr waveforms in the time domain

The Sasaki-Nakamura equation with source describing a propagating mode with frequency ω\omega takes the canonical form (see Appendix B of [721])

[∂x2+V(ω,x)]ξ~(ω,x)=S(ω,x),\left[\partial_{x}^{2}+V(\omega,x)\right]\tilde{\xi}(\omega,x)=S(\omega,x)\,, (4.24)

where xx is the tortoise coordinate and V⁡(x)V(x) has the asymptotic limits

V⁡(ω,x)∼{kH2x→−∞,ω2−1/x2x→+∞,\displaystyle V(\omega,x)\sim\begin{cases}k_{\rm H}^{2}&x\to-\infty\,,\\ \omega^{2}-1/x^{2}&x\to+\infty\,,\end{cases} (4.25)

with kH≡ω−m​ΩHk_{\rm H}\equiv\omega-m\Omega_{\rm H}. Here we omit the (ℓ,m)(\ell,\,m) subscripts for brevity. The TD signal ξ⁡(t−x)\xi(t-x) is given by the inverse Laplace transform of ξ~​(ω,x)\tilde{\xi}(\omega,x). Employing the Green’s function technique (see Section 4.1), the inhomogeneous solution is

ξ~​(ω,x)=ξ~∞​(ω,x)W⁡(ω)​∫−∞xd​x′​ξ~+​(ω,x′)​S​(ω,x′)+ξ~+​(ω,x)W⁡(ω)​∫x∞d​x′​ξ~∞​(ω,x′)​S​(ω,x′),\tilde{\xi}(\omega,x)=\frac{\tilde{\xi}_{\infty}(\omega,x)}{W(\omega)}\int_{-\infty}^{x}dx^{\prime}\tilde{\xi}_{+}(\omega,x^{\prime})S(\omega,x^{\prime})+\frac{\tilde{\xi}_{+}(\omega,x)}{W(\omega)}\int_{x}^{\infty}dx^{\prime}\tilde{\xi}_{\infty}(\omega,x^{\prime})S(\omega,x^{\prime})\,, (4.26)

where W⁡(ω)W(\omega) is the Wronskian of ξ~∞\tilde{\xi}_{\infty} and ξ~+\tilde{\xi}_{+}, and the two homogeneous solutions, ξ~+​(ω,x)\tilde{\xi}_{+}(\omega,x) and ξ~∞​(ω,x)\tilde{\xi}_{\infty}(\omega,x), have the asymptotic form

ξ~+∼{e−i​kH​xx→−∞,𝒜out​(ω)​ei​ω​x+𝒜in​(ω)​e−i​ω​xx→+∞,\displaystyle\tilde{\xi}_{+}\sim\begin{cases}e^{-ik_{\rm H}x}&x\to-\infty\,,\\ {\cal A}_{\rm out}(\omega)e^{i\omega x}+{\cal A}_{\rm in}(\omega)e^{-i\omega x}&x\to+\infty\,,\end{cases} (4.27)
ξ~∞∼{ℬout​(ω)​ei​kH​x+ℬin​(ω)​e−i​kH​xx→−∞,ei​ω​xx→+∞.\displaystyle\tilde{\xi}_{\infty}\sim\begin{cases}{\cal B}_{\rm out}(\omega)e^{ik_{\rm H}x}+{\cal B}_{\rm in}(\omega)e^{-ik_{\rm H}x}&x\to-\infty\,,\\ e^{i\omega x}&x\to+\infty\,.\end{cases} (4.28)

For signals observed in the far zone (x→∞x\to\infty) we have

ξ~​(ω,x)≃ξ~∞​(ω,x)2​i​ω​𝒜in​∫−∞∞d​x′​ξ~+​(ω,x′)​S​(ω,x′)=ei​ω​x​𝒜out2​i​ω​𝒜in​∫−∞∞d​x′​ξ~+​(ω,x′)𝒜out​S​(ω,x′),\tilde{\xi}(\omega,x)\simeq\frac{\tilde{\xi}_{\infty}(\omega,x)}{2i\omega{\cal A}_{\rm in}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx^{\prime}\tilde{\xi}_{+}(\omega,x^{\prime})S(\omega,x^{\prime})=\frac{e^{i\omega x}{\cal A}_{\rm out}}{2i\omega{\cal A}_{\rm in}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx^{\prime}\frac{\tilde{\xi}_{+}(\omega,x^{\prime})}{{\cal A}_{\rm out}}S(\omega,x^{\prime})\,, (4.29)

which can be rewritten as

ξ~​(ω,x)=[h~G​(ω)×T~​(ω)]​ei​ω​x,\tilde{\xi}(\omega,x)=[\tilde{h}_{\rm G}(\omega)\times\tilde{T}(\omega)]e^{i\omega x}\,, (4.30)

with

h~G​(ω)≡𝒜out2​i​ω​𝒜in,T~​(ω)≡∫−∞∞d​x′​ξ~+​(ω,x′)𝒜out​S​(ω,x′).\tilde{h}_{\rm G}(\omega)\equiv\frac{{\cal A}_{\rm out}}{2i\omega{\cal A}_{\rm in}}\,,\ \ \tilde{T}(\omega)\equiv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx^{\prime}\frac{\tilde{\xi}_{+}(\omega,x^{\prime})}{{\cal A}_{\rm out}}S(\omega,x^{\prime})\,. (4.31)

Note that the two functions h~G\tilde{h}_{\rm G} and T~\tilde{T} are independent of the overall scale of the homogeneous solutions ξ~+\tilde{\xi}_{+} and ξ~∞\tilde{\xi}_{\infty}, since 𝒜≀⊓⊔/𝒜⟩\{\cal A_{\rm out}}/{\cal A_{\rm in}} and ξ~+/𝒜≀⊓⊔{\tilde{\xi}_{+}}/{\cal A_{\rm out}} are invariant with respect to the overall scale transformation of ξ~+/∞\tilde{\xi}_{+/\infty}. While h~G\tilde{h}_{\rm G} is determined only by the Green’s function, T~\tilde{T} contains all the initial data and source information. Neglecting the time dependence of QNM amplitudes, the TD waveform is then given by

h⁡(t−x)=12​π​∫−∞+i​ϵ∞+i​ϵd​ω​ξ~​(ω,x)​e−i​ω​t=∑nBn(SN)​Tn​e−i​ωn​(t−x)+(prompt response term)+(branch cut term),\displaystyle\begin{split}h(t-x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty+i\epsilon}^{\infty+i\epsilon}d\omega\tilde{\xi}(\omega,x)e^{-i\omega t}&=\sum_{n}B_{n}^{\rm(SN)}T_{n}e^{-i\omega_{n}(t-x)}\\ &+\text{(prompt response term)}+\text{(branch cut term)}\,,\end{split} (4.32)

where for simplicity T~​(ω)\tilde{T}(\omega) is assumed to not have any poles in the complex-ω\omega plane, and Tn≡T~​(ωn)T_{n}\equiv\tilde{T}(\omega_{n}). The relevant integration contour is shown in Fig. 25. The prompt response and branch cut terms correspond to the green-dashed and red-dotted lines in Fig. 25, respectively. The first term in Eq. (4.32) above represents the QNM contribution to the waveform. The total QNM amplitude is Bn(SN)×TnB_{n}^{\rm(SN)}\times T_{n}, where the complex “excitation factors” Bn(SN)B_{n}^{\rm(SN)}, defined as in Eq. (2.32) in terms of the asymptotic amplitudes 𝒜out/in{\cal A}_{\rm out/in} of the Sasaki-Nakamura equation, are determined solely by the Green’s function (here we omit the ℓ,m\ell,m subscripts for brevity). The “source factors” TnT_{n} depend on the initial data and on the specific source exciting the perturbations. The overall amplitude of each QNM, i.e., the so-called “excitation coefficient” CnC_{n}, is given by the product Cn=Bn(SN)​TnC_{n}=B_{n}^{\rm(SN)}T_{n}.

The ringdown component of ξ\xi, i.e., the first term on the right-hand side of Eq. (4.32), can be derived using a QNM eigenfunction decomposition [155]. Substituting Eq. (4.26) into Eq. (4.32), one finds that the QNM part has the form

ξ∼2​π​i​∑nResω=ωn​[ξ~​(ω)​e−i​ω​t],=∑n[𝒜out​(ωn)2​ωn​(d​𝒜in/d​ω)ω=ωn​ξ~q​(ωn,x)​∫−∞∞d​x′​ξ~q​(ωn,x)​S​(ωn,x′)]​e−i​ωn​t,\displaystyle\begin{split}\xi&\sim 2\pi i\sum_{n}\text{Res}_{\omega=\omega_{n}}\left[\tilde{\xi}(\omega)e^{-i\omega t}\right]\,,\\ &=\sum_{n}\left[\frac{{\cal A}_{\rm out}(\omega_{n})}{2\omega_{n}(d{\cal A}_{\rm in}/d\omega)_{\omega=\omega_{n}}}\tilde{\xi}_{\rm q}(\omega_{n},x)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx^{\prime}\tilde{\xi}_{\rm q}(\omega_{n},x)S(\omega_{n},x^{\prime})\right]e^{-i\omega_{n}t}\,,\end{split} (4.33)

where

ξ~q​(ωn,x)≡ξ~∞​(ωn,x)=ξ~+​(ωn,x)/𝒜out\tilde{\xi}_{\rm q}(\omega_{n},x)\equiv\tilde{\xi}_{\infty}(\omega_{n},x)=\tilde{\xi}_{+}(\omega_{n},x)/{\cal A}_{\rm out} (4.34)

is the QNM eigenfunction. It can be checked that Eq. (4.33) reduces to the ringdown component of Eq. (4.32) in the limit x→∞x\to\infty. Note that the QNM eigenfunction ξ~q\tilde{\xi}_{\rm q} is divergent both at the horizon and at infinity. To obtain a finite value of the source factor TnT_{n} in Eq. (4.31), it is useful to perform an analytic continuation of the areal coordinate r′​(x′)r^{\prime}(x^{\prime}) and to change the contour of the spatial integral so that the integral has no divergence at the horizon and at infinity [155, 731].

For simplicity of exposition, in the above expression the time dependence of the QNM amplitudes has been neglected, as taking it into account gives rise to more complicated expressions [155]. The full waveform ξ⁡(t−x)\xi(t-x) including these contributions, as well as the prompt response and branch cut portions, is instead given by the convolution of the two TD waveforms

ξℓ​m​(t−x)=hG,ℓ​m​(t−x)∗Tℓ​m​(t),\xi_{\ell m}(t-x)=h_{{\rm G},\ell m}(t-x)*T_{\ell m}(t)\,, (4.35)

where the convolution is defined as

(f∗g)​(t)≡∫−∞∞d​τ​f​(τ)​g​(t−τ)(f*g)(t)\equiv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\tau f(\tau)g(t-\tau) (4.36)

in terms of the functions

hG,ℓ​m​(t−x)\displaystyle h_{{\rm G},\ell m}(t-x) ≡12​π​∫−∞+i​ϵ∞+i​ϵd​ω​h~G,ℓ​m​(ω)​ei​ω​x​e−i​ω​t,\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty+i\epsilon}^{\infty+i\epsilon}d\omega\tilde{h}_{{\rm G},\ell m}(\omega)e^{i\omega x}e^{-i\omega t}\,, (4.37)
Tℓ​m​(t)\displaystyle T_{\ell m}(t) ≡12​π​∫−∞∞d​ω​T~ℓ​m​(ω)​e−i​ω​t,\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega\tilde{T}_{\ell m}(\omega)e^{-i\omega t}\,, (4.38)

where we have restored the subscript (ℓ,m)(\ell,m), that had been omitted for simplicity earlier.

The Kerr Green’s function contribution to the TD waveform for the dominant quadrupolar mode, hG,22​(t−x)h_{{\rm G},22}(t-x), is shown in Fig. 28, and it exhibits a ringdown phase at late times. The waveform is computed by numerically integrating the Sasaki-Nakamura equation and by directly reading off 𝒜in/out{\cal A}_{\rm in/out} from the homogeneous solution. The TD waveform is found by using a contour on the real-ω\omega axis and an integration interval in the range [−4​M, 4​M][-4M,\,4M]. The full waveform ξ⁡(t−x)\xi(t-x) shown in Fig. 29 was found by taking the convolution with the numerically computed source term of [723], and it corresponds to a particle plunging along an equatorial geodesic into a Kerr BH with varying spin, neglecting radiation reaction on the particle trajectory.

The excitation of QNMs in the extreme mass ratio limit has been studied using different methods to construct the source term. Early papers computed complete gravitational waveforms in the extreme mass-ratio limit within the EOB framework [732, 733, 734, 735], considering a PN-driven trajectory with a generic test-particle source term [37]. In other works, the loss of energy and angular momentum of the small body was taken into account by generalizing the Ori-Thorne procedure [728] to describe the transition from inspiral to plunge. For example, the dependence of QNM excitation on the inspiral-to-plunge transition in the Schwarzschild background can be studied using an analytical form of the trajectory [736, 737]. Several works have explored trajectories describing the transition from inspiral to plunge [738, 739, 740] and the worldline of small bodies following initially circular but misaligned orbits [729] in the Kerr background. This work was the basis for subsequent studies of the excitation of Kerr QNMs [741, 742] where the Teukolsky equation was solved with high precision in the TD, following methods developed in [341, 730].

As in this approach it is not possible to split the QNM, prompt and tail components of the Green’s function, the QNM amplitudes need to be extracted a posteriori from the full solution by fitting a superposition of damped sinusoids with frequencies corresponding to the QNM spectrum. This methodology is described in detail in Section 5.

Rather than finding the QNM amplitudes from fits of the gravitational waveforms, an alternative is to analytically compute the excitation factor Eℓ​m​nE_{\ell mn} and the source factor Tℓ​m​nT_{\ell mn} from first principles. The source factor calculation in the Schwarzschild case was pioneered by Leaver [155]. It involves the integration of the QNM eigenfunctions ξq​(ωn,x)\xi_{\rm q}(\omega_{n},x) in Eq. (4.34) in standard Schwarzschild coordinates, which yields divergent results at both the horizon and infinity. The source factor integral can be regularized, either by subtracting divergent terms (as in [743]) or by analytical continuation of the radial coordinate into the complex plane and contour deformation (as in [155], see also [744, 745, 494, 95]). A similar source factor calculation for a particle plunging along the spin axis of a Kerr BH, based on the regularization scheme developed in [743], can be found in [164] (see also recent work in [746, 747]). A generalization of these calculations to generic orbits is required to understand QNM excitation and to improve waveform models for extreme mass ratio binaries, but it is technically complicated. A promising avenue in this direction is the extension of self-force techniques [748] beyond the inspiral phase [749, 750].

4.2.3 Kerr excitation factors

The excitation factors Bℓ​m​nB_{\ell mn}, defined as the residues of the Green’s function at the QNM poles, quantify the “intrinsic excitability” of QNMs. It is sometimes useful to introduce also the quantity Eℓ​m​n≡Bℓ​m​n/ωℓ​m​n2E_{\ell mn}\equiv B_{\ell mn}/\omega_{\ell mn}^{2} [162], which is useful to take into account the fact that the strain amplitude hh and the Newman-Penrose scalar are related by two time derivatives (Ψ4∼h¨\Psi_{4}\sim\ddot{h}). The excitation factors were first computed in the Schwarzschild case [155, 731, 744, 165, 163]. The Kerr case was initially investigated in [745, 163], and later extended to n=3n=3 and up to ℓ=7\ell=7 [164], to n=20n=20 for ℓ=2\ell=2 [162], and to multipoles with ℓ>2\ell>2 [751]. The excitation factors are now known in the scalar, electromagnetic and gravitational case up to ℓ=7\ell=7 and to n=7n=7, thanks to technical improvements to achieve high accuracy [94, 154, 95]. Excitation factor calculations require the homogeneous solution of the perturbation equation for general complex frequencies, which can be achieved using the Mano-Suzuki-Takasugi (MST) method [157]. This technique was applied in [164, 154]. In [95], the Sasaki-Nakamura equation with a general complex frequency was solved instead. An alternative is to use Heun functions to obtain the relevant expressions for the Kerr-de Sitter spacetime, and then extrapolate to the Kerr case by setting the cosmological constant to zero [162, 752]. The high-ℓ\ell expansion method was also applied to the computation of Schwarzschild excitation factors [241, 707]. The accuracy of this method for low ℓ\ell’s can be improved by including higher-order terms [753].

The Kerr excitation factors are shown in Fig. 30 for ℓ=m=2\ell=m=2 and varying overtone number. The absolute value of the excitation factor peaks around n=5,6n=5,6. However, the overtone excitation coefficients are ultimately weighted by the source factor, so it is not possible to draw definitive implications on the excitations of overtones in actual ringdown signals just by looking at the excitation factors. The peak of the excitation factor shifts towards higher overtone numbers for higher multipoles (see Fig. 31). As shown in Fig. 32, E22​nE_{22n} grows with spin for all overtones up to a≃0.9​Ma\simeq 0.9M, at which point the n=5, 6n=5,\,6 overtones display a peak, with the n=5n=5 overtone being strongly suppressed in the near-extremal case. This behavior is caused by mode repulsion (see Section 2.3).

By definition, the excitation factors Eℓ​m​nE_{\ell mn} correspond to the QNM amplitudes in the Green’s function waveform hG,ℓ​mh_{{\rm G},\ell m} of Eq. (4.37). Since constant-valued QNM amplitudes depend on the time at which the exponential decay starts, some care is required in specifying the time at which the excitation factor is defined. In other words, Eℓ​m​nE_{\ell mn} is ambiguous up to a factor of ei​ωℓ​m​n​t∗e^{i\omega_{\ell mn}t_{*}}, where the parameter t∗t_{*} encodes the ambiguity in the starting time of ringdown, and it should be defined at a time such that the QNM expansion is convergent [162, 751, 754], as carefully investigated in [754]. The ringdown phase in hG,ℓ​mh_{{\rm G},\ell m} can be reconstructed using a superposition of QNMs weighted by the excitation factors, hEh_{\rm E}:

hG,ℓ​m≃hE,ℓ​m≡∑nP=0NPEℓ​m​nP​e−i​ωℓ​m​nP​(t−x−D∗)+∑nR=0NREℓ​m​nR​e−i​ωℓ​m​nR​(t−x−D∗).h_{{\rm G},\ell m}\simeq h_{{\rm E},\ell m}\equiv\sum^{N_{\rm P}}_{n_{\rm P}=0}E_{\ell mn_{\rm P}}e^{-i\omega_{\ell mn_{\rm P}}(t-x-D_{*})}+\sum^{N_{\rm R}}_{n_{\rm R}=0}E_{\ell mn_{\rm R}}e^{-i\omega_{\ell mn_{\rm R}}(t-x-D_{*})}\,. (4.39)

Here t∗t_{*} is fixed to t∗=D∗≡−2​M​log⁡[1−(a/M)2]t_{*}=D_{*}\equiv-2M\log[1-(a/M)^{2}] [754], i.e. the “starting time” of the ringdown, in the sense that for t−x<D∗t-x<D_{*} the QNM expansion does not converge (see Fig. 33). The two indices nPn_{\rm P} and nRn_{\rm R} label prograde and retrograde overtones, respectively. The number of prograde and retrograde overtones in the sum, NPN_{\rm P} and NRN_{\rm R}, must be large enough to precisely reconstruct the ringdown. With NP=20N_{\rm P}=20 and NR=5N_{\rm R}=5, one can reconstruct the ringdown part of hG,ℓ​mh_{{\rm G},\ell m} within a mismatch of ℳ≲10−3{\cal M}\lesssim 10^{-3} (see Fig. 33), where the mismatch is defined as

ℳ≡1−|⟨hG,ℓ​m|hE,ℓ​m⟩⟨hG,ℓ​m|hG,ℓ​m⟩​⟨hE,ℓ​m|hE,ℓ​m⟩|,{\cal M}\equiv 1-\left|\frac{\braket{h_{{\rm G},\ell m}|h_{{\rm E},\ell m}}}{\sqrt{\braket{h_{{\rm G},\ell m}|h_{{\rm G},\ell m}}\braket{h_{{\rm E},\ell m}|h_{{\rm E},\ell m}}}}\right|\,, (4.40)

in terms of the scalar product

⟨a⁡(u)|b⁡(u)⟩≡∫D∗∞d​u′​a​(u′)​b∗​(u′),\braket{a(u)|b(u)}\equiv\int_{D_{*}}^{\infty}du^{\prime}a(u^{\prime})b^{*}(u^{\prime})\,, (4.41)

where u≡t−xu\equiv t-x. Note that this analysis does not rely on any fits, as the excitation factors are computed from first principles. It turns out that the excitation factors computed in [162] are defined at the earliest time at which the QNM expansion is convergent [754]. Even more accurate reconstructions of the TD signal (including early times and even late-time tails) are possible by considering expansions in terms of the QNMs of destabilized potentials [752].

4.3 Quadratic modes in Schwarzschild

Initial contributors: Bucciotti, Kuntz, Riotto

Until recently, most spectroscopy efforts have been dedicated to understanding the physical excitation mechanisms and detectability of the linear ringdown spectrum. However, a debate on the domain of validity of linear perturbation theory in describing BH binary dynamics [161, 378] has sparked a community-wide initiative to systematically investigate nonlinear effects, such as quadratic mode excitation, absorption-induced changes in BH mass and spin, and transient effects. Among these, significant attention has been given to the new modes appearing in the spectrum at higher orders in perturbation theory [755, 756, 757, 758, 759, 760]. The quadratic modes or quadratic QNMs (QQNMs) appearing at second order are the topic of this section. These additional families of QNM frequencies naturally arise from the nonlinear nature of Einstein’s equations, and were recently confidently extracted from nonlinear binary merger simulations [761, 762, 763, 378, 540].

Following these breakthroughs, various analytical and numerical techniques were swiftly employed to characterize the amplitudes and the dependence on initial data of these modes for Schwarzschild and Kerr BHs [764, 765, 766, 767, 297, 768, 769, 770, 771, 297, 772, 277, 279]. These predictions are currently being incorporated as additional components in the construction of BBH waveform templates. Remarkably, not only the QQNM frequencies are calculable from perturbation theory, but also their relative amplitudes with respect to the linear modes can be fully obtained within perturbation theory only. This makes quadratic modes very clean probes of BH physics, as all of their properties are determined from perturbation theory alone. This section deals with the Schwarzschild case, while Kerr QQNMs are described in Section 4.4 below.

4.3.1 Quadratic modes in equatorial symmetry

Let us expand around the Schwarzschild metric g¯μ​ν\bar{g}_{\mu\nu} to second order in a bookkeeping parameter ε\varepsilon representing the small amplitude of the perturbations:

gμ​ν=g¯μ​ν+ε​hμ​ν(1)+ε2​hμ​ν(2)+𝒪⁡(ε3).g_{\mu\nu}=\bar{g}_{\mu\nu}+\varepsilon h^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}+\varepsilon^{2}h^{(2)}_{\mu\nu}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{3})\,. (4.42)

Linear perturbations hμ​ν(1)h_{\mu\nu}^{(1)} obey the standard RWZ equations (2.7), so that their propagating modes h+(1)h_{+}^{(1)} and h×(1)h_{\times}^{(1)} can be written far from the BH as

h+(1)−i​h×(1)=Mr​∑ℓ​m​n​𝔪𝒜ℓ​m​n(1)​𝔪​e−2−i​ωℓ​m​n𝔪​(t−r)​Yℓ​m​(θ,ϕ).h_{+}^{(1)}-ih_{\times}^{(1)}=\frac{M}{r}\sum_{\ell mn\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{A}_{\ell mn}^{(1)\mathfrak{m}}e^{-i\omega_{\ell mn}^{\mathfrak{m}}(t-r)}\hphantom{a}_{-2}Y^{\ell m}(\theta,\phi)\,. (4.43)

In this equation, the frequencies ωℓ​m​n𝔪\omega_{\ell mn}^{\mathfrak{m}} belong to the linear QNM frequency spectrum, and 𝒜ℓ​m​n(1)​𝔪\mathcal{A}_{\ell mn}^{(1)\mathfrak{m}} are the linear QNM amplitudes. Both depend on the mirror mode number 𝔪=±\mathfrak{m}=\pm, which distinguishes ordinary and mirror modes (see Eq. (2.20)). Note that for a Schwarzschild BH, the QNM frequencies ωℓ​m​n𝔪=ωℓ​0​n𝔪\omega_{\ell mn}^{\mathfrak{m}}=\omega_{\ell 0n}^{\mathfrak{m}} do not depend on mm. In the following discussion, the 𝔪ℓ​m​n{}_{\ell mn}^{\mathfrak{m}} indices will often be suppressed to avoid clutter.

We will start by making the simplifying assumption that the perturbations satisfy equatorial (or reflection, or planar) symmetry. In the general case where the progenitors’ intrinsic angular momenta (“spin”) are not aligned with the orbital angular momentum, the spins precess around the total angular momentum and this assumption is violated (see Section 5), but for the moment let us neglect spin precession and focus on nonprecessing binaries; this assumption will be dropped in Section 4.3.2. In this case the parity of a mode is (−1)ℓ+m(-1)^{\ell+m}, i.e., all metric perturbations satisfy the Zerilli equation for ℓ+m\ell+m even and the Regge-Wheeler equation for ℓ+m\ell+m odd (in a more generic setting, metric perturbations would contain both even and odd components for a fixed ℓ+m\ell+m). Furthermore, equatorial symmetry imposes a relation between the amplitudes of mirror and ordinary modes:

𝒜ℓ⁡(−m)​n(1)​(−𝔪)=(−1)ℓ​𝒜∗ℓ​m​n(1)​𝔪\mathcal{A}_{\ell(-m)n}^{(1)(-\mathfrak{m})}=(-1)^{\ell}{\mathcal{A}^{*}}_{\ell mn}^{(1)\mathfrak{m}} (4.44)

The second-order perturbations hμ​ν(2)h_{\mu\nu}^{(2)} can be split into parity-even (Zerilli) and parity-odd (Regge-Wheeler) sectors, each characterized by a Regge-Wheeler or Zerilli variable Ψ±(2)\Psi^{\pm(2)}, with frequency ω\omega and angular momentum numbers (ℓ,m)(\ell,m), using the same definitions as at first order. By plugging the metric decomposition into Einstein’s equations, at order ε2\varepsilon^{2} one obtains the equations of motion of Ψ±(2)\Psi^{\pm(2)},
