d2​Ψ±(2)d​r∗2+ω2​Ψ±(2)−V2±​(r)​Ψ±(2)=S,\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}\Psi^{\pm(2)}}{\mathrm{d}r_{*}^{2}}+\omega^{2}\Psi^{\pm(2)}-V_{2}^{\pm}(r)\Psi^{\pm(2)}=S\;, (4.45)

where V2±V_{2}^{\pm} is the Regge-Wheeler or Zerilli potential (see Eqs. (2.8) and (2.9)), we have suppressed the subscript denoting the spin of the perturbation from Ψ2±(2)=Ψ±(2)\Psi^{\pm(2)}_{2}=\Psi^{\pm(2)} to avoid confusion, and SS is a source term quadratic in the linear perturbation hμ​ν(1)h_{\mu\nu}^{(1)}. This simple quadratic dependence allows us to focus on a source given by a single pair of linear QNMs, the general case being obtained by superposition. Three essential properties of the quadratic source term SS can be derived by squaring the linear QNMs in Eq. (4.43):

  • (1)

    It contains a sum of terms oscillating at frequencies ω1+ω2\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}, where ωi\omega_{i} are the frequencies of the two linear modes 11 and 22 entering the square. In particular, since regular modes can couple to mirror modes, the real parts of the QNM frequencies can be added or subtracted, while the imaginary parts always add.

  • (2)

    The product of two spin-weighted spherical harmonics Yℓ1​m1s{}_{s}Y_{\ell_{1}m_{1}} and Yℓ2​m2s{}_{s}Y_{\ell_{2}m_{2}} needs to be expressed as a sum of spin-weighted spherical harmonics, which means the source will be proportional to a 3​j3j symbol (ℓ1ℓ2ℓm1m2−m)\begin{pmatrix}\ell_{1}&\ell_{2}&\ell\\ m_{1}&m_{2}&-m\end{pmatrix} ensuring the usual selection rules:

    ℓ=|ℓ1−ℓ2|,…,ℓ1+ℓ2,m=m1+m2.\ell=|\ell_{1}-\ell_{2}|,\dots,\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}\,,\qquad m=m_{1}+m_{2}\,. (4.46)

    In fact, the only dependence of the source term on mm, m1m_{1} and m2m_{2} is fully contained in the 3​j3j symbol because of angular momentum conservation.

  • (3)

    The amplitude of the source is quadratic in the linear mode amplitudes 𝒜(1)\mathcal{A}^{(1)}.

This nonlinear source term was computed in early works [755, 773, 774, 775] for the case ℓ=ℓ1=ℓ2=2\ell=\ell_{1}=\ell_{2}=2, and in [758, 757] for ℓ=4\ell=4, ℓ1=ℓ2=2\ell_{1}=\ell_{2}=2. The generic ℓ,ℓ1,ℓ2\ell,\ell_{1},\ell_{2} case was tackled in [776, 777, 756], although only in recent work [769, 768] expressions for the source term became publicly available (see Appendix A). In the most general case, the source for a single product of two linear modes has the following form:

S=ℱ1​(r)​Ψ1(1)​Ψ2(1)+ℱ2​(r)​(Ψ1(1))′​Ψ2(1)+ℱ3​(r)​Ψ1(1)​(Ψ2(1))′+ℱ4​(r)​(Ψ1(1))′​(Ψ2(1))′,\displaystyle S=\mathcal{F}_{1}(r)\Psi_{1}^{(1)}\Psi_{2}^{(1)}+\mathcal{F}_{2}(r)(\Psi_{1}^{(1)})^{\prime}\Psi_{2}^{(1)}+\mathcal{F}_{3}(r)\Psi_{1}^{(1)}(\Psi_{2}^{(1)})^{\prime}+\mathcal{F}_{4}(r)(\Psi_{1}^{(1)})^{\prime}(\Psi_{2}^{(1)})^{\prime}\,, (4.47)

where Ψ1(1)\Psi_{1}^{(1)} and Ψ2(1)\Psi_{2}^{(1)} are linear mode wavefunctions (Regge-Wheeler or Zerilli variables, depending on the parity of ℓ+m\ell+m) and the four functions ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i} depend on (ℓ,m)(\ell,m) as well as (ℓ1,m1,n1,𝔪1)×(ℓ2,m2,n2,𝔪2)(\ell_{1},m_{1},n_{1},\mathfrak{m}_{1})\times(\ell_{2},m_{2},n_{2},\mathfrak{m}_{2}). A priori, the quadratic frequency ω\omega appearing in SS could belong to the linear QNM spectrum. If this happens, the resulting QQNM amplitude would only renormalize the linear amplitude. This does not occur for Schwarzschild QNMs in vacuum, because the sum of two QNM frequencies does not belong to the discrete spectrum. For nonvacuum spacetimes, where models for the source term SS matter, this case is instead realized, because SS contains in general a continuum of frequencies. While the QQNM frequencies are trivial to find (ω=ω1+ω2\omega=\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}), the calculation of their amplitudes requires solving Eq. (4.45).

By definition, QQNMs are solutions to the second-order equations (4.45) with QNM boundary conditions, ψ(2)∝r∗→∞ei​ω​r∗\psi^{(2)}\mathrel{\mathop{\propto}\limits_{{r_{*}\rightarrow\infty}}}e^{i\omega r_{*}} and ψ(2)∝r∗→−∞e−i​ω​r∗\psi^{(2)}\mathrel{\mathop{\propto}\limits_{{r_{*}\rightarrow-\infty}}}e^{-i\omega r_{*}}. To impose these boundary conditions, observe that Eq. (4.45) is a linear inhomogeneous equation, whose solutions are the sum of a particular solution and a combination of homogeneous solutions. Imposing the QNM boundary conditions completely fixes the coefficients of the homogeneous solutions, thus removing any ambiguity. Instead, the inhomogeneity of Eq. (4.45) is what completely determines the amplitude of QQNMs, in contrast with linear QNMs, where the equation is homogeneous.

The second-order equation (4.45) can be solved with standard methods already used to solve for the linear spectrum, e.g., WKB [765], uniform approximation [764], or the well-known Leaver algorithm [769, 768] (see Appendix A). However, as noted in [755, 773, 774, 775, 776, 777, 756], a complication arises due to the source term diverging at the boundaries. In the particular case of the QNM problem, imposing QNM boundary conditions e.g. at infinity in Eq. (4.45) implies that S∝r∗→∞ei​ω​r∗/r2S\mathrel{\mathop{\propto}\limits_{{r_{*}\rightarrow\infty}}}e^{i\omega r_{*}}/r^{2}, but one finds from expression (4.47) that S∝r∗→∞ei​ω​r∗S\mathrel{\mathop{\propto}\limits_{{r_{*}\rightarrow\infty}}}e^{i\omega r_{*}} instead [758, 769]. Thus, it seems at first that QNM boundary conditions are incompatible with second-order perturbations. The solution to this conundrum is that these divergences are spurious, and they should cancel out when expressing QNM amplitudes in the GW strain (4.43) in a regular gauge at infinity, while the Regge-Wheeler gauge employed to derive Eq. (4.45) entails a poor asymptotic scaling [756]. In the particular case of the QNM setting, a workaround was proposed in [758, 769]: one can redefine a new, regular master scalar

Ψ~(2)​(r)=Ψ(2)​(r)+Δ⁡(r)​Ψ1(1)​Ψ2(1),\tilde{\Psi}^{(2)}(r)=\Psi^{(2)}(r)+\Delta(r)\Psi_{1}^{(1)}\Psi_{2}^{(1)}\,, (4.48)

where Δ⁡(r)=a2​r2+a1​r\Delta(r)=a_{2}r^{2}+a_{1}r is chosen to cancel the divergences. The regular variable obeys a differential equation at second order similar to Eq. (4.45), but with a modified source term obeying the correct asymptotics. One can also check that Δ⁡(r)\Delta(r) encodes the divergences in the change of gauge needed at second order to go from the Regge-Wheeler gauge to the transverse-traceless gauge, where the GW strain (4.43) is most easily extracted [769].

Employing this gauge, the amplitude prediction for all relevant QQNMs in the strain (4.43) can be computed using Leaver’s algorithm [768, 769]. Since the source is proportional to a product of linear amplitudes, the ratio of quadratic to linear amplitudes

ℛ=𝒜(2)/(𝒜1(1)​𝒜2(1))\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{A}^{(2)}/(\mathcal{A}^{(1)}_{1}\mathcal{A}^{(1)}_{2}) (4.49)

can be predicted [768], and it is shown for several combinations of linear modes (including mirror modes) in Fig. 34.

Note in particular that ℛ=0.154​e−0.068​i\mathcal{R}=0.154e^{-0.068i} for the QQNM (220+)×(220+)→(44)(220+)\times(220+)\rightarrow(44), which is typically the most excited nonlinear mode in quasi-circular binary mergers (see Section 4.5). This is a small number (even if its smallness was not required for perturbation theory to be valid, as this only requires 𝒜(2)≪𝒜(1)\mathcal{A}^{(2)}\ll\mathcal{A}^{(1)}), but could be within reach of XG detectors [778, 772, 779] (see Section 7.2.1 for a detailed discussion). Combinations of regular modes with mirror modes or with overtones can also have non-negligible ℛ\mathcal{R}, e.g. in the dominant ℓ=2\ell=2 multipole [768, 769], as also observed in numerical simulations [780]. In particular, combining a mode with its exact mirror is interesting because it produces quadratic modes which are purely imaginary and still have a nonzero amplitude (see also Section 5.4).

4.3.2 Beyond equatorial symmetry

The previous discussion was based on assuming equatorial symmetry for the QNM amplitudes. Going beyond that assumption, each single (ℓ,m)(\ell,m) linear metric perturbation will contain both even (P=+P=+, Zerilli) and odd (P=−P=-, Regge-Wheeler) parities. It was thus first conjectured in [297], and then explicitly shown [770], that in full generality quadratic modes are not completely characterized by a single number (the ratio ℛ\mathcal{R}), but they also depend on the linear modes’ parity. This dependence could explain some of the discrepancies found in the literature concerning the value of the ratio ℛ\mathcal{R} [297, 767, 762, 771, 761, 540]. A single quadratic mode thus depends on four numbers, which represent the four different ratios ℛP1×P2→P\mathcal{R}_{P_{1}\times P_{2}\rightarrow P} combining different parities among each other [769]. Indeed, although there seem to be eight different ways to combine ±×±→±\pm\times\pm\rightarrow\pm, they are in fact restricted by parity invariance, which imposes

(−1)ℓ1​P1×(−1)ℓ2​P2=(−1)ℓ​P,(-1)^{\ell_{1}}P_{1}\times(-1)^{\ell_{2}}P_{2}=(-1)^{\ell}P\,, (4.50)

so that the parity PP of the QQNM is fixed by the individual parities of linear modes. To find the value of the quadratic amplitude in this generic case, a polarization parameter can be introduced, encoding the deviation from equatorial symmetry:

𝔭ℓ​m​n𝔪=(−1)m​𝒜∗ℓ⁡(−m)​n(−𝔪)𝒜ℓ​m​n𝔪.\mathfrak{p}_{\ell mn}^{\mathfrak{m}}=(-1)^{m}\frac{{\mathcal{A}^{*}}_{\ell(-m)n}^{(-\mathfrak{m})}}{\mathcal{A}_{\ell mn}^{\mathfrak{m}}}\,. (4.51)

As before, the 𝔪ℓ​m​n{}_{\ell mn}^{\mathfrak{m}} indices will be suppressed in the following (𝔭ℓ​m​n𝔪→𝔭\mathfrak{p}_{\ell mn}^{\mathfrak{m}}\to\mathfrak{p}) to avoid clutter.

The parameter 𝔭\mathfrak{p} can also be thought of as a measure of the parity content of a given mode, i.e., 𝔭=(𝒜++i​𝒜−)/(𝒜+−i​𝒜−)\mathfrak{p}=(\mathcal{A}_{+}+i\mathcal{A}_{-})/(\mathcal{A}_{+}-i\mathcal{A}_{-}), where 𝒜±\mathcal{A}_{\pm} is the amplitude of the even (odd) component of the GW strain in Eq. (4.43) [769]. Equatorial symmetry imposes 𝔭=(−1)ℓ+m\mathfrak{p}=(-1)^{\ell+m} (consistent with either 𝒜+\mathcal{A}_{+} or 𝒜−\mathcal{A}_{-} being zero), but in the general case 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is a complex number. At second order, the quadratic ratio ℛ\mathcal{R} and the polarization parameter 𝔭(2)\mathfrak{p}^{(2)} of the quadratic mode are given by

ℛ\displaystyle\mathcal{R} =14​∑P1,P2ℛP1×P2→P​(1+P1​𝔭1(1))​(1+P2​𝔭2(1)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{P_{1},P_{2}}\mathcal{R}_{P_{1}\times P_{2}\rightarrow P}\big(1+P_{1}\mathfrak{p}_{1}^{(1)}\big)\big(1+P_{2}\mathfrak{p}_{2}^{(1)}\big)\,, (4.52)
𝔭(2)\displaystyle\mathfrak{p}^{(2)} =∑P1,P2P​ℛP1×P2→P​(1+P1​𝔭1(1))​(1+P2​𝔭2(1))∑P1,P2ℛP1×P2→P​(1+P1​𝔭1(1))​(1+P2​𝔭2(1)),\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{P_{1},P_{2}}P\,\mathcal{R}_{P_{1}\times P_{2}\rightarrow P}\big(1+P_{1}\mathfrak{p}_{1}^{(1)}\big)\big(1+P_{2}\mathfrak{p}_{2}^{(1)}\big)}{\sum_{P_{1},P_{2}}\mathcal{R}_{P_{1}\times P_{2}\rightarrow P}\big(1+P_{1}\mathfrak{p}_{1}^{(1)}\big)\big(1+P_{2}\mathfrak{p}_{2}^{(1)}\big)}\,, (4.53)

where the sum runs over all parities of the linear modes P1P_{1}, P2P_{2}, PP being given by Eq. (4.50), and ℛP1×P2→P\mathcal{R}_{P_{1}\times P_{2}\rightarrow P} are the quadratic ratios for individual parities. In equatorial symmetry 𝔭i=(−1)ℓi+mi\mathfrak{p}_{i}=(-1)^{\ell_{i}+m_{i}} (i=1,2i=1,2), recovering previous results with parities given by Pi=(−1)ℓi+miP_{i}=(-1)^{\ell_{i}+m_{i}}. It is interesting to consider ℛ\mathcal{R} as a function of the linear polarization parameters ℛ⁡(𝔭1(1),𝔭2(1))\mathcal{R}(\mathfrak{p}_{1}^{(1)},\,\mathfrak{p}_{2}^{(1)}), fixing the remaining quantum numbers. The variations of ℛ\mathcal{R} coming from its dependence on 𝔭\mathfrak{p} are plotted in Fig. 35 (see also [770]) for the self-coupling case (220+)×(220+)→(44)(220+)\times(220+)\rightarrow(44). In addition, it was numerically noticed that the the following combination vanishes identically:

ℛ⁡(+1,+1)+ℛ⁡(−1,−1)−2​ℛ​(0,0)≡0.\mathcal{R}(+1,+1)+\mathcal{R}(-1,-1)-2\mathcal{R}(0,0)\equiv 0\,. (4.54)

As a consequence, there is a linear relation between the four definite parity ratios ℛP1×P2→P\mathcal{R}_{P_{1}\times P_{2}\to P}, only three of them being independent. This property generalizes to Kerr, as will be explained in the next section.

4.4 Quadratic modes in Kerr

Initial contributors: Ma, Yang

An essential tool to investigate quadratic effects in Kerr BHs is the second-order Teukolsky formalism [781, 759, 760, 782, 783], that has been applied to compute QQNMs and mode couplings [297, 772]. Here we summarize the main results of this body of work.

4.4.1 Classification of mode couplings.

As in Section 2.1.1, a QQNM can be represented in terms of the linear modes that drive it with the notation (ℓ1,m1,n1,𝔪1,ℓ2,m2,n2,𝔪2)(\ell_{1},m_{1},n_{1},\mathfrak{m}_{1};\ell_{2},m_{2},n_{2},\mathfrak{m}_{2}), and its time and azimuthal dependence are given by e−i⁡(ωℓ1,m1,n1𝔪1+ωℓ2,m2,n2𝔪2)​t​ei⁡(m1+m2)​ϕe^{-i(\omega_{\ell_{1},m_{1},n_{1}}^{\mathfrak{m}_{1}}+\omega_{\ell_{2},m_{2},n_{2}}^{\mathfrak{m}_{2}})t}e^{i(m_{1}+m_{2})\phi}. By the usual angular momentum selection rules, this QQNM appears in the harmonics with azimuthal number mQ=(m1+m2)m_{Q}=(m_{1}+m_{2}). In the following, to reduce clutter in the notation, we denote (l,m,n,𝔪)(l,m,n,\mathfrak{m}) by a single multi-index LL, and (l,−m,n,−𝔪)(l,-m,n,-\mathfrak{m}) by L¯\bar{L}.

A QQNM can be excited by interactions between four distinct linear modes: L1,L¯1,L2L_{1},\bar{L}_{1},L_{2}, and L¯2\bar{L}_{2}, with respective amplitudes A1A_{1}, A−1A_{-1}, A2A_{2}, and A−2A_{-2}. These interactions can be categorized into four channels:

  • •

    L1⊗L2L_{1}\otimes L_{2} (hereafter +⁣+++): The two linear modes, L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}, generate frequency components ωℓ1,m1,n1𝔪1\omega_{\ell_{1},m_{1},n_{1}}^{\mathfrak{m}_{1}} and ωℓ2,m2,n2𝔪2\omega_{\ell_{2},m_{2},n_{2}}^{\mathfrak{m}_{2}} in the linearized metric. The interaction between these components results in the QQNM frequency.

  • •

    L¯1⊗L2\bar{L}_{1}\otimes L_{2} (hereafter −⁣+-+): The linear mode L¯1\bar{L}_{1} generates a frequency component −ω¯ℓ1−m1​n1−𝔪1-\bar{\omega}_{\ell_{1}-m_{1}n_{1}}^{-\mathfrak{m}_{1}} in the linearized metric, which is numerically equal to ωℓ1​m1​n1𝔪1\omega_{\ell_{1}m_{1}n_{1}}^{\mathfrak{m}_{1}} due to Eq. (2.20). At the same time, the second linear mode L2L_{2} produces a frequency component ωℓ2,m2,n2𝔪2\omega_{\ell_{2},m_{2},n_{2}}^{\mathfrak{m}_{2}}. The product of these components leads to the QQNM frequency.

  • •

    L1⊗L¯2L_{1}\otimes\bar{L}_{2} (hereafter +⁣−+-): This case is analogous to −⁣+-+, but with the roles of L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} exchanged (1↔2)(1\leftrightarrow 2).

  • •

    L¯1⊗L¯2\bar{L}_{1}\otimes\bar{L}_{2} (hereafter −⁣−--): The two linear modes, L¯1\bar{L}_{1} and L¯2\bar{L}_{2}, generate frequency components −ω¯ℓ1,−m1,n1−𝔪1-\bar{\omega}_{\ell_{1},-m_{1},n_{1}}^{-\mathfrak{m}_{1}} and −ω¯ℓ2,−m2,n2−𝔪2-\bar{\omega}_{\ell_{2},-m_{2},n_{2}}^{-\mathfrak{m}_{2}} in the linearized metric, which are numerically equal to ωℓ1​m1​n1𝔪1\omega_{\ell_{1}m_{1}n_{1}}^{\mathfrak{m}_{1}} and ωℓ2​m2​n2𝔪2\omega_{\ell_{2}m_{2}n_{2}}^{\mathfrak{m}_{2}}. Their coupling leads to the QQNM frequency. Intriguingly, a careful calculation [772, 297] shows that this coupling channel always vanishes identically, regardless of the types of parent modes and the spin of the Kerr BH.

The representation of LL and L¯\bar{L} is a more natural basis than the parity basis for analyzing QQNMs for a generic Kerr background, as the time and azimuthal dependence are conveniently factorized to calculate individual channels using the Teukolsky formalism. In addition, the vanishing coupling between two conjugate modes L¯1\bar{L}_{1} and L¯2\bar{L}_{2} is nontrivial, and is most conveniently expressed in the LL basis. As a result, the total amplitude of the QQNM, AQA_{Q}, can be written as

AQ=\displaystyle A_{Q}= ℛ+⁣+​A1​A2+ℛ+⁣−​A1​A¯−2+ℛ−⁣+​A¯−1​A2,\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{++}A_{1}A_{2}+\mathcal{R}_{+-}A_{1}\bar{A}_{-2}+\mathcal{R}_{-+}\bar{A}_{-1}A_{2}\,, (4.55)

where ℛ+⁣+,ℛ−⁣+\mathcal{R}_{++},\mathcal{R}_{-+}, and ℛ+⁣−\mathcal{R}_{+-} depend only on the dimensionless spin of the Kerr BH. This equation is the Kerr counterpart of Eq. (4.52) in the Schwarzschild case. In general, the four linear modes L1,2L_{1,2} and L¯1,2\bar{L}_{1,2} are excited independently, and so are their amplitudes A±1,±2A_{\pm 1,\pm 2}. Therefore, the connection between the quadratic amplitude and the linear amplitudes is initial-data dependent. In the special case of parity symmetry (as is the case for, e.g., nonprecessing binary mergers), mirror and ordinary mode amplitudes satisfy Eq. (4.44). Consequently we have

ℛtotal≡AQA1​A2=\displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\rm total}\equiv\frac{A_{Q}}{A_{1}A_{2}}= ℛ+⁣++(−1)ℓ2​ℛ+⁣−+(−1)ℓ1​ℛ−⁣+.\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{++}+(-1)^{\ell_{2}}\mathcal{R}_{+-}+(-1)^{\ell_{1}}\mathcal{R}_{-+}. (4.56)

In this case, the amplitude ratio becomes an intrinsic property of the Kerr BH, and reflects the total excitability of the QQNM.

4.4.2 Excitation of a mirror QQNM

Similarly to linear QNMs, where LL and L¯\bar{L} are mirrored counterparts, a QQNM (L1;L2)(L_{1};L_{2}) also has its mirror, represented by (L¯1;L¯2)(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2}). Here we show that their respective amplitude ratios are directly related via the parity transformation P−P_{-}, defined by (θ,ϕ)→(π−θ,ϕ+π)(\theta,\phi)\to(\pi-\theta,\phi+\pi).

Under the parity transformation, a strain h⁡(θ,ϕ)h(\theta,\phi) is mapped to h¯​(π−θ,ϕ+π)\bar{h}(\pi-\theta,\phi+\pi) [784]. Consequently, a linear QNM transforms as follows:

ALe−i​ωL​uSℓ​m−2(θ,ϕ;cL)\displaystyle A_{L}e^{-i\omega_{L}u}{}_{{}_{-2}}S_{\ell{m}}(\theta,\phi;c_{L}) →A¯L​ei​ω¯L​u​S¯ℓ​m−2​(π−θ,ϕ+π,cL)\displaystyle\to\bar{A}_{L}e^{i\bar{\omega}_{L}u}{}_{-2}\bar{S}_{\ell m}(\pi-\theta,\phi+\pi;c_{L})
=(−1)ℓ+mA¯Le−i​ωL¯​uSℓ−m−2(θ,ϕ;cL¯),\displaystyle=(-1)^{\ell+m}\bar{A}_{L}e^{-i\omega_{\bar{L}}u}{}_{{}_{-2}}S_{\ell{-m}}(\theta,\phi;c_{\bar{L}}), (4.57)

where we have used Eqs. (2.15) and (2.20). Therefore, the parity transformation takes the mode LL with amplitude ALA_{L} to the mode L¯\bar{L} with amplitude (−1)ℓ+m​A¯L(-1)^{\ell+m}\bar{A}_{L}.

Now consider the mirror QQNM (L¯1;L¯2)(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2}) and its +⁣+++ channel, where L¯1\bar{L}_{1} with amplitude AL¯1A_{\bar{L}_{1}} interacts with L¯2\bar{L}_{2} with amplitude AL¯2A_{\bar{L}_{2}}. The quadratic amplitude excited through this channel can be written as

A(L¯1;L¯2)+⁣+=ℛ+⁣+(L¯1;L¯2)​AL¯1​AL¯2.\displaystyle A^{++}_{(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2})}=\mathcal{R}_{++}^{(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2})}A_{\bar{L}_{1}}A_{\bar{L}_{2}}. (4.58)

Since the Kerr BH spin is an axial vector and is unaffected by parity transformations, the parity-transformed +⁣+++ channel remains a real process for the same Kerr BH. This leads to a QQNM (L1;L2)(L_{1};L_{2}) with amplitude (−1)ℓQ+mQ​A¯(L¯1;L¯2)+⁣+(-1)^{\ell_{Q}+m_{Q}}\bar{A}^{++}_{(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2})}, excited by two linear modes L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} with amplitudes (−1)ℓ1+m1​A¯L¯1(-1)^{\ell_{1}+m_{1}}\bar{A}_{\bar{L}_{1}} and (−1)ℓ2+m2​A¯L¯2(-1)^{\ell_{2}+m_{2}}\bar{A}_{\bar{L}_{2}}, respectively. By definition, we have

ℛ+⁣+(L1;L2)≡(−1)ℓQ+mQ​A¯(L¯1;L¯2)+⁣+(−1)ℓ1+ℓ2+m1+m2​A¯L¯1​A¯L¯2=(−1)ℓQ+ℓ1+ℓ2​ℛ¯+⁣+(L¯1;L¯2),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{++}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}\equiv\frac{(-1)^{\ell_{Q}+m_{Q}}\bar{A}^{++}_{(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2})}}{(-1)^{\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}+m_{1}+m_{2}}\bar{A}_{\bar{L}_{1}}\bar{A}_{\bar{L}_{2}}}=(-1)^{\ell_{Q}+\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}}\bar{\mathcal{R}}_{++}^{(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2})}, (4.59)

where we have used the relation mQ=m1+m2m_{Q}=m_{1}+m_{2}. In fact, this argument extends to any channel, leading to

ℛc1​c2(L1;L2)=(−1)ℓQ+ℓ1+ℓ2​ℛ¯c1​c2(L¯1;L¯2),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{c_{1}c_{2}}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}=(-1)^{\ell_{Q}+\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}}\bar{\mathcal{R}}_{c_{1}c_{2}}^{(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2})}, withc1,c2=(±,±).\displaystyle{\rm with}\quad c_{1},c_{2}=(\pm,\pm). (4.60)

The physical interpretation of Eq. (4.60) is clear: the amplitude ratio for a given channel of a QQNM is directly related to the amplitude ratio of the corresponding channel of the mirrored QQNM.

4.4.3 Quadratic effect of parity-definite QNMs.

By leveraging Eq. (4.60), we now show that the QQNM excited by parity-definite QNMs also has a definite parity.

Let us first consider two linear parity-definite modes

ALi​e−i​ωLi​u+(−1)ℓi+mi​Pi​A¯Li​e−i​ωL¯i​u,\displaystyle A_{L_{i}}e^{-i\omega_{L_{i}}u}+(-1)^{\ell_{i}+m_{i}}P_{i}\bar{A}_{L_{i}}e^{-i\omega_{\bar{L}_{i}}u}, withi=1,2,\displaystyle{\rm with}\quad i=1,2, (4.61)

where we have omitted the angular dependence for brevity. It is straightforward to show, by Eq. (4.57), that Pi=±1P_{i}=\pm 1 corresponds to even (odd) parity. The linear QNMs excite a QQNM (L1;L2)(L_{1};L_{2}) and its mirror (L¯1;L¯2)(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2}), which read

AL1​AL2​e−i⁡(ωL1+ωL2)​u​[ℛ+⁣+(L1;L2)+(−1)ℓ2+m2​P2​ℛ+⁣−(L1;L2)+(−1)ℓ1+m1​P1​ℛ−⁣+(L1;L2)]+e−i⁡(ωL¯1+ωL¯2)​u\displaystyle A_{L_{1}}A_{L_{2}}e^{-i(\omega_{L_{1}}+\omega_{L_{2}})u}\left[\mathcal{R}_{++}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}+(-1)^{\ell_{2}+m_{2}}P_{2}\mathcal{R}_{+-}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}+(-1)^{\ell_{1}+m_{1}}P_{1}\mathcal{R}_{-+}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}\right]+e^{-i(\omega_{\bar{L}_{1}}+\omega_{\bar{L}_{2}})u}
×P1​P2​A¯L1​A¯L2​[(−1)ℓ1+ℓ2+m1+m2​ℛ+⁣+(L¯1;L¯2)+(−1)ℓ1+m1​P2​ℛ+⁣−(L¯1;L¯2)+(−1)ℓ2+m2​P1​ℛ−⁣+(L¯1;L¯2)].\displaystyle\times P_{1}P_{2}\bar{A}_{L_{1}}\bar{A}_{L_{2}}\left[(-1)^{\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}+m_{1}+m_{2}}\mathcal{R}_{++}^{(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2})}+(-1)^{\ell_{1}+m_{1}}P_{2}\mathcal{R}_{+-}^{(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2})}+(-1)^{\ell_{2}+m_{2}}P_{1}\mathcal{R}_{-+}^{(\bar{L}_{1};\bar{L}_{2})}\right]. (4.62)

Using Eq. (4.60), the second term (namely, that involving ωL¯1+ωL¯2\omega_{\bar{L}_{1}}+\omega_{\bar{L}_{2}}) can be converted to

(…)+e−i⁡(ωL¯1+ωL¯2)​u\displaystyle(\ldots)+e^{-i(\omega_{\bar{L}_{1}}+\omega_{\bar{L}_{2}})u}
×P1​P2​(−1)ℓQ+mQ​A¯L1​A¯L2​[ℛ¯+⁣+(L1;L2)+(−1)ℓ2+m2​P2​ℛ¯+⁣−(L1;L2)+(−1)ℓ1+m1​P1​ℛ¯−⁣+(L1;L2)].\displaystyle\times P_{1}P_{2}(-1)^{\ell_{Q}+m_{Q}}\bar{A}_{L_{1}}\bar{A}_{L_{2}}\left[\bar{\mathcal{R}}_{++}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}+(-1)^{\ell_{2}+m_{2}}P_{2}\bar{\mathcal{R}}_{+-}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}+(-1)^{\ell_{1}+m_{1}}P_{1}\bar{\mathcal{R}}_{-+}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}\right]. (4.63)

Notice that the bracket of the mirror QQNM is now the complex conjugate of the first bracket in Eq. (4.62), which immediately reveals that the parity of the QQNM (L1;L2)(L_{1};L_{2}) is P1​P2P_{1}P_{2}. This can be summarized into the rule:

(even)⊗(even)→(even),(odd)⊗(odd)→(even),(odd)⊗(even)\displaystyle({\rm even})\otimes({\rm even})\to({\rm even}),\quad({\rm odd})\otimes({\rm odd})\to({\rm even}),\quad({\rm odd})\otimes({\rm even}) →(odd),\displaystyle\to({\rm odd}),

which extends the rule in Eq. (4.50) to the Kerr case. Similar to nonprecessing binaries, we can define a total amplitude ratio RparitytotalR^{\rm total}_{\rm parity} for the parity-definite QQNM

ℛparitytotal=ℛ+⁣+(L1;L2)+(−1)ℓ2+m2​P2​ℛ+⁣−(L1;L2)+(−1)ℓ1+m1​P1​ℛ−⁣+(L1;L2),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\rm total}_{\rm parity}=\mathcal{R}_{++}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}+(-1)^{\ell_{2}+m_{2}}P_{2}\mathcal{R}_{+-}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}+(-1)^{\ell_{1}+m_{1}}P_{1}\mathcal{R}_{-+}^{(L_{1};L_{2})}\,, (4.64)

which is also initial-data independent.

4.4.4 Computational methods.

The discussion of quadratic mode couplings in the Kerr BH spacetime presented so far has been somewhat qualitative. We now turn to two quantitative methods to compute the values of the amplitude ratios ℛc1​c2\mathcal{R}_{c_{1}c_{2}}.

The first method adopts an analytical approach [297]. Consider the second-order perturbation of Ψ4\Psi_{4},

Ψ4=ϵ​Ψ4(1)+ϵ2​Ψ4(2)+𝒪⁡(ϵ3),\displaystyle\Psi_{4}=\epsilon\Psi_{4}^{(1)}+\epsilon^{2}\Psi_{4}^{(2)}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,, (4.65)

with ϵ\epsilon being a book-keeping parameter. The dynamics of Ψ4(2)\Psi_{4}^{(2)} is governed by [781]

𝒯⁡[Γ¯4​Ψ4(2)]=S4(2),\displaystyle\mathcal{T}\left[\bar{\Gamma}^{4}\Psi_{4}^{(2)}\right]=S_{4}^{(2)}, (4.66)

where the Teukolsky operator 𝒯\mathcal{T} is defined in Eq. (2.2), Γ=r+i​a​cos⁡θ\Gamma=r+ia\cos\theta, and the source term S4(2)S_{4}^{(2)} is a complicated function of the linearized metric ha​b(1)h_{ab}^{(1)}. The perturbative metric ha​b(1)h_{ab}^{(1)} is defined by the expansion

ga​b=ga​b(0)+ϵ​ha​b(1)+ϵ2​ha​b(2)+𝒪⁡(ϵ3).g_{ab}=g^{(0)}_{ab}+\epsilon h_{ab}^{(1)}+\epsilon^{2}h_{ab}^{(2)}+\mathcal{O}\left(\epsilon^{3}\right)\,. (4.67)

For a Kerr BH, a linear QNM is described in terms of Ψ4(1)\Psi_{4}^{(1)}. Therefore, to derive the source term S4(2)S_{4}^{(2)} in Eq. (4.66), it is necessary to solve for ha​b(1)h_{ab}^{(1)} from Ψ4(1)\Psi_{4}^{(1)} through a process known as metric reconstruction. This method was pioneered by Chrzanowski [501] and Cohen and Kegeles [785, 504] for source-free scenarios. To be specific, it introduces an auxiliary scalar called the “Hertz potential,” which satisfies the s=2​(s=−2)s=2\,(s=-2) Teukolsky equation in the outgoing (ingoing) radiation gauge. Once determined, the linearized metric ha​b(1)h_{ab}^{(1)} and all Newman-Penrose spinors can be derived by differentiating the Hertz potential. Wald elegantly showed that this is feasible through an operator identity linking the Teukolsky operator and the linearized Einstein operator, which governs the dynamics of the linearized metric [786].

Metric reconstruction is performed analytically in the outgoing radiation gauge in [297], as this gauge directly relates the solution to physical observables at infinity. The procedure is made analytically tractable by using commutation relations between three derivative operators and other quantities in the Newman-Penrose formalism [297]. It was later realized that this approach is very similar to the Held formalism [787, 788].

The reconstruction yields an analytic expression for the source S4(2)S_{4}^{(2)}, which depends on both rr and θ\theta:

S4(2)=\displaystyle S_{4}^{(2)}= A1​(r,θ)​[ℒ2†​S​(θ)]2+A2​(r,θ)​[S⁡(θ)​ℒ1†​ℒ2†​S​(θ)]+A3​(r,θ)​[3​i​a​sin⁡θ​S​ℒ2†​S​(θ)]\displaystyle A_{1}(r,\theta)\left[\mathcal{L}_{2}^{\dagger}S(\theta)\right]^{2}+A_{2}(r,\theta)\left[S(\theta)\,\mathcal{L}_{1}^{\dagger}\mathcal{L}_{2}^{\dagger}S(\theta)\right]+A_{3}(r,\theta)\left[3ia\sin\theta\,S\,\mathcal{L}_{2}^{\dagger}S(\theta)\right]
+A4​(r,θ)​[a​sin⁡θ​S​(θ)]2,\displaystyle+A_{4}(r,\theta)\left[a\sin\theta S(\theta)\right]^{2}, (4.68)

where S⁡(θ)S(\theta) is the spin-weighted −2-2 spheroidal harmonic. The operator ℒn†\mathcal{L}_{n}^{\dagger} is given by

ℒn†=∂θ+icscθ∂ϕ+iasinθ∂t+ncotθ.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{n}^{\dagger}=\partial_{\theta}+i\csc\theta\partial_{\phi}+ia\sin\theta\partial_{t}+n\cot\theta. (4.69)

The angular dependence of the coefficients A1..4A_{1..4} is solely determined by Γ\Gamma: A1..4∼Γj/Γ¯kA_{1..4}\sim\Gamma^{j}/\bar{\Gamma}^{k}, with j=0,1j=0,1 and k=1..7k=1..7. Asymptotically, the source follows S4(2)∼𝒪⁡(r2)S_{4}^{(2)}\sim\mathcal{O}(r^{2}). Since the source S4(2)S_{4}^{(2)} cannot be separated into a product of purely angular and radial components, an angular projection of the equation is necessary. This can be performed by using the orthogonality of spin-weighted spheroidal harmonics with different ℓ\ell, but same ω\omega and mm [297].

Finally, the second-order Teukolsky equation in Eq. (4.66) can be solved using the shooting method along a complex contour, as shown in Fig. 11. Two solutions satisfying the QNM boundary condition are shot separately on the left and right vertical paths. The value of ℛc1​c2\mathcal{R}_{c_{1}c_{2}} can be obtained by matching the two solutions in the middle [297].

The second method [772] uses hyperboloidal slicing [348, 303, 302, 305] to solve the reduced second-order Teukolsky equation [782, 783]. The coordinates (T,Φ,R)(T,\Phi,R) are defined by the transformations

d​T=d​t+r2+a2Δ​d​r−2​(1+2​Mr)​d​r,d​Φ=d​ϕ+a​d​rΔ,R=1r.\displaystyle\mathrm{d}T=\mathrm{d}t+\frac{r^{2}+a^{2}}{\Delta}\mathrm{d}r-2\left(1+\frac{2M}{r}\right)\mathrm{d}r\,,\quad\mathrm{d}\Phi=\mathrm{d}\phi+\frac{a\mathrm{d}r}{\Delta}\,,\quad R=\frac{1}{r}\,. (4.70)

A pseudospectral method, where all quantities are expanded in Chebyshev polynomials in the radial direction and spin-weighted spherical harmonics in the angular directions, is adopted to treat the system fully numerically.

The source of the reduced second-order Teukolsky equation is computed numerically from the Einstein tensor. Specifically, considering the second-order perturbation of the metric in Eq. (4.67), the Einstein tensor can be written as

Ga​b​[ga​b]=ϵ​Ga​b(1)​[ha​b(1)]+ϵ2​Ga​b(1)​[ha​b(2)]+ϵ2​Ga​b(2)​[ha​b(1),ha​b(1)]+𝒪⁡(ϵ3).\displaystyle G_{ab}[g_{ab}]=\epsilon G_{ab}^{(1)}[h_{ab}^{(1)}]+\epsilon^{2}G_{ab}^{(1)}[h_{ab}^{(2)}]+\epsilon^{2}G_{ab}^{(2)}[h_{ab}^{(1)},h_{ab}^{(1)}]+\mathcal{O}\left(\epsilon^{3}\right)\,. (4.71)

Einstein’s equations at second order lead to

Ga​b(1)​[ha​b(2)]=−Ga​b(2)​[ha​b(1),ha​b(1)].G_{ab}^{(1)}[h_{ab}^{(2)}]=-G_{ab}^{(2)}[h_{ab}^{(1)},h_{ab}^{(1)}]\,. (4.72)

Therefore, −Ga​b(2)[ha​b(1),ha​b(1)]/8π-G_{ab}^{(2)}[h_{ab}^{(1)},h_{ab}^{(1)}]/8\pi acts as an effective stress-energy tensor driving the metric at second order, which can then be converted to the source term for the reduced Teukolsky equation [772]. Using the outgoing radiation gauge, the reduced second-order Teukolsky equation [782, 783] is equivalent to the Campanelli-Lousto approach [781]: Ψ4(2)\Psi_{4}^{(2)} arises solely from ha​b(2)h_{ab}^{(2)}, and the quadratic contribution from ha​b(1)h_{ab}^{(1)} vanishes. Finally, the equation is solved with the QNM boundary conditions to compute ℛc1​c2\mathcal{R}_{c_{1}c_{2}}. As an example, in Fig. 36 we show the quadratic ratios ℛ+⁣+\mathcal{R}_{++} and ℛtotal\mathcal{R}^{\rm total}, as defined in Eq. (4.56), for the QQNM (220+,220+)(220+;220+), across BH spins χ∈[0,0.95]\chi\in[0,0.95]. They are in remarkable agreement with the values obtained from numerical simulations.

One limitation of both methods is their inability to handle purely decaying QQNMs, which have vanishing real frequencies. For an alternative treatment of these modes, see Section 5.4.

4.5 Nonlinear numerical experiments: perturbation theory vs. full numerical relativity

Initial contributors: Cheung, Mitman, Redondo-Yuste, Zhu

The physics driving the relaxation of a BH to equilibrium, for instance, after a BBH merger, is mostly understood through the lens of linear perturbation theory. After a transient phase, the newly formed BH is assumed to be perturbatively close to its final state, and therefore the relaxation is expected to be well described as a superposition of QNMs with amplitudes that depend on the initial perturbation, followed by a late-time tail. However, GR is a nonlinear theory, and especially in the strong-field regime, nonlinearities are expected to have a significant impact. The goal of this section is to review the description of BH ringdown by comparing nonlinear and perturbative results.

Because of their nonlinear character, Einstein’s equations are very hard to solve analytically. This is particularly true in the dynamical, strong-field regime, where most known approximation schemes fail. However, continuous progress in the field of NR allows for numerical solutions with increasingly high accuracy.

Some problems in NR can also be addressed within BH perturbation theory. Paradigmatic examples are wave scattering off a BH [789, 228, 790, 791, 792] and the head-on collision of two BHs [793, 794, 795, 761, 796]. It is by virtue of these numerical experiments, where perturbation theory can be compared directly with fully nonlinear solutions, that we can understand more precisely the nonlinear content of the ringdown.

We first review numerical methods to deal with gravitational perturbations of BHs at the linear level and at higher orders, focusing on the comparison between the amplitude ratio between QQNMs and QNMs found from perturbative calculations and from scattering experiments. Then we consider fully nonlinear numerical experiments, including wave scattering and BBH mergers. We close by discussing how a time-varying background affects the relaxation of BHs at both the perturbative and nonlinear level.

4.5.1 Perturbation theory

Consider the problem of gravitational radiation scattering off a BH. In perturbation theory, the metric can be written as ga​b=ga​b(0)+∑n=1ϵn​ha​b(n)g_{ab}=g^{(0)}_{ab}+\sum_{n=1}\epsilon^{n}h^{(n)}_{ab}, where ga​b(0)g^{(0)}_{ab} is the background Kerr metric, and ϵ≪1\epsilon\ll 1 is a small book-keeping parameter. The stress-energy tensor is assumed to be zero at all perturbative orders, i.e., we are not concerned with how the gravitational perturbation is generated, but rather with its evolution and propagation. Thus, we consider the time evolution of some initial data,

ha​b(n)​(t=0)=h̊a​b(n),∂tha​b(n)​(t=0)=k̊a​b(n),h_{ab}^{(n)}(t=0)=\mathring{h}_{ab}^{(n)}\,,\qquad\partial_{t}h_{ab}^{(n)}(t=0)=\mathring{k}_{ab}^{(n)}\,, (4.73)

where tt is a causal coordinate. For example, one can choose tt to be the Boyer–Lindquist coordinate time tt or, alternatively, the hyperboloidal time parameter τ\tau (see Section 2.5). The quantities h̊a​b(n)\mathring{h}_{ab}^{(n)} and k̊a​b(n)\mathring{k}_{ab}^{(n)} are functions of the spatial coordinates alone. The evolution of the initial data is determined uniquely by linear equations at each order that can be written in the form

(ℰ​h(n))a​b=𝒮(n)​(h(1),…,h(n−1)),(\mathcal{E}h^{(n)})_{ab}=\mathcal{S}^{(n)}(h^{(1)},\dots,h^{(n-1)})\,, (4.74)

where (ℰ​h)a​b(\mathcal{E}h)_{ab} is the linearized Einstein tensor (given by the Lichnerowicz operator in the Lorenz gauge), and 𝒮(n)\mathcal{S}^{(n)} are source terms that involve second- and higher-order perturbations of the Einstein equations [797]. As discussed previously, lower-order metric perturbations act as an effective stress-energy tensor for the higher-order perturbations.

Perhaps the most relevant question in scattering experiments is how to specify the initial data {h̊a​b(n),k̊a​b(n)}\{\mathring{h}_{ab}^{(n)},\mathring{k}_{ab}^{(n)}\}. Once this is done, solving Eqs. (4.74) order by order is relatively straightforward from the mathematical point of view. Most early works on scattering in linear perturbation theory considered Gaussian-like profiles [789, 228, 798, 799, 800]. These have the advantage of being simple to implement, and of illustrating interesting physical content. For instance, one can directly characterize the excitation of different QNMs as a function of the width or of the spatial spread of the initial data [800, 801]. The disadvantage of using simple initial data like Gaussian wave packets is that it is harder to directly compare the results with nonlinear evolutions of the Einstein equations.

There are three ways to overcome this obstacle.

The simplest approach is to prescribe initial data for nonlinear simulations that mimic those chosen in perturbation theory [791, 771, 426]. Brill wave initial data [791] provide a natural way of doing this when the perturbed BH does not rotate. Another alternative for rotating BHs is to specify an initial guess for {h̊a​b(n),k̊a​b(n)}\{\mathring{h}_{ab}^{(n)},\mathring{k}_{ab}^{(n)}\}, and rescale the metric by a conformal factor. The shift and conformal factor that solve the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints can be found numerically using, e.g., the conformal thin sandwich method [771, 426]. Then, one can read off the actual metric perturbations and their time derivatives.

An alternative approach, the so-called “close limit approximation” (CLA) [802], consists of starting from exact initial data that describe two BHs. Originally, the initial data were based on the Misner wormhole solution that describes a wormhole with a single asymptotic region [803], and parameterized by the distance between the two mouths. If this distance is small enough, both mouths are enclosed by a common apparent horizon, and the Misner wormhole can be written explicitly as a perturbation around Schwarzschild, order by order in the distance between the mouths of the wormhole. This problem was studied at second order in perturbation theory in a series of papers [802, 804, 805] that found very good agreement with nonlinear simulations, even for cases where the perturbative solution was not expected to hold up. The CLA was extended to Brill–Lindquist initial data in [806, 807], and to Bowen–York initial data in [808]. An extension to rotating backgrounds is more challenging since the Kerr metric cannot be written as a conformally flat metric, although there are ways to overcome this difficulty [809, 810, 811].

A third approach is the Lazarus program [812, 781, 813, 814, 815, 816, 817]. The idea here is to read out the initial data for the perturbations around a Kerr BH directly from a snapshot of a numerical simulation, once the two merging BHs are very close to each other. This allowed to obtain hybrid waveforms (fully nonlinear during the late stages of the inspiral, and based on perturbation theory to describe the merger-ringdown) which, nonetheless, showed excellent agreement with NR simulations that were evolved through the merger, once those became available [818].

Once the initial data are prescribed, one has to solve the perturbation equations. We now describe the main practical methods employed for the solution, with a focus on perturbations around rotating BHs. We refer the interested reader to [819] for an equivalent calculation for second-order perturbations in Schwarzschild. The method presented here is based on [759, 760]; alternative methods designed to describe perturbations sourced by the motion of point masses [820, 797] are not covered here.

Let {la,na,ma,m¯a}\{l^{a},n^{a},m^{a},\bar{m}^{a}\} be a null tetrad aligned along the principal null directions. We work in the Newman-Penrose formalism (see [748] for a review), and denote by D=la​∇aD=l^{a}\nabla_{a}, Δ=na​∇a\Delta=n^{a}\nabla_{a} the contractions of the covariant derivatives along the principal null directions. We will use the Geroch-Held-Penrose operators ð,ð′\eth,\eth^{\prime} to compute the covariant derivatives in the remaining directions. As discussed in Section 2.1, the vacuum first-order metric perturbation in the radiation gauge ha​b(1)h_{ab}^{(1)} is governed only by one homogeneous equation for the linear perturbation of the Weyl scalar with maximum spin weight, Ψ4(1)\Psi_{4}^{(1)}. This is the Teukolsky equation, which we can write in terms of Newman-Penrose quantities (see e.g. [1] for definitions) as

𝒪⁡[Ψ4(1)]≡[(Δ+4​μ+μ¯)​(D+4​ϵ−ρ)−(ð′+4​π−τ¯)​(ð−τ)−3​Ψ2]​Ψ4(1)=0.\mathcal{O}[\Psi_{4}^{(1)}]\equiv\Bigl[(\Delta+4\mu+\bar{\mu})(D+4\epsilon-\rho)-(\eth^{\prime}+4\pi-\bar{\tau})(\eth-\tau)-3\Psi_{2}\Bigr]\Psi_{4}^{(1)}=0\,. (4.75)

The second-order metric perturbations can also be encoded in the perturbation of the maximal spin weight Weyl scalars, e.g., Ψ4(2)\Psi_{4}^{(2)}, and they also satisfy the Teukolsky equation, but in this case, with a source [781]:

𝒪⁡[Ψ4(2)]=𝒯⁡[ha​b(1)].\mathcal{O}[\Psi_{4}^{(2)}]=\mathcal{T}[h^{(1)}_{ab}]\,. (4.76)

The source term cannot be written directly in terms of Ψ4(1)\Psi_{4}^{(1)}, but instead it involves different metric components of ha​b(1)h^{(1)}_{ab}, perturbations of spin coefficients, as well as perturbations of other Weyl scalars. The issue of finding these quantities from a solution Ψ4(1)\Psi_{4}^{(1)} of the homogeneous Teukolsky equation is known as the metric reconstruction problem, and many different approaches have been proposed to solve it [501, 504, 786, 782, 821, 822, 823]. The approach put forward in [759] is easily implemented in order to reconstruct ha​b(1)h^{(1)}_{ab} in the absence of matter fields, and it casts the metric in the outgoing radiation gauge, which is well behaved numerically. In simple words, it consists in solving a set of seven nested transport equations (i.e., first order differential equations which do not involve time derivatives). The procedure is lengthy, but the resulting equations can easily be solved numerically. However, this framework is not well suited to push the formalism to higher orders in perturbation theory [759, 760].

Once the source term is known, the inhomogeneous Teukolsky equation can be solved. A particularly efficient solution technique uses pseudospectral methods in hyperboloidal slicing. By choosing hyperboloidal coordinates {T,R,θ,ϕ}\{T,R,\theta,\phi\}, the boundary conditions that select QNMs are satisfied automatically, since the constant-TT slices become null at the horizon and at future null infinity (see Section 2.5.4). A generic unknown ff (e.g., Ψ(1)\Psi^{(1)}) is then decomposed in a spectral basis,

f=∑ℓ,nfℓ,n​(T)​Tn​(x)​Pℓ​ms​(−cos⁡θ)​e−i​m​ϕ,f=\sum_{\ell,n}f_{\ell,n}(T)T_{n}(x){}_{s}P_{\ell m}(-\cos\theta)e^{-im\phi}\,, (4.77)

where x=2​R/r+−1x=2R/r_{+}-1 is the compact radial coordinate, Tn​(x)T_{n}(x) are Chebsyhev polynomials, and Pℓ​ms{}_{s}P_{\ell m} are spin-weighted associated Legendre polynomials. The Teukolsky equation can be written in a first-order form as ∂T𝐯=𝐀​∂R𝐯+𝐁​𝒟2​𝐯+𝐂𝐯\partial_{T}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{A}\partial_{R}\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{B}\mathcal{D}^{2}\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{C}\mathbf{v}, where 𝒟2\mathcal{D}^{2} is the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the sphere, and the matrices 𝐀,𝐁,𝐂\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C} are read from the equation. In this form, the variables are evolved in time using, e.g., an explicit Runge–Kutta method.

We can choose initial data corresponding to a Gaussian profile for Ψ4(1)\Psi_{4}^{(1)}, setting Ψ4(2)=0\Psi_{4}^{(2)}=0. Initially, the rest of the metric fluctuations are assumed to be zero (e.g., hl​l(1)=0h^{(1)}_{ll}=0). This is not consistent with Ψ4(1)≠0\Psi_{4}^{(1)}\neq 0. However, if the initial data have compact support, one can show [760] that constraint violating modes propagate towards the horizon, and therefore they will exit the computational domain after a short amount of time T=TRT=T_{R}. Then, in a certain sense, the “real” initial data are only specified at T=TRT=T_{R}, the time after which the evolution of Ψ4(2)\Psi_{4}^{(2)} is started.

This method was used in [767, 771] to extract the amplitude ratio between the QQNM (220)×(220)(220)\times(220) and its parent mode (220)(220). In [767] the amplitude of the modes was inferred with an agnostic algorithm based on Bayesian methods; in [771], it was found by minimizing the mismatch between the signal and a template containing a superposition of QNMs. In both cases the recovered amplitudes were checked to be stable and independent of the starting time of the fit (within a certain appropriate range), and the two methods are in very good agreement. More interestingly, these studies indicate that the ratio between these modes as computed from perturbation theory is in very good agreement with the value extracted with nonlinear, NR simulations of merging BHs. In addition, both works show that the ratio between QQNMs and QNMs is only mildly dependent on the properties of the Gaussian pulse used as initial data. A summary of the different results for this nonlinear ratio is shown in Fig. 36. Note the good agreement between second-order perturbation theory calculations (including both TD scattering experiments and FD calculations) and the fully nonlinear evolutions.

4.5.2 Fully nonlinear numerical experiments

The perturbative regime can also be studied through numerical experiments which solve the full Einstein equations. Fully nonlinear simulations of BH spacetimes have a long history [824]. In fact, the first attempts at simulating BBH collisions by Hahn and Lindquist in 1964 [825] predate the usage of the term “black hole” to describe these objects. Here we discuss simulations of waves scattering off isolated BHs, as well as BBH mergers.

Wave packet scattering

One of the first “modern” fully nonlinear evolutions of a single perturbed BH [791] studies a time-symmetric GW falling into a single BH in full NR and compares the results to the corresponding first-order evolution. The outgoing GW in the fully nonlinear simulation is well-modeled by the expected fundamental QNM and the result agrees remarkably well with the perturbative solution, as long as the amplitude of the infalling perturbation is small. For larger perturbations, however, the mass of the BH can change by a large fraction, and the outgoing radiation can be significantly different from the predictions of first-order perturbation theory.

More recent work considers infalling radiation on an isolated BH to investigate whether certain modes of the outgoing radiation exhibit a quadratic scaling with respect to the initial amplitude of the perturbation [792]. This work simulates infalling radiation of varying amplitude with angular structure corresponding to (ℓ,m)=(2,0)(\ell,m)=(2,0) or (2,2)(2,2). In the (2,0)(2,0) case, excitations in the (4,0)(4,0) and (6,0)(6,0) modes scale as the square and cube of the initial perturbation’s amplitude. By Fourier transforming the resulting waveform, the dominant frequency in the (4,0)(4,0) mode is found to be twice that of the dominant frequency in the (2,0)(2,0) mode, while two frequencies are found in the (6,0)(6,0) mode: one is three times the (2,0)(2,0) mode frequency, and the other is very close to the frequency of the (2,0)(2,0) mode. For the (2,2)(2,2) case, the (2,0)(2,0), (4,0)(4,0), and (4,4)(4,4) modes exhibit a very similar quadratic behavior, while the (4,2)(4,2), (6,2)(6,2), and (6,6)(6,6) modes exhibit a cubic behavior.

In conclusion, these pioneering investigations already provide strong numerical evidence that a clear nonlinear structure in the ringdown should generically be present (and predictable) given the initial amplitude and angular structure of the perturbation.

Head-on mergers

To date, all of the observed GW events, including those with a clear ringdown signal, come from binary compact object mergers. If nonlinear QNMs are within reach of current observatories, the first detections will most likely come from the ringdown of a remnant BH produced by a binary merger. To understand the experimental data, it is essential to study the excitation of nonlinear QNMs in NR simulations of binary mergers.

Astrophysically realistic simulations should target BBHs in inspiraling (and typically approximately circular) orbits, that eventually merge and form a single, spinning remnant. The advantage of studying head-on collisions is that these systems are more symmetric (hence easier to simulate) and that the amplitude of the emitted GWs, including linear and nonlinear QNMs, can be controlled by tuning the initial speed (or equivalently, the center-of-mass energy) of the colliding BHs [826, 827, 828, 829, 126, 761]. This is particularly useful to measure the scaling relationship between the amplitudes of nonlinear QNMs and their linear parent modes, because a set of simulations with a wide range of initial speeds can probe the relationship over a large range of amplitudes. Quasi-circular simulations, while more realistic, typically span a smaller range of collision energies, so the scaling relationship can only be probed in a more restricted range of amplitudes.

In [761], head-on collisions of nonspinning, equal mass BHs are simulated with the GRChombo code [830] over a relatively broad range of center-of-mass Lorentz factor boosts γ∈[1.2,3.2]\gamma\in[1.2,3.2] (i.e., β=v/c∈[0.553,0.95]\beta=v/c\in[0.553,0.95]) with the specific goal of measuring the excitation of nonlinear QNMs. Under these symmetry assumptions, the simulation domain can be reduced to two dimensions. The remnant is a nonrotating Schwarzschild BH, so the frequencies of QNMs with the same azimuthal number mm are degenerate, meaning that each mode can be labeled by (ℓ,n)(\ell,n). By extracting the gravitational perturbations in terms of Ψ4\Psi_{4}, this work finds QQNMs sourced by the (2,0)×(2,0)(2,0)\times(2,0) and (2,0)×(4,0)(2,0)\times(4,0) linear QNMs in the ℓ=4\ell=4 and ℓ=6\ell=6 harmonics, respectively, with amplitudes spanning an order of magnitude over the simulations. The second-order mode amplitudes scale quadratically with the amplitudes of their parent linear modes and the phases are the sum of the corresponding linear phases, as expected, implying that nonlinear QNMs are definitely present in these ultrarelativistic head-on simulations.

Inspiralling mergers

The first evidence of QQNMs in BBH ringdown waveforms was presented more than a decade ago in [831]. The work is mostly focused on the construction of fits of the linear QNM amplitudes as a function of the parameters of the progenitor through the analysis of 68 nonspinning BBH mergers with mass ratios between [1, 15]. Interestingly, the QNM superpositions that seem to best describe the (4,4)(4,4) and (5,5)(5,5) multipoles of the Ψ4\Psi_{4} Weyl scalar are found to contain mode frequencies close to the (2,2,0)×(2,2,0)(2,2,0)\times(2,2,0) and (2,2,0)×(3,3,0)(2,2,0)\times(3,3,0) QQNMs.

More recent studies focusing on QQNMs in BBH simulations [761, 762], independently confirm the presence of QQNMs in quasi-circular, nonprecessing NR simulations using the SpEC code [832]. The amplitudes of the QQNMs scale quadratically with the amplitudes of their parent modes, providing clear evidence that QQNMs with the expected nonlinear behavior are present in quasi-circular BBH merger simulations. This result has since received even more support through the analysis of a larger set of quasi-circular, nonprecessing BBH simulations presented in [833]: see, e.g., Fig. 9 of. [833]. Another recent analysis focused on the stability of overtone fitting in NR waveforms finds evidence of at least four QQNMs in the dominant (2,2)(2,2) mode of quasi-circular, nonprecessing BH mergers [780]. For highly-spinning remnants, there is evidence for QQNMs sourced by the linear QNM pairs (2,−2,0,−)×(4,4,0,+)(2,-2,0,-)\times(4,4,0,+), (3,−2,0,−)×(4,4,0,+)(3,-2,0,-)\times(4,4,0,+), (2,2,0,+)×(2,0,0,+)(2,2,0,+)\times(2,0,0,+), and (2,2,0,+)×(2,0,0,−)(2,2,0,+)\times(2,0,0,-). A second high-accuracy simulation producing a remnant with smaller spin shows evidence of the same four modes, as well as weaker evidence of the presence of QQNMs sourced by the (2,2,0,+)×(3,0,0,+)(2,2,0,+)\times(3,0,0,+), (2,2,0,+)×(3,0,0,−)(2,2,0,+)\times(3,0,0,-), (2,2,0,+)×(4,0,0,+)(2,2,0,+)\times(4,0,0,+), and (2,2,0,+)×(4,0,0,−)(2,2,0,+)\times(4,0,0,-) pairs.

While the QQNM frequencies can be simply predicted from BH perturbation theory, their angular structure is nontrivial. In particular, even though the angular structure of the parent modes is represented by spheroidal harmonics with an oblateness parameter equal to the product of the spin and the QNM frequency, the source at second order in perturbation theory is not separable, and its angular dependence is a complicated combination of spin-weighted spheroidal harmonics [297]. This complexity can be illustrated numerically by leaving the spherical-spheroidal QQNM mixing coefficients as free parameters when fitting the ringdown phase of NR waveforms over the two-sphere. This analysis finds that the angular structure of the QQNMs does not match simple (and naive) expectations [834], as suggested in [297]. This complexity offers interesting opportunities: spatial information can be extracted from NR by fitting a feature with known time dependence to all of the spherical harmonic modes, allowing the shape of the feature to be reconstructed. This program was initiated in [834] and called “BH cartography.” BH cartography allows us, at least in principle, to determine the viewing angles that maximize the amplitude of the quadratic QNMs. This can be an important guide for future searches.

Horizons

The QNMs observed in binary merger signals represent perturbations propagating out to infinity. However, GWs also propagate into the BH horizon. It has been shown that the shear of the out-going light rays at the common horizon of a BBH merger can be accurately described by a superposition of QNMs that match those observed at infinity [835]. It is then natural to expect that nonlinear QNMs should also be observable within the evolution of the shear, as the dynamics of the horizon should be nonlinear. Indeed, the (2,0)×(2,0),(2,0)×(4,0)(2,0)\times(2,0),(2,0)\times(4,0) and possibly the (2,0)×(6,0)(2,0)\times(6,0) or (4,0)×(4,0)(4,0)\times(4,0) QQNM are found, respectively, in the ℓ=2,4,6\ell=2,4,6 horizon shear modes in head-on BBH collisions [836]. The amplitudes of the QQNMs follow the expected quadratic scaling relationship with respect to the parent linear QNMs. However, the scaling coefficient is found to be different when studying a set of simulations with two BHs of fixed mass ratios but varying initial momentum, versus simulations with varying mass ratios but fixed initial momentum. This is unexpected, given that quadratic amplitude ratios should be independent of initial conditions, beside parity. Further work is needed to understand the source of the discrepancy.

4.5.3 Changing background

During a BBH coalescence, a significant portion of the system’s energy resides outside the newly formed horizon as perturbations, some of which fall back into the BH while others propagate to infinity, producing the ringdown waveform. Infalling of perturbations increase the remnant BH’s mass (as computed from the apparent horizon properties) by as much as 5% in equal-mass mergers [837, 426]. This substantial change in the BH background raises questions about the validity of traditional perturbation theory at the peak of the waveform. Specifically, can the GWs be modeled as a superposition of QNMs when the underlying spacetime itself is evolving? If so, to what extent?

This issue is not new, as debates around nonlinearity in ringdown go back to early efforts like the Lazarus project [812, 781, 813, 814, 815, 816, 817], prior to the first nonlinear simulation of BBH merger [837], and continued when these simulations first became available [838, 839]. Early comparisons between time evolutions of identical initial data describing a single perturbed BH in NR and in linear perturbation theory show that nonlinear waveforms can significantly deviate from their linear counterparts when the amplitude of the initial perturbation is sufficiently large [815].

Another way to quantify this nonlinear effect is to perform perturbation theory on a time-dependent background. A good toy model is provided by the Vaidya spacetime, where the change in the background is driven by accretion of null dust (instead of the in-falling perturbations characteristic of BBH mergers) and a nonlinearly changing mass function can be arbitrarily specified. The scalar QNMs of the Vaidya spacetime are known [840] and its nonadiabatic behavior was quantified in a study of time-dependent Reissner-Nordström BHs [841]. The imprint on changing QNM frequencies in a Vaidya spacetime with a mass function resembling what is observed in BBH mergers was studied for gravitational perturbations in [335]. If the mass function changes slowly, the frequencies follow an adiabatic evolution such that the product ω​M\omega M remains approximately constant. This simple model can be improved by studying the problem perturbatively in the derivatives of the mass function [427]. Including this information in the ringdown model can significantly improve the fit of the waveform in a changing-mass background, even when the change due to the mass function is far from adiabatic [335].

Alternatively, one can try to capture the time-evolution of the background through an adiabatic approximation [299]. This work compares the nonlinear and linear evolution of a spherically symmetric scalar field in an asymptotically AdS Schwarzschild BH background, with initial data given by an exact QNM profile. Because of spherical symmetry and the “compact” nature of the spacetime provided by the AdS boundary conditions, the numerical evolutions are very accurate. For the linear evolution, the mass flux of the scalar field is tracked through the horizon, and the background mass is updated as a function of time during the course of the evolution. Reference [299] shows that an infalling linear mode can nonlinearly excite other scalar modes due to the changing mass of the background. A similar study of linear gravitational perturbations of (asymptotically flat) Kerr BHs yields similar results [425].

In general, these ad hoc adiabatic approximations are in agreement with the qualitative predictions based on Vaidya spacetimes, yielding credibility to both. However these approximations do not fully capture the nonlinear features present in the BH ringdown. In particular, the key assumptions of spherical symmetry (in the Vaidya spacetime) and adiabaticity (in postulating the mass-varying Teukolsky equation in [425]) are only rough approximations. A more self-consistent numerical assessment of the imprints of a changing mass and spin [426] compares the ringdown waveform of a linearly and nonlinearly perturbed Kerr BH with spin a=0.7a=0.7 using a setup similar to [815]. The perturbation is a Gaussian pulse. Constraint-satisfying initial data are constructed using the conformal thin sandwich method [842] and evolved both linearly and nonlinearly with consistent gauge conditions to first order. A comparison of the waveforms and of their decomposition into QNMs shows that the the fully nonlinear QNM amplitudes deviate from the linear predictions at third order in the initial perturbation amplitude, as expected from perturbation theory. It is perhaps more surprising that perturbations leading to ∼5%\sim 5\% changes in BH mass and spin (typical in astrophysical mergers) lead to nonlinear distortions in the mode amplitudes that can reach ∼50%\sim 50\% near the peak of the waveform. In addition, the phase difference between the linear and nonlinear waveforms displays a nonlinear drift in the frequency of the waveform, causing rapid dephasing between nonlinear and linear waveforms for large perturbations.

Despite these significant nonlinear effects, a linear QNM model using fixed QNM frequencies based on the remnant BH mass and spin remains surprisingly accurate from the peak amplitude onward, in the sense that the residual and stability of the fit for linear and nonlinear waveforms are comparable [426]. This remarkable success of the linear QNM model can be attributed to the overlap between the nonlinear phase (where the BH mass and spin are rapidly evolving) and the transient, which is already present at the linear level. This suggests that the linear transient is the bottleneck for measuring and constraining nonlinear effects, such as the time dependence of the QNM frequency. However, the simple time-symmetric Gaussian pulse initial data used in [426] are unlikely to be a good approximation of post-merger perturbations for generic binaries. More realistic initial data are required to better understand nonlinear effects in realistic BBH mergers.

Some promising results in this direction emerge from a comparison of fully nonlinear head-on BH collisions with perturbative evolutions of test-particle infalls with compatible initial data. The resulting ringdown waveforms are in remarkable agreement (see [796] and Fig. 53), suggesting that nonlinear effects are suppressed in this case. More work is needed to understand if this suppression occurs for more general, astrophysically realistic mergers, and how the evolution of the BH spin (which is identically zero in head-on collisions) affects these results.

5 Ringdown modeling in gravitational waveforms

Misner proposed the following problem for my Ph.D. thesis. Take two of these entities that are now called black holes. Revolving around each other, they come close as energy is radiated away in the form of gravitational waves. They coalesce into an ellipsoidal “Schwarzschild surface” still rotating and radiating. Study the whole process, computing all the characteristics of the emitted gravitational radiation. Fine, I said, thy will be done! At the time, I did not realize the magnitude of this problem. Had I pursued it, I might have entered the Guinness book of records as the oldest graduate student alive, that too without financial support.

C.V. Vishveshwara, On the black hole trail…: a personal journey, text of the lecture delivered on February 17, 1996 on the occasion of the XVII Meeting of the Indian Association for General Relativity and Gravitation held at the Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Madras.

The ultimate goal of the techniques described in the previous chapter is to build a model of the ringdown waveform that can be used in GW data analysis. This is the formidable problem that Misner assigned to Vishveshwara for his Ph.D. thesis more than 50 years ago. In this chapter we consider various aspects of this problem. We start by reviewing a large body of work to extract stationary QNM amplitudes from numerical simulations of BBH mergers, and to understand their dependence on the binary parameters (Section 5.1). The extraction of the QNM amplitudes is conceptually challenging because they generally become time-dependent as we approach the nonlinear merger. This has been addressed through several phenomenological models, reviewed in Section 5.2. In Section 5.3 we discuss our current understanding of the power-law tails following the ringdown regime, both in the test-particle limit and for comparable mass mergers. To ensure that the ringdown physics extracted from numerical simulations is frame-invariant, one must transform from the initial binary frame used in the simulations to an appropriate remnant frame through a “BMS frame fixing.” This procedure, and the permanent net change in the GW strain between early and late times (“GW memory”), are discussed in Section 5.4. Finally, we review recent progress in our understanding of the correspondence between QNMs and horizon dynamics (Section 5.5).

5.1 Stationary amplitudes dependence on binary parameters: numerical extraction

Initial contributors: Baibhav, Carullo, Forteza, Hughes, London

The QNM frequencies and damping times are solely dictated by the mass and spin of the remnant BH. Instead, the initial conditions arising during the perturbation phase, prior to the ringdown, influence the excitation of the modes, i.e., their amplitudes and phases. In the context of BBH mergers, the ringdown follows immediately after the merger of the two progenitor BHs, which thus provides the initial conditions for the ringdown phase, and sets the QNM amplitudes and phases. Thus there is an intrinsic link between the parameters of the initial binary system (determining the merger configuration) and the values of the ringdown complex amplitudes Cn′C_{n^{\prime}} capturing the spacetime geometry right after merger. All GW ringdown models based on QNM superpositions embed this information in the values of Cn′C_{n^{\prime}}, either implicitly or explicitly. Since the amplitudes Cn′C_{n^{\prime}} depend on the contribution of the initial perturbation, Tn′T_{n^{\prime}}, a complete characterization of the ringdown amplitudes would require a knowledge of Tn′T_{n^{\prime}}, but these coefficients are currently unknown with the exception of a few simplified scenarios (see Section 4.2.2). Lacking a direct analytical computation, the coefficients Cn′C_{n^{\prime}} can be estimated using NR simulations of coalescing BBH systems with varying masses and spins. This is the main topic of this section.

For brevity we will use a multi-index n′→(ℓ​m​n,±)n^{\prime}\rightarrow(\ell mn,\pm), where the (ℓ​m​n)(\ell mn) indices refer to the decomposition of the signal in spheroidal harmonics Sℓ​m​n​(θ,φ,a​ω)S_{\ell mn}(\theta,\varphi,a\omega), and the index ±\pm labels either prograde or retrograde modes (also referred to as co-/counter-rotating modes). For most of the parameter space of interest, C+≫C−C_{+}\gg C_{-}. Notable exceptions are binaries with large spins counter-aligned with respect to the orbital angular momentum, highly precessing binaries, or Schwarzschild BHs, in which the two branches of the solution converge to a single one with C+=C−∗C_{+}=C_{-}^{*}. We will usually drop the ±\pm indices to simplify the notation, and restore them only in cases where counter-rotating modes play a significant role. Typically, these complex amplitudes are split into an amplitude and phase as follows:

Cℓ​m​n=Aℓ​m​n​ei​ϕℓ​m​n.C_{\ell mn}=A_{\ell mn}e^{i\phi_{\ell mn}}\,. (5.1)

To understand how the Cℓ​m​nC_{\ell mn}’s enter the gravitational waveform detected by far-away observers, it should first be recalled that ringdown is a dynamical process, as extensively discussed in Section 4.1 (see also Chapter 4.B of [843]). Hence, the early ringdown phase will include the dynamical excitation of QNMs, with corresponding time-dependent amplitudes Cℓ​m​n​(t)C_{\ell mn}(t). Such a dynamical “activation” regime exists even in the linear theory. The merger waveform from BBH numerical simulations will include this dynamical regime, driven by the dynamical multipolar structure of the background, together with other nonlinear contributions, such as those due to a time-varying mass M⁡(t)M(t) and spin χ⁡(t)\chi(t). Following the terminology introduced in Chapter 4 of [843], it is only when the transient effects have decayed that the ringdown enters into a “stationary” regime, where amplitudes can be represented as constants Cℓ​m​n​(t)=Cℓ​m​nC_{\ell mn}(t)=C_{\ell mn}, as most commonly assumed. Given the current lack of first-principles models for the dynamical excitation of QNMs, in the following we will also assume to be in the “stationary” regime. It is important to select the appropriate time window where this approximation is valid in order to construct a physically meaningful QNM amplitudes model and to avoid overfitting. The lower limit of this time window is often (somewhat improperly) called the “linear ringdown starting time,” but it would be more appropriate to refer to it as the “linear stationary ringdown starting time.” In Section 5.2 we present a phenomenological extension to the dynamical regime (compare and contrast with Sections 4.3 and 4.4, where we discussed nonlinear contributions).

In the stationary regime, QNM amplitudes contribute to the linear GW BBH ringdown strain as

h+−i​h×=MD​∑ℓ≥2,m,n,±Aℓ​m​n±​ei​ϕℓ​m​n±​ei​ωℓ​m​n±​(t−tref)​Sℓ​m​n​(θ,φ,a​ω)+(tails),h_{+}-ih_{\times}=\frac{M}{D}\sum_{\ell\geq 2,m,n,\pm}A_{\ell mn}^{\pm}e^{i\phi_{\ell mn}^{\pm}}e^{i\omega_{\ell mn}^{\pm}(t-t_{\rm ref})}S_{\ell mn}(\theta,\varphi,a\omega)+\text{(tails)}\,, (5.2)

where ωℓ​m​n±\omega_{\ell mn}^{\pm} represent the two branches of prograde/retrograde modes (also known as co/counter-rotating or ordinary/mirror modes) introduced in Eq. (2.20). The amplitude parameters of the merger remnant can be modeled as a function of the parameters of the binary progenitors, namely the mass ratio qq (the total mass scales out), the progenitor BH spins χ→i=1,2\vec{\chi}_{i=1,2}, and the orbital parameters related to eccentricity, so that

Aℓ​m​n\displaystyle A_{\ell mn} →Aℓ​m​n(q,χ→i||,χ→i⟂,E,J),\displaystyle\rightarrow A_{\ell mn}(q,\vec{\chi}_{i||},\vec{\chi}_{i\perp},E,J)\,,
ϕℓ​m​n\displaystyle\phi_{\ell mn} →ϕℓ​m​n(q,χ→i||,χ→i⟂,E,J),\displaystyle\rightarrow\phi_{\ell mn}(q,\vec{\chi}_{i||},\vec{\chi}_{i\perp},E,J)\,, (5.3)

where E,JE,J are any two independent gauge-invariant quantities representing eccentric degrees of freedom. We have also decomposed each spin vector into components that are parallel and perpendicular to L→\vec{L}, the orbital angular momentum vector, as χ→i=(χ→i||,χ→i⟂)\vec{\chi}_{i}=(\vec{\chi}_{i||},\vec{\chi}_{i\perp}). Other useful combinations in the case where the progenitor spins are aligned with the orbital angular momentum (“spin-aligned” case) are χ±=(q​χ1±χ2)/(1+q)\chi_{\pm}=(q\chi_{1}{\pm}\chi_{2})/(1+q), with χ1,2\chi_{1,2} the components of the spins along the direction of L→\vec{L}. In the broader GW literature, χ+\chi_{+} (the spin combination entering at the lowest PN order in the phasing [315]) is also referred to as the “effective spin,” χeff\chi_{\rm eff}.

The relevance of modes with different ℓ​m​n{\ell mn}’s varies in different regions of the parameter space of the progenitor parameters. Greater asymmetry in the system enhances the contribution of higher harmonics with ℓ>2\ell>2. For instance, for nonprecessing systems with χ→i⟂=0\vec{\chi}_{i\perp}=0, asymmetric ringdown modes with ℓ>2\ell>2 are typically excited when the progenitors have unequal masses and misaligned spins. Similarly, these modes are excited for systems with significant orbital precession. Therefore, the ringdown phase can also reveal information about the past dynamics of BBH systems [844], provided that the relations in Eq. (5.3) are known.

The simplest way to determine these relations is through phenomenological fits of NR waveforms. In general, the ansatzes used for these fits are informed by: (i) numerical waveforms from the extreme-mass ratio case, a simplified limiting scenario for which analytical intuition is more easily developed; and (ii) PN predictions for the amplitude and phase in the inspiral. Albeit not trivial in principle, soon after NR simulations of coalescing binaries became available, it was realized that most modes exhibit a dependence on the progenitors parameters that is similar to those derived from PN theory [838, 839, 845, 844, 846, 847]. This has led to the widespread usage of PN-inspired fitting formulas for predicting the QNM amplitudes. To date, there is no analytical computation extending these scalings to the merger regime for comparable-mass binaries.

5.1.1 Fitting methods and ringdown starting times

There are various methods to extract all “detectable” QNMs from NR and perturbative waveforms while avoiding overfitting. Standard nonlinear least squares techniques, like the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm, are suboptimal and ill-conditioned (see [780] for a discussion). Variants of Prony’s algorithm (namely, the Kumaresan-Tufts and matrix pencil methods) should be better suited to extracting QNM parameters from GW signals [848]. Early studies of the QNM content of binary merger waveforms used either nonlinear least squares [838] or Prony methods [839].

A later, comprehensive study used ordinary linear least-squares (OLS) fitting method to estimate the amplitudes of spheroidal QNMs for each spherical multipole, and a greedy algorithm to select the optimal set of QNMs that best fit NR waveforms 10​M10M after the peak of the Penrose scalar Ψ4\Psi_{4} [831]. This greedy algorithm starts with a single QNM and iteratively adds more QNMs, ensuring that each addition significantly reduces the fitting error. The process ends when adding more than two QNMs fails to improve, or worsens, the fit. To ensure the extraction of physical QNM components, this method also checks for the stability of the extracted QNM amplitudes. Namely, given the assumption of constant Cℓ​m​nC_{\ell mn} within the stationary regime in which Eq. (5.2) is valid, the algorithm checks that extracting them at different times should yield the same value within a given tolerance (“amplitudes time stability criterion”). Similarly, physical QNMs are expected to show smooth changes under variation of binary parameters (“amplitudes parametric stability criterion”), something that can be imposed by constructing “global fit” models across the parameter space of the progenitor binary.

Another approach to find the QNM content of the ringdown is to decompose the waveform into two components: one “parallel” and one “perpendicular” to the QNM. This projection is achieved through a normalized time-integral overlap between a QNM superposition and the numerical waveform: see e.g. [849]. The ringdown start time is defined as the moment when the energy parallel to the QNM reaches its maximum. The ringdown starting time corresponds to the lower limit of integration at which the energy along the QNM is maximized. This concept, introduced by Nollert [850], is referred to as the “energy maximized orthogonal projection” (EMOP) and it has been used to calculate the mode excitation for both nonspinning [839] and nonprecessing waveforms [849]. Other studies find the peak of the strain of each individual mode, and fit at a fixed time after the peak [851, 852]. Yet another method chooses the ringdown starting time in the observed waveform by assessing how closely the strong-field spacetime resembles that of a Kerr BH. The idea is to generate a map that associates each time in the gravitational waveform with a value of a certain “Kerrness” measure, by tracking outgoing null characteristics from the strong and near-field regions to the wave zone [853].

A systematic TD fitting algorithm can be specifically designed to enforce time and parametric stability while avoiding overfitting [540]. First, the excited modes in NR data are identified agnostically, i.e., without assuming which specific QNMs are present in the data [378]. The algorithm then iteratively discards time-unstable modes, i.e., those whose amplitudes and phases strongly deviate from a constant under changes in the fitting window. The starting time for each mode is determined by imposing a stability criterion on its amplitude.

In alternative, one can use a FD filter [763]. The idea is to remove a chosen QNM component from the TD ringdown signal. After filtering out the primary QNMs, the method allows for the extraction of subdominant effects, such as retrograde modes and second-order contributions, that might otherwise be masked by the stronger dominant modes. Filters yield results that are equivalent to conventional fitting methods employing amplitude maximization. They offer a significant speed increase, at the cost of preventing an agnostic identification of the mode content of the waveform.

While most studies fit the QNM content of individual spherical harmonic components of the waveform, one can also fit various dominant modes across all angles on the two-sphere, accounting for mode-mixing and mapping the NR waveforms to the super-rest frame (see Section 5.4), as required by the Teukolsky formalism [50]. This has been incorporated in many recent works, including those exploring the robustness of QNM fits, such as Refs. [780, 854, 855, 833].

Most of the studies mentioned above use PN-inspired formulas to fit the amplitudes and phases as functions of binary properties. This approach is useful to understand the physical content of amplitude models, but it can miss complex patterns that are not captured by the analytical predictions (e.g. for precessing and eccentric binaries), or lead to fits of limited accuracy. Higher accuracy can be achieved with Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). Ringdown waveform models based on GPR (rather than closed-form analytic expressions) starting at 20​M20M after the peak typically have higher accuracy [856, 857, 858]. The GPR implementation of [857] is available in the postmerger package [859]. Another advantage of GPR is that it provides an estimate of the fitting uncertainty that can be used in data analysis [860, 861, 862].

As we pointed out at the beginning of this section, least squares fitting can be ill-conditioned when applied to damped sinusoids with unknown frequencies, making it highly sensitive to numerical noise and unmodeled physics. The Variable Projection (VarPro) algorithm used in [780] helps mitigate the ill-conditioning associated with least squares fitting, allowing for a more stable extraction of the amplitudes of highly damped modes, such as overtones.

5.1.2 Fundamental mode harmonics in spin-aligned quasi-circular systems

Initial systematic fits of the amplitudes of nonspinning [838, 839] and spin-aligned [844, 846] binaries as a function of the parameters of the binary progenitors were later extended to include both amplitudes and phases for the dominant multipoles of nonspinning [831] and spin-aligned [863] binaries. These fits, that rely on the MAYA [864] and Cardiff [865] NR simulation catalogs and take into account the effect of spherical-spheroidal mode-mixing, were later revisited and extended by several authors [849, 540, 857, 856], exploiting improved fitting algorithms and higher-accuracy simulations from the SXS catalog [866].

In Fig. 37 we compare the amplitude at the peak of the fundamental QNMs for some of the dominant multipolar indices (ℓ,m)(\ell,m) found with some of the fitting algorithms described above [831, 540, 857]. In the left panel we plot the amplitude as a function of the mass ratio for nonspinning binary waveforms. The hierarchy of the modes follows the sequence (ℓ,m)=(2,2),(3,3),(2,1),(4,4)(\ell,m)=(2,2),(3,3),(2,1),(4,4), except as the system approaches the equal-mass (and equal-spin) limit. As the mass ratio approaches unity, odd-mm modes are suppressed [839, 867] and the (4,4)(4,4) mode becomes the most important subdominant mode. This transition is driven by the symmetry of the system: for equal-mass, equal-spin binaries (q=1q=1 and χ1=χ2\chi_{1}=\chi_{2}), the modes with odd mm vanish due to the requirement that the system is invariant under a rotation by an angle π\pi around the axis of the binary [315]. However, for asymmetric mass ratios (q≳2q\gtrsim 2), the relative amplitudes of higher modes increase very rapidly.

In the right panel of Fig. 37 we show how the multipolar QNM amplitude hierarchy changes when the BH spins are included. The amplitudes of the (2,2)(2,2), (3,3)(3,3), and (4,4)(4,4) fundamental QNMs depend only weakly on the spin parameters, while the (2,1)(2,1) mode shows a more significant sensitivity to spin [845], as expected for m=ℓ−1m=\ell-1 “magnetic” multipoles [315]. In the top right panel we plot the amplitudes of equal-mass systems (q=1q=1) as a function of χ−\chi_{-} for χ+=0\chi_{+}=0 and q=1q=1. In this case the BH spins are anti-aligned with each other, i.e., χ1=χ−=−χ2\chi_{1}=\chi_{-}=-\chi_{2}. Again, the odd-mm modes vanish from symmetry arguments at q=1q=1 and χ−=0\chi_{-}=0, with the amplitude growing proportionally to |χ−||\chi_{-}|. In particular, the (2,1)(2,1) mode amplitude increases significantly with spin, as predicted by PN theory, where the amplitude of this mode scales with χ−\chi_{-} [845, 315]. This is because the (2,1)(2,1) mode contains spin-dependent terms at a lower PN order [845, 868], making it more sensitive to spin effects compared to other modes. In contrast, multipoles with even mm, such as the (2,2)(2,2) and (4,4)(4,4) modes, exhibit a much weaker dependence on the spins. For moderately large asymmetric spins (|χ−|≳0.25|\chi_{-}|\gtrsim 0.25), the (2,1)(2,1) multipole dominates over the (3,3)(3,3) and (4,4)(4,4) multipoles.

In the bottom right panel of Fig. 37, we show the amplitude of the modes as a function of the spin of the more massive BH for q=8q=8. For large positive spins (χ1≳0.5\chi_{1}\gtrsim 0.5), the (2,1)(2,1) mode becomes subdominant compared to the (4,4)(4,4) mode [869]; conversely, for negative spins (χ1≲−0.25\chi_{1}\lesssim-0.25), the (2,1)(2,1) mode grows larger than the (3,3)(3,3) mode [869].

In [649], similar fits have been used to point out that the amplitude-phase correlation predicted by NR simulations spans only a limited portion of the allowed parameter space for spin-aligned quasi-circular systems. This suggests the possibility to carry out an “amplitude-phase ringdown consistency test”: anomalous amplitude-phase measurements could be flagged to reveal unmodeled physics, or even effects beyond GR [649].

5.1.3 Overtones in spin-aligned quasi-circular systems

One of the earliest comparisons between analytical predictions and BBH waveforms computed within NR [838] shows that the inclusion of three overtones (with complex frequencies fixed to the asymptotic values of the BH mass and spin) improves the mismatch between QNM superpositions and the NR signal at early times.
