However, these early comparisons already note that a simple superposition of large numbers of overtones with fixed mass and spin close to the waveform peak does not take into account near-peak transient or nonlinear effects [838, 839], and so their physical interpretation is unclear. Later work finds robust fits of the n=1n=1 overtone at late times (in the stationary regime) that display both time stability and parametric stability [831, 863].

In the attempt to match the entire post-peak waveform using QNM superpositions, EOB models often employ the superposition of a large number (N=7N=7) of overtones up to the waveform peak. In fact, additional phenomenological components with frequencies that do not belong to the Kerr QNM spectrum, called “pseudo-QNMs,” are needed to bridge the gap between the lowest QNM frequency and the merger frequency [870, 871, 872]. Over time, QNM superpositions of overtones and pseudo-QNMs have become a crucial component of early EOB models [870, 871, 872]. Because of issues with the parametric stability of these phenomenological fits, together with the improved accuracy of alternative phenomenological templates [873] (see Section 5.2), these QNM superpositions are no longer used in most of the latest EOB models.

The inclusion of one or two overtones close to the waveform peak significantly improves the extraction of the fundamental mode frequency and damping time (and hence of the remnant’s mass and spin), typically leading to ∼1%\sim 1\% accuracy [849]. However, this study did not address the issue of the parametric stability of global fits across the parameter space (that is achieved instead for the fundamental mode).

A later study considered a superposition of N=7N=7 overtones with frequencies fixed to their asymptotic Kerr values, showing that this combination of QNMs can fit a GW150914-like NR simulation from the SXS catalog with very high accuracy [161]. This study stressed the validity of linear and stationary QNMs superpositions in accurately describing the post-merger waveform, and sparked a lively debate on the problem of fitting a large number of modes to the entire post-peak waveform, on the quantification of the nonlinear and transient content of these signals, and on the implications of these modeling assumptions for observational follow-up studies on real data (see Section 6). Given the short lifetime of the overtones, these follow-up studies highlighted the importance of accounting for time and parametric stability to discern between physical QNMs and other contributions to the waveform. Refs. [874, 875] challenged the parametric stability of overtone amplitudes with n>1n>1, and showed that stable fits across the parameter space can not be achieved from the waveform peak, but only at later times (during what we called the “stationary regime”).

As previously mentioned, the fact that multiple overtones can be extracted by fitting does not necessarily guarantee their physical significance. For example, adding more modes can help by overfitting the nonlinear and transient structure of the signal, particularly near the peak. Comprehensive linear and nonlinear studies show that these additional modes (especially the highest overtones) can enable a more accurate extraction of the fundamental mode and of the first overtone, which at late times carry the majority of information about the remnant properties, by “fitting-away” the poorly understood nonlinear and transient portion of the signal [378, 539, 541]. The risk of overfitting can be illustrated by e.g. considering “unphysical hybrids” (Appendix E of [378]) constructed by stitching together two different signals h1h_{1} and h2h_{2}: in this case, a superposition of overtones (h1h_{1}) can accurately – but unphysically – fit the post-merger of h2h_{2}.

An agnostic extraction of QNMs is necessary to identify the mode content of the ringdown and to mitigate the risk of overfitting [378, 767, 540]. Rather than assuming the presence of known overtones in a given (ℓ,m)(\ell,m) multipole, agnostic fits treat the complex frequencies as free parameters. The agnostic approach leads to stronger tests of mode excitation and it is conceptually more similar to the spirit of the original BH spectroscopy proposal (in fact, it can be thought of as the infinite-SNR limit of the observational BH spectroscopy program). Without considering nonlinear contributions, the agnostic fits of the ℓ=m=2\ell=m=2 multipole in [378] can only reliably identify the fundamental mode, the first overtone, and some retrograde modes (in addition to modes related to spherical-spheroidal mode mixing). Higher overtones (n>1n>1) are not as easy to identify using free-frequency fittings and standard least squares methods on extrapolated SXS waveforms [378]. This conclusion remains valid even when fitting with as many as 10 damped sinusoids [540].

While agnostic fitting using least squares methods allows for unbiased identification of excited modes, it may struggle to detect highly damped modes in the presence of even small numerical noise. This is because agnostic QNM fitting is numerically ill-conditioned – i.e., it is extremely sensitive to numerical noise and other underlying unmodeled physics. Being very short-lived, overtones are particularly sensitive to unmodeled contributions and hard to extract: even subdominant tail effects can obscure the identification of highly damped overtones [378, 780]. This presents a challenge for performing BH spectroscopy with high overtones.

These issues can be partially addressed by reducing the impact of numerical noise and improving the robustness of the fitting process. By adopting a superior fitting method known as Variable Projection (VarPro) to help mitigate the issue related to ill-conditioning in least square fitting, correctly normalizing the time unit by the Christodoulou mass, and using simulations with higher accuracy augmented by Cauchy Characteristic Evolution (CCE) rather than polynomial extrapolation at future null infinity – which avoids spurious contributions related to recoil that could spoil the fit (see also Section 5.3) – it is possible to identify as many as nine overtones with relatively time-stable amplitudes [780]. This is achievable for simulations that produce remnants spinning faster than the GW150914 remnant, when accounting for quadratic contributions, and by “dropping” unstable modes outside of the initial fitting window, which results in partial fits discontinuities for highly damped modes. A stable fit could be achieved starting at 4−8​M4-8M after the peak strain (depending on the binary parameters), after transient contributions have sufficiently decayed away.

While at intermediate times most QNMs were found to follow the expected decay, sizable departures from constant amplitudes are present for certain modes. The n=8,9n=8,9 QNMs deviate from a constant scaling from the start of the time-grid, and the jumps due to mode dropping further contribute to constant-scaling deviation. As previously highlighted, the employed model assumes that all modes are constant in the same time-window. Extracting constant amplitudes of different modes in different windows leaves open the possibility that higher overtones can “fit away” other physical contributions [378, 539, 876], such as the QNMs or mass-spin dynamical growth, prompt response and nonperturbative terms. Future studies will need to address these remaining issues related to time-stability.

The parametric stability of overtone amplitudes across the binary parameter space was not addressed in [780], but it has been achieved for the n=1n=1 overtone in the stationary regime (typically ∼10​M\sim 10M after the peak strain, depending on the binary parameters) by several authors: see e.g. [831, 875, 540, 856] for global fits of the complex amplitudes of spin-aligned BBH constructed. The amplitude ratio between the first overtone and the fundamental mode is mainly determined by χf\chi_{f}, and this holds true for both the (2,2)(2,2) and (3,3)(3,3) modes. In the right panel of Fig. 38, based on [540], we show the amplitude ratios between the first overtone and the fundamental mode, A221/A220A_{221}/A_{220} (purple) and A331/A330A_{331}/A_{330} (orange), as functions of the remnant spin χ\chi, along with the ratio of excitation factors E221/E220E_{221}/E_{220} (purple dashed) and E331/E330E_{331}/E_{330} (orange dashed). Recall that the amplitudes Aℓ​m​nA_{\ell mn} are the product of the excitation factor Eℓ​m​nE_{\ell mn} and the integral term Tℓ​m​nT_{\ell mn}, with Eℓ​m​nE_{\ell mn} solely determined by the remnant spin and independent of the initial conditions of the binary system, while Tℓ​m​nT_{\ell mn} depends on both the initial configuration of the system and the source of perturbations. For low values of the remnant spin χ\chi, the amplitude ratios and excitation factor ratios have similar values, but as the remnant spin increases, these two ratios diverge significantly. This interesting numerical result has not yet been confirmed by analytical arguments.

The fits of [833] display parametric stability across quasi-circular, nonprecessing BBH mergers for the (2,±2,n≤2,±)(2,\pm 2,n\leq 2,\pm) QNMs, as well as for various other QNMs, such as the (3,±3,n≤2,±)(3,\pm 3,n\leq 2,\pm) and (2,±1,n≤1,±)(2,\pm 1,n\leq 1,\pm). This is possible through an automated QNM extraction routine that performs a reverse search in time for QNM frequencies using VarPro, and only adds QNMs to the model if their complex amplitudes can be shown to be stable (within some tolerance) as a function of the starting time of the fit over some time interval of fitting times whose length depends on the QNM’s damping time. On average, the overtones are found to be stable at times ≳8​M\gtrsim 8M after the peak of the strain, with some slight variation across parameter space and overtone number [833]. Stability was enforced through tolerance thresholds derived from test cases. In the future it will be important to extend these fits to higher overtones by adopting “mode-dropping” techniques or GPR methods to incorporate the noise level in the fit through a Bayesian formulation (rather than tolerance thresholds).

While the (2,2,n≤1,+)(2,2,n\leq 1,+) QNMs are found across every simulation, the (2,2,2,+)(2,2,2,+) QNM is found in ∼60%\sim 60\% of the simulations and the (2,2,3,+)(2,2,3,+) QNM is found only in ∼3%\sim 3\% (primarily equal-mass and high-spinning) binaries. Overtones in other (ℓ,m)(\ell,m) modes are found slightly less often than in the (2,2)(2,2) mode. The dependence of the n≤2n\leq 2 prograde overtones for the (2,2)(2,2) and (3,3)(3,3) multipoles on the binary’s effective spin and mass ratio is shown in Fig. 39.

When several overtones can be found across many NR simulations, it is possible to perform a more robust analysis of the relationship between the (2,±2,n,±)(2,\pm 2,n,\pm) amplitudes and their excitation factors [161, 162, 540, 833]. By fixing three degrees of freedom (two for the overall scale of the source function and one for the time at which the QNMs are extracted), it can be shown that the (2,±2,n≤2,±)(2,\pm 2,n\leq 2,\pm) QNMs track almost exactly their excitation factors, with very good agreement as a function of nn for the amplitudes, and slightly larger disagreement for the phases [833]. This is shown in Fig. 40, which appears to differ with the right panel of Fig. 38 because the amplitude ratios in [540] are always taken at the peak of the strain. This suggests that there may be something inherent to the BH scattering potential or the remnant perturbation in BBH mergers that naturally excites the overtones at the level predicted by their excitation factors. Consequently, there may be a physical reason to expect the excitation of a large number of overtones, even if demonstrating their stability in numerical simulations is challenging [378, 539, 541, 780]. More work on overtone excitation using either scattering experiments or NR simulations of BBH mergers is needed to confidently confirm this hypothesis.

In summary, despite many recent advancements in the characterization of low (n≤2n\leq 2) overtones at intermediate times, many of the complications related to the excitation of higher-order overtones close to the waveform peak remain. A definitive solution to the debate on the physical meaning of the overtone contributions close to the peak may only be possible through analytical models of overtone excitation on a dynamical background, including transient effects. The extent to which these effects are at play in comparable mass systems, together with the robust determination of the time-window in which a stationary description is valid are still subject of active investigation.

5.1.4 Amplitudes in precessing quasi-circular systems

Precession effects in the ringdown resulting from a BBH coalescence appear due to a misalignment between the progenitors spins 𝝌i\boldsymbol{{\chi}}_{i} and the orbital angular momentum L. In the inspiral, this is most conveniently described in two frames: one with the zz-axis along the total angular momentum J, the other along L. Wigner D-matrices D​(R)μ​mℓD(R)^{\ell}_{\mu m} can be used [877, 878] to transform between the two frames:

hℓ​m′=∑μ=−llD​(R)μ​mℓ​hℓ​μ,h^{\prime}_{\ell m}=\sum_{\mu=-l}^{l}D(R)^{\ell}_{\mu m}h_{\ell\mu}\,, (5.4)

where RR is the quaternion representing the time-dependent rotation. This rotation changes the strain modes detected by far-away inertial observers, and can be interpreted as a “mode-mixing” yielding a “spread” of dominant harmonics into sub-dominant harmonics. This implies a corresponding re-ordering of their amplitudes compared to the spin-aligned case. As an example, binaries with strong in-plane spin components induce larger excitation amplitudes for modes with ℓ=m≠2\ell=m\neq 2. This effect has been well-studied in the context of IMR modeling [879, 880, 881, 882, 870, 883, 872, 884, 885].

In the ringdown, these two frames become those anchored to either the spin of the final BH 𝝌f\boldsymbol{{\chi}}_{f} (the “preferred direction” of the background) or to L (the direction of the perturbation). Knowledge of the rotation matrix allows to un-mix individual modes from the higher harmonic modes [886]. Such approach shows how QNM superpositions with free amplitudes achieve small mismatches and remnant errors if higher harmonics are added and unmixed through Eq. (5.4).

Moreover, the QNM amplitudes are also affected by the intrinsically distinct nature of the precessing perturbation. In particular, NR fits of QNM superpositions with free amplitudes [887] can be used to identify systems where strong precession leads to, e.g., a louder excitation of the (2,1,0,±)(2,1,0,\pm) or (2,0,0,±)(2,0,0,\pm) QNMs than the (2,2,0,±)(2,2,0,\pm) QNMs, as shown in Fig. 41. It is particularly interesting that subleading modes can become dominant: as shown in Fig. 41, it is possible for the amplitude |A(2,1,0)||A_{(2,1,0)}| to be larger than |A(2,2,0)||A_{(2,2,0)}| for large mass-ratio systems [887]. Specializing the above picture to a single time-independent rotation between the remnant’s spin and the total angular momentum flux d​J/d​td\textbf{J}/dt, this enhancement can be well-explained by “rotating” the spin-aligned amplitudes predicted in, e.g., [846]. This approach is motivated by perturbative studies in the extreme-mass-ratio case [729, 741, 742, 888], detailed below in Section 5.1.7. Each individual mode in Fig. 41 is fit in the canonical super-rest frame of the remnant, the one used in BH perturbation theory, mitigating the mode-mixing effects due to the remnant kick velocity [889, 50, 890]. Apart from this effect, precessing systems can also lead to distinct excitation of ±m\pm m modes due to the breaking of reflection symmetry, as shown in Fig. 3 of [887]. This reflection symmetry breaking is also important in the modeling of the entire waveform [884, 888].

An alternative approach involves the development of surrogate models for the ringdown mode amplitudes of quasi-circular precessing BBHs [858]. The fits are provided in a coordinate frame where the zz-axis is aligned with the spin direction of the remnant BH. The amplitudes are fitted as a function of six parameters (6D model): the asymmetric mass ratio δ=(q−1)/(q+1)\delta=(q-1)/(q+1), with q=m1/m2≥1q=m_{1}/m_{2}\geq 1; the symmetric and antisymmetric combinations of the spin components parallel to the orbital angular momentum, χs=(q​χ1​z+χ2​z)/(1+q)\chi_{\rm s}=(q\chi_{1z}+\chi_{2z})/(1+q) and χa=(q​χ1​z−χ2​z)/(1+q)\chi_{\rm a}=(q\chi_{1z}-\chi_{2z})/(1+q); the angle θf\theta_{f} between the orbital angular momentum at the ISCO and the spin of the remnant χf\chi_{f}; the angle ϕk\phi_{k} between χf\chi_{f} and the direction of the recoil; and the magnitude of the recoil velocity vkv_{\rm k}. Additionally, slightly less accurate fits are also provided for a 7D model involving δ\delta and the individual BHs’ Cartesian spin components. Note that these two models include only the fundamental modes (n=0n=0) and do not take into account spherical-spheroidal mode mixing. The waveforms are aligned at a reference time defined by the point of maximum energy projection (tEMOPt_{\text{EMOP}}), as introduced in [839]. In particular, the amplitudes are modeled starting at 20​M20M after tEMOPt_{\text{EMOP}}. The surrogates are constructed for all ℓ=2\ell=2 modes, as well as for the ℓ=3,m=3\ell=3,m=3 mode, using a Gaussian process regression method and the SXS NR catalog.

In Fig. 42 we show the mismatch between the calibrated amplitude ringdown templates and the waveforms of the SXS NR catalog. A metric εNR\varepsilon^{\rm NR} that quantifies the goodness of fit is defined as

εNR=∫t0100​M|hl​mNR−hl​mfit|2​𝑑t∫t0100​M|hl​mNR|2​𝑑t,\varepsilon^{\rm NR}=\frac{\int_{t_{0}}^{100M}\left|h_{lm}^{\rm NR}-h_{lm}^{\rm fit}\right|^{2}dt}{\int_{t_{0}}^{100M}\left|h_{lm}^{\rm NR}\right|^{2}dt}, (5.5)

where hl​mfith_{lm}^{\rm fit} is the QNM model with amplitude determined by the fitting procedure, and hl​mNRh_{lm}^{\rm NR} is the NR waveform. The median percentage errors for these fits are 3.1% and 6.4% for the (2,2)(2,2) and (2,1)(2,1) modes, respectively, and approximately 13% for the (3,3)(3,3) and the real components of the (2,0)(2,0) modes. While the model’s accuracy is sufficient for current detector sensitivities, it will need to be improved for use with future and more sensitive detectors. The current limitations arise dominantly from the sparsity and uneven distribution of available NR simulations across the parameter space.

5.1.5 Eccentricity

Similar to other binary properties, orbital eccentricity leaves an imprint on the ringdown amplitudes and phases. However, since eccentricity tends to be radiated away during the binary inspiral [891], its effects become apparent in the ringdown only if it has not been fully radiated away. This implies that eccentric effects can observable in the ringdown only if the system formed shortly before merger, or if eccentricity has been enhanced by other mechanisms. This is possible in dense environments (such as e.g. globular or nuclear star clusters [892]), due e.g. to the presence of a third body or matter distributions. These considerations lead to the expectation that only a fraction of systems will be affected by eccentric corrections. Nevertheless, in order to achieve searches of new physics using BH ringdown (one of the major goals of the BH spectroscopy program), it is imperative to construct complete models of the binary dynamics, including sub-dominant effects. Failure to do so would result in false violations of the predictions of GR [893].

In Fig. 43 we report the values of the A330/A220A_{330}/A_{220} amplitude ratio as a function of the residual orbital eccentricity e0e_{0} at 10 Hz (i.e., when the binary enters the LVK band) [649]. Significant departures from the quasi-circular case start around e0≃0.6e_{0}\simeq 0.6, while an initial eccentricity e0>0.3e_{0}>0.3 would be enough to have significant departures in the phase difference δ​ϕ330=m/2​ϕ330−ϕ220\delta\phi_{330}=m/2\,\phi_{330}-\phi_{220} [649]. The amplitudes shown in Fig. 43 are multi-valued functions, because two parameters are required to fully specify a noncircular orbit, and these amplitudes do not include the required dependence on a second parameter. In addition the amplitudes are plotted as functions of a gauge-dependent parameter, so it is not immediately obvious how to compare amplitudes across different simulations or how to use them data-analysis. Moreover, to successfully model noncircular orbits we must incorporate the time-dependence of the noncircular parameter(s).

These issues can be addressed by using a parameterization based on gauge-invariant combinations of the binary’s energy and angular momentum was [895]. By shifting the focus from orbit-based to dynamics-based quantities (i.e., ADM energy and angular momentum), this parameterization can account for generic noncircular planar orbits, including bounded eccentric orbits and dynamical captures. The time dependence is incorporated by considering combinations of the ADM energy and angular momentum evolved up to the merger time by using the GW fluxes. This approach differs from previous approaches that define time-dependent eccentric parameters in the inspiral by interpolating the waveform [896, 897, 898], and it can be applied to arbitrarily short waveforms.

A specific combination of these parameters – an effective “impact parameter” at merger bmrgb_{\text{mrg}}, inspired by the test-mass limit in an EOB description [899] (see Section 5.2) – captures the main dependence of the quantities characterizing the merger remnant. In Fig. 44 we observe that the merger amplitude is a monotonic function of b^mrg\hat{b}_{\text{mrg}} in the equal-mass, nonspinning case. Similar results hold for the merger frequency, the remnant BH mass and the remnant BH spin for spin-aligned binaries with different mass ratios. This simple dependence makes it possible to construct global fits of these quantities (that enter as inputs of IMR models when attached to inspiral predictions) across the parameter space of spin-aligned binaries. The same parameterization can be used to fit the ringdown amplitudes of the dominant fundamental modes [852]. In the right panel of Fig. 44 for (ℓ,m,n)=(2,2,0)(\ell,m,n)=(2,2,0). we see that noncircular orbits can have a large impact on the merger and ringdown amplitudes, with relative changes larger than 50%50\% compared to the quasi-circular case in the domain of NR calibration, and even higher when extrapolating beyond this domain. Models of the post-merger amplitudes of eccentric systems in the extreme mass-ratio regime exist within the EOB framework [899] (see Section 5.2 below for more details).

A noncircular binary is characterized, in general, by two additional parameters (e.g. the eccentricity and radial phase/anomaly in the bounded case, or the energy and angular momentum (E,J)(E,J) in the generic case), but the left panel of Fig. 44 shows a monotonic dependence in terms of a single parameter. This suggests some sort of “quasi-universality” of the merger regime, which to a good approximation seems to be entirely captured by b^mrg\hat{b}_{\text{mrg}}. An interpretation of this result in terms of the orbital features can be found in [852], but an analytical explanation would be desirable.

5.1.6 Retrograde modes

The excitation of retrograde modes is related to the presence of a perturbation which rotates in the opposite direction relative to the spin of the background spacetime (see e.g. [735]). These modes matter most when the progenitor spins are aligned antiparallel to the binary’s orbital angular momentum. This is pedagogically depicted in Fig. 45, depicting two situations in which: (a) the remnant spin of a BH resulting from a binary merger is parallel to the progenitors orbital angular momentum; (b) the remnant spin is opposite to the orbital angular momentum. This latter case arises depending on the binary mass ratio, spin magnitudes and spin directions (see e.g. [900, 901]). In situation (a) the prograde modes dominate the signal, while retrograde modes are maximally excited in situation (b). This intrinsic excitation is observed-independent, as it is set by the binary properties.

The excitation of retrograde modes should instead not be confused with the magnitude of the m=±|m|m=\pm|m| signal components. The mm index accounts for the spherical decomposition of the signal, and the relevance of the +|m|+|m| vs −|m|-|m| component depends on the observer location on the sky, set by a reference frame (ι,φ)(\iota,\varphi). Focusing for concreteness on the m=±2m=\pm 2 mode, an observer located on the positive side of the z-axis will only receive contributions from the m=+2m=+2 modes, and will see the binary rotate with a positive orbital frequency. Instead, an observer located on the negative z-axis will only receive contributions from the m=−2m=-2 modes, observing a binary rotating with an orbital frequency equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to observers located on the positive z-axis. For m=0m=0, both descriptions lose meaning, and the two modes are degenerate.

The intuitive excitation picture presented above is confirmed by NR fits [863, 851, 540]. The retrograde mode is found more strongly excited in the (2,1)(2,1) multipole than in the (2,2)(2,2) multipole [540].

For binary modeling purposes, it is instead more convenient to define “prograde” and “retrograde” modes as those co/counter-rotating with the BBH orbit, rather than with the remnant BH spin. This definition coincides with the remnant-spin based one (used in Section 2.1) when the remnant spin is aligned with the BBH orbital direction, but it becomes opposite when the remnant spin is flipped (see also Fig. 12 of [540]). This alternative definition offers practical advantages. In BBH simulations, the orbital direction is easy to control, while the remnant spin direction depends nontrivially on the initial conditions. By defining modes relative to the binary’s orbital motion, one ensures that as the initial parameters (e.g., q,χ+,χ−q,\chi_{+},\chi_{-}) are varied smoothly, the amplitudes and phases of the dominant component also varies smoothly, even when the remnant spin direction flips. In contrast, adopting the (perturbative) remnant-spin based definition would lead to discontinuous transitions in QNM frequency, amplitudes, and phases when the remnant spin flips. Comparing to the remnant-spin based definition used in Section 2.1, IMR models always include the dominant component co- and counter-rotating modes, switching among the two depending on the final spin direction. Under the orbit-based definition, IMR models typically include only prograde modes, as these capture the dominant late-time frequency trend and allow for smooth fits even when the final spin direction changes, even when including a single component. In the future, both co-rotating and counter-rotating modes should be included. Their combination gives rise to mode-mixing, as observed in several studies conducted in the test-mass limit [902, 734, 903, 735, 904, 899] (see also Section 5.2). This effect has been modeled for test particles falling into a Kerr BH using QNM superpositions with constant amplitudes [904], and more recently, a procedure to incorporate this effect in QNM-factorized phenomenological ringdown models was applied to test particles falling into a Schwarzschild BH [899]. However, counter-rotating modes have yet to be included in IMR models for binaries with generic mass ratios.

5.1.7 Inclined extreme mass ratio inspirals

As we discussed in Section 4.2, test-particle studies are valuable laboratories to develop an intuitive picture in a rigorous perturbative framework, which can then be applied to the modeling of comparable-mass systems. A detailed QNM analysis of extreme-mass-ratio inspirals can be found in [741] (which builds on previous work in [742]). This study uses the procedure described in [729] to construct worldlines describing the inspiral and plunge of a small body on initially circular but misaligned orbits of Kerr BHs. These worldlines in turn are used to build the Teukolsky source term for point particles following such trajectories and to compute the resulting gravitational waveforms following [341]. The final cycles of the resulting waveforms are Kerr QNMs, with different modes excited in a predictable way depending on the larger BH’s spin parameter aa, an angle II describing the misalignment of the smaller body’s orbital plane relative to the BH spin, and an angle θfin\theta_{\rm fin} which describes where on the event horizon the smaller body plunges into the BH [741, 742]. Similarly to what is done in the comparable-mass case, by fitting to the final cycles of the waveforms to the functional form [377]

h⁡(t)\displaystyle h(t) =\displaystyle= μD∑ℓ​m​n[𝒜ℓ​m​ne−i⁡[ωℓ​m​n​(t−t0)−φℓ​m​n]Sℓ​m​na​ωℓ​m​n(θ,ϕ)\displaystyle\frac{\mu}{D}\sum_{\ell mn}\bigg[\mathcal{A}_{\ell mn}e^{-i[\omega_{\ell mn}(t-t_{0})-\varphi_{\ell mn}]}S^{a\omega_{\ell mn}}_{\ell mn}(\theta,\phi) (5.6)
+𝒜ℓ​m​n′ei⁡[ωℓ​m​n∗​(t−t0)+φℓ​m​n′]Sℓ​m​na​ωℓ​m​n(π−θ,ϕ)∗].\displaystyle+\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{\ell mn}e^{i[\omega^{*}_{\ell mn}(t-t_{0})+\varphi^{\prime}_{\ell mn}]}S^{a\omega_{\ell mn}}_{\ell mn}(\pi-\theta,\phi)^{*}\bigg]\;.

(where μ\mu is the mass of the secondary body, DD is distance from the system to point where h⁡(t)h(t) is measured and ∗ denotes complex conjugation), one can determine the amplitude 𝒜ℓ​m​n\mathcal{A}_{\ell mn} and phase φℓ​m​n\varphi_{\ell mn} of mode (ℓ,m,n)(\ell,m,n) in the waveform. Figure 46 illustrates how the geometry of the system influences the resulting GWs, and the mixture of modes which enter the TD waveform.

It is worth noting that θfin\theta_{\rm fin} is essentially an accidental phase parameter: a system with inclination angle II will have 90∘−I≤θfin≤90∘+I90^{\circ}-I\leq\theta_{\rm fin}\leq 90^{\circ}+I (for I≤90∘I\leq 90^{\circ}) or I−90∘≤θfin≤270∘−II-90^{\circ}\leq\theta_{\rm fin}\leq 270^{\circ}-I (for I>90∘I>90^{\circ}). Two systems which are identical in all ways except for their initial position along their orbit will plunge with different values of θfin\theta_{\rm fin}, and as a consequence excite very different mixtures of QNMs. This is illustrated in Fig. 47, which shows how the mode amplitude 𝒜220\mathcal{A}_{220} and phase φ220\varphi_{220} vary with θfin\theta_{\rm fin} for a set of systems which all have a=0.5​Ma=0.5M, I=60∘I=60^{\circ}. Despite the fact that the systems are identical in many of their most important properties, the amplitude of this important QNM can vary significantly depending on how the plunging body crosses the horizon. A rapidly spinning remnant BH with extreme mass ratio may be advantageous for detecting QNMs, as it results in a long-lived ringdown and enhanced excitation of higher multipole modes [905, 906]. In an extension of these studies, significant excitation of higher multipole modes was also observed in intermediate mass ratio mergers [746], where the energy and angular momentum losses are taken into account by utilizing the Ori-Thorne procedure [728].

5.2 Time-dependent amplitudes: phenomenological models

Initial contributors: Albanesi, Pompili

5.2.1 Basic concepts

The EOB approach, originally introduced in [907, 908, 909, 910, 911], provides a framework to construct semi-analytic waveform models covering the entire coalescence of compact-object binaries (i.e., the inspiral, plunge, merger and ringdown). The basic idea of EOB models is to map the motion of the two bodies, typically described in terms of PN equations of motion, into the motion of a particle in an effective metric. The latter is a deformation of a BH solution, where the parameter that tunes this deformation is the symmetric mass ratio η≡q/(1+q)2\eta\equiv q/(1+q)^{2}. Through this mapping, EOB models naturally incorporate the test-mass limit and, as a consequence, information from perturbation theory can be used to improve their reliability. Moreover, since the advent of numerical simulations [837, 818, 912], the EOB framework has integrated information from NR simulations, offering highly accurate waveform models that are routinely used in GW data analysis of IMR signals. Numerical simulations are used both to calibrate analytically unknown coefficients in the EOB Hamiltonian, adding phenomenological contributions to the poorly modeled near-merger waveform, to select the unknown optimal polynomial orders to be chosen in resummation procedures, and to build phenomenological post-merger models that are matched to the inspiral-plunge waveform.

The complete EOB waveform is usually constructed by attaching a merger-ringdown waveform, hℓ​mmerger−RD​(t)h_{\ell m}^{\rm merger-RD}(t), to an inspiral-plunge one, hℓ​minsp−plunge​(t)h_{\ell m}^{\rm insp-plunge}(t), at a suitable matching time t=tmatcht=t_{\rm match}, around the peak of the EOB orbital frequency (which approximately corresponds to merger time), that is [908]:

hℓ​m​(t)=hℓ​minsp−plunge​(t)​h^ℓ​mNQC​(t)​Θ​(tmatchℓ​m−t)+hℓ​mmerger−RD​(t)​Θ​(t−tmatchℓ​m),h_{\ell m}(t)=h_{\ell m}^{\rm insp-plunge}(t)\hat{h}_{\ell m}^{\rm NQC}(t)\,\Theta\left(t_{\rm match}^{\ell m}-t\right)+h_{\ell m}^{\rm merger-RD}(t)\,\Theta\left(t-t_{\rm match}^{\ell m}\right)\,, (5.7)

where Θ⁡(t)\Theta(t) is the Heaviside step function. The inspiral-plunge waveform modes are based on a resummation of the PN GW modes [913, 902, 914, 868, 915, 916, 917], evaluated on the dynamics obtained from the EOB equations of motion [907, 908, 910]. The smooth connection of the inspiral-plunge waveform with the merger-ringdown waveform is achieved by applying the numerically tuned next-to-quasi-circular corrections [902] h^ℓ​mNQC\hat{h}_{\ell m}^{\rm NQC}, which are particularly relevant during the plunge, when the radial motion dominates the dynamics. In the rest of this section, we focus on the modeling of the merger-ringdown waveform modes.

5.2.2 Ringdown as a QNM superposition

As previously mentioned, early EOB models represented the merger-ringdown waveform as a linear superposition of QNMs [908, 838, 918, 902, 919, 920, 921, 922, 734, 903, 923, 735, 924, 925, 870, 871, 926, 872]. This approach, inspired by results for the infall of a test mass into a BH [927] and the close-limit approximation [802], was initiated in [908], where the inspiral waveform was matched to the least-damped QNM of the remnant BH at the light-ring crossing. Notably, the final mass and spin were estimated from the EOB Hamiltonian and angular momentum at the end of the plunge, thus providing the first semi-analytical estimate of such quantities for a remnant generated by a BBH merger. Later works confirmed the goodness of the EOB estimates for the remnant properties [838, 928, 926], but recent models compute these quantities from more accurate NR fits [900, 929]. To ensure continuity between the EOB inspiral-plunge waveform and the QNM ansatz, the introduction of two free coefficients in the amplitude and phase of the merger-ringdown waveform was needed, and determined by imposing C1C_{1} continuity conditions at the matching time. With the 2005 NR breakthrough [837, 818, 912], the picture delineated in [908], which put forward the first model for the entire IMR waveform in the comparable-mass regime, was revealed to be qualitatively, and to some extent quantitatively, correct [838]. There, the underlying picture was inspired by the study of the test-mass case, a useful laboratory for many EOB developments in the comparable-mass regime.

The inclusion of three overtones up to the waveform peak was first considered in [838] (see Section 5.1.3). The relevance of higher overtones in the comparable-mass regime was confirmed and used to complete a pre-merger EOB model in [918], with free parameters fixed by requiring continuity. A study in the test-mass limit also found that higher QNM overtones are required in order to improve the frequency of the inspiral-plunge waveform, and thus achieve a smoother transition [902]. Further, the latter work introduced the idea of performing the match of the QNM ansatz with the inspiral-plunge EOB waveform on a time-extended interval around the peak of the orbital frequency, a procedure also known as matching comb. While these refined methods led to reliable results for nonspinning binaries [902, 919, 921, 924, 926], the ringdown frequency obtained from the QNM superposition was found to rise too quickly after merger for spin-aligned binaries and higher harmonics. To address this problem, pseudo-QNMs, i.e., fictitious modes, were introduced [922]. These complex frequencies were phenomenologically determined to improve the transition from the inspiral-plunge EOB frequency, to the one of QNM superpositions assuming the asymptotic Kerr mass and spin values.

5.2.3 QNM-factorized phenomenological ringdown models

The necessity to include pseudo-QNMs highlighted the need to include other physical effects beyond the pure QNM description, such as transient contributions. While analytical computations from first principles of such effects are still ongoing, a practical solution is to build physical intuition, and then provide phenomenological ansatzes. The seminal work of [930] described the full waveform in terms of a rotating source and produced closed-form fits of the waveform frequency. Later, a phenomenological description of the ringdown which is still employed in state-of-the-art EOB and TD Phenom models was proposed [873]. The basic idea is to consider a multiplicative decomposition of the waveform by factorizing the contribution of the co-rotating fundamental QNM. Focusing on the dominant (ℓ,m)=(2,2)(\ell,m)=(2,2) mode h22/η=A22​e−i​ϕ22h_{22}/\eta=A_{22}e^{-i\phi_{22}}, the QNM-rescaled signal reads

h^22​(τ)=ei​ω220​τ+i​ϕ220​h22​(τ),\hat{h}_{22}(\tau)=e^{i\omega_{220}\tau+i\phi_{22}^{0}}h_{22}(\tau), (5.8)

where ω220\omega_{220} is the MM-rescaled complex fundamental frequency, τ=(t−t0)/M\tau=(t-t_{0})/M, and t0t_{0} corresponds to the peak of the (2,2) amplitude. Under the assumption of a pure QNM superposition with constant amplitudes cic_{i}, the rescaled signal can be written as

h^22QNM​(τ)=c0+c1​e−i⁡(ω221−ω220)​τ+c2​e−i⁡(ω222−ω220)​τ+⋯.\hat{h}_{22}^{\rm QNM}(\tau)=c_{0}+c_{1}e^{-i(\omega_{221}-\omega_{220})\tau}+c_{2}e^{-i(\omega_{222}-\omega_{220})\tau}+\cdots. (5.9)

Note that while the damping coefficients of the QNMs increase with nn, the real parts remain relatively unchanged, especially if the spin of the remnant is large. As a consequence, the differences ω221−ω220\omega_{221}-\omega_{220}, ω222−ω220\omega_{222}-\omega_{220}, …\dots in Eq. (5.9) are approximately constant and imaginary. Therefore, Eq. (5.9) describes approximate straight lines in the complex plane. However, when looking at the QNM-rescaled waveform obtained from equal-mass NR simulations, only the ones which correspond to nonspinning or anti-aligned configurations are approximately straight, as shown in the left panel Fig. 48. On the contrary, spin-aligned configurations show a snail-shaped behavior, thus indicating that a pure QNM ansatz is not suitable for their description. From this perspective, the role of pseudo-QNMs ω221′\omega_{221}^{\prime} [922, 923, 924, 871] for positive-spin configurations was needed to account for the rotation of the curve in the h¯22{\bar{h}}_{22} plane by having ω221′−ω220\omega_{221}^{\prime}-\omega_{220} with significant nonzero real frequency difference. However, a different strategy was employed in [873]. In the following, we drop the (ℓ,m)(\ell,m) indices to simplify the notation. By decomposing the QNM-rescaled waveform h^\hat{h} in amplitude and phase as

h^=Ah^​ei​ϕh^,\hat{h}=A_{\hat{h}}e^{i\phi_{\hat{h}}}, (5.10)

one can see that the shapes of the amplitude Ah^A_{\hat{h}} and phase ϕh^\phi_{\hat{h}} are reminiscent of activation-like functions, as shown in the right panels of Fig. 48 for the equal-mass case with individual BH spins χ≡χ1=χ2=0.97\chi\equiv\chi_{1}=\chi_{2}=0.97 (dashed blue). To model such activation-like behavior, the following ansatz was proposed

A~​(τ)\displaystyle\tilde{A}(\tau) =c1A​tanh⁡(c2A​τ+c3A)+c4A,\displaystyle=c_{1}^{A}\tanh\left(c_{2}^{A}\tau+c_{3}^{A}\right)+c_{4}^{A}, (5.11)
ϕ~​(τ)\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}(\tau) =−c1ϕ​ln⁡(1+c3ϕ​e−c2ϕ​τ+c4ϕ​e−2​c2ϕ​τ1+c3ϕ+c4ϕ).\displaystyle=-c_{1}^{\phi}\ln\left(\dfrac{1+c_{3}^{\phi}e^{-c_{2}^{\phi}\tau}+c_{4}^{\phi}e^{-2c_{2}^{\phi}\tau}}{1+c_{3}^{\phi}+c_{4}^{\phi}}\right). (5.12)

Some of these coefficients were constrained by requiring continuity conditions at t0t_{0} and fixing the asymptotic behavior for large τ\tau (see [873] for the explicit expressions). The remaining coefficients were instead determined by a least-square fit performed on NR waveforms.

The results of this fit are shown for the χ=0.97\chi=0.97 case in the right panels of Fig. 48 (red). Even though transient effects, overtones, and nonlinearities are not explicitly encapsulated in Eq. (5.11) and (5.12), these effects are effectively included in the merger-ringdown model, since these phenomenological ansatzes are calibrated on NR simulations. Note that at late times h^\hat{h} is approximately constant, indicating that in the late ringdown, before the transition to the tail regime (see Section 5.3), only the contribution of the fundamental QNM is still relevant.

The fitted coefficients, together with the numerical quantities needed for the continuity conditions at t0t_{0}, depend smoothly on χ=χ1=χ2\chi=\chi_{1}=\chi_{2}, thus allowing a simple polynomial fit approximation over the whole spin range (see, e.g., Fig. 6 of [873]). Later works [931, 932, 933, 934, 935] considered also unequal-mass binaries and progenitors with different individual spins, thus providing closed-form descriptions of the post-merger waveform over the whole parameter space of quasi-circular spin-aligned binaries, which are currently used in state-of-the-art EOB and phenomenological TD models [936, 937, 938].

While initial work focused on the (2,2)(2,2) mode, the same methodology can be readily applied to higher-modes. For each complex (ℓ,m)(\ell,m) mode, the fit can be started from the peak of the corresponding amplitude [939]. However, fits for the higher harmonics can robustly be performed even starting from the peak of the (2,2)(2,2) amplitude [869]. This choice facilitates the matching of the post-merger model with the inspiral-plunge EOB waveform, especially for the multipoles whose peaks are strongly delayed with respect to the (2,2)(2,2) amplitude, such as the (2,1)(2,1) mode.

The templates in Eq. (5.11) and (5.12) describe a monotonic amplitude and frequency evolution, so they are not directly applicable to modes with post-merger oscillations due to mode mixing [838, 940, 941]. For comparable-mass binaries, this occurs primarily in the (3,2)(3,2) and (4,3)(4,3) modes, and is related to the mismatch between the spherical harmonic basis used for extraction in NR simulations, and the spheroidal harmonic basis employed in perturbation theory [940]. The previous template was recently extended [934] to such contributions in the (3,2)(3,2) and (4,3)(4,3) modes by applying Eqs. (5.11), (5.12) to the spheroidal harmonics [39] (3,2,0)(3,2,0) and (4,3,0)(4,3,0), which maintain a monotonic amplitude and frequency evolution. The (3,2)(3,2) and (4,3)(4,3) spherical harmonics can be reconstructed by combining the (3,2,0)(3,2,0) and (4,3,0)(4,3,0) spheroidal harmonics with the (2,2)(2,2) and (3,3)(3,3) spherical harmonics, using suitable mode mixing coefficients [941]. Another source of mode mixing is the beating between co-rotating and counter-rotating modes, as noticed in several studies conducted in the test-mass limit [902, 734, 903, 735, 904, 899]. While this effect is also visible in the (2,2) ringdown waveform generated by the infall of a test particle in a Schwarzschild BH, it is even more relevant in some higher harmonics, such as the (2,1) and (3,2) ones, or for orbital angular momenta anti-aligned with the Kerr spin [904]. A procedure to include this effect in QNM-factorized phenomenological ringdown models at late times has been recently proposed and applied to test particles falling in a Schwarzschild BH [899]. While this methodology seems to retain its validity in the comparable-mass case, as shown in the example reported in Fig. 32 of [935], it has yet to be included in EOB models for generic mass ratios.

The methodology of [873] has also been recently extended to the oscillatory contribution in real-valued m=0m=0 modes by applying a complexification of the physical signal with a Hilbert transform [942]. In these cases, the description has to be completed by including null memory contributions, discussed in more detail in Section 5.4.

The closed-form nature of the merger-ringdown waveform also makes it well-suited for BH spectroscopy analyses, either by introducing parameterized deviations to the QNM complex frequencies within the complete IMR EOB model [943, 944, 945, 946, 947], or by using the merger-ringdown waveform as a standalone post-merger model [948]. The same model has also been applied to theories of gravity beyond GR [553, 530], provided the QNM frequencies in the alternative theory are known. These applications are discussed in more detail in Section 6.

5.2.4 Eccentric and precessing orbits

In recent years, EOB models have been generalized to describe generic orbits [949, 950, 951, 952, 953, 885, 954, 955, 917, 956]. However, the post-merger signal of these models is still described using the quasi-circular ringdown waveform described above. For moderate eccentricity, such modeling still yields accurate results due to the circularization of the dynamics during the inspiral, and works reasonably well even in the dynamical capture scenario [957, 958, 959]. However, the accuracy of these models could be improved by including noncircular information from NR data in the ringdown waveform, as shown in [958]. Motivated by these considerations, gauge-invariant combinations of evolved energy and angular momentum, well suited to model post-merger effects were introduced in [895]. Closed-form descriptions of the remnant properties and waveform quantities at merger were also provided, which could be used to improve the post-merger waveforms of EOB models for generic orbits. Fully eccentric post-merger models have instead been explored in the test-mass limit [960, 899], where an alternative to Eq. (5.11) has also been proposed [960].

For binaries with generic spins, the same construction is applied to the waveform in the co-precessing frame [884, 938, 961, 962]. The co-precessing frame is a noninertial frame that tracks the instantaneous motion of the orbital plane, in which the gravitational radiation resembles the one of an aligned-spin binary [879, 963, 882, 964, 880] (up to asymmetries over the orbital plane [784, 965]). However, spin precession introduces specific effects that require additional consideration. To convert the waveform from the co-precessing frame to the inertial observer’s frame, one must describe the rotation between the two, often parameterized by a set of time-dependent Euler angles (α⁡(t),β⁡(t),γ⁡(t))(\alpha(t),\beta(t),\gamma(t)), which extends beyond merger. A phenomenological prescription, informed by NR simulations [881], was then employed [884, 938, 961, 962] to show that the co-precessing frame continues to approximately precess around the direction of the final angular momentum, with a precession frequency ωprec=ωR,220−ωR,210\omega_{\rm{prec}}=\omega_{R,220}-\omega_{R,210}, where ωR,ℓ​m​n\omega_{R,\ell mn} denotes the real part of the complex ωℓ​m​n\omega_{\ell mn} QNM frequency. As noted in Section 5.1.4, such a rotation induces a re-ordering of the amplitudes of different modes as compared to the nonprecessing scenario [963, 966, 886], leading to particularly large amplitudes for modes with ℓ=m≠2\ell=m\neq 2 [742, 967, 968, 887]. The rotation prescription used in EOB and Phenom models provides an accurate approximation if the (ℓ,m)=(2,0)(\ell,m)=(2,0) QNM amplitude in the remnant frame is negligible. However, for highly precessing binaries in which the (2,0)(2,0) QNM can be strongly excited, this assumption may be a source of systematics [887].

Finally, the QNM frequencies determined from BH perturbation theory are applicable in a frame in which the final spin of the remnant BH is aligned with the zz-direction (the so-called 𝐉\mathbf{J}-frame). A relationship between the QNM frequencies in the 𝐉\mathbf{J}-frame and an effective ringdown frequency in the co-precessing frame was derived in [883]:

ωR,ℓ​m​0CP=ωR,ℓ​m​0J−m⁡(1−|cos⁡β|)​ωprec ,\omega_{R,\ell m0}^{\mathrm{CP}}=\omega_{R,\ell m0}^{\mathrm{J}}-m\left(1-\left|\cos\beta\right|\right)\omega_{\text{prec }}, (5.13)

This relation was employed in the construction of recent phenomenological IMR models [962, 291].

5.3 Tails

Initial contributors: De Amicis, Khanna

A signal characterized by a slow decay in time, persisting after the main body of radiation has passed, is usually called a “tail effect.” In this section we review past and recent progress on modeling the tail signal that characterizes the late-time response of a BH spacetime to a perturbation. We will refer to effects originated by initial data perturbations of a BH in vacuum as “initial-data driven” tails, and to spacetime effects due to moving perturbing bodies (arising e.g. in the relativistic two-body problem) as “source-driven” tails.

5.3.1 Initial data-driven tails: spherically symmetric case

Late-time tails were first predicted by Price in the context of linear relaxation of the gravitational field following nonspherical collapse [421, 711]. He showed that for an observer at finite distances, the signal follows an inverse power-law falloff; in particular, that ∼t−(2​ℓ+2+x)\sim t^{-(2\ell+2+x)}, where x=0x=0 if a static mode is initially present, and x=1x=1 otherwise.

This result was later generalized in [155, 710, 165, 969, 970] by means of a Green’s function approach. These studies found that tails are generated by the back-scattering of low frequency signals with the long-range curvature of the background. In particular, Leaver [155] computed the late-time signal observed at null infinity as u−ℓ−2u^{-\ell-2} for all retarded times uu, where ℓ\ell the waveform’s multipole index, at leading order in a small-frequency expansion. At finite distances, the late-time response is first dominated by a transient radiative tail u−ℓ−2u^{-\ell-2}, while Price’s prediction is recovered only after some time. The duration of this radiative transient increases with the distance of the observer’s location [971]: this work showed that the radiative transient is the most relevant for real observations of astrophysical sources.

Corrections to the leading-order expansion of [155] were computed in Refs. [165, 970], for tails observed at finite distances. For example, a superposition of faster decaying power laws ∼t−(2​ℓ+3+2​m)\sim t^{-(2\ell+3+2m)}, originating from sub-leading orders in the small frequency expansion ω​M≪1\omega M\ll 1, was found in [165]. It is important to note that these faster decaying power laws come from corrections to the Green’s function that propagate the late-time signal. Corrections to Price’s law including more terms in the large distance (r≫Mr\gg M) expansion for the background potential were computed in [970]. Such corrections are logarithmic and belong to the class of potentials analyzed also in Refs. [710, 712], leading to logarithmic corrections in the coordinate time tt for the late-time signal.

Different approaches to compute late-time tails, likewise exploiting the key role of back-scattering off the large-scale background curvature, can be found in [972, 973, 974, 969].

Analytical predictions for late-time tails as observed at finite distances [421, 711], and radiative tails at null infinity ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+} [155], were later investigated numerically: see in particular [975, 976] for numerical evolutions of the spherical collapse of a scalar field, and [802, 799, 801, 971, 977] for perturbative numerical evolutions.

5.3.2 Initial data-driven tails: Kerr case

The asymptotic late-time, power-law (tnt^{n}) decay rates of matter fields in Kerr BH spacetime have been a matter of significant debate for several years. Initial difficulties were related to the complex mode coupling which arises in the spinning case, and required the development of sophisticated mathematical and computational techniques [978, 979, 980, 981, 982, 983, 984, 985]. The following late-time decay rate expressions for scalar fields in sub-extremal BHs were found in [984, 985]:

n={−(ℓ′+ℓ+3)forℓ′=0,1,−(ℓ′+ℓ+1)otherwise.\quad n=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}-(\ell^{\prime}+\ell+3)&\mathrm{for}\quad\ell^{\prime}=0,1,\\ -(\ell^{\prime}+\ell+1)&\mathrm{otherwise}.\end{array}\right.\\ (5.14)

along r=constr={\rm const} and ℋ+\mathscr{H}^{+}, and

nℐ+={−ℓ′forℓ≤ℓ′−2,−(ℓ+2)forℓ≥ℓ′,\quad n^{\mathscr{I}^{+}}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}-\ell^{\prime}&\mathrm{for}\quad\ell\leq\ell^{\prime}-2,\\ -(\ell+2)&\mathrm{for}\quad\ell\geq\ell^{\prime},\end{array}\right. (5.15)

along null infinity ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+}, where ℓ′\ell^{\prime} refers to the initial field multipole, and ℓ\ell is the multipole of interest. These rates refer to axisymmetric multipoles, and were obtained by carefully studying the inter-mode coupling effects that are present in the Kerr spacetime due to frame-dragging. The nonaxisymmetric results do not change, except for fact that both ℓ′\ell^{\prime} and ℓ\ell are bounded from below by the value of mm [986].

To illustrate in some detail the role of mode coupling, let us consider for example an initial multipole ℓ′=2\ell^{\prime}=2, and study the multipoles ℓ=0,2,4,6\ell=0,2,4,6. The evolution equations for each of these multipoles may be found in [986]. They are expanded in powers of the BH spin χ=a/M\chi=a/M and denoted as fℓ(2​n)f^{(2n)}_{\ell}, where 2​n2n refers to the power of χ\chi in the expansion, and ℓ\ell to the multipole moment. Each equation has the form

□​fℓ(2​n)+Vℓ​(ρ)​fℓ(2​n)=Sℓ(2​n),\Box f^{(2n)}_{\ell}+V_{\ell}(\rho)\,f^{(2n)}_{\ell}=S^{(2n)}_{\ell}\,, (5.16)

where the effective potential is given by

Vℓ​(ρ)=1ρ2​(1−2​Mρ)​[ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)+2​Mρ],V_{\ell}(\rho)=\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\,\left(1-\frac{2M}{\rho}\right)\,\left[\ell(\ell+1)+\frac{2M}{\rho}\right]\,, (5.17)

and Sℓ(2​n)S^{(2n)}_{\ell} is a sum of terms involving differential operators operating on lower–order iteration modes with multipoles ℓ−2\ell-2, ℓ\ell, and ℓ+2\ell+2. The radial variable ρ\rho is defined via r=M+ρ2−2​M​ρ+M2​(1−χ2)r=M+\sqrt{\rho^{2}-2M\rho+M^{2}(1-\chi^{2})}, so that the horizon is always at 2​M2M.

Each of the solutions of these inhomogeneous equations is the sum of a general solution of the homogeneous equation, plus a particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation. The nontrivial, nonzero homogeneous solution is the one corresponding to the mode present in the initial data. There are ten possible channels of excitation from the initial f2(0)f^{(0)}_{2} mode to the final f2(6)f^{(6)}_{2} mode, schematically represented in Fig. 49. Notice that three channels include direct coupling between modes that are separated by more than one order. A detailed study of such excitation channels established the dominant channels that predict the final decay rates of the ℓ=2\ell=2 multipole [986]. The same rates were recently confirmed by a rigorous mathematical analysis of mode-coupling effects in Kerr spacetime [985].

In Table 5 we summarize late-time power-law decay rates for extremal Kerr. The table, built using extensive numerical solutions [987], lists the fall-off rates for scalar perturbations along r=constr={\rm const}, along ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+}, and along ℋ+\mathscr{H}^{+}, for the case of no initial data supported on ℋ+\mathscr{H}^{+}. It also reports the corresponding decay rates when the initial data are supported on ℋ+\mathscr{H}^{+}. It is interesting to note that along ℐ+\mathscr{I}^{+}, horizon data do not change the decay rate.

There are relatively few generalizations of these results beyond the scalar case (e.g. [988]). However, the spin-weight of the matter field does not impact the asymptotic rates [422]. Therefore, it is expected that the dominant GW mode (hℓ​mh_{\ell m} with ℓ=m=2\ell=m=2) at future null infinity should have a late-time tail decay of 1/u41/u^{4} which has been confirmed in studies such as Ref. [988].

5.3.3 Source-driven tails: perturbative test-particle results

The initial data studies reviewed in the previous section suggest that tail effects are typically strongly suppressed compared to the QNM emission. Hence, while the study of late-time tails has attracted considerable attention from the mathematical point of view, their contributions to GW templates has typically been considered negligible for any near-future observations. Here we discuss work showing that the tail can be considerably enhanced when BH perturbations are driven by an orbiting body along noncircular orbits. This indicates that the relevance of tails in GW source modeling should be revisited.

Perturbative numerical evolutions of a test particle falling along generic orbits into a Schwarzschild BH found an enhancement of late-time tails as the progenitor’s binary eccentricity increases [899]. This observation was highlighted and exploited in [989] to attempt the first extraction of late-time tails in nonlinear simulations (see Section 5.3.4), and later investigated in depth in [420, 990].

A perturbative analytical model for late-time tails emitted by eccentric particle trajectories developed in [420] following a strategy similar to [155] predicts late-time, post-merger tails observed at ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+} as an integral over the system past history of the form

Ψℓ​mtail​(u)=∫−∞ud​t′​𝒮ℓ​m​[r⁡(t′),φ⁡(t′)](u−t′)ℓ+2,\Psi^{\rm tail}_{\ell m}(u)=\int_{-\infty}^{u}dt^{\prime}\frac{\mathcal{S}_{\ell m}\left[r(t^{\prime}),\varphi(t^{\prime})\right]}{\left(u-t^{\prime}\right)^{\ell+2}}\,, (5.18)

where 𝒮ℓ​m\mathcal{S}_{\ell m} a function of the test particle’s trajectory (r⁡(t′),φ⁡(t′))\left(r(t^{\prime}),\varphi(t^{\prime})\right), and Ψℓ​m\Psi_{\ell m} is a master function linearly related to the GW strain at future null infinity [420]. This expression illustrates the hereditary nature of late-times tails: the post-ringdown strain is inherited from the inspiral in a nonlocal fashion, similarly to what is observed in PN theory [991].

From Eq. (5.18) one can accurately predict the scaling of late-time tails with the eccentricity, as shown by the comparison with perturbative numerical waveforms in Fig. 50 [420]. The perturbative numerical waveforms are computed with the RWZHyp code [734, 992], by simultaneously solving the RWZ equations (initially setting the Ψ\Psi field and its derivative to zero) and the Hamiltonian equation of motion for the test particle. The signal is computed at ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+} and the trajectories are driven by a (fully analytical) PN-expanded radiation-reaction, which allows for the evolution of generic orbits up to merger, instead of focusing on geodesic plunges. The semi-analytical predictions were obtained by feeding the numerical trajectory into the model of Eq. (5.18). A similar agreement holds for generic planar bounded orbits, including dynamical captures and radial infalls [420].

An enhancement of the tails with increasing eccentricity was found also in the Kerr background [990], as shown in Fig. 51. While the tail amplitude is clearly enhanced with increasing eccentricity, its dependence on the BH spin χ\chi is less clear, and analytical predictions are not available yet. The numerical results in the range χ=[−0.6,0.6]\chi=[-0.6,0.6] show clear evidence that the amplitude increases for large negative spins (anti-aligned with the orbital angular momentum), but they are inconclusive for co-aligned spins. Through a series of numerical experiments on generic orbits, the last apastron before merger was isolated as the portion of the trajectory contributing the most to tail enhancement, both in the Schwarzschild and in the Kerr cases [420, 990].

When the trajectories include the last apastron passage, a strong tail excitation is observed. On the contrary, no tails are observed when that part of the trajectory is ignored. An expansion of the late-time tail model of Eq. (5.18) valid in the limits r≫1r\gg 1 and L≪1L\ll 1 (where LL is the angular momentum of the test particle) yields, for the motion near apastron [420]:

Ψℓ​mTail​(u)=∫Ti​nTfd​t′​rℓ​(t′)​e−i​m​φ​(t′)​Pℓ​m​(cos⁡θ0)(u−t′)ℓ+2⋅[a1−a12​r˙2+a2​r˙​Lr+(a3+a12)​L2r2],\begin{gathered}\Psi^{\rm Tail}_{\ell m}(u)=\int_{T_{in}}^{T_{f}}dt^{\prime}\frac{r^{\ell}(t^{\prime})e^{-im\varphi(t^{\prime})}P_{\ell m}\left(\cos\theta_{0}\right)}{\left(u-t^{\prime}\right)^{\ell+2}}\cdot\left[a_{1}-\frac{a_{1}}{2}\dot{r}^{2}+a_{2}\dot{r}\frac{L}{r}+\left(a_{3}+\frac{a_{1}}{2}\right)\frac{L^{2}}{r^{2}}\right]\,,\end{gathered} (5.19)

where

a1=a0(ℓ+1)(ℓ+2),a2=a04im,a3=a0[ℓ(ℓ+1)−2m2−2],a0=cℓ8​π​μℓ⁡(ℓ+1)​[ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)−2].\begin{split}&a_{1}=a_{0}\left(\ell+1\right)\left(\ell+2\right)\,,\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ a_{2}=a_{0}4im\,,\\ &a_{3}=a_{0}\left[\ell(\ell+1)-2m^{2}-2\right]\,,\ \ \ a_{0}=c_{\ell}\frac{8\pi\mu}{\ell(\ell+1)\left[\ell(\ell+1)-2\right]}\,.\end{split} (5.20)

Here μ\mu is the test particle mass, and θ0\theta_{0} is a constant angle determining the planar motion. This equation implies that the integral (hence the tail effect) is enhanced for motion at large rr and with small angular velocity, due to the oscillating phase e−i​m​ϕ​(t′)e^{-im\phi(t^{\prime})}. Therefore the late-time tail is maximized for radial infalls from large distances, as corroborated by a series of numerical evolutions [420]. For generic binaries, the larger is the last orbit’s eccentricity, the further is the last apastron location, and the smaller is the angular velocity near this point (due to Kepler’s second law). These conditions imply an enhanced emission of tails at the last apastron before merger, an effect that is later observed in the post-ringdown strain. The oscillatory contribution and alternating sign of the expansion terms also imply an “interference” pattern that suppresses tail contributions for more “circular” motions: tail effects are maximized for systems with small phase variations, such as radial infalls. Since the oscillatory factor in the integral always reduces to unity for m=0m=0, the tail will be enhanced in the m=0m=0 modes of generic (eccentric and quasi-circular) orbits, as shown in [942].

Long-lived, perturbative numerical waveforms [420] show that late-time tails converge slowly and (in general) nonmonotonically towards Price’s law prediction u−ℓ−2u^{-\ell-2} [155]. Expanding Eq. (5.18) for u≫Tfu\gg T_{f}, with TfT_{f} the time of merger, it was found that source-driven late-time tails, computed through Price’s law propagator [155], are not an inverse power law, but rather a superposition of an infinite number of inverse power laws:

Ψℓ​mTail​(u)=1uℓ+2⋅∫−∞Tfd​t′​𝒮ℓ​m​[r⁡(t′),φ⁡(t′)]​[1+∑n=1∞(ℓ+1+n)!n!​(ℓ+1)!​(t′u)n].\begin{gathered}\Psi^{\rm Tail}_{\ell m}(u)=\frac{1}{u^{\ell+2}}\cdot\int_{-\infty}^{T_{\rm f}}dt^{\prime}\mathcal{S}_{\ell m}\left[r(t^{\prime}),\varphi(t^{\prime})\right]\left[1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\left(\ell+1+n\right)!}{n!\left(\ell+1\right)!}\left(\frac{t^{\prime}}{u}\right)^{n}\right]\,.\end{gathered} (5.21)

A large number of these power-law contributions (at least O⁡(100)O(100)) is required to obtain the transient emission to a reasonable degree of accuracy [796].

The excitation coefficient of each fast-decaying contribution depends on the history of the system and on the details of the specific orbit it describes, enclosed in the trajectory function 𝒮ℓ​m\mathcal{S}_{\ell m}. For generic orbits, corrections to Price’s law due to the source give rise to a long-lived transient, while homogeneous perturbation theory results can only be recovered at asymptotically late times. Note how faster-decaying corrections in Eq. (5.21) are source-driven, hence conceptually different from higher-order corrections to the tail propagator computed (e.g.) in [165].

The above discussion pertains to the sub-extremal Kerr case. In the near-extremal regime, the late-time behavior is different and rather peculiar. As the BH approaches extremality, a remarkable superposition of overtones due to a “superradiance resonance cavity” implies that the ringdown transitions from an exponential decay to a 1/u1/u behavior [174, 47]. Numerical investigations [993] confirm this prediction, as shown in Fig. 52.

Moreover, this overtone superposition imparts a peculiar evolution to QNM frequencies during ringdown [994]. In the near-extremal regime, the u−1u^{-1} decay is due to the collective excitation of zero-damped modes [47]. For extremal BHs, the u−1u^{-1} decay is eternal instead of transient.

5.3.4 Tails in nonlinear evolutions

The above discussion was limited to perturbation theory, as until recently the identification of late-time tails in nonlinear binary mergers seemed out of reach because of the small amplitude of tails in quasi-circular binaries. Motivated by tails enhancement in highly eccentric binaries, and by the understanding of the large-radius origin of this effect discussed above, two independent studies extracted late-time tails in fully nonlinear 3+1 evolutions of head-on BBH mergers [796, 995].

Tails identification in previous simulations had been challenging because standard evolutions employed imperfect boundary conditions at the outer simulation boundary, imposing no incoming radiation towards the source. In curved spacetime this condition does not hold due to the presence of tails. Hence, if the boundary is too close to the source, enforcing no incoming radiation implies cutting a large portion of spacetime inside which tails are generated, and thus quenching the tail signal. Moreover, due to the nonexact nature of the boundary conditions, when the evolved radiation reaches the boundary it generates a nonphysical signal, that later travels back to the observer’s location and spoils the extraction of the tail [996, 997]. This second subtlety depends on the observer’s location: if the extraction radius is far from the source, the extrapolated late-time signal is characterized by an initial transient following the proper ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+} behavior (i.e., what would be observed by real detectors [971]); if instead the extraction radius is close to the source, the tail signal is suppressed.

By analyzing several Cauchy evolutions, in which the signal was computed at different finite-radii locations and then extrapolated towards null infinity [998, 999, 1000, 966, 784, 1001], it is possible to robustly extract the late-time tail by fixing the observer’s radii and the outer boundary to be very far from the GW source [796].

A different strategy based on Cauchy-Characteristic Matching [1002, 1003, 1004, 1005, 1006, 1007] was adopted in [995]. This method combines (i) a Cauchy integration performed up to an outer boundary, used to evolve a characteristic system from this location; and (ii) characteristic evolution to impose correct boundary conditions at each time step of the Cauchy evolution. In this way it is possible to include the back-scattered signal (i.e., tail effects) in the full numerical integration.

These results are summarized in Figs. 53 and 54, respectively.

In Fig. 53 we show fully nonlinear numerical evolutions of head-on collisions with mass ratios q=[1,2,3]q=[1,2,3] from an initial separation D0=100​MD_{0}=100M, with initial ADM energy equal to the total rest-mass of the system MM. The NR results are compared with perturbative waveforms computed with the RWZHyp code [903, 992] for a test particle of mass μ\mu falling from the same distance and with initial energy E0=μE_{0}=\mu. Beyond clear signatures of a slow tail decay, Fig. 53 shows that the binary mass ratio has a small effect on the excitation of tails, and that there is remarkable agreement between perturbative and fully nonlinear waveforms from the peak of the strain of the (20)(20) multipole up to late-times. This observation adds to a large body of literature indicating the surprising predictive power of BH perturbation theory in the nonlinear comparable-mass case [1008, 1009, 1010]. Radial infalls are admittedly “simpler” than quasi-circular inspirals as radiation reaction is suppressed, but it would be interesting to better understand this striking agreement by analytical methods.

The results in Fig. 54 refer instead to a head-on collision with mass-ratio q=1q=1 and initial separation D0=110​MD_{0}=110M. Here the tail signal is reconstructed starting from early times, and the QNM contributions to the strain are removed using the filters developed in [763, 1011, 1012]. The tail signal is always present (although initially subdominant) during the BH ringdown. The impact of tails on waveform modeling has yet to be investigated. A fit of the late-time behavior of the Weyl scalar Ψ4\Psi_{4} is compatible with an inverse power-law (u+19.1)−3.79(u+19.1)^{-3.79}. This decay is slower than Price’s prediction, and in agreement with the perturbative predictions of [796].

The nonlinear signal shown in Fig. 53 displays a slower late-time decay with respect to perturbative source-driven results, in agreement with [995]. This can be tentatively explained by the presence of nonlinearities: hereditary tails depend, at any time, on the entire history of the system, hence they can amplify nonlinearities and make them relevant even at very late times.

Recent work focused on a new late-time nonlinear effect that does not originate from long-range back-scattering and is not hereditary [717, 1013, 1014, 1015]. This signal, referred to as a “nonlinear tail” because of its inverse power-law behavior arising at second-order in perturbation theory, decays slower than Price’s law and it presumably originates from coupled linear QNMs in the second-order source, mediated through the prompt response propagator [717, 1013, 1014, 1015].

5.4 BMS frames and memory

Initial contributors: Magaña Zertuche, Mitman, Stein

In GR, the perturbed remnant formed at the end of a BBH coalescence asymptotes to a Kerr BH, but the metric is not expressed in the coordinates normally used in BH perturbation theory. Instead, the coordinates are transformed within the symmetry group of future null infinity ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+} — the final destination of outgoing gravitational radiation. For example, in general the remnant BH receives a “kick” (i.e., a boost) relative to center-of-momentum frame of its progenitor binary. Consequently, the radiation that one observes from the boosted remnant BH will not be the usual ringdown expected from perturbation theory: because of the boost, the frequencies will be Doppler shifted and the angular structure will be beamed by relativistic aberration. To ensure that the extracted ringdown physics is frame-invariant, one must transform from the initial binary frame to an appropriate remnant frame. In this section we review the characterization of this frame and its implications.

5.4.1 Basic formalism

In the 1960s, Bondi, van der Burg, Metzner, and Sachs (BMS) [1016, 1017, 1018, 1019, 1020] sought to better understand the asymptotics of gravitational radiation by fixing as much coordinate gauge freedom as possible. They began by considering an arbitrary metric written in Bondi-Sachs coordinates with gauge conditions gr​r=0g_{rr}=0, gr​A=0g_{rA}=0, and ∂rdet⁡(γA​B)=0\partial_{r}\mathrm{det}\left(\gamma_{AB}\right)=0:

d​s2\displaystyle ds^{2} =−U​e2​β​d​u2−2​e2​β​d​u​d​r+r2​γA​B​(d​xA−𝒰A​d​u)​(d​xB−𝒰B​d​u),\displaystyle=-Ue^{2\beta}du^{2}-2e^{2\beta}dudr+r^{2}\gamma_{AB}\left(dx^{A}-\mathcal{U}^{A}du\right)\left(dx^{B}-\mathcal{U}^{B}du\right)\,, (5.22)

where capital Latin indices range over {θ,ϕ}\{\theta,\phi\}, u≡t−ru\equiv t-r, and UU, β\beta, 𝒰A\mathcal{U}^{A}, and γA​B\gamma_{AB} are arbitrary functions of the coordinates (u,r,θ,ϕ)(u,r,\theta,\phi). Since radiation decays with distance, they specialized to metrics that approach the standard Minkowski metric in the large radius limit. Consequently, as r→∞r\rightarrow\infty they imposed the conditions

U→1,β→0,𝒰A→1,γA​B→(100sin2⁡θ).\displaystyle U\rightarrow 1,\quad\beta\rightarrow 0,\quad\mathcal{U}^{A}\rightarrow 1,\quad\gamma_{AB}\rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&\sin^{2}\theta\end{pmatrix}. (5.23)

This asymptotic restriction is often called being in “Bondi gauge” or some “Bondi frame” and provided an early notion of “asymptotic flatness.” Gravitational radiation is now entirely encoded in the 1/r1/r part of γA​B\gamma_{AB}. However, there is a remaining ambiguity regarding the coordinate freedom of radiation on the boundary of the spacetime, i.e., what is the set of transformations of the asymptotic coordinates (u,θ,ϕ)(u,\theta,\phi) that preserve the form of the metric described in Eqs. (5.22) and (5.23).

One may expect that since the conditions in Eq. (5.23) make the metric asymptote to the Minkowski metric as r→∞r\to\infty, then these coordinate freedoms should simply be the ten elements of the Poincaré group. A bit surprisingly, this intuition turns out to be only nearly correct. Instead, the symmetry group of future null infinity is an extension of the more familiar Poincaré group, in which the usual spacetime translations are replaced by a larger set of direction-dependent spacetime translations called “supertranslations.” Fortunately, one can intuit why supertranslations are symmetries of future null infinity through the following realization. Take a family of inertial observers placed about a 2-sphere of radius rr, and consider the limit as r→∞r\to\infty along outgoing null rays, thus approaching ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+}. Their world lines will asymptote to null geodesics tangent to ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+}. These generators are causally disconnected from each other, as all future-directed null rays starting on ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+} stay tangent to ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+}. Therefore, one can freely translate each generator, i.e., an arbitrary point on the two-sphere, without changing this asymptotic boundary.

Thus the symmetry group of future null infinity is not the usual Poincaré group, but an infinite-dimensional extension called the BMS group [1018, 1019]. As a result, whenever one works with radiation from the perturbed BH formed by a BBH coalescence, one must always control the BMS freedoms of future null infinity to ensure that their analysis is in the frame of the remnant [889, 50, 762, 890].

To do this, one needs to understand how a BMS transformation, i.e., an element of the BMS group, transforms asymptotic data. As shown by the original works [1016, 1017, 1018, 1019, 1020], a BMS transformation changes the asymptotic coordinates via

(u,ζ)↦(u′,ζ′)≡(k⁡(ζ,ζ¯)​(u−α⁡(ζ,ζ¯)),a​ζ+bc​ζ+d),\displaystyle(u,\zeta)\mapsto(u^{\prime},\zeta^{\prime})\equiv\left(k(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})\left(u-\alpha(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})\right),\frac{a\zeta+b}{c\zeta+d}\right), (5.24)

where ζ≡ei​ϕ​cot⁡(θ/2)\zeta\equiv e^{i\phi}\cot(\theta/2) is the complex stereographic projective coordinate,

k⁡(ζ,ζ¯)≡1+|ζ|2|a​ζ+b|2+|c​ζ+d|2\displaystyle k(\zeta,\bar{\zeta})\equiv\frac{1+|\zeta|^{2}}{|a\zeta+b|^{2}+|c\zeta+d|^{2}} (5.25)

is the conformal factor, (a,b,c,d)(a,b,c,d) are complex coefficients with a​d−b​c=1ad-bc=1 that encode the Lorentz rotation and boost, and α⁡(ζ,ζ¯)\alpha(\zeta,\bar{\zeta}) is a real, smooth function that encodes the supertranslation. From this coordinate transformation, by examining how the tetrad on ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+} transforms [1001], one can then ascertain that the usual GW strain hh and the five Weyl scalars transform as

h′​(u′,ζ′)\displaystyle h^{\prime}(u^{\prime},\zeta^{\prime}) =1k​e−2​i​λ¯​[h⁡(u,ζ)−2​ð2​α],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}e^{-2i\bar{\lambda}}\left[h(u,\zeta)-2\eth^{2}\alpha\right], (5.26)
ΨA′​(u′,ζ′)\displaystyle\Psi_{A}^{\prime}(u^{\prime},\zeta^{\prime}) =1k3​e(2−A)​i​λ​∑a=A4(4−Aa−A)​(−1k​ð​u′)a−A​Ψa​(u,ζ),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k^{3}}e^{(2-A)i\lambda}\sum\limits_{a=A}^{4}\begin{pmatrix}4-A\\ a-A\end{pmatrix}\left(-\frac{1}{k}\eth u^{\prime}\right)^{a-A}\Psi_{a}(u,\zeta), (5.27)

where A∈{0,1,2,3,4}A\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}, λ\lambda is the spin phase with

ei​λ≡[∂ζ¯′∂ζ¯​(∂ζ′∂ζ)−1]12=c​ζ+dc¯​ζ¯+d¯,\displaystyle e^{i\lambda}\equiv\left[\frac{\partial\bar{\zeta}^{\prime}}{\partial\bar{\zeta}}\left(\frac{\partial\zeta^{\prime}}{\partial\zeta}\right)^{-1}\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{c\zeta+d}{\bar{c}\bar{\zeta}+\bar{d}}\,, (5.28)

and

ðf=−12(sinθ)+s(∂θ+icscθ∂ϕ)[(sinθ)−sf]\displaystyle\eth f=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\sin\theta)^{+s}(\partial_{\theta}+i\csc\theta\partial_{\phi})\left[(\sin\theta)^{-s}f\right] (5.29)

is the usual Geroch-Held-Penrose spin-weight operator [20] (see Appendix B).

Apart from this, the remaining information one needs is what BMS transformation must actually be applied to the system to map it to the canonical frame of the remnant. Extracting this transformation is typically referred to as “BMS frame fixing” [889, 762, 890]. It consists of constructing functions of asymptotic data which measure the failure of the system to be in some canonical frame. For example, to measure how much a system is boosted out of its center-of-mass frame, one can study the center-of-mass charge and extract the boost from said function. For fixing the entire BMS freedom, one requires three charges: a rotation charge to fix the rotation, a center-of-mass charge to fix the boost and translation, and a supermomentum charge, which extends the usual notion of a four-momentum charge, to fix the supertranslation. Definitions of these charges and how one can use them to fix the BMS frame are provided in [762, 890].

5.4.2 Conserved charges and memory effect

When a generalization of Noether’s theorem [1021, 1022] is applied to the BMS group, we find new (non)conservation laws that extend the usual Poincaré conservation laws. In particular, when considering the conservation law stemming from supertranslations, one finds

Re⁡[ð2​h]=12​(m+14​∫−∞u|h˙|2​𝑑u),\displaystyle\mathrm{Re}\left[\eth^{2}h\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left(m+\frac{1}{4}\int_{-\infty}^{u}|\dot{h}|^{2}du\right)\,, (5.30)

where

m≡Re⁡[Ψ2+14​h˙​h¯]\displaystyle m\equiv\mathrm{Re}\left[\Psi_{2}+\frac{1}{4}\dot{h}\bar{h}\right] (5.31)

is the Bondi mass aspect, a direction-dependent generalization of the mass on future null infinity ℐ+\mathcal{I}^{+}. The second term in Eq. (5.30) is a directional energy flux. When these equations are restricted to the ℓ=0\ell=0 and ℓ=1\ell=1 spherical harmonics, this conservation law yields the usual mass and momentum Poincaré conservation laws. However, for the ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 components, a brand new conservation law is encoded, yielding additional information on gravitational radiation. In particular, the first term is simply the usual mass multipole moment source, e.g., the mass quadrupole, while the second term is a source that corresponds to the flux of gravitational radiation sourcing even more radiation. Furthermore, because the flux of radiation can never be negative, the second term implies that the strain will experience a permanent net change between early and late times.

This phenomenon is known as the “GW memory effect” [1023, 1024, 1025, 1026, 1027]. It corresponds to the permanent net displacement that two inertial observers will experience due to a flux of gravitational radiation passing by them.
