Given the flexibility of damped sinusoid sums, additional modes in the ringdown template can, in principle, improve the fit by capturing nonstationarities, increasing the probability of false detections when the model contains multiple modes. The inclusion of multiple detectors characterized by independent noise processes helps to alleviate the impact of specific noise realizations that necessarily affect each signal.

We can assess the impact of noise on a given event in two steps, by adding a simulated signal (“injection”) with parameters close to those expected (e.g. estimated from some preferred analysis) into: (i) simulated Gaussian noise; and (ii) real noise around the GW event. Repeating step (ii) by injecting at different times, we can “sample” the true detector noise process and quantify the impact of real noise on the results (see e.g. Refs. [460, 1080, 945]). These studies can rapidly become computationally intensive because of high noise variability, uncertainty in the parameters of the detected signal, and the necessity to include different QNM combinations and starting times [460].

6.2 Current status of observations

Initial contributors: Caneva, Carullo, Farr, Finch, Westerweck

6.2.1 Fundamental quadrupolar mode observations

The observation of a coincident transient signal in the two LIGO interferometers on September 14, 2015 [1105] marked not only the historical discovery of GWs and the first observation of a binary BH merger, but also the first detection of the dominant QNM frequency of a BH. The signal power within the detector band was sufficiently large to isolate the post-peak signal and extract the dominant frequency and damping time in the ringdown waveform. Given the remnant BH parameters extracted under the assumption that GR correctly describes the entire signal, the expected frequency and damping time of the fundamental (ℓ,m,n)=(2,2,0)(\ell,m,n)=(2,2,0) mode correspond to f220≃250​Hz,τ220≃4​msf_{220}\simeq 250\,\mathrm{Hz},\,\tau_{220}\simeq 4\,\mathrm{ms}. The LVK collaboration compared this expectation against a measurement obtained under the simplest possible assumption: a single damped sinusoid post-peak [543, 1055]. Given the statistical uncertainty on the signal peak location and the uncertainty on the starting time of a single-QNM ringdown, the analysis was repeated at multiple starting times past the waveform peak. For the system parameters under consideration, an analysis assuming a single QNM was predicted to yield an estimate in agreement with the fundamental mode around a timescale of tstart≃3​ms≃10​Mt_{\rm start}\simeq 3\,\mathrm{ms}\simeq 10M, with MM the total mass of the binary system expressed in seconds units. The analysis result is in agreement with this expectation, as shown in Fig. 61.

Despite its consistency with the predictions of GR, the LVK ringdown-only analysis of GW150914 was based on a FD technique that did not apply a window or gating and in-painting filters to the data [1055]. As discussed in the previous subsection, this approach can lead to biased results. This realization is what sparked the development of TD and nonstandard FD methodologies capable of isolating a specific signal portion. These were applied to a re-analysis of the presence of the fundamental QNM in GW150914 at late times [529]. This confirmed the robustness of the detection of the dominant mode against differences in details of the data analysis (such as PSD estimation, data conditioning, etc.) with high statistical confidence, as quantified e.g. by the BF comparing the hypothesis for the presence of a damped sinusoid signal hypothesis vs. pure noise, ℬns≃e14.6\mathcal{B}^{s}_{n}\simeq e^{14.6} [529]. Additional searches found no evidence for multiple fundamental modes in the signal beyond the quadrupolar harmonic [1052, 529].

GWTC-3 GW150914 was the first GW event shown to be consistent with a BBH signal as predicted by GR. Since then, the LVK collaboration has validated the predictions of GR in the strong-field regime by performing a variety of tests on an expanding collection of GW events [460, 546, 529]. Over the years, this list of events has been extended with additional binary merger detections during the first, second, and third observing runs (O1–O3). The third GWTC [1108] includes 90 compact binary coalescence events; however, not all events are used for testing GR (TGR). The TGR analyses apply stringent event selection criteria to ensure the astrophysical origin of the candidate event. Only events detected by at least two interferometers that would be generated by a random noise fluctuations in less than a thousand years are considered. Applying these conditions to GWTC-3 leads to a subset of 48 events passing the FAR threshold and the two-detector detection criterion. Once this subset is established, additional criteria are imposed depending on the specific strategy of each GR test. Probing the nature of the merger remnant is a crucial part of the TGR studies, which the LVK achieves using two complementary approaches: the TD analysis pyRing and the parameterized analysis pSEOB.

pyRing The pyRing analysis uses the truncated TD likelihood formulation described in Section 6.1.3. A hierarchical analysis strategy using templates with increasing levels of complexity (described in Section 6.1.6) is used to extract information from the observed signal with varying degrees of agnosticism. The templates employed in the analysis are, in order of encoded information: Damped sinusoids (here abbreviated to DS), Kerr and KerrBinary. The analysis is repeated for each template over a grid of fixed starting times to ensure that the estimated quantities converge toward their GR values, as expected. For simplicity, results for each model are reported only at a nominal start time tnomt_{\text{nom}}, defined as the time after the peak t0t_{0} when the QNM superposition model is expected to become valid. For analyses up to GWTC-3, the Kerr template, including a combination of the (ℓ=m=2\ell=m=2, n=0n=0) and (ℓ=m=2\ell=m=2, n=1n=1) QNMs, was the most sensitive. The inclusion of an overtone phenomenologically models the early time portion of the signal, thereby capturing more power. Additional selection criteria are imposed on the list of events passing the TGR selection process to ensure that only events with detectable ringdown signals are thoroughly analyzed, reducing computational cost. This is determined by a first analysis of all events using the most sensitive template: if the analysis favors the presence of a signal over Gaussian noise, as well as yielding estimates of the remnant’s mass and spin which are informative relative to the prior distributions, the event is included in the “ringdown catalog.” Out of the 48 events, only 22 make the cut. The analysis starting time for each model is defined relative to the best estimate of the peak strain h+2+h×2h_{+}^{2}+h_{\times}^{2} time t0t_{0}, as determined by the IMR analysis under the assumption of GR. The sky position is also fixed to values pre-determined by IMR analyses.

The simplest model, DS, is an agnostic framework for testing the consistency of ringdown emission with GR in which the signal is a simple superposition of QNMs. The frequency, damping time, logarithmic amplitude and phase of each mode are free parameters, each with uniform priors. Spectroscopic measurements of QNMs are achieved by comparing the observed frequencies and damping times with the theoretical predictions from BH perturbation theory. The comparison between the frequency and damping time obtained for the 22 analyzed events agrees with the IMR predictions for the fundamental ℓ=|m|=2,n=0\ell=|m|=2,n=0 mode at ts​t​a​r​t=10​Mt_{start}=10M. Searches based on other templates are discussed in detailed below.

6.2.2 Searches for additional modes

Spectroscopic tests of the Kerr nature of the merger remnant require the detection of more than one mode. Here we review the current status of searches for multiple modes.

Overtones in GW150914 As discussed in Section 5.1.3, the authors of [161] suggested that the post-peak GW signal from BBH mergers like GW150914 could be described to high accuracy by a sum of damped sinusoids corresponding to the final-state linear ringdown modes of the remnant BH, provided that enough overtones are included. Motivated by this suggestion, Isi et al. [1053] fit a Kerr model to post-peak GW150914 data using the TD methods discussed in Section 6.1.3. They consider a fixed time offset between the Hanford and Livingston detectors, corresponding to a signal originating at right ascension α=1.95​rad\alpha=1.95\,\mathrm{rad} and declination δ=−1.27​rad\delta=-1.27\,\mathrm{rad}; additionally, they constrain the signal to be left-circularly polarized (consistent with a face-off viewing angle, ι=180∘\iota=180^{\circ}). These values are consistent with the sky location and orientation for the GW150914 event determined by an analysis of the full signal [1127]. Isi et al. [1053] show that a single-tone Kerr ringdown model, with only the (2,2,0)(2,2,0) fundamental mode, fitted to the Hanford and Livingston detector data sampled at a 2 kHz sample rate starting at tH=1126259462.423t_{H}=1126259462.423 (the peak time employed in Ref. [543]), recovers a final-state mass and spin that are inconsistent with the values inferred from the full signal analysis. The analysis duration is T=0.5T=0.5\,s, and a direct correlation method is used to estimate the ACF.

In contrast, using a two-tone (fundamental (2,2,0)(2,2,0) plus overtone (2,2,1)(2,2,1)) Kerr model at the estimated peak time, Ref. [1053] recovers a mass and spin that are instead consistent with the analysis of the full signal. In the two-tone model, the posterior mean amplitude of the overtone is 3.6 standard deviations from zero; this is the leftmost result shown in Fig. 62. Relaxing the Kerr assumption and allowing the frequency and damping rate of the overtone to vary from the Kerr value consistently with the fundamental mode’s frequency and damping rate, as described in Section 3.2, recovers posteriors on the deviations δ​f221\delta f_{221} and δ​τ221\delta\tau_{221} compatible with δ​f221=δ​τ221=0\delta f_{221}=\delta\tau_{221}=0; the measurement of δ​f221=−0.05±0.2\delta f_{221}=-0.05\pm 0.2 establishes that the data are consistent with the Kerr overtone frequency at the 20%20\% level [1053]. In the three-tone model, neither the first nor second overtone amplitudes are individually bounded away from zero, but their joint posterior excludes the origin at similarly high credibility. Subsequently, Isi et al. [1051] demonstrated similar results for two-tone models applied to GW150914-like waveforms from NR calculations in realistic detector noise at SNRs comparable to GW150914, at least partially validating the applicability of the two-tone Kerr model in these contexts as an effective description of the post-peak data. Their inference framework is implemented in the publicly available ringdown package (see Appendix A).

Cotesta et al. [1080] re-assess these results. They note that (i) the peak-time distribution of GW150914 spans a width of 22\,ms (at 2​σ2\sigma credibility), or several tMt_{M}, and this uncertainty can not be neglected; (ii) the fixed reference time used in Isi et al. [1053] underestimates the average peak time of h+2+h×2h_{+}^{2}+h_{\times}^{2} (see the top panel of Fig. 62). The analysis of Cotesta et al. is similar to Isi et al. [1053], but it uses the independent and publicly available pyRing package (see Appendix A). They report a fluctuating posterior on the overtone amplitude across a range of analysis times consistent with the estimates from full-signal models, finding a much smaller significance for the overtone presence and negative Bayesian evidence (see Figs. 62 and 63). They repeat a similar analysis for GW150914-like signals added to LIGO detector noise, which suggests that noise fluctuations could induce spurious evidence for the presence of an overtone. Such a significantly different posterior on the overtone amplitude is not only due to the inclusion of peak-time uncertainty – it is also found at a reference time compatible with Isi et al. [1053]. Compared to Isi et al., Cotesta et al. use a higher sampling rate (∼16​kHz\sim 16\,\rm kHz instead of ∼2​kHz\sim 2\,\rm kHz), an analysis duration of T=0.1​sT=0.1s, and an identical method to estimate the ACF through the ringdown package.

Isi & Farr [1081] performed a subsequent re-analysis at a sampling rate of ∼2​kHz\sim 2\,\mathrm{kHz}, with a Fourier-transform based ACF estimation and with a duration T=0.2​sT=0.2\,\mathrm{s} (arguing that this is sufficiently long to capture virtually the entire signal power). The re-analysis notes how the estimated overtone amplitude decays consistently with the expectation of exponential damping [1081], even in a range of times consistent with estimates of the peak of the strain. A subsequent Comment [1094] later identified two issues with the analysis in Cotesta et al. [1080]: an insufficient analysis duration (T=0.1​sT=0.1\,\mathrm{s}, instead of the original T=0.2​sT=0.2\,\mathrm{s}), and a shift of one timestamp (or 0.06​ms0.06\,\mathrm{ms}) in the likelihood time axis with respect to the detector data axis. A re-analysis accounting for these issues, presented in Carullo et al. [1082], finds negligible differences with respect to previous work by the same authors in Cotesta et al. [1080]. The remaining differences with the analyses of Isi et al. [1053, 1081] are attributed to different sampling rates and ACF estimation methods: recall that Ref. [1081] switched to an FFT-based estimate, similar to the one employed within the standard LVK spectroscopy searches [1052, 460], but different from the direct correlation originally employed in Isi et al. [1053] and (in the attempt to reproduce their results) by Cotesta et al. [1080].

Finch & Moore [1086] also analyze GW150914 with the method discussed in Section 6.1.7, which allows for a variable damped-sinusoid starting time in the analysis at the cost of introducing a wavelet-based model for the early time signal. Marginalizing over the starting time estimates from [1127], they find that the Bayesian evidence for the two-tone model is lower than for the single-tone model by a small factor (log10⁡B1​Q​N​M2​Q​N​M≃−0.2\log_{10}B_{1\mathrm{QNM}}^{2\mathrm{QNM}}\simeq-0.2). The time-marginalized posterior on the overtone amplitude has a mean ∼1.8\sim 1.8 times its standard deviation away from zero. This marginalized result is shown in Fig. 62. At the same starting time used by Isi et al. [1053], the posterior on the overtone amplitude agrees with the results of Ref. [1053], and the evidence for the overtone is positive, log10⁡B1​Q​N​M2​Q​N​M≃0.9\log_{10}B_{1\mathrm{QNM}}^{2\mathrm{QNM}}\simeq 0.9. However, when assuming a fixed starting time corresponding to the peak-time median (as in the top panel of Fig. 62) the evidence drops to log10⁡B1​Q​N​M2​Q​N​M≃0\log_{10}B_{1\mathrm{QNM}}^{2\mathrm{QNM}}\simeq 0.

Ma et al. [1011, 1012] use a rational filter to target and remove specific QNM frequencies from the data. They report a log base-10 BF as high as ∼2.8\sim 2.8 in favor of a model with an overtone, but note that this is sensitive to the ringdown starting time. We chose not to include their results in Figs. 62 and 63, because the interpretation of their reported BF is affected by the filtering technique they use.

Crisostomi et al. [1087] report a mild (∼2​σ\sim 2\sigma) evidence for the presence of an overtone, making use of a calibrated simulation-based inference pipeline. This number is based on the credible region at which the (calibrated) two-dimensional (A220,A221)(A_{220},\,A_{221}) posterior excludes A221=0A_{221}=0, for some preferred choice of ringdown start time and sky position.

Yi-Fan Wang et al. [1083] employ gating and in-painting (see Section 6.1.4) to perform the analysis at multiple (fixed) ringdown starting times, focusing on data analysis systematics. Their “fiducial” analysis with a sampling rate of 8192 Hz (shown in Figs. 62 and 63) reports log base-10 BFs ranging from ∼−0.4\sim-0.4 to 1.41.4 and an overtone amplitude median over standard deviation of ∼1.9\sim 1.9 to 2.82.8 (over the 1-sigma uncertainty on tpeakt_{\mathrm{peak}}).

Correia et al. [1084] also use gating and in-painting. However, by allowing the switch-on time of the gate (tat_{a}) to vary as a free parameter within the analysis, they are able to marginalize over the ringdown starting time and sky position. They find that simply allowing the switch-on time of the gate to vary would result in the gate being pushed as late as possible, effectively excising all signal from the data (see also [1085] for details). To address this issue, the pre-ringdown signal is simultaneously modeled with the IMRPhenomXPHM approximant, where now the data after tat_{a} is gated out. The pre-ringdown and ringdown analyses only share as parameters the gate time and sky position. As in Finch & Moore, their result consists of a single marginalized analysis with a log base-10 BF of ∼0.04\sim 0.04 in favor of the overtone, and an overtone amplitude median over standard deviation of ∼1.2\sim 1.2.

Finally, Hai-Tian Wang et al. [1090] employ the ℱ\mathcal{F}-statistic method. This consists of analytically maximizing over the ringdown amplitudes and phases. The overtone significance is quantified in terms of an “ℱ\mathcal{F}-statistic information criterion” (analogous to, but different from, a BF) with reported values ranging between ∼−1.3\sim-1.3 and 0.30.3.

In Figs. 62 and 63 we summarize the amplitude estimates for the overtone in a two-tone Kerr model applied to GW150914 at various starting times, from a selection of the works summarized above. It is now broadly accepted that in order to obtain agreement for the final mass and spin between the ringdown-only and full-signal analyses, it is necessary to include at least one overtone when the ringdown analysis starts close to the peak strain time. This conclusion, however, is SNR-dependent: louder signals would require an increasing number of overtones. The level of statistical significance for a nonzero overtone amplitude, quantified via the posterior median over standard deviation, varies between 1​σ1\sigma and 4​σ4\sigma for a range of times within the estimated peak time of the signal. Values at the median time quoted in Fig. 62 range within [1.4,2.6]​σ[1.4,2.6]\sigma, while time-marginalized estimates range instead in the [1.2,1.8]​σ[1.2,1.8]\sigma interval. The Bayesian evidence in favor of the overtone model presents wider variations, with log base-10 BFs ranging between −0.5-0.5 and 44. Time-marginalized evidences are uninformative or slightly disfavor the inclusion of an overtone ([−0.2,0.04][-0.2,0.04]), while estimates at the median time range within [−0.4,0.8][-0.4,0.8].

Significant disagreement remains on the interpretation of the results. Several authors have questioned the physical significance of a constant-amplitude QNM model starting at the peak, which ignores the dynamical nature of the BH relaxation process (including the time-dependent nature of the background and of the QNM amplitudes, as well as possible nonlinear couplings): see the discussion in Section 5.1.3.

Higher harmonic searches in GWTC-3 The multimodal search employed by pyRing involves performing model selection between different hypotheses, represented by models with varying mode content in the templates used to fit the data. These models include Kerr and KerrBinary [863] templates. The start times of the analysis are chosen to be 10​M10M and 15​M15M, respectively. Two baseline models represent the fundamental mode hypothesis: the Kerr template and the KerrBinary template with only the (2,2)(2,2) mode. The higher mode hypotheses are constructed by augmenting the fundamental mode with additional modes:

  • •

    Kerr templates include (2,2,0)+(ℓ,m,n)(2,2,0)+(\ell,m,n) and (2,2,0)+(2,2,1)+(ℓ,m,n)(2,2,0)+(2,2,1)+(\ell,m,n), where (ℓ,m,n)=(3,3,0),(3,2,0),(2,1,0),(2,0,0)(\ell,m,n)=(3,3,0),(3,2,0),(2,1,0),(2,0,0), added individually and independently.

  • •

    KerrBinary templates include all (3,3),(2,1),(3,2),(4,4),(4,3)(3,3),(2,1),(3,2),(4,4),(4,3) modes simultaneously (overtones are only “implicitly” included in this parameterization).

Additional hypotheses are introduced to refine the sensitivity of multi-modal analyses. First, the search assumes reflection symmetry in the Kerr amplitudes, such that modes with opposite mm signs are related by the nonprecessing symmetry

Aℓ,−|m|,n=(−1)ℓ​Aℓ,|m|,n∗.A_{\ell,-|m|,n}=(-1)^{\ell}A^{\ast}_{\ell,|m|,n}\,. (6.15)

This symmetry is valid for remnants of nonprecessing binary mergers. To enhance sensitivity to higher modes, the analysis is performed under two conditions. First, no restriction is imposed on the relative magnitude of the modes. Second, an amplitude hierarchy constraint is imposed between the fundamental and higher order modes: Aℓ,m,n/A2,2,0<0.9A_{\ell,m,n}/A_{2,2,0}<0.9, consistent with expectations for quasi-circular spin-aligned binaries with moderate mass ratios [649, 1057]. This suppresses bi-modalities arising in the previous unconstrained search, that degrade sensitivity to multi-modal detections. Since the above templates do not account for precession, the reflection symmetry assumption is relaxed in an additional analysis to accommodate scenarios where the progenitor binary’s spins are misaligned with the orbital angular momentum. This approach includes precessing binaries, which break the above symmetry between the mode amplitudes [315, 1128, 1129]. A log BF is used to quantify the evidence for the presence of higher modes relative to the fundamental mode, providing a statistical basis for hypothesis selection.

No significant evidence for the presence of higher modes was found in the LVK events using any of the search strategies we discussed so far [460], with the exception of one event: GW191109_010717. However, the apparent detection in this case was attributed to nonstationarities in the data, so GW191109_010717 was excluded from the combined results. This particular event shows weak evidence for the (3,2,0)(3,2,0) and (2,1,0)(2,1,0) modes at t<5​Mt<5M, but with overestimated values of the remnant mass MfM_{f} and spin afa_{f}, consistently with a starting time outside of the model validity regime. Another event (GW200224_222234) shows weak, but not fully convincing, statistical evidence for the presence of the (2,2,1)(2,2,1) overtone.

In Fig. 64 we compare the GR remnant parameters predicted by the full IMR waveforms and by the Kerr ringdown template including the (2,2,0)(2,2,0) mode. For all events that pass the noise contamination selection criteria, the IMR predictions agree with the properties inferred from the ringdown alone. The one exception is GW170729, which however does not pass the noise contamination selection criteria. This is a good example of how noise contamination can lead to false violations of GR.

The KerrPostmerger template, based on the TEOBPM [873] ansatz, has been implemented in pyRing [948] in preparation for the fourth LVK observing run (O4). This template is the most sensitive ringdown-only data analysis model to date. While similar to the KerrBinary template, KerrPostmerger is NR-calibrated and designed to model the time-dependent amplitudes and phase, so it can effectively capture nonlinearities, overtone excitation, and transient effects in the early post-merger signal. A total of 18 events from GWTC-3 pass the threshold of having a ln⁡B>3\ln B>3 in favor of a signal over noise with the KerrPostmerger template. These events were re-analyzed using the KerrPostmerger template, considering the modes (ℓ,m)=[(2,2),(3,3),(2,1)](\ell,m)=[(2,2),(3,3),(2,1)]. More specifically, the multi-modal search uses four different KerrPostmerger templates at the peak of the IMR waveform, tnomt_{\text{nom}}, which include the following combinations:

  • •

    only the (2,2)(2,2) mode;

  • •

    (2,2)+(ℓ,m)(2,2)+(\ell,m), with (ℓ,m)=[(2,1)],[(3,3)],[(2,1)+(3,3)](\ell,m)=[(2,1)],[(3,3)],[(2,1)+(3,3)].

These higher-order modes are chosen because they are more likely to be detectable. Their detectability can be estimated semi-analytically using the relation

ln⁡B22ℓ​m∝12​(1−FF2)​SNRopt2,\ln B^{\ell m}_{22}\propto\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{FF}^{2})\,\text{SNR}^{2}_{\text{opt}}\,, (6.16)

valid in the high-SNR limit. Here, FF denotes the fitting factor, defined as the normalized best-match between a KerrPostmerger template containing higher modes and one with only the (2,2)(2,2) mode. The quantity SNRopt\text{SNR}_{\text{opt}} is the optimal SNR, calculated as the signal power divided by the noise power, integrated over the detector’s bandwidth.

For nearly equal mass binaries (q∼1q\sim 1), which are prevalent among current GW observations, the excitation of higher modes during the ringdown phase is minimal, and their detection is challenging. For example, detecting the (3,3)(3,3) mode with a detection threshold of ln⁡B22ℓ​m=3\ln B^{\ell m}_{22}=3 would require an SNRopt≳50\text{SNR}_{\text{opt}}\gtrsim 50, while typical events in the current catalogs have ringdown SNRopt≲15\text{SNR}_{\text{opt}}\lesssim 15.

The higher modes are more excited for large mass ratio binaries (q∈[2,3]q\in[2,3]), reducing the required SNRopt\text{SNR}_{\text{opt}} for detection. For these systems, the (3,3)(3,3) mode becomes detectable in loud events with SNRopt∼[10,15]\text{SNR}_{\text{opt}}\sim[10,15], particularly at larger inclinations (ι>π/4\iota>\pi/4). This highlights the importance of mass ratio and inclination for the observability of higher modes. The (3,3)(3,3) mode in particular stands out as the easiest to observe, often requiring a lower SNRopt\text{SNR}_{\text{opt}} compared to modes like (2,1)(2,1) for systems with moderate mass ratios. Higher modes such as (3,2)(3,2) and (4,4)(4,4), on the other hand, require substantially larger SNRopt\text{SNR}_{\text{opt}} for detection – typically above 25 for mass ratios q≲2q\lesssim 2 and inclinations ι>π/4\iota>\pi/4.

These observations reinforce the need to carefully account for the system’s parameters when predicting the detectability of higher modes. Furthermore, the detection threshold itself plays a significant role. Reducing the threshold increases the likelihood of observing higher modes, even at lower SNR, but it also necessitates careful control of false positives due to noise. Future studies should refine these estimates by incorporating realistic noise simulations and accounting for systematic uncertainties, such as modeling inaccuracies and the determination of the ringdown starting time.

Model selection between the (2,2)(2,2) and (2,2)+ℓ​m(2,2)+\ell m templates yields BFs that overall do not show a preference for higher modes in the analyzed data, as shown in Fig. 65. Four events (GW170729, GW190521_074359, GW200129_065458, GW200224_222234) exhibit a low but positive BF, and for these events, adding the (3,3)(3,3) mode yields posteriors that favor higher mass ratios. Once can probe the sensitivity of the results to the starting time of the analysis by varying it within the 95% credible interval of the IMR peak time. Within this range, some events show BF peaks, with corresponding posterior distributions shifting towards higher mass ratios. Even when the (3,3)(3,3) mode is not confidently detected, its inclusion in the model improves the recovered parameter estimates. For GW200129_065458 and GW200224_222234, a BF increase is observed at later times (outside the IMR peak time support region). However, since the KerrPostmerger template assumes given values for the amplitudes defined at the peak time, starting the fit outside the domain of definition for the amplitudes could introduce biases. Once again, a careful selection of the starting time is important to avoid systematic errors due to modeling assumptions.

Higher harmonics: GW190521 On May 21, 2019, 03:02:29 UTC, the two LIGO detectors and the Virgo interferometers detected the GW190521 signal [1095]. Assuming the quasi-circular waveform families NRSur, SEOB and Phenom (see Section 5), all including both higher harmonics and spin precession effects, the signal is found to be consistent with a merger of two nearly equal mass BHs, with a high total mass, and component spins preferentially large and oriented along the equatorial plane. This is the heaviest BH merger detected with high confidence to date. The high mass leads to the merger occurring at comparatively low frequency, placing the ringdown signal at the lower end of the detector spectrum – around 60​Hz60\,\rm Hz, a region with degraded detector sensitivity and larger impact from detector noise [1065].

A later study found support for large unequal mass ratio, highlighting the significant impact of prior distributions on the inferred parameters [1130]. The study employed an early version of the IMRPhenomXPHM model, at the time still under development. Subsequent follow-ups [1131, 1132], using an improved version of IMRPhenomXPHM, confirmed a multi-modal likelihood. The support for the unequal mass configuration was reduced, with the bulk of the posterior distribution falling close to the equal mass regime [1131]. However, the unequal mass peak yielded the highest likelihood, with a peak larger by a factor ∼7\sim 7 [1132] compared to the equal mass case. The significant impact of the prior distribution on the mass ratio was also confirmed. These findings enhanced prospects for the excitation of modes beyond the fundamental quadrupolar one. Due to the prominence of the merger-ringdown signal component, several studies investigated in detail the post-merger emission of GW190521, searching for the presence of multiple modes.

A first search for multiple modes by the LVK collaboration [1096] employed the Damped sinusoids, Kerr (assuming unconstrained amplitudes parameterizations compatible with spin precession) and KerrBinary (spin aligned) models, with a tpeakt_{\rm peak} estimate based on the NRSur IMR model. The Kerr model contained the modes with ℓ=m=2\ell=m=2, and up to n=0,1,2n=0,1,2, targeting overtones of the fundamental quadrupolar mode. The KerrBinary model contained instead all modes ℓ=2,3,4\ell=2,3,4 with m=ℓ,ℓ−1m=\ell,\ell-1 and n=0n=0, targeting multiple fundamental modes. The ringdown analysis used the pyRing software package (see Appendix A) and a TD truncated likelihood function [1051]. Multi-mode models were found to yield posteriors on final mass and spin consistent with those of the full IMR signal, and also with those from the single-mode model with ℓ=m=2\ell=m=2, n=0n=0, as shown in Figure 66. There was no strong evidence in favor of modes beyond the fundamental quadrupolar one, as quantified by BFs.

A subsequent study employed Damped sinusoids and Kerr models to search for multiple modes [1057]. The gating and inpainting method implemented in PyCBC (see Appendix A) was used to restrict the analysis to a data segment following the chosen signal starting time.

In the Damped sinusoids search, additional constraints were imposed to extract multiple modes from the data. Each sinusoid was restricted to an individual frequency band around its central frequency. The resulting posterior distribution in frequency and damping time, shown in Fig. 67, displays a narrow peak near the values expected for the (2,2,0)(2,2,0) mode from the IMR analysis. A secondary peak was found at a higher frequency. Assuming the first peak to match (ℓ,m,n)=(2,2,0)(\ell,m,n)=(2,2,0) indicates that the secondary peak is consistent with the expected (ℓ,m,n)=(3,3,0)(\ell,m,n)=(3,3,0) mode. This feature was most clearly present at tref+6​mst_{\rm ref}+6\,\rm ms after the reference time used in this analysis (see Table 8). It suggests the presence of a secondary feature compatible with a damped sinusoid, but this does not on its own provide statistical evidence, since filtering bands have to be selected a priori.

Equatorial reflection symmetry of the initial perturbation and priors on the amplitudes of the subdominant modes restricted to A330/A220<0.5A_{330}/A_{220}<0.5, A221/A220<5A_{221}/A_{220}<5, valid only for binaries with aligned spins [649], were assumed. The authors looked for various mode combinations, including (ℓ,m,n)=[(2,2,0),(2,2,1),(2,1,0),(3,3,0)](\ell,m,n)=[(2,2,0),(2,2,1),(2,1,0),(3,3,0)]. Statistical evidence for these mode combinations in terms of BFs within the Kerr model is quantified in Fig. 68. Evidence favoring the presence of the (2,2,0)+(3,3,0)(2,2,0)+(3,3,0) and (2,2,0)+(3,3,0)+(2,1,0)(2,2,0)+(3,3,0)+(2,1,0) mode combinations was found, compared to models containing only the (2,2,0)+(2,1,0)(2,2,0)+(2,1,0) or the (2,2,0)+(2,2,1)(2,2,0)+(2,2,1) combinations. The excitation of the (3,3,0)(3,3,0) mode is indicative of a high mass ratio binary, in disagreement with the NRSur posterior measurement, which is points instead to a more equal-mass system. The largest BF (∼56\sim 56) was found at tpeakharm+6​mst^{\rm harm}_{\rm peak}+6\,\rm ms, where tpeakharm=max𝑡​∑ℓ​mhℓ​m​(t)=1242442967.445t^{\rm harm}_{\rm peak}=\underset{t}{\max}\sum_{\ell m}h_{\ell m}(t)=1242442967.445 GPS time is estimated from the NRSur IMR model assuming a uniform prior on the mass ratio. Using the reported Mfdet≃330​M⊙M_{f}^{\rm det}\simeq 330M_{\odot} [1057], this translates to tpeakharm+3.7​Mfdett^{\rm harm}_{\rm peak}+3.7\,M_{f}^{\rm det}. The analysis was repeated for the model with no equatorial symmetry, while maintaining the priors on amplitude ratios. In this case, the BF for the (2,2,0)+(3,3,0)(2,2,0)+(3,3,0) model peaked at 42, also at tpeakharm+6​mst^{\rm harm}_{\rm peak}+6\,\rm ms. Later studies on populations of simulated signals, intended to mimic the full signal of GW190521 under the same assumptions of this initial analysis, found the BFs to be robust against noise fluctuations. They also assigned a consistent statistical quantification to the Damped sinusoids results [1133]. There, support for a mode compatible with larger mass ratios was found when assuming the IMRPhenomTPHM model, unlike the IMRPhenomXPHM and NRSur models. Assuming the IMRPhenomTPHM model, they also validated the correlation between unequal mass-ratios and Bayes Factors, consistent with the GW190521 analysis [1134].

There is some uncertainty related to the choice of the reference tpeakt_{\rm peak}: the difference of the first two entries in Table 8 results in a shift of ∼4.7​ms\sim 4.7\,{\rm ms} compared to the estimate of tpeakpol=max𝑡​(h+2+h×2)t^{\rm pol}_{\rm peak}=\underset{t}{\max}(h_{+}^{2}+h_{\times}^{2}) used in [1095], which is based on the NRSur model with a uniform prior on the source-frame component masses. Thus, depending on the waveform model and on the definition of tpeakt_{\rm peak}, the largest BF is found in the range [1, 3.7]​Mf[1,\,3.7]\,M_{f} after the signal peak. If the tpeakt_{\rm peak} estimate from the NRSur is unbiased, this is well outside the regime where one would expect the fundamental mode to be excited. Compared to tpeakharmt^{\rm harm}_{\rm peak}, the tpeakpolt^{\rm pol}_{\rm peak} reference time makes use of the polarizations, yielding a larger statistical uncertainty O⁡(7−10​ms)O(7-10\,{\rm ms}) [1096]. Such uncertainty should also be accounted for in computing the “time-marginalized” evidence (see Section 6.1.7). Moreover, higher harmonics in spin-aligned systems can peak at significantly later times compared to the fundamental mode: from Table VI of [939] or Appendix E of [869], the (3,3)(3,3) multipole can peak up to 5​M5M after the (2,2)(2,2) mode, while the (2,1)(2,1) multipole should can peak up to 12​M12M after the (2,2)(2,2) mode, for nonspinning systems with moderate mass ratios. Such time delays are not taken into account by QNM superpositions, which assume that all modes are already excited at the starting time of the analysis. In addition, the prior assumptions on the spin-aligned quasi-circular amplitudes do not take into account the effect of spin precession and eccentricity, while both effects may be relevant for this particular event [1106, 1135, 957].

If one relaxes either the assumption of equatorial symmetry or the amplitude ratio constraints, and assumes the NRSur tpeakpolt^{\rm pol}_{\rm peak} estimate, there is no evidence for a secondary mode in the regime of validity of QNM superpositions [460].

A subsequent study [968], based on the ringdown software package (see Appendix A), assumes a Kerr model and implements a TD likelihood function. This study uses relaxed assumptions on the amplitudes, computes tpeakharmt^{\rm harm}_{\rm peak} through the NRSur model and uses improved data conditioning, looking for evidence of multiple modes and analyzing the consistency of the corresponding model parameters with those from the full IMR waveform. It notes that assuming a single (ℓ,m,n)=(2,2,0)(\ell,m,n)=(2,2,0) mode, the remnant parameter posteriors do not fully overlap with the NRSur IMR analysis. Instead, a fit assuming (2,2,0)+(2,1,0)(2,2,0)+(2,1,0) or (2,2,0)+(2,1,0)+(3,2,0)(2,2,0)+(2,1,0)+(3,2,0) yields complete overlap with the IMR analysis, suggesting that these multi-modal templates recover signal content that was not captured in the previous model. Nonvanishing amplitudes for these three modes are preferred up until the signal peak, with the (2,1,0)(2,1,0) amplitude being comparable in magnitude to the (2,2,0)(2,2,0) amplitude. This surprising feature is conjectured to arise from strong precession. However it is unclear if such large amplitudes are compatible with the near-equal mass system and inclination angle inferred with NRSur: in fact, studies of ringdown modeling for precessing binaries do not predict such large intrinsic amplitudes for comparable-mass systems, but only for larger mass ratios [887, 858]; nevertheless, viewing angle effects could conceivably amplify the observed (2,1,0)(2,1,0) or (2,0,0)(2,0,0) amplitudes over the (2,2,0)(2,2,0) mode in nearly equal-mass binaries [887].

The authors of Ref. [968] use the leave-one-out cross-validation to quantify the statistical evidence of mode detection and allow for model comparison. As shown in Fig. 69 (which shows also the statistical uncertainty on tpeakharmt^{\rm harm}_{\rm peak} computed from NRSur), they find no significant statistical preference for additional modes after the peak.

The assumptions in these different studies are compared in Table 8. In summary, there are three primary hypotheses to explain the ringdown of GW190521: (i) there are no observable sub-dominant ringdown modes, consistent with the equal-mass posterior from the LVK NRSur analysis [1095]; (ii) the (3,3,0) mode is observable, but the remnant mass, coalescence time, and mass ratio are inconsistent with the NRSur analysis [1057]; (iii) other mode combinations – including the (2,1,0) and possibly the (3,2,0) modes – are preferred, as they agree with the remnant parameter posteriors inferred from the NRSur analysis if restricted to the highly precessing part of the posterior. The (2,1,0) and (2,2,0) mode amplitudes are comparable. In both cases (ii) and (iii), statistical preference for additional modes is observed close to the peak, where the validity of a QNM model is questionable.

It is hard to find conclusive evidence for any of these competing hypotheses for various reasons: there are no waveforms modeling precession with an accuracy comparable to NRSur beyond q=6q=6; it is hard to marginalize over the starting time of models that use only the fundamental QNMs; and we do not have compelling analytical models for the early ringdown regime, where constant-amplitude QNM superpositions are generally not valid. Even if we were to overcome these difficulties, the short duration of the GW190521 event would likely still make its interpretation problematic.

6.3 Tests of general relativity: observational results

Initial contributors: Carullo, Silva

6.3.1 Parameterized (theory-agnostic) tests

In the data analysis language of this chapter, the original, agnostic BH spectroscopy program consists of (i) assuming a Damped sinusoids template, (ii) measuring at least three frequencies or damping times, and (iii) inverting these measurements to check that they yield estimates of the remnant mass and spin consistent with the predictions of GR. The measurements of two parameters are, in principle, sufficient to obtain the Kerr BH mass and spin. The third measurement (and any further measurements) can then be used to yield null tests of GR [376, 377], similar to those routinely performed for binary pulsars (see e.g. Fig. 8 of [432]). The idea is illustrated in Fig. 70.

This simple, robust approach allows for model-independent tests of gravity and investigations of the nature of the compact binary merger remnant. However, even in this simplest version of the test, we can only map the frequency measurements to the remnant parameters if we know which modes are excited. As we discussed earlier, in reality the starting time is unknown, and effects such as spin precession and eccentricity drastically complicate the mode excitation pattern, so identifying which modes are excited can be challenging. This issue is particularly relevant for the faint signals observed at current sensitivities, but it should be less pressing in the loud observations that will be possible with XG detectors (see Section 7).

These simple, agnostic BH spectroscopy tests were initially proposed and explored on simulated LISA data assuming loud, pure ringdown signals and using the Fisher matrix approximation [377, 1136]. A first Bayesian analysis [534] proposed to use a set of agnostic parameterized deviations from the GR spectrum of the form

fℓ​m​n​(M,a)\displaystyle f_{\ell mn}(M,a) =fℓ​m​nKerr​(M,a)⋅[1+δ​fℓ​m​n],\displaystyle=f^{\rm Kerr}_{\ell mn}(M,a)\cdot[1+\delta f_{\ell mn}], (6.17a)
τℓ​m​n​(M,a)\displaystyle\tau_{\ell mn}(M,a) =τℓ​m​nKerr​(M,a)⋅[1+δ​τℓ​m​n],\displaystyle=\tau^{\rm Kerr}_{\ell mn}(M,a)\cdot[1+\delta\tau_{\ell mn}], (6.17b)

where δ​ωℓ​m​n\delta\omega_{\ell mn} and δ​τℓ​m​n\delta\tau_{\ell mn} control the deviations from the Kerr QNM oscillation frequencies and damping times, respectively (see Section 3.2.1). This parameterization was leveraged to construct posterior probability distributions for the set of independent parameters (M,a,δ​fℓ​m​n,δ​τℓ​m​nM,a,\delta f_{\ell mn},\delta\tau_{\ell mn}), obtained using Monte Carlo or Nested Sampling [1137] techniques for simulated pure ringdown signals in XG detectors. In the spirit of the agnostic approach described earlier, the measurement of nonzero deviation parameters in the presence of more than a single damped sinusoid would indicate a deviation from GR. Compared to an agnostic superposition of damped sinusoids, this parameterization reduces the number of free parameters from 4​N4N to 2+2​N2+2N, where NN is the number of modes. This increases the sensitivity to possible GR deviations and reduces correlations in the presence of a large number of modes. It is also possible to establish a direct connection to the mass and spin parameters of the remnant, instead of identifying them a posteriori (as in the agnostic approach). The evidence for deviations from GR can be quantified through an overall BF between all the possible combinations of parameterized GR deviations and the GR case, where all the deviation parameters are equal to zero [1138, 1139].

These initial studies made the simplifying assumption that the simulated data consisted of a pure superposition of damped sinusoids, with no preceding signal. In Ref. [536] this assumption was overcome through a windowing function, so that the inference can be formulated in the FD with small SNR loss. The parameterized tests described above were applied to forecast the capabilities of the LVK network to constrain δ​f220\delta f_{220} and δ​τ220\delta\tau_{220} at design sensitivity. A similar windowing technique, now applied to the whitened signal, was introduced in [1054]. This work highlighted the key role of sky position and starting times and proposed some strategies to take into account the uncertainty on these parameters. A summary of these early forecasts and more recent developments can be found in Section 7.1 below.

The parameterization of Eq. (6.17) can in principle capture any deviations from the GR spectrum. However, at finite SNR, including a large number of deviation parameters will increase the prior volume and broaden the posterior distribution, and make the result uninformative. Besides, due to the sensitivity of GW interferometers to phase measurements, frequency deviations are typically better measured than the corresponding damping times [535]. These considerations imply that certain combinations of deviation parameters are better suited to capturing GR deviations without unnecessarily increasing the prior volume. The optimal parameter combinations also depend on the functional dependence of the Kerr QNM spectrum on the BH spin. For example, in a search relying on the (ℓ,m,n)=(2,2,0)+(2,2,1)(\ell,m,n)=(2,2,0)+(2,2,1) mode combination, it is more convenient to add parameterized modifications to the (ℓ,m,n)=(2,2,1)(\ell,m,n)=(2,2,1) mode, rather than the (ℓ,m,n)=(2,2,0)(\ell,m,n)=(2,2,0) mode [1051]. For an arbitrary number of modes, to avoid useless repetitions of posterior samples representing the same physical state, the sampling algorithm must distinguish the different modes by attaching a “label” to each mode [1140]. For an agnostic superposition of damped sinusoids, this mode switching issue is typically addressed by ordering the modes by increasing frequency, since frequencies are better measured. This choice is not unique: we can order in terms of any other mode parameter, at the expenses of sampling efficiency if the posterior distributions for the same parameter of two different modes overlap. There is no loss of generality by labeling in terms of a single parameter (but there would be if we imposed more than one ordering condition). For Kerr BHs, the ordering is intrinsically given by the GR spectrum. However, when we consider tests based on Eq. (6.17) mode switching can (in principle) happen, especially for overtones (which are in close in frequency and have poorly measured damping times), and the (required) ordering choice can affect one-dimensional marginalized constraints [529]. Similar ideas are discussed in Refs. [1141, 1142] in the context of the identification of binary merger progenitors.

So far, complex amplitudes and other extrinsic parameters were considered free, in the sense that they are directly constrained from the data. When the complex amplitudes are not free to vary, but predicted by GR as well (as in the KerrBinary, KerrPostmerger or templates), consistency tests become possible even with a single mode [948, 649]. The result is a model-dependent test of GR that can be performed using weaker signals, but now under more stringent assumptions on the emission process (for example, at present, most amplitude models are limited to quasi-circular orbits).

Pushing this idea even further, it is possible to measure frequency deviations using ringdown signals by considering the entire IMR waveform. In the pSEOB framework [943, 944, 945, 946, 947], this idea is implemented with a parameterized EOB waveform model (see Section 5.2 for more details). The analysis includes the entire IMR waveform rather than isolating the post-merger ringdown phase. Its assumes that the GR predictions apply up to the merger phase and describes the merger-ringdown with phenomenological time-dependent amplitudes, similarly to the KerrPostmerger search based on the TEOB template [948] (cf. Section 5.2). Each QNM present in the baseline GR waveform model is modified using the parameterization of Eq. (6.17). For example, focusing on the dominant (2,2,0) mode, the pSEOB analysis would yield a posterior distribution on δ​f220\delta f_{220} and δ​τ220\delta\tau_{220}. This approach has two main advantages: it leverages the SNR of the full IMR signal, and it does not require a separate estimation of the ringdown starting time parameters. A drawback of the approach is that it is inevitably subject to a larger number of GR constraints. The mass and the spin that determine the QNM frequencies are largely constrained from the inspiral contributions, the inspiral-plunge and merger-ringdown “stitching” time. In addition, the mode amplitudes and phases are calibrated against NR simulations in GR, and the modifications to the QNM frequencies assume continuity with the GR spectrum. For these reasons, the pSEOB analysis will in general work best if the deviations from the baseline GR model – either from modifications to the QNM frequencies or from unmodeled physics – are perturbatively small. If instead the deviations lay outside the pSEOB’s “functional space,” the test is expected to be biased towards GR, and it should not be as effective at characterizing possible sources of new physics. In fact, when considering the performance of parameterized tests of GR, it is important to distinguish between the “detection” of a beyond-GR signature and its “characterization” [550]. Highly informed templates like pSEOB should be able to flag an inconsistency with GR even if deviations are “large,” but they are expected to under-perform more agnostic templates when it comes to identifying physical shifts in the system parameters.

Results Observational constraints on parameterized deviations from the fundamental mode of the form (6.17) using GW150914 can be found in [943, 1052], while other papers consider catalogs of LVK events [944, 529, 460, 948, 947]. The first ringdown-only constraints based on (2,2,0)+(2,2,1)(2,2,0)+(2,2,1) QNM superpositions starting at the signal peak found |δ​f221|<0.4|\delta f_{221}|<0.4, |δ​τ221|<0.8|\delta\tau_{221}|<0.8 at 90%90\% credibility [1053]. A re-analysis using a wavelet approach found similar results [1086]. These constraints were later refined by combining multiple events using the GWTC-2 [529] and GWTC-3 [460] LVK catalogs. The most up-to-date analysis, shown in the left panel of Fig. 71, finds |δ​f221|<0.28|\delta f_{221}|<0.28 at 90%90\% credibility. These constraints are based on a hierarchical method to combine single-event inferences which allows for the possibility of having different deviations in different GW events [1143, 1144]. The idea is to impose that the parent distribution of each realization is a Gaussian with parameters μ\mu, σ\sigma, and quantify the agreement with GR (in which case the distribution would be a delta function). The latest LVK data imply μ=0.01±0.18\mu=0.01\pm 0.18, σ<0.22\sigma<0.22, indicating no evidence for GR violations at the population level [460]. The combined BF is 𝒪G​Rm​o​d​G​R=−0.90±0.45\mathcal{O}_{GR}^{modGR}=-0.90\pm 0.45 in favor of GR, while the damping time deviations were found to be uninformative [460].

Similar tests on GW190521 can be found in [1057]. Their analysis using the dominant (2,2,0)+(3,3,0)(2,2,0)+(3,3,0) Kerr combination and an amplitude model compatible with spin-aligned binaries starting at ∼tpeakharm+3.7​Mf\sim t_{\rm peak}^{\rm harm}+3.7\,M_{f} finds |δ​f330|<0.09|\delta f_{330}|<0.09 at 90%90\% credibility. A generic Kerr amplitude model assuming the (2,2,0)+(2,1,0)+(3,2,0)(2,2,0)+(2,1,0)+(3,2,0) combinations starting at ∼tpeakharm\sim t_{\rm peak}^{\rm harm} finds that measurements of the deviation parameters on the fundamental mode, δ​f220\delta f_{220} and δ​τ220\delta\tau_{220}, are uninformative; however δ​f320<0.2\delta f_{320}<0.2 at 90%90\% credibility, while the lower bound on this deviation parameter is prior driven. A KerrPostmerger combination of the (2,2)+(3,3)(2,2)+(3,3) modes at tpeakpolt_{\rm peak}^{\rm pol} yields |δ​f22|<0.4|\delta f_{22}|<0.4, δ​τ22<0.5\delta\tau_{22}<0.5 for the loudest signals, with uninformative bounds on the (3,3)(3,3) deviation parameters.

These results are valid phenomenological consistency tests of GR. They are somewhat analogous to similar results obtained by varying the phenomenological (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) merger-ringdown calibration parameters of Phenom waveform families [543, 546, 529], which yield constraints at the 10%10\% level (90%90\% credibility). However these bounds are not necessarily genuine “no-hair” tests in the spirit of the original spectroscopy proposal, because constant-amplitude superpositions at the peak need not represent the physical QNM content of the system (see [378, 836, 539, 1082, 876] and Section 5.1.3). Similar considerations apply to GW190521 constraints involving the (3,3,0)(3,3,0) mode [1057] and other mode combinations [968], because the starting time of the analysis is close to the peak and model systematic uncertainties are important. For other results based on IMR consistency see [1145] and Section IVB in [460].

Less agnostic (and more informative) constraints can be found using the ParSpec parameterization (3.31) following [547]. Here, the idea is to perform a series expansion of the frequencies in terms of the remnant spin, in which the deviations from GR are introduced as a perturbative correction in the (small) coupling constant that characterizes beyond-GR modifications. These perturbative corrections can be either scale-free or dimensionful. This parameterization was implemented in pyRing and applied to all events with detectable ringdown signals in the GWTC-2 catalog [550]. For dimensionless couplings (p=0p=0 in the ParSpec notation), the bounds is δ​f220(0)=−0.05±0.05\delta f^{(0)}_{220}=-0.05\pm 0.05, while for dimensionful corrections of the form ℓp=αp\ell_{p}=\sqrt[p]{\alpha} one finds ℓ2<23​km\ell_{2}<23\mathrm{km}, ℓ4<35​km\ell_{4}<35\mathrm{km}, ℓ6<42​km\ell_{6}<42\mathrm{km}. The case of an individual charge (corresponding to Kerr-Newman BHs in GR for p=2p=2) was studied in [551, 552]. At current sensitivities, the LVK spin measurements yield upper bounds on the normalized BH charge parameter q<0.33q<0.33 (90%90\% credibility) for the best measured events. Ringdown measurements with future detectors would be able to directly measure hypothetical charges q≃0.5q\simeq 0.5, and even lower values of the charge should be measurable through IMR consistency tests [551]. Even better constraints may be possible by developing full IMR templates of Kerr-Newman mergers, based e.g. on the numerical simulations in Refs. [124, 125].

The larger SNR available in the pSEOB pipeline – initially introduced in Ref. [943] building upon the EOBNRv2HM waveform model for quasi-circular, nonspinning BBHs [923] – leads to more optimistic predictions: it would take approximately 30 GW150914-like BBHs detected by Advanced LIGO and Virgo at design sensitivity to carry out no-hair tests by measuring the frequencies of both the (2,2,0)(2,2,0) and (3,3,0)(3,3,0) modes, and the decay time of the (2,2,0)(2,2,0) mode with an accuracy of ≲5%\lesssim 5\% at the 2​σ2\sigma level [943]. Follow-up work [944] incorporated the parameterization (6.17) into the quasi-circular spin-aligned waveform model SEOBNRv4HM [869]. By hierarchically combining the results from individual events up to the O3a observing run, they find the constraints δ​f220=0.03−0.09+0.10\delta f_{220}=0.03^{+0.10}_{-0.09} and δ​τ220=0.10−0.39+0.44\delta\tau_{220}=0.10^{+0.44}_{-0.39} at 90% credibility.

The pSEOB analysis was augmented in [945] (using SEOBNRv4HM_PA [1146] as the baseline GR model) to incorporate additional fractional changes to (i) the instant at which the GW mode amplitude peaks, (ii) the instantaneous frequency at this time, and (iii) the value of the peak amplitude. By modifying (a subset) of the quantities that describe the merger, the resulting pSEOB model becomes more flexible in capturing potential strong-field deviations from GR, and expands the functional space covered by the model. As an example, Ref. [945] analyzed GW150914 allowing for fractional changes in the GW mode amplitude δ​A\delta A (assumed to be the same for all GW modes present in SEOBNRv4HM_PA), in addition to δ​f220\delta f_{220} and δ​τ220\delta\tau_{220}. These three parameters were constrained to be δ​A=0.03−0.20+0.29\delta A=0.03^{+0.29}_{-0.20}, δ​f220=0.041−0.084+0.151\delta f_{220}={0.041}^{+0.151}_{-0.084}, and δ​τ220=0.04−0.29+0.27\delta\tau_{220}={0.04}^{+0.27}_{-0.29} at 90% credibility. The frequency and damping times constraints are compatible with those found for the same event in Ref. [944] (where amplitude variations were not considered) – namely, δ​f220=0.05−0.07+0.11\delta f_{220}=0.05^{+0.11}_{-0.07} and δ​τ220=0.07−0.23+0.26\delta\tau_{220}=0.07^{+0.26}_{-0.23}.

A particularly interesting result of Ref. [945] is that the GW200129 event displays strong violations of GR on the peak-amplitude parameter δ​A\delta A (the QNM deviation parameters remain compatible with GR). This result was interpreted as a false violation of GR originating either from waveform systematics (mismodeling of spin precession that is not present in the baseline GR waveform model) or from data-quality issues, depending on the interpretation of this particular event. This case study is an important cautionary tale: waveform systematics, noise artifacts or astrophysics can easily lead to false violations of GR even at current sensitivities [893].

The pSEOB framework was recently extended to include spin precession effects [947], using the quasi-circular, spin-precessing SEOBNRv5PHM model [962] as the GR baseline.The analysis of a hierarchical combination of events finds δ​f220=0.00−0.06+0.06\delta f_{220}=0.00^{+0.06}_{-0.06} and δ​τ220=0.15−0.24+0.26\delta\tau_{220}=0.15^{+0.26}_{-0.24} at 90% credibility. These results are broadly consistent with those reported by the LVK Collaboration (using an earlier version of the pSEOB model for aligned-spin binaries) for the same events.

The pSEOB pipeline is now among the standard battery of GR tests performed by the LVK Collaboration. The latest bounds [947] from a hierarchical combination of events are

δ​f220=0.01±0.04,andδ​τ220=0.17−0.13+0.14.\delta{f}_{220}=0.01\pm 0.04,\quad\textrm{and}\quad\delta{\tau}_{220}=0.17^{+0.14}_{-0.13}. (6.18)

Because a sufficiently high inspiral SNR is typically required to break the degeneracy between δ​f220\delta f_{220} and the remnant’s mass MfM_{f}, events are normally analyzed if SNR≥8\rm SNR\geq 8 in both the pre- and post-merger regimes [944]. The corresponding two-dimensional posterior distributions are shown in Fig. 71. There, we report both the hierarchically-combined results mentioned above and a joint deviation obtained by multiplying the single-event likelihoods, which includes the GR value only in the tails of the posterior distribution. This result may still be compatible with the statistical uncertainty of the analysis, given the finite number of events [1147].

6.3.2 Theory-specific tests

Recent progress in calculations of QNMs emitted by rotating BHs in modified theories of gravity (cf. Section 3.1) allows us to place constraints on these theories using ringdown data. These searches for new physics have improved sensitivity relative to previous agnostic tests, at the expense of assuming a specific theory of gravity. Reference [553] used the (ℓ,m,n)=(2,2,0)(\ell,m,n)=(2,2,0) QNM calculations to linear order in spin in EdGB, dCS, and cubic and quartic EFTs of GR from Refs. [489, 440, 492]. These computations fix the theory-agnostic parameters up to linear order in the ParSpec spin expansion, while all other theory-agnostic parameters (at quadratic and higher orders in spin) were set to zero. In other words, the two lowest powers in the spin expansion include beyond-GR correction, whereas higher-order terms in the spin expansion are the same as in GR. The resulting theory-informed ParSpec parameterization was then used to modify the h22h_{22} mode of the pSEOB waveform model (cf. Section 6.2.1). and to carry out a full Bayesian parameter estimation analysis of two events: GW150914 and GW200129. The analysis does not constrain EdGB gravity, but it places upper bounds on the fundamental length scale of dCS gravity (ℓdCS⩽38.7\ell_{\rm dCS}\leqslant 38.7 km) as well as cubic- (ℓcEFT⩽38.2\ell_{\rm cEFT}\leqslant 38.2 km) and quartic-order (ℓqEFT⩽51.3\ell_{\rm qEFT}\leqslant 51.3 km) EFTs of GR at 90% credible level. Note that dCS gravity is a good example of a theory which is presently unconstrained by inspiral-only analyses, while it can be constrained using merger-ringdown radiation.

This “pSEOB plus ParSpec” approach has some limitations. For example, it does not accommodate the two branches of gravitational QNMs that generally arise in modified gravity theories because of isospectrality breaking. In particular, Ref. [553] made an educated guess by adopting the branch that has the slowest decaying f220f_{220} QNM. Moreover, linear-in-spin beyond-GR predictions are not accurate enough to describe typical BBH merger remnants, which have Kerr parameters af≃0.7a_{f}\simeq 0.7. A third important limitation (and a typical assumption of the pSEOB approach) is that the inspiral part of the waveform was assumed to be the same as in GR.

These shortcomings were addressed to some extent in Refs. [525, 1148, 1149]. Specifically, Ref. [525] used the results from Ref. [497, 498] to construct a prograde (ℓ,m,n)=(2,2,0),(2,2,1)(\ell,m,n)=(2,2,0),(2,2,1) ringdown model, including corrections to the spectrum for the cubic and quartic EFTs of GR up to twelfth order in a small spin expansion, and allowing for isospectrality breaking. This model was used to perform a complete Bayesian analysis of all events in the GWTC-3 catalog with clear and confident ringdown signatures within the pyRing infrastructure (cf. Section 6.2.1). By combining posterior distributions of single events from GWTC-3, the length scale associated to these higher-curvature terms is bound to be ℓEFT≲35\ell_{\rm EFT}\lesssim 35 km. In [1149], the results from [511, 512, 527] were used to construct a similar ringdown model, accurate up to a≲0.75a\lesssim 0.75, incorporating isospectrality breaking for quadratic gravity theories. This model was applied to analyze the most informative ringdown signals in the GWTC-3 catalogs using pyRing. By combining the posterior distributions of all analyzed events, the authors find a constraint on the quadratic-gravity coupling length scale of ℓEFT≲34−47\ell_{\rm EFT}\lesssim 34-47 km, as well as the first constraint on axi-dilaton gravity, ℓAD≲34\ell_{\rm AD}\lesssim 34 km. Results from Refs. [553, 525] are shown in Fig. 72.

Full IMR analyses including both inspiral and ringdown deviations induced by an EsGB term and EFT higher-curvature corrections [530, 1148] analyzed only low-mass signals, for which the ringdown contributions are negligible.

6.4 Echoes: data analysis methods and observational status

Initial contributors: Abedi, Lo

Here we summarize observational efforts to search for GW echoes (see Section 3.3). Some initial studies suggested positive evidence for echoes in the data following BBH merger events in LVK data [662, 1150]. However, subsequent efforts have reported both positive [1151, 1152, 1153, 1154] and negative or inconclusive findings [1155, 1156, 1157, 1158, 682, 1159, 1160, 529, 1161, 1162, 1163, 460, 1164, 687]. The disagreement stem from different choices of statistical methodologies and/or models, but there is full agreement on the fact that current data show no conclusive detection of echoes. The detection debate has stimulated improvements in both models and statistical techniques, highlighting that extensive detection campaigns and higher SNRs are required to robustly detect and characterize echoes.

6.4.1 Classification of echo analysis approaches

Efforts to detect echoes in GW signals have predominantly relied on three different methodologies:

  • •

    Waveform-dependent approaches: These studies use specific assumptions about the expected form of the echo signal, often based on physical parameters of the post-merger remnant, such as its mass and spin. Examples include studies that assume echo templates from scenarios with potential quantum gravitational structures near the horizon [662, 1155, 1156, 682, 1159, 529, 1161, 1162, 460, 1154, 687, 1158]. These approaches are limited by the degree of agreement between template models and actual echo waveforms, but would deliver the most sensitive constraints if the data were described by the echo models under consideration. Highly faithful models are hard to achieve, given the vast landscape of theoretical possibilities. An imperfect representation of the echo signal (catching most but not all of the signal power) is expected to be effective at detecting echoes [1154], but the unbiased characterization of the underlying physics depends heavily on accurate waveform templates. Some of the waveform models for GW echoes are implemented in a publicly available python package, echoes_waveform_model [681] (see Appendix A).

  • •

    Weakly modeled approaches: These methods try to avoid specific waveform assumptions by focusing on generic signatures or patterns indicative of echoes, allowing for a broader search for potential deviations from the GR waveform. Model-agnostic analyses, such as those by [1151, 1150, 1157, 1152, 1163, 1165, 1154, 1153, 1164], but may be more sensitive to noise and statistical interpretation issues. For well-modeled scenarios, they will also naturally be less sensitive.

  • •

    Electromagnetic confirmation: A complementary line of investigation explores potential electromagnetic counterparts to GW echoes. For example, astrophysical considerations suggest that the remnant of GW170817 collapsed into a BH within tcoll≲2​st_{\rm{coll}}\lesssim 2\,\mathrm{s} [1166, 1167, 1168, 1169, 1170, 1171, 1172, 1173, 1174]. If the collapse were delayed, an echo signal for this event at around ≃1\simeq 1s after the merger could independently confirm or refute the existence of echoes [1151, 1175, 1176]. In this scenario, the echoes are generated by GWs with a resonant harmonic frequency, arising from the cavity between the angular momentum barrier and the near-horizon membrane formed following the collapse of a binary neutron star merger into a BH.

6.4.2 Early claims and up-to-date understanding

We will now discuss two different, early echo searches in GW data and their current understanding.

Binary black hole mergers in O1 A simple phenomenological template for echoes, the “ADA model,” was introduced in [662]. Searches using this template indicated tentative evidence for echoes at a significance level of approximately 2.5​σ2.5\sigma in data collected during the first LIGO observing run (“O1”) [1107]. Significance levels were interpreted using a two-tailed Gaussian probability, where p-values of 68% and 95% correspond to 1​σ1\sigma and 2​σ2\sigma, respectively.

These data were subsequently re-analyzed by different groups using different data analysis methodologies, finding no evidence for echoes [1155, 1156, 1157, 1158, 682, 1159, 1160, 529, 1161, 1162, 1163, 460, 1164, 687]. Another independent study [1157] used a weakly-modeled approach, based on the coherent WaveBurst (cWB) software, not originally designed to search for echoes. They initially identified post-merger features that could be interpreted as echoes, but subsequent rigorous re-analysis by the same group found no evidence for these features [1164].

In Table 9 we summarize the results obtained by various groups for the O1 events. Here, the smaller the p-value, the stronger the evidence against the null hypothesis. A p-value of =2.87×10−7=2.87\times 10^{-7} corresponds to the probability of observing a result ≥5​σ\geq 5\sigma (in one tail) under a Gaussian distribution if the null hypothesis is true. Jeffreys’ scale for interpreting BFs [1177] classifies a BF in the range of 10 to 100 as strong evidence, and a BF greater than 100 as decisive evidence. It is important to note that p-values and BFs are distinct statistical quantities with no known mathematical relationship. Since both quantities are used for hypothesis testing, we report them both in this table and elsewhere in this section.

Binary neutron star merger (GW170817) A search for echoes following the binary neutron star merger GW170817 used the weakly-modeled approach proposed in [1151], and focused on scenarios where the merger results in either prompt or rapid collapse into a BH. Echoes are hypothesized to arise due to Planck-scale modifications near the event horizon, repeating with a characteristic time delay (Δ​techo)(\Delta t_{\rm echo}) estimated to be ∼4.7ms​(1+1/1−χ2)\sim 4.7^{\rm{ms}}\ (1+1/\sqrt{1-\chi^{2}}) for a 2.7​M⊙2.7M_{\odot} BH.

The search targeted fundamental echo frequencies fecho=Δ​techo−1f_{\rm echo}=\Delta t_{\rm echo}^{-1} in the range [63, 92][63,\,92]\,Hz, and identified potential signals within the first second post-merger. By cross-correlating spectrograms from LIGO detectors, periodic peaks corresponding to echo harmonics were claimed with 4.2​σ4.2\sigma significance. This signal, observed approximately 11\,s after the BNS merger GW170817 [1151], was interpreted as evidence that the remnant collapsed into a BH at that time. The claim was disputed by a subsequent reanalysis [1160] and contested on theoretical grounds [630].

6.4.3 Combined event search

Bayesian inference and advanced statistical inference pipelines have been used to quantify the likelihood of echo signals across multiple events. In particular, a recent effort [1158] applied a waveform inspired by stimulated Hawking radiation (the Boltzmann echo model [1154, 1158] shown in Fig. 73) to a set of 47 highly-confident LVK BBH merger events in the GWTC-3 catalog [1108], each with a false alarm rate of less than 10−3​yr−110^{-3}\ \text{yr}^{-1} [529]. The study used a fixed echo amplitude AA across events, allowing for the calculation of combined BFs as a measure of signal strength across multiple events. It also assumed that the echo model is identical across all events; while this assumption is not expected to be physically well-motivated, it is a reasonable minimal framework to facilitate the combination of multiple events. The analysis found no statistically significant evidence for this signal in GWTC-3 data. The Bayesian evidence for most events falls within the range of 0.3–1.6, with the hypothesis of a common (nonvanishing) echo amplitude for all mergers being weakly disfavored at 2:5 odds. The one exception was GW190521, the most massive event observed so far, which shows a positive evidence of 9.2, but the significant waveform systematic uncertainties affecting this event complicate its interpretation [957, 1135, 1179]. An optimal combination of posteriors yields an upper limit on the universal echo amplitude of A<0.4A<0.4 at 90% confidence level, whereas typical models predict A∼1A\sim 1.

Later work used Bayesian analysis techniques suitable to combine multiple events, such as hierarchical methods [1180, 1144], to further improve detection reliability [1158]. By assuming that individual events follow a parent distribution in echo amplitude, with parameters fitted across the dataset, the method can analyze weak or inconclusive signals by integrating information across a population of potential echo candidates. The result is a posterior function that estimates the parameters of interest while accounting for uncertainties and selection biases in individual detections, improving over previous work that assumed equal echo properties across events. The analysis assumes a target Gaussian distribution 𝒫¯(A,A¯,σ)=e−(A−A¯)2/2σ2/2​π​σ2\bar{\mathcal{P}}(A,\bar{A},\sigma)=e^{-(A-\bar{A})^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}/\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}} characterized by a mean A¯\bar{A} and a standard deviation σ\sigma. These parameters are then combined hierarchically [1158, 1144, 1180], as described by the equation:

𝒫⁡(A¯,σ)=∫∏i=Eventsd​Ai​Bi​(Ai)​𝒫¯​(Ai,A¯,σ).\mathcal{P}(\bar{A},\sigma)=\int\prod_{i=\rm{Events}}dA_{i}B_{i}(A_{i})\bar{\mathcal{P}}(A_{i},\bar{A},\sigma)\,. (6.19)

Here, p⁡(A¯,σ)p(\bar{A},\sigma) represents the posterior function for the hierarchical combination of events, yielding the parameters A¯\bar{A} and σ\sigma, and ℬi​(Ai)\mathcal{B}_{i}(A_{i}) is the BF as a function of echo amplitude AiA_{i} for event ii. The values of A¯\bar{A} and σ\sigma inferred from this analysis are shown in Fig. 74. The mean amplitude A¯\bar{A} peaks around 0.350.35, while σ\sigma peaks close to zero. This indicates minimal spread among the events, suggesting consistency across the dataset.

Subsequent analyses from the LVK collaboration and affiliated groups also searched for echoes in multiple signals, using both waveform-dependent [460, 687] and weakly-modeled [1181, 1160, 1164] approaches. They obtained no evidence for echoes, as shown in Fig. 75.

6.4.4 Summary of current status and future prospects

Despite extensive efforts, a definitive detection of echoes remains elusive. Finding a consistent and statistically significant signal across multiple events is challenging due to the sensitivity of the echo templates to waveform modeling, noise, and the inherent complexities of GW signals. Continued developments in waveform modeling and more extensive datasets from future observing will improve the situation.

Echo searches are among the science goals outlined in the LISA White Papers on waveform modeling [1182] and fundamental physics [1183]. One of the challenges lies in accurately modeling the near-horizon reflection effects due to quantum phenomena. The vast range of possible models and large prior uncertainties make it less likely to detect weak signals. Current models often rely on simplifying assumptions for both the near-horizon regime and the angular momentum barrier. Additionally, the effects of nonlinearities are typically excluded from these models, which can significantly reduce their accuracy. On the data analysis side, the practical challenges are equally significant. Echoes are expected to be faint signals, often buried in noise, making their detection difficult. The sensitivity of echo templates to small variations in the waveform, noise characteristics, and even the underlying BH properties demands highly precise and computationally expensive data analysis techniques. For example, injection studies have shown that the true positive detection probability for large BFs (greater than 8) is only 35±735\pm 7% [1154]. This probability is expected to be even lower if the models used are not sufficiently accurate, which is currently the case. These challenges require further methodological refinements, independent confirmation (e.g. from potential electromagnetic counterparts), advancements in waveform modeling (e.g. by incorporating nonlinear effects and more complex boundary conditions), and more extensive observational datasets.

Future ground-based XG detectors are expected to probe the reflectivity of compact objects up to values close to the BH one due to the large SNR of compact binary coalescences [684, 398, 675]. If measured with the Einstein Telescope (ET), an event like GW150914 would have a ringdown SNR of 𝒪⁡(200)\mathcal{O}(200) [1184], improving the measurability of the reflectivity by one order of magnitude with respect to the LVK detector network [685]. Similar improvements are predicted also for QNM frequency measurements and “ordinary” BH spectroscopy tests [1185, 1186, 1187, 1184].

A population of horizonless compact objects would give rise to a stochastic GW background of GW echoes. Reference [1188] estimated the detectability of this background with Voyager and ET as a function of the amplitude of the first echo relative to the ringdown. Furthermore, if the remnant of a compact binary coalescence is a highly spinning horizonless compact object, the ergoregion instability would spin down the remnant by GW emission, until the condition for stability is satisfied. The incoherent superposition of the GW signals from all sources in the population would produce a stochastic GW background due to spin loss [1189]. The LVK network at design sensitivity, ET and LISA can place stringent constraints on the percentage of perfectly reflecting horizonless compact objects from the astrophysical population [1189].

Finally, assuming the quantization of the BH horizon area dictates the QNMs of the prompt ringdown [643]. Current LVK observations already place interesting constraints on the quantization parameter [1190]. Thanks to the discontinuous limit of this proposal against the spectrum of QNMs predicted in classical GR, this scenario can be entirely ruled out from a population of 𝒪⁡(20)\mathcal{O}(20) GW150914-like events at design sensitivity [1190].

7 Future prospects

It is evident that if we adopt this point of view toward concepts, namely that the proper definition of a concept is not in terms of its properties but in terms of actual operations, we need run no danger of having to revise our attitude toward nature. […] Furthermore, if we remember that the operations to which a physical concept are equivalent are actual physical operations, the concepts can be defined only in the range of actual experiment, and are undefined and meaningless in regions as yet untouched by experiment. It follows that strictly speaking we cannot make statements at all about regions as yet untouched, and that when we do make such statements, as we inevitably shall, we are making a conventionalized extrapolation, of the looseness of which we must be fully conscious, and the justification of which is in the experiment of the future.

Percy W. Bridgman,

The logic of modern physics,

The Macmillan Company (1927)

Future detectors such as ET [1191], Cosmic Explorer (CE) [1192] and LISA [1193] will attain at least an order of magnitude increase in sensitivity with respect to current interferometers, open up entirely new observational windows, and pave the way to new explorations of gravity and physics beyond the Standard Model [1194, 1195, 1196]. Among these, a long-sought goal is the robust measurement of multiple QNMs in ringdown waveforms. However, the large SNR of future detectors means that systematic errors will become dominant over statistical errors, and demands improvements in both GW source modeling and data analysis [893].

In this section we review the prospects for multi-mode ringdown detections that will allow for straightforward, linear tests of gravity (Section 7.1); we expand the discussion to nonlinear tests of gravity and parameterized searches for new physics that will be possible with XG detectors (Section 7.2); and we outline the data analysis challenges that we must overcome to take full advantage of these observations (Section 7.3).

7.1 Multi-mode observations and rates

Initial contributors: Bhagwat, Chirenti, Pacilio

The detection of multiple ringdown modes is the first step in realizing the promise of BH spectroscopy as a tool for testing GR [12, 376, 377]. At its heart the idea is simple: each mode detected in the signal provides a pair (ωR,ωI)(\omega_{R},\omega_{I}), which can be related to the parameters MM and aa of the resulting Kerr BH [1197, 1198]. Detecting multiple modes then allows to perform consistency tests that the same parameters MM and aa are recovered from each mode – a condition that can be formulated in rigorous statistical terms [534, 535, 943]. Thus, BH spectroscopy is a probe of the background geometry and of the dynamical equations governing the ringdown perturbations [1199, 7]. Moreover, using NR fits for the amplitudes and phases of each mode provides additional constraints [536, 1200, 649].
